chapters.title: Book I — The gods in council—minerva’s visit to ithaca—the challenge from telemachus to the suitors.
paragraphs: Tell me, Muse, about that clever hero who traveled to many lands after he destroyed the great city of Troy. He visited many cities and learned about different peoples and their ways. He suffered greatly on the seas, trying to save his own life and bring his men home safely. But no matter what he did, he couldn't save his crew—they died because of their own foolishness when they ate the sacred cattle that belonged to the Sun-god Hyperion. So the god made sure they never reached home. Tell me all about these adventures, daughter of Zeus, from whatever you know about them.

Now all the other warriors who had survived the battles and shipwrecks of the Trojan War had made it safely home—all except Odysseus (also called Ulysses). Though he longed desperately to return to his wife and homeland, he was trapped by the goddess Calypso. She had taken him to her cave on a lonely island and wanted to marry him. Years passed, and finally the gods decided it was time for him to return to Ithaca. But even then, when he would be among his own people, his troubles wouldn't be over. All the gods now felt sorry for him—all except Poseidon (called Neptune by the Romans), the god of the sea, who still hunted him without mercy and wouldn't let him reach home.

Now Poseidon had traveled far away to visit the Ethiopians, a people who lived at the edge of the world, split into two groups—one facing west, the other east. He had gone there to enjoy a great feast of sheep and cattle they were offering him. Meanwhile, the other gods gathered in the palace of Zeus on Mount Olympus. Zeus, the king of gods and men, spoke first. At that moment he was thinking about Aegisthus, who had been killed by Orestes, son of Agamemnon. So Zeus said to the other gods:

"Look how humans blame us gods for their troubles, when really it's their own foolishness that causes their problems! Take Aegisthus—he chose to steal Agamemnon's wife and then murder Agamemnon himself, even though he knew it would mean his death. I sent Mercury (Hermes) to warn him not to do either of these terrible things, because Orestes would surely take revenge when he grew up and returned home. Mercury gave him this warning out of kindness, but Aegisthus wouldn't listen. Now he has paid the full price for his crimes."

Then Athena (called Minerva by the Romans) said, "Father Zeus, son of Cronus, king of all kings, Aegisthus got exactly what he deserved, and so would anyone else who acts like he did! But I'm not worried about Aegisthus—it's Odysseus who breaks my heart. I think of him suffering on that lonely island surrounded by sea, far from all his friends. It's a forest-covered island in the middle of the ocean, where a goddess lives. She's the daughter of Atlas, that giant who holds up the pillars that separate heaven and earth and watches over the deepest parts of the sea. This daughter of Atlas has trapped poor Odysseus and keeps trying to make him forget his homeland with sweet words and magic, so that he's sick of life and dreams only of seeing the smoke rising from his own house again. Yet you, sir, pay no attention to this! Didn't Odysseus honor you with many burnt offerings when he was fighting at Troy? Why do you stay so angry with him?"

Zeus replied, "My dear daughter, what are you saying? How could I ever forget Odysseus? There's no more clever man on earth, and no one has been more generous in his sacrifices to us immortal gods who live in heaven! But remember, Poseidon is still furious with Odysseus for blinding the eye of Polyphemus, king of the Cyclopes (one-eyed giants). Polyphemus is Poseidon's son by the sea-nymph Thoosa, daughter of the sea-king Phorcys. That's why, though Poseidon won't kill Odysseus outright, he torments him by preventing him from getting home. Still, let's put our heads together and figure out how to help him return. Poseidon will have to accept it if we all agree—he can hardly fight against all of us."

Athena answered, "Father Zeus, son of Cronus, king of all kings, if the gods have now decided that Odysseus should return home, we should first send Mercury to Calypso's island to tell her we've made up our minds and that Odysseus must be allowed to leave. Meanwhile, I'll go to Ithaca to encourage Odysseus's son Telemachus. I'll give him courage to call together all the Greek leaders and speak boldly to the suitors who are pursuing his mother Penelope. These men keep eating his sheep and cattle! I'll also help him travel to Sparta and Pylos to see if he can learn anything about his dear father's return—this will make people respect him."

With these words, Athena put on her gleaming golden sandals that could carry her swift as the wind over land or sea. She grabbed her mighty bronze-tipped spear, so strong and sturdy, which she uses to defeat armies of heroes who anger her. Down she swooped from the highest peaks of Mount Olympus, and instantly she was in Ithaca, standing at the gateway of Odysseus's house. She had disguised herself as a visitor named Mentes, chief of the Taphian people, and she carried a bronze spear. There she found the arrogant suitors sitting on the hides of oxen they had killed and eaten, playing board games in front of the house. Servants and pages bustled around serving them—some mixing wine with water in large bowls, some cleaning the tables with wet sponges and setting them up again, others cutting up huge amounts of meat.

Telemachus spotted her long before anyone else did. He was sitting sadly among the suitors, thinking about his brave father and how he would throw all these men out of the house if he could return and reclaim his honor as in the old days. Lost in these thoughts, he noticed Athena and went straight to the gate, annoyed that a stranger should be kept waiting outside. He took her right hand in his and offered to hold her spear. "Welcome to our house," he said. "After you've eaten, please tell us why you've come."

He led the way as he spoke, and Athena followed. When they were inside, he took her spear and placed it in a spear-rack against a strong wooden post, alongside many other spears that had belonged to his missing father. He led her to a beautifully decorated chair and spread a fine cloth beneath it. There was also a footstool for her feet, and he placed another seat nearby for himself, away from the suitors, so she wouldn't be bothered by their noise and rudeness while eating, and so he could ask her freely about his father.

A servant girl brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin so they could wash their hands. She set a polished table beside them. Another servant brought bread and offered them many delicious foods from the house's stores. The carver brought them plates of various meats and placed golden cups at their sides, while a servant brought wine and poured it out for them.

Then the suitors came in and took their places on benches and chairs. Servants poured water over their hands, maids passed around baskets of bread, pages filled the mixing bowls with wine and water, and everyone reached for the good food spread before them. When they had eaten and drunk their fill, they wanted music and dancing, which are the perfect ending to any feast. So a servant brought a lyre to Phemius, the bard, whom they forced to sing for them. As soon as he touched his lyre and began to sing, Telemachus leaned close to Athena and spoke quietly so no one else could hear.

"I hope you won't be offended by what I'm about to say," he whispered. "Singing is easy for those who don't have to pay for it, and all this feasting comes at the expense of a man whose bones may be rotting in some wilderness or ground to powder by the ocean waves. If these men saw my father return to Ithaca, they'd pray for faster legs rather than more money, because gold wouldn't save them then! But sadly, he has met some terrible fate, and even when people sometimes say he's coming home, we no longer believe them. We'll never see him again. But please, tell me truthfully—who are you and where do you come from? Tell me about your city and your parents, what kind of ship brought you here, and how your crew got you to Ithaca. What nation do they come from? You certainly didn't walk here! Also tell me honestly—are you a stranger to this house, or have you been here before in my father's time? In the old days we had many visitors, because my father traveled widely himself."

Athena answered, "I'll tell you everything truthfully. I am Mentes, son of Anchialus, and I'm king of the Taphians. I've come here with my ship and crew on a voyage to foreign lands, heading to Temesa with a cargo of iron, planning to bring back copper. My ship is anchored over there away from town, in Rheithron harbor beneath the wooded mountain Neritum. Our fathers were friends long ago, as old Laertes will tell you if you ask him. They say he never comes to town anymore and lives alone in the countryside, struggling to get by with just an old woman to care for him and prepare his meals when he comes in tired from working in his vineyard. People told me your father had returned home, which is why I came—but apparently the gods are still keeping him away. He's not dead, though, I'm sure of it! He's probably trapped on some island in the middle of the ocean, held prisoner by savage people against his will. I'm not a prophet and don't know much about omens, but something tells me from heaven that he won't be away much longer. He's so resourceful that even if he were chained in iron, he'd find a way to escape and come home. But tell me truly—can Odysseus really have such a handsome son as you? You look amazingly like him, especially around the eyes and head. We were close friends before he sailed for Troy with all the finest Greek warriors. Since then, neither of us has seen the other."

"My mother says I'm Odysseus's son," Telemachus replied, "but it's a wise child who truly knows his own father. I wish I were the son of someone who had grown old peacefully on his own land. Since you ask, there's no more unlucky man under heaven than the one they say is my father."

Athena said, "There's no danger of your family line dying out while Penelope has such a fine son as you! But tell me truly—what's the meaning of all this feasting? Who are these people and what's it all about? Is this some banquet or wedding celebration? It doesn't seem like anyone's bringing their own food. And these guests—how terribly they're behaving! What a riot they're making throughout the whole house! It's enough to disgust any decent person who sees them."

"Sir," said Telemachus, "since you ask—as long as my father was here, all was well with us and our house. But the gods have decided otherwise and have hidden him away more completely than any man has ever been hidden before. I could bear it better if he had died—if he had fallen with his men at Troy, or died peacefully among friends when his fighting days were over. Then the Greeks would have built a burial mound over his ashes, and I would have inherited his glorious reputation. But now the storm winds have swept him away to some unknown place. He's vanished without leaving a trace, and I've inherited nothing but grief. And that's not the end of my troubles! The gods have sent me sorrows of another kind. All the nobles from the nearby islands—Dulichium, Same, and wooded Zacynthus—plus all the leading men of Ithaca itself, are eating up our house while pretending to court my mother. She won't give them a clear 'no,' but she won't end the matter either. So they're destroying our property, and soon they'll destroy me too."

"Really?" exclaimed Athena. "Then you definitely need Odysseus to come home! Give him his helmet, shield, and a couple of spears, and if he's still the man I knew when I first met him in our house—when he was drinking and celebrating, fresh from his trip to Ephyra where he'd gone to get poison for his arrows from Ilus, son of Mermerus (Ilus feared the eternal gods and wouldn't give him any, but my father helped him because he was so fond of Odysseus)—if he's still that man, these suitors will have a quick and sorry end to their wooing!

"But listen! It's up to heaven to decide whether he'll return and take revenge in his own house or not. However, I strongly urge you to start trying to get rid of these suitors immediately. Take my advice—tomorrow morning call all the Greek heroes to an assembly. Present your case to them and call heaven to witness your words. Tell the suitors to go away, each to his own home. If your mother's heart is set on remarrying, let her return to her father's house. He'll find her a husband and provide all the wedding gifts such a beloved daughter deserves. As for you, let me convince you to take the best ship you can find, with a crew of twenty men, and go searching for your long-missing father. Someone might tell you something useful, or you might receive some heaven-sent message—people often learn things this way. First go to Pylos and ask Nestor; then continue to Sparta to visit Menelaus, since he was the last of the Greeks to return home. If you hear that your father is alive and on his way back, you can put up with these suitors' waste for another year. But if you learn of his death, come home immediately. Hold proper funeral ceremonies for him, build a memorial mound, and help your mother remarry. After you've done all this, think carefully about how—by fair means or foul—you can kill these suitors in your own house. You're too old to act like a helpless child anymore! Haven't you heard how people praise Orestes for killing Aegisthus, his father's murderer? You're a fine, strong-looking young man—show your courage and make a name for yourself in the stories people tell! Now I must return to my ship and crew, who will be impatient if I keep them waiting longer. Think over what I've said and remember my advice."

"Sir," answered Telemachus, "you've been so kind to talk with me as if I were your own son, and I'll do everything you've told me. I know you're eager to continue your voyage, but please stay a little longer. Let me offer you a bath and refreshment first. Then I'll give you a gift before you leave—something beautiful and valuable, a keepsake that dear friends give to each other."

Athena replied, "Don't try to delay me—I need to leave right away. As for any gift you'd like to give me, save it for when I return, and I'll take it home with me then. Choose something really nice for me, and I'll give you something equally valuable in return."

With these words, she flew away like a bird into the air. But she had filled Telemachus with courage and made him think about his father more than ever. He felt the change in himself, wondered at it, and realized that the stranger had been a god. So he walked straight back to where the suitors were sitting.

Phemius was still singing, and his audience sat in rapt silence as he told the sad story of the Greeks' difficult journey home from Troy and all the troubles that Athena had sent upon them. Penelope, daughter of Icarius, heard his song from her room upstairs. She came down the great staircase, not alone but accompanied by two of her servant women. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the wooden posts that supported the roof of the covered walkway, with a modest maiden on either side of her. She held a veil over her face and wept bitterly.

"Phemius," she cried, "you know many other stories about the deeds of gods and heroes that singers love to perform. Sing one of those for the suitors, and let them drink their wine in silence. But stop this sad tale! It breaks my sorrowful heart and reminds me of my lost husband, whom I mourn constantly. His name was honored throughout all of Greece!"

"Mother," Telemachus answered, "let the bard sing whatever he chooses. Poets don't create the troubles they sing about—it's Zeus who sends both good and bad fortune to people according to his will. This singer means no harm by performing the sad story of the Greeks' return from Troy. People always appreciate the newest songs most. Make up your mind to bear it. Odysseus isn't the only man who never came back from Troy—many others died there too. Now go back inside the house and tend to your daily work—your weaving, your spinning, and managing the servants. Speaking in public is men's business, and especially mine, since I am the master of this house."

She returned to the house in amazement, taking her son's words to heart. Going upstairs with her servant women to her room, she grieved for her dear husband until Athena brought sweet sleep to her eyes. But the suitors made a loud commotion throughout the covered walkways, each one praying that he might share her bed.

Then Telemachus spoke up: "Shameless and rude suitors! Let's enjoy our feast peacefully now without fighting, since it's wonderful to hear a man with such a godlike voice as Phemius has. But tomorrow morning, meet me in a full assembly so I can formally tell you to leave. Go feast at each other's houses, taking turns, at your own expense. But if you choose to keep sponging off one man, then heaven help me—Zeus will make you pay in full! And when you fall in my father's house, there will be no one to avenge you."

The suitors bit their lips when they heard him and marveled at his bold speech. Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, said, "The gods seem to have taught you to be boastful and speak big words! May Zeus never let you become king in Ithaca as your father was before you."

Telemachus answered, "Antinous, don't be angry with me, but if the gods will it, I'll gladly be king too. Do you think that's the worst fate you can imagine for me? It's not bad to be a leader—it brings both wealth and honor. Still, now that Odysseus is gone, there are many great men in Ithaca, both old and young, and someone else might become the leader. But I will definitely be master in my own house and rule over the servants that Odysseus won for me."

Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, replied, "It's up to heaven to decide who will be our leader, but you should certainly be master of your own house and possessions. As long as there are people living in Ithaca, no one should use violence against you or rob you. But now, my good fellow, I want to know about this stranger. What country does he come from? What family is he from, and where is his land? Did he bring you news about your father's return, or was he here on his own business? He seemed like a wealthy man, but he left so suddenly—he was gone in a moment before we could get to know him."

"My father is dead and gone," answered Telemachus, "and even when rumors reach me, I don't believe them anymore. My mother sometimes calls for a fortune-teller to question him, but I pay no attention to his predictions. As for the stranger, he was Mentes, son of Anchialus, chief of the Taphians, and an old friend of my father's." But in his heart, he knew it had been the goddess.

The suitors then returned to their singing and dancing until evening came. When night fell on their entertainment, they went home to bed, each to his own house. Telemachus's bedroom was high up in a tower that overlooked the courtyard. He went there, deep in thought and brooding. A good old woman, Euryclea, daughter of Ops the son of Pisenor, walked ahead of him carrying two blazing torches. Laertes had bought her with his own money when she was quite young, paying the value of twenty oxen for her. He showed her as much respect in his household as he did his own wife, but he never slept with her because he feared his wife's anger. She was the one who now lit Telemachus to his room—she loved him more than any of the other women in the house because she had been his nurse when he was a baby. He opened his bedroom door and sat on his bed. As he took off his shirt, he handed it to the kind old woman, who folded it neatly and hung it on a peg beside his bed. Then she left the room, pulled the door shut with its silver handle, and slid the bolt home using a leather strap. But Telemachus lay under his woolen blanket, thinking all night long about his planned journey and the advice that Athena had given him.

chapters.title: Book II — Assembly of the people of ithaca—speeches of telemachus and of the suitors—telemachus makes his preparations and starts for pylos with minerva disguised as mentor.
paragraphs: When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, Telemachus rose and dressed himself. He tied his sandals to his feet, strapped his sword over his shoulder, and left his room looking like a god. He immediately sent messengers to call all the people together for an important meeting. When everyone had gathered, he walked to the assembly place carrying his spear—not alone, for his two faithful dogs came with him. The goddess Athena (called Minerva by the Romans) made him look so noble and handsome that everyone stared in wonder as he passed by. When he took his place in his father's chair, even the oldest leaders stepped aside to make room for him.

Aegyptius, an old man bent over with age but full of wisdom, spoke first. His son Antiphus had sailed with Odysseus to Troy, the city famous for its horses, but the terrible one-eyed giant called the Cyclops had killed him when they were trapped in his cave. The monster had even cooked the young man for dinner! Aegyptius still had three sons left—two worked on the family farm, while the third, Eurynomus, was one of the suitors pestering Penelope to marry them. But their father could never get over losing Antiphus, and tears still rolled down his cheeks as he began to speak.

"Men of Ithaca," he said, "listen to my words. Ever since Odysseus left us, we have never called a meeting like this until today. So who could it be, young or old, who finds it so urgent to bring us all together? Has he heard news of an enemy army approaching and wants to warn us? Or does he want to discuss some other important matter? I'm sure he's a good man, and I hope Zeus will grant him whatever his heart desires."

Telemachus took this as a good sign and stood up at once, his heart bursting with everything he needed to say. He walked to the center of the assembly, and the trusted herald Pisenor handed him the speaker's staff. Then, turning to Aegyptius, he said, "Sir, I am the one who called this meeting, as you'll soon learn, because I am the one suffering the most. I haven't heard of any enemy army that I need to warn you about, and this isn't about any public business. My problem is personal, and it comes from two terrible disasters that have struck my family. First, I've lost my wonderful father, who was your leader and treated each of you like his own children. Second—and this is much worse—my entire inheritance will soon be completely destroyed. The sons of all your most important families are bothering my mother, trying to force her to marry one of them. They're too cowardly to go to her father Icarius and ask him to choose a husband for her and provide a proper dowry. Instead, day after day they lounge around my father's house, killing our cattle, sheep, and fat goats for their feasts, and drinking enormous amounts of our wine without a care. No family fortune can survive such waste! We have no Odysseus to protect us anymore, and I'm not strong enough to fight them off. I'll never be as great a warrior as he was, but I would defend my home if I could! I can't stand this treatment any longer—my house is being ruined and disgraced. Have some respect for your own consciences and for what people will think! Fear the anger of the gods too, or they might become furious and punish you. I beg you by Zeus and Themis (the goddess of justice who watches over all meetings like this)—don't abandon me to face this alone! Unless my brave father Odysseus somehow wronged you Greeks and you want revenge on me by helping these suitors. Honestly, if someone has to eat up all my food and property, I'd rather it be you—at least then I could demand you pay me back and take you to court until I got every bit back. But now I have no way to stop them!"

With these words, Telemachus threw his speaking staff to the ground and burst into tears. Everyone felt very sorry for him, but they all sat in silence. No one dared to give him an angry answer—except Antinous, who spoke like this:

"Telemachus, you rude show-off! How dare you try to blame us suitors? It's your mother's fault, not ours—she's incredibly clever and sneaky. For almost four years now, she's been driving us crazy by encouraging each of us and sending us private messages, but she doesn't mean a word of what she says. And then there was that other trick she played on us. She set up a huge weaving frame in her room and began working on an enormous piece of fine cloth. 'My dear suitors,' she told us, 'Odysseus is surely dead, but please don't pressure me to remarry right away. Wait—I don't want my weaving skills to be forgotten—until I finish this burial shroud for the hero Laertes, to have ready when death takes him. He's very wealthy, and the women of our island will gossip terribly if he's buried without a proper shroud.'

"That's what she said, and we agreed to wait. Every day we could see her working on that huge tapestry, but every night she would sneak back by torchlight and unravel all the stitches she'd made! She fooled us like this for three whole years without us catching on. But in the fourth year, one of her maids who knew what she was doing told us the truth, and we caught her red-handed undoing all her work. So she had to finish the shroud whether she wanted to or not. Now we suitors give you this answer, so you and all the Greeks will understand: 'Send your mother away and tell her to marry whichever man she and her father choose!' We don't know what will happen if she keeps tormenting us much longer with her proud attitude about all the skills Athena has taught her, and because she's so incredibly clever. We've never heard of such a woman before! We know about famous queens from the old days like Tyro, Alcmena, and Mycene, but none of them could compare to your mother. It wasn't fair of her to treat us this way, and as long as she keeps this up, we'll keep eating up your inheritance. I don't see why she would change her mind, since she gets all the honor and fame while you're the one paying for it. Understand this clearly: we won't return to our own lands until she finally chooses one of us to marry."

Telemachus answered, "Antinous, how can I throw out the mother who gave birth to me and raised me? My father is far away and we don't even know if he's alive or dead. It would cost me a fortune to send her back to Icarius—I'd have to pay him a huge penalty for returning his daughter. Not only would he punish me harshly, but the gods would punish me too. When my mother leaves the house, she'll call upon the Furies—terrifying goddesses who punish people who harm their families—to get revenge on me. Besides, it would be a shameful thing to do, and I won't consider it. If you don't like this, then leave my house and go feast at each other's homes, taking turns paying for your own parties. But if you choose to keep living off one man like parasites, then may Zeus help me! Zeus will make you pay for this, and when you die in my father's house, no one will come to avenge you."

Just as he finished speaking, Zeus sent two eagles from the top of the mountain. They flew side by side, riding the wind in their majestic flight. When they reached the middle of the assembly, they suddenly wheeled around in circles, beating their powerful wings and staring down with deadly looks at everyone below. Then they fought fiercely, tearing at each other with their claws, before flying off toward the right over the town. The people watched in amazement and wondered what this strange sight could mean. Then Halitherses, who was the best prophet and reader of omens among them, spoke honestly and clearly to everyone:

"Listen to me, men of Ithaca, and especially you suitors, because I see disaster coming for you! Odysseus won't be away much longer—in fact, he's very close to home and will soon bring death and destruction, not just to you but to many others of us who live in Ithaca. Let's be wise now and stop this evil behavior before he returns. The suitors should do this on their own—it would be better for them. I'm not making wild guesses here; everything has happened to Odysseus exactly as I predicted when the Greek army left for Troy and he went with them. I said that after suffering greatly and losing all his men, he would return home in the twentieth year, and no one would recognize him. Now all of this is coming true."

Eurymachus, son of Polybus, then said, "Go home, old man, and make prophecies to your own children, or something bad might happen to them! I can read these bird signs much better than you can. Birds are always flying around in the sky, but they rarely mean anything special. Odysseus died in some distant land, and it's too bad you didn't die along with him, instead of babbling here about omens and making Telemachus even angrier than he already is. I suppose you think he'll give you some reward for your family, but I tell you this—and it will definitely happen—when an old man like you, who should know better, talks a young person into causing trouble, first of all his young friend will only suffer more for it (he won't gain anything because we suitors will stop him), and second, we'll make you pay a fine so heavy you won't like it one bit. As for Telemachus, I warn him in front of all of you to send his mother back to her father, who will find her a husband and provide all the wedding gifts such a precious daughter deserves. Until then, we'll keep pestering him with our marriage proposals, because we're not afraid of anyone. We don't care about him and his fancy speeches, or about any of your fortune-telling. You can preach all you want, but we'll only hate you more for it. We'll go back to eating up Telemachus's property without paying him anything, until his mother stops tormenting us by keeping us waiting day after day in suspense, each of us competing for such a perfect prize. Besides, we can't go marry other women like we normally would, not with the way she's been treating us."

Then Telemachus said, "Eurymachus, and all you other suitors, I won't say anything more or beg you any further, because the gods and the people of Ithaca now know my situation. Just give me a ship and a crew of twenty men to sail here and there, and I'll go to Sparta and to Pylos to search for my father who has been missing for so long. Someone might tell me news about him, or (people often hear things this way) some message from heaven might guide me. If I hear that he's alive and on his way home, I'll put up with the waste you suitors are causing for another twelve months. But if I hear that he's dead, I'll return immediately, hold his funeral ceremony with all proper honors, build a burial mound in his memory, and make my mother marry again."

After saying this, he sat down. Then Mentor, who had been Odysseus's friend and had been left in charge of everything with full authority over the servants, rose to speak. He addressed them plainly and honestly:

"Listen to me, men of Ithaca. I hope you never again have a kind and fair ruler, or one who will govern you justly, because not one of you remembers Odysseus, who ruled you like a loving father! I'm not nearly as angry with the suitors—if they choose to act violently because of their wicked hearts, and gamble their lives betting that Odysseus won't return, they can continue their arrogant behavior and eat up his property. But I'm shocked at how all the rest of you just sit there without even trying to stop such scandalous behavior—which you could do if you wanted to, since there are many of you and only a few of them."

Leiocritus, son of Evenor, answered him saying, "Mentor, what nonsense is this, telling people to stop us? It's hard for one man to fight many over food. Even if Odysseus himself came back and tried to throw us out while we're feasting in his house, his wife—who wants him back so badly—would have little reason to celebrate, because he'd be killed if he fought against such overwhelming odds. There's no sense in what you've been saying. Now, you people go about your business, and let his father's old friends, Mentor and Halitherses, help this boy on his journey—if he goes at all, which I doubt. He's more likely to stay here until someone comes and tells him something."
With that, he broke up the assembly, and everyone went back home, while the suitors returned to Odysseus's house.
Then Telemachus walked alone to the seashore, washed his hands in the gray waves, and prayed to Athena.

"Hear me," he cried, "you goddess who visited me yesterday and told me to sail across the seas searching for my father who has been missing so long. I want to obey you, but the Greeks, especially these wicked suitors, are preventing me from doing so."

As he prayed, Athena came close to him, looking and sounding exactly like Mentor. "Telemachus," she said, "if you're made of the same stuff as your father, you won't be foolish or cowardly from now on, because Odysseus never broke his word or left a job half-finished. If you take after him, your voyage won't be useless. But unless you have the blood of Odysseus and Penelope flowing through your veins, I don't see much hope of you succeeding. Sons are rarely as good as their fathers—they're usually worse, not better. Still, since you're not going to be foolish or cowardly anymore, and you do have some of your father's wisdom, I have hope for your mission. But never join forces with any of those stupid suitors, because they have no sense or virtue, and they don't think about death and the doom that will soon fall on all of them—they'll all die on the same day. As for your voyage, it won't be delayed long. Your father was such a dear friend of mine that I'll find you a ship and come with you myself. Now go home and mingle with the suitors while you get supplies ready for your trip. Pack everything carefully—wine in jars, and barley meal (which is essential food) in leather bags. I'll go around town and quickly gather volunteers. There are many ships in Ithaca, both old and new. I'll look them over for you and choose the best one. We'll get her ready and set sail without delay."

So spoke Athena, daughter of Zeus, and Telemachus wasted no time doing as the goddess instructed. He went home feeling determined, and found the suitors skinning goats and roasting pigs in the courtyard. Antinous immediately came up to him and laughed as he took his hand, saying, "Telemachus, my hotheaded friend, don't hold any more grudges in your words or actions, but eat and drink with us like you used to. The Greeks will provide everything you need—a ship and a handpicked crew—so you can sail to Pylos right away and get news of your noble father."

"Antinous," answered Telemachus, "I can't eat peacefully or enjoy myself with men like you. Wasn't it enough that you wasted so much of my good property while I was still a boy? Now that I'm older and understand more, I'm also stronger, and whether here among these people or by going to Pylos, I'll do you all the harm I can. I will go, and my trip won't be pointless—though thanks to you suitors, I have neither my own ship nor crew, and must travel as a passenger, not a captain."
As he spoke, he pulled his hand away from Antinous's grip. Meanwhile, the others continued preparing dinner around the buildings, mocking him cruelly as they worked.

"Telemachus means to kill us all," said one young suitor. "I suppose he thinks he can bring warriors to help him from Pylos, or maybe from Sparta, where he seems determined to go. Or maybe he'll even go to Ephyra to get poison to put in our wine and murder us!"

Another said, "Maybe if Telemachus gets on a ship, he'll be like his father and die far from his friends. In that case, we'd have plenty to do, because then we could divide up all his property among ourselves. As for the house, we could let his mother and whoever marries her have that."

This was how they talked. But Telemachus went down into the high, spacious storage room where his father's treasure of gold and bronze lay piled on the floor, and where the linen and spare clothes were kept in wooden chests. There was also a supply of fragrant olive oil, and jars of old, perfectly aged wine—pure and fit for a god to drink—lined up against the wall in case Odysseus should return home after all. The room was secured with well-made doors that opened in the middle, and the faithful old housekeeper Euryclea, daughter of Ops (son of Pisenor), was in charge of everything day and night. Telemachus called her to the storage room and said:

"Nurse, draw off some of the best wine you have, except for what you're saving for my father's personal use, in case the poor man should escape death and find his way home again. Give me twelve jars, and make sure they all have tight lids. Also fill some well-sewn leather bags with barley meal—about twenty measures total. Get all these things ready immediately, and don't tell anyone about it. I'll take everything away tonight as soon as my mother goes upstairs to bed. I'm traveling to Sparta and Pylos to see if I can hear any news about my dear father's return."

When Euryclea heard this, she began to cry and spoke lovingly to him: "My dear child, whatever put such an idea into your head? Where in the world do you want to go—you, who are the only hope of this household? Your poor father is dead and gone in some foreign country nobody knows about, and as soon as you leave, these wicked men will plot to kill you and divide all your possessions among themselves. Stay here with your own people, and don't go wandering around risking your life on the empty ocean."

"Don't worry, nurse," answered Telemachus. "My plan has heaven's blessing. But swear you won't tell my mother about any of this until I've been gone ten or twelve days, unless she discovers I've left and asks you directly. I don't want her to ruin her beauty by crying."

The old woman swore solemnly that she wouldn't tell, and after she completed her oath, she began drawing the wine into jars and packing the barley meal into bags, while Telemachus returned to the suitors.

Then Athena thought of something else. She took on his appearance and went around the town to each member of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sunset. She also went to Noemon, son of Phronius, and asked to borrow a ship—which he was very happy to provide. When the sun had set and darkness covered the land, she got the ship into the water, loaded all the equipment that ships normally carry, and positioned her at the end of the harbor. Soon the crew arrived, and the goddess spoke encouragingly to each of them.

Next, she went to Odysseus's house and cast a deep sleep over the suitors. She made their drinks affect their minds and caused them to drop their cups, so that instead of staying up drinking, they staggered back to town to sleep with their eyes heavy and drowsy. Then she took on Mentor's appearance and voice, and called Telemachus to come outside.
"Telemachus," she said, "the men are on board and at their oars, waiting for you to give your orders, so hurry up and let's go."

With that, she led the way, and Telemachus followed her. When they reached the ship, they found the crew waiting by the water, and Telemachus said, "Come on, men, help me load the supplies on board. Everything's packed and ready in the storeroom, and my mother doesn't know anything about this, nor do any of the servants except one."

He led the way and the others followed. When they had loaded everything as he directed, Telemachus went aboard with Athena going first and taking her seat at the stern of the ship, while Telemachus sat beside her. The men untied the ropes and took their places on the rowing benches. Athena sent them a favorable wind from the west that whistled over the deep blue waves. Telemachus told them to grab the ropes and raise the sail, and they did exactly as he commanded. They set the mast in its socket in the crossbeam, raised it up, and secured it with the forestays. Then they hoisted their white sail high with ropes made of twisted cowhide. As the sail billowed out with the wind, the ship flew through the deep blue water, and foam hissed against her bow as she sped forward. They secured everything throughout the ship, filled the mixing bowls to the brim, and poured drink offerings to the immortal gods who live forever, but especially to the gray-eyed daughter of Zeus.
And so the ship sailed swiftly on her way through the watches of the night from darkness until dawn.

chapters.title: Book III — Telemachus visits nestor at pylos.
paragraphs: As the golden sun rose from the sparkling sea to light up both gods and humans, Telemachus and his crew reached Pylos, the city ruled by old King Neleus. The people of Pylos had gathered on the beach to offer a special sacrifice to Poseidon, the god of earthquakes and the sea. There were nine groups of people, with five hundred men in each group, and each group had nine black bulls to sacrifice. The people were eating the inner parts of the animals and burning the thigh bones on fires as an offering to Poseidon when Telemachus arrived. His crew furled their white sails, anchored their ship, and went ashore.

Athena led the way with Telemachus following close behind. She turned to him and said, "Telemachus, you must not be shy or nervous! You've come on this long voyage to find out what happened to your father and where he might be buried. So walk right up to old Nestor and see what he can tell you. Ask him to tell you the truth - he will not lie to you, for he is a wise and honest man."

"But how can I do that, Mentor?" Telemachus replied nervously. "How should I speak to Nestor? I've never had long conversations with important grown-ups before, and I'm embarrassed to start questioning someone so much older and wiser than me."

"Some things will come to you naturally, Telemachus," Athena answered kindly. "And the gods will help you find the right words. I'm sure the gods have been watching over you since the day you were born."

She walked quickly ahead, and Telemachus followed her footsteps until they reached the place where all the groups of Pylian people had gathered. There they found Nestor sitting with his sons, while his men were busy preparing dinner - some putting chunks of meat on long metal spits to roast, while other pieces were already cooking over the fires. When the people saw the strangers, they crowded around them warmly, took them by the hands, and invited them to sit down. Nestor's son Pisistratus immediately offered his hand to both visitors and seated them on soft sheepskins that were spread on the sand near his father and his brother Thrasymedes. Then he gave them portions of the cooked meat and poured wine into a golden cup, offering it first to Athena (who was still disguised as Mentor) with a respectful greeting.

"Please offer a prayer, sir," Pisistratus said politely, "to King Poseidon, for you are joining his feast. When you have prayed properly and poured out your drink offering, pass the cup to your young friend so he can do the same. I'm sure he prays to the gods too, for no person can live without the gods' help. But since he's younger than you and closer to my own age, I'll give you the honor of going first."

As he spoke, he handed Athena the golden cup. She thought it was very proper and respectful of him to offer it to her first. She began praying earnestly to Poseidon: "O great god who surrounds the earth with your seas, please grant the prayers of your faithful servants! Most especially, we ask you to bless Nestor and his sons. And please reward all these good people of Pylos for the wonderful sacrifice they're offering you. Finally, grant Telemachus and me success in the important mission that brought us here to Pylos in our ship."

When she finished her prayer, she handed the cup to Telemachus, and he prayed in the same way. Soon the outer pieces of meat were fully roasted and taken off the spits. The servants gave everyone their fair share, and they all enjoyed an excellent dinner. As soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, Nestor, the noble knight of Gerene, began to speak.

"Now that our guests have finished their meal," he said, "it's time to ask who they are. Who are you, strangers, and from what port have you sailed here? Are you merchants trading goods? Or do you sail the seas as pirates, fighting against everyone you meet?"
Telemachus answered boldly, for Athena had filled him with courage to ask about his father and make a good impression.

"Nestor, son of Neleus, honor of all the Greeks," he said, "you ask where we come from, and I will tell you truly. We come from Ithaca, the island beneath Mount Neritum, and what I want to discuss is a personal matter, not public business. I'm searching for news of my poor father Odysseus, who they say helped you destroy the city of Troy. We know what happened to each of the other heroes who fought at Troy, but as for Odysseus, the gods have hidden from us even the knowledge of whether he's dead or alive. No one can tell us where he died - whether he fell in battle on land or was lost at sea in the waves. That's why I come to you as a humble visitor, hoping you might tell me about his sad end. Did you see it with your own eyes, or did you hear about it from some other traveler? He was surely a man born for trouble and adventure. Please don't soften your words out of pity for me - tell me plainly exactly what you saw. If my brave father Odysseus ever served you faithfully, either by his words or actions when you Greeks were suffering at Troy, please remember that kindness now and tell me the whole truth."

"My young friend," Nestor replied, "your words bring back memories of great sorrow, for we brave Greeks suffered terribly - both at sea when we went raiding under Achilles' command, and when we fought before the great city of King Priam. Our finest men all died there: Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus who was wise as the gods, and my own dear son Antilochus, who was incredibly fast and brave in battle. But we suffered even more than this! What human voice could tell the whole story? Even if you stayed here questioning me for five or six years, I couldn't tell you everything the Greeks endured, and you'd get tired of my tale and sail home before I finished. For nine long years we tried every kind of trick and strategy, but fate was against us. During all that time, no one could match your father's cleverness - if you really are his son! I can hardly believe my eyes - you talk exactly like him! No one would believe that people of such different ages could speak so similarly. He and I never disagreed about anything, whether in camp or in council meetings. We worked together with one heart and mind, always advising the Greeks on the best course of action.

"But when we had finally conquered Priam's city and were setting sail for home as the gods scattered us to different places, then Zeus decided to cause trouble for the Greeks on their journey home. They hadn't all been wise or thoughtful, and so many came to bad ends because of the anger of Zeus's daughter Athena, who caused a bitter quarrel between the two sons of Atreus - Agamemnon and Menelaus.

"The sons of Atreus called a meeting that wasn't proper, for it was sunset and the Greeks were heavy with wine. When they explained why they had gathered everyone together, it turned out that Menelaus wanted to sail home immediately, but this made Agamemnon angry. He thought we should wait until we had offered great sacrifices to calm Athena's anger. What a fool he was! He should have known he couldn't change her mind, for when the gods make a decision, they don't change it easily. So the two brothers stood there exchanging harsh words, while the Greeks jumped to their feet with a cry that split the air, divided in their opinions about what to do.

"That night we rested, but we nursed our anger, for Zeus was planning trouble for us. In the morning, some of us launched our ships and put our belongings and women aboard, while the rest - about half our number - stayed behind with Agamemnon. We who made up the other half set sail, and our ships sailed smoothly because the gods had calmed the sea. When we reached the island of Tenedos, we offered sacrifices to the gods, longing to get home. But cruel Zeus didn't want us to reach home yet, and he caused a second quarrel. Some of our men turned their ships around and sailed back under Odysseus's command to make peace with Agamemnon. But I pressed forward with all the ships that followed me, because I could see that more trouble was brewing. Diomedes, son of Tydeus, came with me too, along with his crews. Later, Menelaus caught up with us at Lesbos and found us trying to decide our route - we didn't know whether to sail outside the island of Chios by Psyra, keeping it on our left, or inside Chios, past the stormy headland of Mimas. So we asked the gods for a sign, and they showed us that we'd be safest if we headed our ships straight across the open sea to Euboea. This we did, and a fair wind sprang up that gave us a quick passage through the night to Geraestus, where we offered many sacrifices to Poseidon for helping us so far on our journey. Four days later, Diomedes and his men anchored their ships at Argos, but I continued on to Pylos, and the wind never failed from the day the gods first made it favorable for me.

"So, my dear young friend, I returned home without hearing anything about the others. I don't know who made it home safely and who were lost. But as I should, I'll share with you freely all the reports that have reached me since I've been here in my own house. They say the Myrmidons (Achilles' warriors) returned home safely under the command of Achilles' son Neoptolemus. So did brave Philoctetes, son of Poias. Idomeneus also lost no men at sea, and all his followers who survived the fighting got home safely with him to Crete. No matter how far from civilization you live, you must have heard about Agamemnon and the terrible end he met at the hands of Aegisthus - and what a fearful punishment Aegisthus received in return! See what a good thing it is for a man to leave a son behind him to act as Orestes did, who killed false Aegisthus, the murderer of his noble father! You too - for you're a tall, good-looking young man - show your courage and make a name for yourself that will be remembered in stories!"

"Nestor, son of Neleus, honor of all Greeks," Telemachus answered, "the Greeks praise Orestes, and his name will live forever because he avenged his father so nobly. I wish the gods would grant me the power to take similar revenge on the shameless suitors who are treating me badly and plotting to ruin me! But the gods have no such happiness in store for my father and me, so we must endure it as best we can."

"My friend," said Nestor, "now that you mention it, I remember hearing that your mother has many suitors who treat you badly and are destroying your property. Do you just accept this quietly, or are the people and the gods against you? Who knows - maybe Odysseus will return after all and make these scoundrels pay in full, either by himself or with an army of Greeks behind him! If Athena were to care for you as much as she did for Odysseus when we were fighting at Troy (I never saw the gods so openly fond of anyone as Athena was of your father), if she would take as good care of you as she did of him, these suitors would soon forget about their courting!"

Telemachus replied, "I can't expect anything like that - it would be far too much to hope for. I don't dare let myself think of it. Even if the gods themselves wanted it, such good fortune could never happen to me."

At this, Athena said, "Telemachus, what are you saying? The gods have long reach when they want to save someone! If it were me, I wouldn't care how much I suffered before getting home, as long as I could be safe once I got there. I'd rather suffer and then return safely than get home quickly only to be killed in my own house like Agamemnon was, through the treachery of Aegisthus and his wife. Still, death is certain, and when someone's time has come, not even the gods can save them, no matter how much they love that person."

"Mentor," answered Telemachus, "let's not talk about this anymore. There's no chance my father will ever come back - the gods decided long ago on his destruction. But there's something else I'd like to ask Nestor about, since he knows more than anyone else. They say he's ruled for three generations, so it's like talking to an immortal! Tell me, Nestor, and tell me truly: how did Agamemnon come to die that way? What was Menelaus doing? How did the coward Aegisthus manage to kill a man so much better than himself? Was Menelaus away from Greek Argos, traveling among other peoples, so that Aegisthus felt bold enough to kill Agamemnon?"

"I'll tell you the truth," answered Nestor, "and you've guessed right about how it happened. If Menelaus had returned from Troy to find Aegisthus still alive in his house, there would have been no proper burial mound for Aegisthus. Instead, his body would have been thrown outside the city for dogs and vultures to eat, and no woman would have mourned him, because he had done such a wicked deed. But we were far away, fighting hard at Troy, while Aegisthus was living comfortably in the heart of Argos, winning over Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra with constant flattery.

"At first she wanted nothing to do with his evil plan, for she was naturally good-hearted. Besides, there was a bard (a singing poet) with her whom Agamemnon had ordered, before leaving for Troy, to guard his wife. But when the gods decided on her destruction, Aegisthus took this bard away to a desert island and left him there for crows and seagulls to devour. After that, she went willingly to Aegisthus's house. Then he offered many burnt sacrifices to the gods and decorated many temples with beautiful tapestries and gold, for he had succeeded far beyond what he had expected.

"Meanwhile, Menelaus and I were on our way home from Troy, getting along well with each other. When we reached Sunium (the southern tip of Athens), Apollo killed Menelaus's steersman Phrontis with his gentle arrows - no one knew better how to handle a ship in rough weather. Phrontis died right there with the steering oar in his hands, so Menelaus, though very eager to continue, had to stop to bury his companion and give him proper funeral rites. When he could sail again and had gotten as far as the dangerous rocks near Cape Malea, Zeus sent trouble his way - making fierce winds blow until the waves rose like mountains. There Zeus divided Menelaus's fleet, taking half toward Crete where the Cydonians live around the river Iardanus. There's a high cliff there stretching into the sea from a place called Gortyn, and all along that coast as far as Phaestus, the sea is rough when the south wind blows. But beyond Phaestus the coast is more sheltered, since even a small headland can provide great protection. Here this part of the fleet was driven onto the rocks and wrecked, though the crews barely managed to save themselves. The other five ships were carried by winds and waves to Egypt, where Menelaus gathered much gold and treasure among people who spoke a foreign language. Meanwhile, Aegisthus back home was plotting his evil deed. For seven years after killing Agamemnon, he ruled in Mycenae, and the people obeyed him. But in the eighth year, Orestes returned from Athens to be his destroyer, and killed his father's murderer. Then he held a funeral feast for his mother and false Aegisthus for all the people of Argos, and on that very same day, Menelaus came home with as much treasure as his ships could carry.

"So take my advice: don't travel far from home for too long, and don't leave your property with such dangerous people in your house. They'll eat up everything you own, and your journey will have been wasted. Still, I do think you should visit Menelaus, who has just returned from a voyage among such distant peoples that no one could hope to get back from such a place once the winds had blown them so far off course. Even birds couldn't fly such distances in a year, so vast and terrible are the seas they'd have to cross. Go to him by ship with your own men, or if you'd rather travel by land, you can have a chariot and horses. Here are my sons who can escort you to Lacedaemon where Menelaus lives. Ask him to tell you the truth, and he won't lie to you, for he's an excellent person."

As he finished speaking, the sun set and darkness came. Then Athena said, "Sir, all you have said is wise. Now, however, order the tongues of the sacrificed animals to be cut out, and mix wine so we can pour drink offerings to Poseidon and the other immortal gods. Then we should go to bed, for it's bedtime. People should leave early and not stay up late at a religious festival."

The daughter of Zeus spoke, and everyone obeyed her words. Servants poured water over the guests' hands to clean them, while young men filled the mixing bowls with wine and water and served everyone their drink offering. Then they threw the tongues of the sacrificed animals into the fire and stood up to make their drink offerings to the gods. When they had made their offerings and each person had drunk as much as they wanted, Athena and Telemachus prepared to return to their ship. But Nestor immediately stopped them.

"May the gods forbid," he exclaimed, "that you should leave my house to sleep on a ship! Do you think I'm so poor and short of blankets and cloaks that I can't provide comfortable beds for both myself and my guests? Let me tell you, I have plenty of rugs and warm coverings, and I will not allow the son of my old friend Odysseus to sleep on the hard deck of a ship - not while I'm alive! And my sons after me will keep the same open-door policy that I have always maintained."

Then Athena answered, "Sir, you have spoken well, and it would be much better for Telemachus to do as you suggest. He will return with you and sleep in your house, but I must go back to give orders to my crew and keep their spirits up. I'm the only older person among them - the rest are all young men about Telemachus's age who have come on this voyage out of friendship. So I must return to the ship and sleep there. Besides, tomorrow I must visit the Cauconians, where someone owes me a large sum of money. As for Telemachus, since he's now your guest, please send him to Lacedaemon in a chariot with one of your sons as his companion. And please provide him with your best and fastest horses."

When she had spoken these words, she flew away in the form of an eagle, and everyone marveled at what they saw. Nestor was amazed and took Telemachus by the hand. "My friend," he said, "I can see that you're going to be a great hero someday, since the gods help you like this while you're still so young! This could only have been one of the gods who live on Mount Olympus - Zeus's mighty daughter Athena, the same goddess who showed such favor to your brave father among the Greeks. Holy queen," he continued, praying to Athena, "please send your blessing on me, my good wife, and my children. In return, I'll sacrifice to you a broad-browed young cow that has never been broken to the yoke by humans. I'll cover her horns with gold and offer her to you in sacrifice."

So he prayed, and Athena heard his prayer. Then he led the way to his own house, followed by his sons and sons-in-law. When they reached the house and had taken their places on the benches and chairs, he mixed them a bowl of sweet wine that was eleven years old - wine that the housekeeper had just opened from its sealed jar. As he mixed the wine, he prayed earnestly and made drink offerings to Athena, daughter of Zeus who carries the magic shield. After they had made their offerings and drunk as much as they wanted, the others went home to bed in their own houses. But Nestor put Telemachus to sleep in the room above the gateway, along with Pisistratus, who was his only unmarried son still living at home. Nestor himself slept in an inner room of the house with his wife, the queen, by his side.

When Dawn appeared with her rosy fingers in the early morning, Nestor got up from his bed and took his seat on the benches of smooth, white marble that stood in front of his house. Here in earlier times had sat Neleus, who was wise as the gods, but he was now dead and had gone to the underworld. So Nestor sat in his father's place, holding the royal scepter as guardian of his people's welfare. His sons gathered around him as they left their rooms: Echephron, Stratius, Perseus, Aretus, and Thrasymedes. The sixth son was Pisistratus, and when Telemachus joined them, they made room for him to sit with them. Then Nestor spoke to them.

"My sons," he said, "hurry to do as I tell you. I want first and most importantly to honor the great goddess Athena, who appeared to me so clearly during yesterday's festival. So one of you go to the fields and tell the herdsman to bring me a cow, and have him bring it here immediately. Another must go to Telemachus's ship and invite all his crew, leaving only two men to guard the vessel. Someone else must run and get Laerces the goldsmith to cover the cow's horns with gold. The rest of you stay here and tell the maids in the house to prepare an excellent meal. Have them bring chairs and firewood for the sacrifice, and tell them to bring me some clear spring water."

At his words, they all hurried off on their different tasks. The cow was brought from the fields, and Telemachus's crew came from the ship. The goldsmith arrived with his anvil, hammer, and tongs for working with gold, and Athena herself came to accept the sacrifice. Nestor provided the gold, and the smith covered the cow's horns with it so the goddess would be pleased with their beauty. Then Stratius and Echephron led the cow by the horns, while Aretus brought water from the house in a decorated pitcher, and in his other hand he carried a basket of barley meal. Strong Thrasymedes stood ready with a sharp ax to strike the cow, while Perseus held a bowl to catch the blood. Then Nestor began by washing his hands and sprinkling the barley meal, offering many prayers to Athena as he threw a lock of hair from the cow's head into the fire.

When they had finished praying and sprinkling the barley meal, Thrasymedes struck his blow and cut through the tendons at the base of the cow's neck. This made all of Nestor's daughters and daughters-in-law, and his respected wife Eurydice (eldest daughter of Clymenus), cry out with joy. Then they lifted the cow's head from the ground, and Pisistratus cut its throat. When the blood had drained and the cow was completely dead, they cut it up according to proper custom. They cut out the thigh bones, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and placed some raw meat on top. Then Nestor laid these on the wood fire and poured wine over them, while the young men stood nearby with five-pronged forks in their hands. After the thigh bones were burned and they had tasted the inner organs, they cut up the rest of the meat into small pieces, put them on spits, and roasted them over the fire.

Meanwhile, lovely Polycaste, Nestor's youngest daughter, gave Telemachus a bath. When she had washed him and rubbed him with olive oil, she brought him a beautiful cloak and tunic. He looked like a god as he came from the bath and sat down beside Nestor. When the outer meat was cooked, they took it off the spits and sat down to eat, served by good servants who kept filling their golden cups with wine. As soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, Nestor said, "Sons, harness Telemachus's horses to the chariot so he can start his journey."

They did exactly as he commanded and quickly harnessed the swift horses to the chariot. The housekeeper packed food for them: bread, wine, and fine foods fit for princes. Then Telemachus climbed into the chariot while Pisistratus took the reins and sat beside him. He whipped the horses, and they flew forward eagerly into the open countryside, leaving the high fortress of Pylos behind them. All day long they traveled, with the yoke swaying on the horses' necks, until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived - he was the son of Ortilochus and grandson of Alpheus. There they spent the night, and Diocles welcomed them with generous hospitality. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared in the morning, they harnessed their horses again and drove out through the gateway and its echoing archway. Pisistratus urged the horses on, and they flew forward willingly. Soon they came to the wheat fields of the open plains, and eventually they completed their journey successfully, so well did their horses carry them.
And when the sun had set and darkness covered the land,

chapters.title: Book IV — The visit to king menelaus, who tells his story—meanwhile the suitors in ithaca plot against telemachus.
paragraphs: They reached the valley city of Lacedaemon, where they drove straight to King Menelaus's palace. They found him celebrating two weddings at once - his daughter was marrying Achilles' brave son, and his own son Megapenthes was getting married too. Menelaus had promised his daughter to Achilles' son back when they were fighting at Troy, and now the gods were making it happen. His son was marrying a girl from Sparta. Megapenthes was born to a servant woman, because the gods never gave Queen Helen any more children after beautiful Hermione, who was as lovely as the goddess Venus herself.

All around the great hall, neighbors and relatives were feasting and having a wonderful time. A musician played his lyre and sang for them, while two acrobats flipped and tumbled in the middle of the crowd, putting on quite a show for everyone.

Telemachus and Nestor's son stopped their horses at the front gate. A servant named Eteoneus saw them and ran quickly back into the house to tell his master. He hurried up to Menelaus and said, "Sir, there are two strangers at our gate - young men who look like they could be sons of Zeus himself! What should we do? Should we take care of their horses, or tell them to find somewhere else to stay?"

King Menelaus got angry and said, "Eteoneus, son of Boethous, you've never been a fool before, but now you're talking like one! Of course we'll take their horses and invite the strangers in for dinner. You and I have stayed at plenty of other people's houses on our long journey home. We must always show kindness to travelers, just as others showed kindness to us."

So Eteoneus hurried back and called the other servants to help. They unhitched the sweating horses from the chariot, tied them up in the stables, and gave them fresh oats and barley to eat. Then they parked the chariot against the courtyard wall and led the two young men into the magnificent palace. Telemachus and Pisistratus gasped in wonder - the walls and floors gleamed like the sun and moon with gold and silver everywhere! After they had looked around in amazement, servants led them to the bathhouse to get cleaned up.

The servants washed them carefully and rubbed sweet-smelling oil on their skin, then gave them fresh woolen cloaks and tunics to wear. The two young men took their seats next to King Menelaus. A maid brought them a beautiful golden pitcher and poured water into a silver bowl so they could wash their hands. She set up a polished table beside them, and another servant brought fresh bread and all kinds of delicious food, while the meat-carver served them portions of the finest cuts and set golden cups beside them.

King Menelaus welcomed them warmly, saying, "Please, eat and enjoy yourselves! After dinner, I'll ask who you are. Young men as noble-looking as you two must come from royal families. You're definitely not the sons of common people - anyone can see you have royal blood!"

He handed them a piece of the best roasted meat that had been saved for him as the guest of honor. They ate heartily of all the good food spread before them. When they had finished eating and drinking, Telemachus leaned close to Pisistratus and whispered so no one else could hear, "Look at all this bronze and gold - and amber and ivory and silver! Everything sparkles so brightly, it's like seeing Zeus's palace on Mount Olympus. I've never seen anything so amazing!"

But Menelaus heard him and said with a smile, "My boys, no one can compete with Zeus - his house and everything in it will last forever. But among ordinary people, well, there might be someone else as wealthy as I am, though I doubt it. It took me nearly eight years of hard traveling to gather all these treasures. I sailed to Cyprus, Phoenicia, and Egypt. I visited the Ethiopians, the Sidonians, and went all the way to Libya, where the lambs are born with horns and the sheep have babies three times a year! Everyone there has plenty of cheese, meat, and milk. But while I was collecting riches in far-off lands, my brother Agamemnon was murdered by his own wife and her lover back home. So all this wealth doesn't bring me much joy. Your parents have probably told you this sad story - how I lost my beautiful home and all my treasures there. I wish I had only a third of what I own now, if it meant all our friends who died at Troy were still alive. I sit here in my palace and weep for all of them. Sometimes I cry out loud, but tears get cold quickly and don't help much. Yet of all the brave warriors we lost, I grieve most for one man. I can't even think of eating or sleeping when I remember him, because no Greek worked harder or risked more than he did. And what did it get him? Nothing but sorrow for all of us who loved him. He's been missing for so long, we don't know if he's alive or dead. His old father Laertes, his faithful wife Penelope, and his son Telemachus - who was just a baby when he left - all live in constant grief, wondering what happened to him."

When Menelaus spoke these words, Telemachus's heart ached thinking of his father Odysseus. Tears spilled from his eyes when he heard his father mentioned, and he quickly pulled his cloak up over his face to hide his crying. Menelaus noticed this and wondered whether he should wait for the boy to speak when he was ready, or ask him right away what was troubling him.

While the king was trying to decide what to do, Queen Helen came down from her perfumed room high in the palace, looking as beautiful as the goddess Diana herself. Her servants Adraste brought her a chair, Alcippe brought a soft wool rug, and Phylo carried her silver sewing box - a gift from Alcandra, the wife of Polybus who lived in Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the world. Polybus had given Menelaus two silver bathtubs, two tripods, and ten bars of gold, while his wife had given Helen wonderful presents: a golden spinning wheel and this silver sewing box that rolled on wheels with a gold rim around the top. Phylo set it beside Helen, filled with fine spun thread, and placed a spindle wound with purple wool on top. Helen sat down, put her feet on a footstool, and began asking her husband questions.

"Do we know who these strangers are, Menelaus?" she asked. "Let me guess - I think I'm right, but I can hardly believe my own eyes! I've never seen anyone - man or woman - who looks so much like someone else as this young man looks like Telemachus, the son Odysseus left behind as a tiny baby when all you Greeks sailed off to fight at Troy because of me and my shameful actions."

"My dear wife," Menelaus replied, "I see exactly the same resemblance you do. His hands and feet are just like Odysseus's, and so is his hair, the shape of his head, and the way his eyes look. What's more, when I was just talking about Odysseus and how much he suffered trying to help me, tears came to this young man's eyes and he hid his face in his cloak."

Then Pisistratus spoke up: "King Menelaus, son of Atreus, you're absolutely right - this is Telemachus. But he's very shy and feels embarrassed about speaking up in front of someone as wise and important as you. My father Nestor sent me to bring him here because he hoped you might be able to give him advice or help. You see, when a father goes away and leaves his son alone, the boy always has trouble at home with no one to protect him. That's exactly how Telemachus feels right now - his father is gone, and there's no one in Ithaca strong enough to stand up for him."

"Well, bless my soul!" exclaimed Menelaus. "So I'm being visited by the son of one of my dearest friends, a man who suffered terribly trying to help me! I always planned to welcome Odysseus with the greatest honor when the gods brought us safely home from our long travels. I was going to build him a city here in my kingdom and give him a fine house. I would have brought him and his family and all his people here from Ithaca, and conquered one of my neighboring cities for them to rule. We would have seen each other all the time, and nothing but death could have separated such close friends. But I suppose the gods didn't want us to have such happiness, since they've prevented that poor man from ever getting home at all."

His words made everyone start crying. Helen wept, Telemachus wept, and so did Menelaus. Even Pisistratus couldn't keep the tears from his eyes as he remembered his dear brother Antilochus, who had been killed by Memnon, son of the Dawn goddess, at Troy. Finally he said to Menelaus:

"Sir, my father Nestor always said you were extremely wise and understanding. So please, if you don't mind, let's not cry during our meal. Morning will come soon enough, and I don't mind weeping then for those who have died. All we can do for the dead is cut our hair short in mourning and shed tears for them. I had a brother who died at Troy - he was one of the best warriors there. I'm sure you knew him. His name was Antilochus. I never got to meet him myself, but everyone says he was incredibly fast and brave in battle."

"My friend," answered Menelaus, "you show wisdom far beyond your years. It's clear you take after your father. You can always tell when someone is the son of a man the gods have blessed with a good wife and fine children - and the gods have blessed Nestor all his life with a peaceful old age, surrounded by sons who are both good and brave. Let's stop all this weeping and get back to our dinner. We can pour water on our hands and wash them clean. Telemachus and I will have plenty of time to talk together in the morning."
So Asphalion, one of the servants, poured fresh water over their hands, and they turned back to the delicious food spread before them.

Then Helen, daughter of Zeus, thought of something that would help. She secretly put a special herb in the wine that takes away all sadness, sorrow, and anger. Anyone who drinks wine mixed with this herb cannot shed a single tear for the rest of the day, even if their parents die right in front of them, or they watch their own brother or son get killed. This powerful medicine had been given to Helen by Polydamna, wife of Thon, a woman from Egypt where all kinds of herbs grow - some that heal and others that can poison. Everyone in Egypt knows about medicine because they're descendants of Paeon, the healing god. After Helen put the herb in the wine bowl and told the servants to pour drinks for everyone, she said:

"Menelaus, son of Atreus, and you fine young men from noble families - for Zeus gives both good fortune and bad as he chooses - feast here and enjoy yourselves while I tell you an exciting story. I can't tell you about every brave thing Odysseus did, but I can share what happened when he was at Troy and all you Greeks were in terrible danger. He covered himself with wounds and cuts, dressed in raggedy clothes like a beggar or slave, and snuck into Troy looking completely different from his usual self. In this disguise he entered the enemy city, and no one suspected who he really was. Only I recognized him and started asking questions, but he was too clever for me. However, after I had bathed him, rubbed oil on his skin, and given him clean clothes, and after I swore a sacred oath not to reveal his identity to the Trojans until he got safely back to your camp, he told me all the Greeks' battle plans. He killed many Trojans and gathered lots of important information before returning to your ships. The Trojan women wailed and mourned, but secretly I was glad, because my heart was already longing for home. I regretted the terrible mistake Venus had made me make when she took me away from my country, my daughter, and my lawful husband - who is certainly not lacking in looks or brains!"

Then Menelaus said, "Everything you've said is absolutely true, my dear wife. I've traveled everywhere and met many heroes, but I've never seen anyone quite like Odysseus. What incredible courage and endurance he showed inside the wooden horse, where all the bravest Greeks were hiding, ready to bring death and destruction to the Trojans! (The wooden horse was a giant hollow statue the Greeks built and hid soldiers inside to trick the Trojans.) You came up to us then - some god who wanted to help Troy must have sent you - and Deiphobus was with you. Three times you walked all around our hiding place and patted it, calling out each of our leaders by name and copying our wives' voices perfectly! Diomedes, Odysseus, and I heard you from inside and wanted to answer or jump out, but Odysseus kept us all quiet and still. Only Anticlus started to respond, but Odysseus clamped his powerful hands over the man's mouth and held them there until Athena led you away. That's what saved all our lives!"

"How sad," said Telemachus, "that all his cleverness couldn't save him in the end, even with his heart as strong as iron. But now, sir, please send us all to bed so we can enjoy the wonderful gift of sleep."

Helen told her maids to set up beds in the guest room by the gate, with fine red blankets and coverlets on top, plus warm woolen cloaks for the visitors to wear. The maids went out carrying torches and prepared the beds, and a male servant led the two young men to their room. So Telemachus and Pisistratus slept in the forecourt, while Menelaus rested in his inner chamber with beautiful Helen beside him.

When rosy-fingered Dawn, child of the morning, appeared in the sky, Menelaus got up and dressed himself. He strapped his sandals on his feet, buckled his sword around his shoulder, and left his room looking as handsome as a god. Then he sat down near Telemachus and said:

"And what, Telemachus, has brought you on this long sea journey to Lacedaemon?" King Menelaus asked. "Are you here on official business for your city, or is this a personal matter? Please tell me everything."

"Your majesty," Telemachus replied, "I've come to see if you know anything about my father. Greedy men are destroying my home and wasting all our wealth. My house is full of troublemakers who keep killing our sheep and cattle, claiming they want to marry my mother. So I'm here begging at your feet, hoping you might tell me about my father's sad fate. Did you see what happened to him with your own eyes, or did you hear about it from another traveler? He was born to face great troubles.
