Please don't hold back any details out of pity for me—tell me plainly exactly what you saw. If my brave father Odysseus ever served you faithfully with words or deeds when you Greeks were fighting the Trojans, remember that kindness now and tell me the whole truth."

When Menelaus heard this, he was deeply shocked. "So!" he exclaimed, "these cowards want to take over a brave man's home? It's like a deer laying her newborn babies in a lion's den, then wandering off to graze in the forest—when the lion returns, he'll quickly destroy them both! That's exactly what Odysseus will do to these suitors. By father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, if Odysseus is still the same man who wrestled with Philomeleides on the island of Lesbos and threw him so hard that all of us Greeks cheered—if he's still that strong and came face-to-face with these suitors, their wedding plans would end very badly! But about your questions—I won't lie or trick you. I'll tell you everything the old sea god told me."

"I was trying to sail home, but the gods trapped me in Egypt because my sacrifices hadn't pleased them enough. The gods are very strict about getting what they're owed. Off the coast of Egypt, about a day's sail with a good strong wind, there's an island called Pharos. It has an excellent harbor where ships can take on fresh water before heading to the open sea. The gods left me stranded there for twenty days without even a breath of fair wind to help me move forward. We would have run out of food and my men would have starved, if a goddess hadn't taken pity on me. She appeared as Eidothea, daughter of Proteus, the old man of the sea, and she had grown quite fond of me."

"She came to me one day when I was alone, as I often was. My men would wander all over the island with fishing hooks, hoping to catch something to eat and ease their terrible hunger. 'Stranger,' she said, 'it seems like you enjoy starving this way—at least it doesn't seem to bother you much, since you just sit here day after day without even trying to escape, while your men are slowly dying.'"

"'Let me tell you,' I said, 'whichever goddess you might be, I'm not staying here by choice. I must have angered the gods who live in heaven. Please tell me—since the gods know everything—which of the immortals is keeping me trapped here, and how I can sail home across the sea.'"

"'Stranger,' she replied, 'I'll explain everything clearly. There's an ancient immortal who lives under the sea near here named Proteus. He's Egyptian, and people say he's my father. He works for Poseidon, god of the sea, and knows every inch of the ocean floor. If you can catch him and hold him tight, he'll tell you about your voyage—what route to take and how to sail home safely. He'll also tell you, if you want to know, everything that's been happening at your house, both good and bad, while you've been away on this long, dangerous journey.'" (Proteus was a sea god who could change his shape and tell the future.)
"'Can you show me some trick to catch this old god without him suspecting anything?' I asked. 'After all, it's not easy for a mortal man to catch a god.'"

"'Stranger,' she said, 'I'll make it perfectly clear. Around noon, when the sun reaches the middle of the sky, the old man of the sea rises from the waves, hidden by the West wind that ruffles the water above his head. As soon as he comes up, he lies down to sleep in a large sea cave. The seals—people call them the sea's children—also come up from the gray water and sleep all around him in groups. They bring a very strong, fishy smell with them. Early tomorrow morning, I'll take you to this place and hide you there. Choose the three best men from your crew, and I'll tell you all the tricks the old man will try on you.'"

"'First, he'll look over all his seals and count them. Then, when he's seen them all and counted them on his fingers, he'll fall asleep among them like a shepherd with his sheep. The moment you see him sleeping, grab him! Use all your strength and hold him tight, because he'll do everything possible to escape. He'll change himself into every kind of creature that walks the earth, and he'll become both fire and water. But you must hold him fast and grip him tighter and tighter, until he starts talking to you and returns to his original form. Then you can loosen your grip and let him go, and ask him which god is angry with you and what you must do to reach home safely.'"

"After saying this, she dove under the waves. I walked back to where my ships were lined up on the shore, my heart heavy with worry. When I reached my ship, we prepared supper since night was falling, and we camped on the beach."

"When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared in the morning, I took the three men I trusted most and walked along the seashore, praying earnestly to heaven. Meanwhile, the goddess brought up four fresh seal skins from the bottom of the sea—she was planning to trick her father. She dug four pits for us to hide in and sat down to wait for us. When we came close, she made us lie down in the pits one by one and threw a seal skin over each of us. Our hiding place would have been unbearable because of the terrible stench of the fishy seals—who would want to sleep next to a sea monster?—but the goddess helped us here too. She put some ambrosia under each man's nose. This divine substance smelled so sweet that it completely blocked out the smell of the seals." (Ambrosia was the food of the gods, with a heavenly fragrance.)

"We waited all morning, watching hundreds of seals come up to sunbathe on the shore. At noon, the old man of the sea came up too. When he found his fat seals, he walked among them and counted them. We were among the first he counted, and he never suspected any trick. As soon as he finished counting, he lay down to sleep. Then we rushed at him with a shout and grabbed him! Immediately he began his old tricks, changing himself first into a lion with a great mane, then suddenly into a dragon, then a leopard, then a wild boar. Next, he became flowing water, and then a tall tree. But we held on tight and never let go. Finally, the clever old creature grew tired and said, 'Which of the gods helped you plan this trap, son of Atreus? What do you want from me?'"

"'You already know the answer, old man,' I replied. 'You'll gain nothing by trying to avoid my questions. I've been trapped on this island for so long, with no way to escape. I'm losing hope. Tell me—since you gods know everything—which immortal is keeping me here, and how I can sail home safely?'"

"'Well then,' he said, 'if you want to finish your voyage and get home quickly, you must offer sacrifices to Zeus and the other gods before you set sail. It's been decided that you won't reach your friends and your own house until you return to the sacred Nile River in Egypt and offer proper sacrifices to the immortal gods who rule heaven. When you do this, they'll let you complete your journey.'"

"I felt heartbroken when I heard I had to make that long, terrible voyage back to Egypt. Still, I answered, 'Old man, I'll do everything you've told me. But now tell me truly—did all the Greeks that Nestor and I left behind when we sailed from Troy make it home safely? Or did any of them die, either on their ships or among friends after their fighting days were over?'"

"'Son of Atreus,' he answered, 'why ask me this? You'd be better off not knowing what I can tell you, because your eyes will surely fill with tears when you hear my story. Many of those you're asking about are dead and gone, but many still survive. Only two of the chief Greek leaders died during their journey home. You were there yourself for the battle. A third Greek leader is still alive but trapped at sea, unable to return. Ajax was shipwrecked when Poseidon drove him onto the great rocks of Gyrae. Still, Poseidon let him escape the water safely, and despite Athena's hatred, Ajax would have survived if he hadn't ruined everything by bragging. He boasted that the gods couldn't drown him even though they'd tried. When Poseidon heard this arrogant talk, he grabbed his trident with both powerful hands and split the rock of Gyrae in two. The base stayed put, but the part Ajax was sitting on fell headfirst into the sea, carrying Ajax with it. So he drank salt water and drowned.'" (Ajax was a Greek warrior known for his pride, which led to his downfall.)

"'Your brother Agamemnon and his ships escaped because Hera protected him. But just as he was about to reach the high cliff of Malea, a heavy storm caught him and carried him far out to sea against his will. The wind drove him to the land where Thyestes once lived, but where Aegisthus was now ruling. Eventually, it seemed he would return safely after all, because the gods changed the wind back to its normal direction and they reached home. Agamemnon kissed his native soil and wept tears of joy at finding himself in his own country.'"

"'Now, Aegisthus had posted a watchman who had been on guard for a whole year, and Aegisthus had promised him two talents of gold for this service. This man had been watching to make sure Agamemnon couldn't sneak back and prepare for war. So when this watchman saw Agamemnon arrive, he immediately told Aegisthus, who began plotting against him. Aegisthus chose twenty of his bravest warriors and hid them on one side of the great hall, while on the other side he prepared a feast. Then he sent his chariots and horsemen to invite Agamemnon to the banquet, but he was planning murder. He got Agamemnon there, completely unaware of the doom waiting for him, and killed him during the feast as if he were slaughtering cattle. Not one of Agamemnon's followers survived, and none of Aegisthus's men either—they were all killed there in the hall.'" (This refers to the famous betrayal where Agamemnon was murdered by his wife's lover upon returning from Troy.)

"When Proteus finished speaking, I felt heartbroken. I sat on the sand and wept, feeling like I could no longer bear to live or see the sunlight. After I had cried and rolled on the ground long enough, the old man of the sea said, 'Son of Atreus, don't waste any more time crying so bitterly—it won't help anything. Find your way home as quickly as possible. Aegisthus might still be alive, but even if Orestes has already killed him before you arrive, you might still make it in time for the funeral.'" (Orestes was Agamemnon's son, who would avenge his father's murder.)

"This comforted me despite all my sorrow, and I said, 'Now I know about those two men. Tell me about the third one you mentioned—is he still alive but stuck at sea, unable to get home? Or is he dead? Tell me, no matter how much it might upset me.'"

"'The third man,' he answered, 'is Odysseus, who lives in Ithaca. I can see him on an island, crying bitterly in the house of the nymph Calypso, who's keeping him prisoner. He can't reach home because he has no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea. As for your own fate, Menelaus, you won't die in Argos. Instead, the gods will take you to the Elysian Fields at the ends of the world. There, fair-haired Rhadamanthus rules, and people live an easier life than anywhere else. In Elysium, there's no rain, hail, or snow. Ocean sends a gentle West wind that sings softly from the sea and gives fresh life to everyone. This will happen to you because you married Helen and are Zeus's son-in-law.'" (The Elysian Fields were a paradise where heroes went after death, and Rhadamanthus was a judge of the dead.)

"As he spoke, Proteus dove under the waves. I returned to the ships with my companions, my heart heavy with worry. When we reached the ships, we prepared supper since night was falling, and camped on the beach. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared in the morning, we dragged our ships into the water and put up our masts and sails. We climbed aboard, took our places on the rowing benches, and struck the gray sea with our oars. I sailed my ships back to the sacred Nile River in Egypt and offered the full sacrifices the gods demanded. After I had calmed heaven's anger, I built a tomb for Agamemnon so his name would live forever. Then the gods sent me a fair wind, and I had a swift journey home."

"Now, as for you—stay here another ten or twelve days, and then I'll send you on your way with wonderful gifts. I'll give you a noble present of a chariot and three horses, plus a beautiful cup. As long as you live, you'll think of me whenever you pour wine offerings to the immortal gods."

"Son of Atreus," Telemachus replied, "please don't ask me to stay longer. I'd be happy to remain with you for another twelve months—I find your stories so fascinating that I'd never miss home or my parents. But my crew, whom I left at Pylos, are already getting impatient, and you're keeping me from them. As for any gift you want to give me, I'd prefer a piece of fine metalwork. I won't take horses back to Ithaca—I'll leave them here to make your stables even more beautiful. You have lots of flat land in your kingdom where clover grows, along with grass and wheat and barley and oats with their white, spreading tops. But in Ithaca, we have no open fields or racetracks. Our country is better suited for goats than horses, and I like it better that way. None of our islands have much level ground suitable for horses, and Ithaca least of all."

King Menelaus smiled warmly and took Telemachus's hand in his own. "Your words show me that you come from a noble family," he said kindly. "I can and will make this trade with you. I'll give you the finest and most valuable treasure in my entire palace. It's a silver mixing bowl made by the god Hephaestus himself, with a golden rim around the edge. King Phaedimus of Sidon gave it to me when I visited his land on my way home from Troy. I want you to have it as my gift."

And so they talked together while more guests arrived at the king's house. The visitors brought sheep and wine, and their wives had packed bread for the journey. Everyone was busy preparing their meals in the courtyards.

Meanwhile, back in Ithaca, the suitors were throwing metal discs and hurling spears at targets on the flat ground in front of Odysseus's house. They acted as rude and demanding as always. Antinous and Eurymachus, the worst troublemakers and leaders of the group, sat together when a man named Noemon came up to speak with Antinous.

"Do we know when Telemachus is coming back from Pylos, Antinous?" Noemon asked. "He borrowed my ship, and I need it back so I can sail to Elis. I have twelve mother horses there with young mules that need to be trained, and I want to bring one back here to break in."

The suitors were shocked to hear this news! They had been sure that Telemachus hadn't gone to King Nestor's city. They thought he was just somewhere on the farms, with the sheep or the swineherd. So Antinous demanded, "When did he leave? Tell me the truth! What young men went with him? Were they free citizens or his servants? And did you give him the ship willingly, or did he take it without asking?"

"I lent it to him," Noemon replied. "What else could I do? When someone of his high rank said he was in trouble and asked for my help, I couldn't possibly say no. The young men who went with him were the best we have. I saw Mentor board the ship as captain—or maybe it was some god who looked exactly like him. I can't understand it, because I saw Mentor here yesterday morning, yet he was supposed to be sailing to Pylos!"

Noemon then returned to his father's house, but Antinous and Eurymachus were furious. They told the other suitors to stop their games and come sit with them. When everyone gathered around, Antinous spoke in anger. His heart was black with rage, and his eyes blazed like fire.

"By the gods, this trip of Telemachus is serious trouble! We were sure it would come to nothing, but the young man has escaped us with a handpicked crew. He'll cause us real problems soon. May Zeus strike him down before he becomes a man! Find me a ship with twenty men, and I'll wait for him in the narrow waters between Ithaca and Samos. He'll be sorry he ever went looking for news of his father!"
The other suitors cheered his words, and then they all went inside the palace buildings.

It wasn't long before Penelope learned what the suitors were planning. A servant named Medon had overheard them talking in the courtyard while they made their evil plans. He hurried to tell his mistress the terrible news. As he entered her room, Penelope said, "Medon, why have the suitors sent you here? Are you supposed to tell my maids to stop their work and cook dinner for those men? I wish they would never eat or court me again, anywhere! Let this be the last time they waste my son's inheritance. Didn't your fathers tell you as children how good Odysseus was to them? He never acted cruelly or spoke harshly to anyone. Kings sometimes favor one person over another, but Odysseus was always fair—which shows how wicked your hearts are, and that gratitude has disappeared from this world."

Then Medon said, "My lady, I wish that was all! But they're plotting something much worse now—may the gods stop their evil plan. They're going to try to murder Telemachus when he returns from Pylos and Sparta, where he went to get news of his father."

Penelope's heart sank, and for a long time she couldn't speak. Her eyes filled with tears, and no words would come. Finally she cried, "Why did my son leave me? Why did he go sailing across the dangerous ocean in those ships that travel so far? Does he want to die without leaving anyone to carry on his name?"
"I don't know," Medon answered. "Maybe some god put the idea in his head, or maybe he decided on his own to find out if his father is dead or alive and coming home."

Then Medon went back downstairs, leaving Penelope in terrible grief. There were plenty of chairs in the house, but she had no desire to sit in any of them. She could only throw herself on the floor of her room and weep. All the servant women, both old and young, gathered around her and began crying too. At last, overcome with sorrow, she wailed,

"My dear women, the gods have given me more suffering than any other woman my age in all of Greece. First I lost my brave, lion-hearted husband, who was the best of men and famous throughout all the land. Now my precious son is at the mercy of wind and waves, and I never even heard he was leaving home! You wicked girls, not one of you thought to wake me from my bed, even though you all knew perfectly well when he was departing. If I had known about this voyage, he would have had to give it up or leave my dead body behind him! Now go quickly and call old Dolius, my gardener, who was given to me when I married. Tell him to rush to Laertes with this news. Maybe Odysseus's old father can think of some plan to get the people on our side against these men who are trying to destroy both his family line and Odysseus's!"

Then the dear old nurse Euryclea said, "You may punish me or let me stay, my lady, but I'll tell you the truth. I knew all about his trip and gave him all the food and wine he wanted. But he made me swear a solemn oath not to tell you for ten or twelve days, unless you asked or found out somehow. He didn't want you to ruin your beauty by crying. Now, my lady, wash your face, change your clothes, and go upstairs with your maids to pray to Athena, daughter of mighty Zeus. She can save him even from the jaws of death. Don't trouble old Laertes—he has enough sorrow already. Besides, I don't think the gods hate Odysseus's family so much. There will be a son to inherit the house and all the beautiful fields around it."

With these words, Euryclea made her mistress stop crying and dried her tears. Penelope washed her face, changed her dress, and went upstairs with her maids. She put some ground barley in a basket and began praying to Athena, the goddess of wisdom and war.

"Hear me," she cried, "daughter of Zeus who carries the mighty shield! If Odysseus ever burned the fat thigh bones of sheep or cattle as offerings to you, remember that now and help me! Save my dear son from the evil plans of the suitors!"
She cried out loudly as she prayed, and the goddess heard her. Meanwhile, the suitors were making noise throughout the covered walkway, and one of them said,
"The queen is getting ready to marry one of us. She has no idea that her son is about to die."

That's what they said, but they didn't know what would really happen. Then Antinous said, "Friends, let's keep our voices down so no one inside hears us. Let's get up and quietly do what we've all agreed on."

He chose twenty men, and they went down to their ship by the seashore. They dragged the vessel into the water and loaded the mast and sails. They tied the oars to the wooden pins with leather straps and raised the white sails, while their servants brought their weapons and armor. Then they anchored the ship a short distance offshore, came back to land, ate their dinner, and waited for darkness to fall.

But Penelope lay in her room upstairs, unable to eat or drink, wondering if her brave son would escape or be killed by the wicked suitors. Like a lioness trapped by hunters closing in from all sides, she worried and worried until she fell into an exhausted sleep on her bed.

Then Athena had another idea. She created a dream vision that looked like Penelope's sister Iphthime, who had married Eumelus and lived in the city of Pherae. The goddess sent this vision to Odysseus's house to comfort Penelope. It came into her room through the hole where the leather strap passed to pull the door shut, and hovered over her head, saying,
"You're sleeping, Penelope, but the gods who live in comfort won't let you weep and be so sad. Your son has done nothing wrong to them, so he will come back to you safely."

Penelope had been sleeping peacefully when she heard a voice in her dreams. She answered, "Sister, why have you come to visit me? You hardly ever come here because you live so far away. Are you telling me I should stop crying and push away all these terrible worries that keep hurting my heart? I've lost my brave husband - he was as fierce as a lion and had every good quality a man could have. Everyone in Greece knew his name! And now my dear son has sailed away on a ship. He's just a boy who has never faced real danger or been around crowds of strangers. I'm even more worried about him than I am about my husband. I shake with fear when I think of him - something terrible might happen to him, either from the people he's visiting or from enemies at sea. So many people want to kill him before he can come home safely."

The dream-visitor replied, "Don't lose hope, and don't be so frightened. Someone very powerful is traveling with your son - someone many people would be grateful to have protecting them. I'm talking about Athena, the wise goddess. She feels sorry for you and your family, and she's the one who sent me to bring you this message of comfort."

"If you're a goddess or someone sent by the gods," Penelope said, "then please tell me about my husband too. Is he still alive somewhere, or has he already died and gone to the underworld where dead spirits live?"
The vision answered, "I won't tell you for sure whether he's alive or dead. There's no point in talking about things that might not be true."
Then the dream-spirit disappeared, slipping away like smoke through the keyhole of the door. But Penelope woke up feeling much better and less worried. The dream had seemed so real and gave her hope.

Meanwhile, the suitors climbed aboard their ship and sailed out to sea, planning to murder young Telemachus. There was a small rocky island called Asteris sitting right in the middle of the water between Ithaca and another island called Samos. This little island had harbors on both sides where ships could hide. The suitors sailed there and hid their ship, waiting like hunters to ambush Telemachus when he sailed by.

chapters.title: Book V — Calypso—ulysses reaches scheria on a raft.
paragraphs: As the golden Dawn woke up next to her husband Tithonus, bringing light to both humans and gods, the mighty gods gathered for their daily meeting. Zeus, the king of all gods who controls thunder and lightning, sat at the head of their council. Then Athena, the wise goddess of war and wisdom, began to speak about brave Odysseus and how much he was suffering, trapped far away on the island of the sea nymph Calypso.

"Father Zeus," she said, "and all you other gods who live forever in happiness, I hope there will never again be a kind and fair ruler! I hope all kings from now on will be cruel and unfair, because not one person remembers Odysseus, who ruled them like a loving father. There he lies, in terrible pain on an island where the nymph Calypso keeps him prisoner. He cannot return to his home because he has no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea. What's worse, evil men are now trying to kill his only son Telemachus, who is traveling home from Pylos and Sparta, where he went looking for news of his father."

"My dear daughter, what are you talking about?" Zeus replied with a smile. "Didn't you send Telemachus on that journey yourself, thinking it would help Odysseus get home and punish those troublemakers? Besides, you have the power to protect Telemachus and bring him home safely, while those bullies will have to run back home without harming him."

After saying this, Zeus turned to his son Hermes, the messenger god. "Hermes, you are our messenger, so go and tell Calypso that we have decided poor Odysseus must return home. No gods or humans will help him on his journey. Instead, he must sail for twenty dangerous days on a raft until he reaches the fertile island of Scheria. There live the Phaeacians, who are related to us gods. They will treat him like one of us and honor him greatly. They will send him home in one of their ships and give him more bronze, gold, and fine clothes than he would have brought back from Troy, even if he had kept all his war prizes and returned without disaster. This is how we have decided he shall return to his country and his friends."

Zeus had spoken, and Hermes, the guide and guardian who could kill with his magic wand, did as he was told. He quickly strapped on his golden sandals that let him fly like the wind over land and sea. He picked up his magic wand that could make people fall asleep or wake up, and flew over the mountains. Then he swooped down through the sky until he reached the ocean, skimming over the waves like a seabird hunting for fish, dipping its feathers in the salty spray. He flew over many exhausting waves until he finally reached Calypso's island, left the sea behind, and walked on land until he came to the cave where the nymph lived.

He found her at home. A large fire crackled on her hearth, and you could smell the sweet scent of burning cedar and sandalwood from far away. She sat at her loom, weaving with a golden shuttle and singing beautifully. Around her cave grew a thick forest of alder, poplar, and sweet-smelling cypress trees, where many large birds had built their nests—owls, hawks, and chattering sea crows that spent their time fishing in the waters. A grapevine heavy with fruit climbed luxuriously around the cave's entrance. Four clear streams flowed in channels close together, winding this way and that to water beds of violets and other lush plants. Even a god couldn't help being amazed by such a beautiful place, so Hermes stood still and admired it. When he had looked his fill, he went inside the cave.

Calypso recognized him immediately—for all gods know each other, no matter how far apart they live—but Odysseus was not there. As usual, he sat on the seashore, staring out at the empty ocean with tears streaming down his face, groaning and breaking his heart with sadness. Calypso offered Hermes a seat and said, "Why have you come to visit me, Hermes? You are always welcome and honored here, though you don't come often. Tell me what you want, and I'll do it right away if I can. But come inside first, and let me give you some refreshments."
As she spoke, she set a table loaded with ambrosia (the food of the gods) beside him and mixed him some red nectar (the drink of the gods). Hermes ate and drank until he was satisfied, then said:

"You ask me why I've come here, goddess to god, and I'll tell you the truth as you want me to. Zeus sent me—it wasn't my idea! Who would want to travel all this way over the sea, where there are no cities full of people to offer me sacrifices and gifts? But I had to come, because none of us gods can disobey Zeus or ignore his commands. He says you're keeping the unluckiest man of all those who fought nine years at Troy and sailed home in the tenth year after destroying that city. On their way home, they angered Athena, who stirred up winds and waves against them. All his brave companions died, and only he was carried here by wind and tide. Zeus commands that you let this man go immediately, for it is his fate not to die here, far from his people, but to return to his house and country and see his friends again."

Calypso shook with rage when she heard this. "You gods should be ashamed of yourselves!" she cried. "You're always jealous and hate it when a goddess falls in love with a mortal man and wants to marry him! Remember when Dawn fell in love with Orion? You precious gods were so furious that Diana killed him on the island of Ortygia. And when Ceres fell in love with Iasion in a plowed field, Zeus heard about it and killed Iasion with his thunderbolts. Now you're angry with me because I have a man here! I found the poor creature clinging all alone to a piece of his broken ship, after Zeus had struck it with lightning and sunk it in the middle of the ocean. All his crew drowned, while he was blown by wind and waves to my island. I grew fond of him and cared for him, and I had planned to make him immortal so he would never grow old. But I cannot disobey Zeus or make his decisions meaningless. So if he insists, the man can sail away again across the seas. But I cannot send him anywhere myself, because I have no ships or sailors. However, I will gladly give him good advice that will help him reach his own country safely."
"Then send him away," said Hermes, "or Zeus will be angry with you and punish you."

With that, Hermes departed, and Calypso went to find Odysseus, having heard Zeus's message. She found him sitting on the beach with his eyes always full of tears, slowly dying of homesickness. He had grown tired of Calypso, and though he was forced to sleep with her in the cave at night, it was her idea, not his. During the day, he spent his time on the rocks and seashore, weeping and crying out in despair, always staring out at the sea. Calypso came close to him and said:

"My poor friend, don't stay here any longer, grieving and wasting your life away. I'm going to send you away willingly. Go cut some wooden beams and build yourself a large raft with a deck on top, so it can carry you safely over the sea. I'll put bread, wine, and water on board to keep you from starving. I'll also give you clothes and send you a fair wind to take you home, if the gods in heaven wish it—for they know more about these things and can arrange them better than I can."

Odysseus shuddered when he heard her. "Now goddess," he answered, "there's something suspicious about all this. You can't really mean to help me get home when you're telling me to do something as terrifying as sailing out to sea on a raft. Not even a well-built ship with a favorable wind would attempt such a distant voyage. Nothing you can say or do will make me get on a raft unless you first solemnly swear that you mean me no harm."

Calypso smiled at this and gently touched his hand. "You're very clever," she said, "but you're completely wrong here. Let heaven above and earth below be my witnesses, along with the waters of the river Styx—and this is the most serious oath a blessed god can take—that I mean you no harm at all. I'm only advising you to do exactly what I would do myself in your situation. I'm being completely honest with you. My heart isn't made of iron, and I feel very sorry for you."

When she finished speaking, she walked quickly ahead of him, and Odysseus followed her steps. So the pair—goddess and man—went on until they reached Calypso's cave, where Odysseus took the seat that Hermes had just left. Calypso set mortal food and drink before him, while her servants brought ambrosia and nectar for herself. They began eating the good food placed before them. When they had satisfied themselves with food and drink, Calypso spoke:

"Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, so you want to leave for your own homeland right away? Good luck to you! But if you only knew how much suffering awaits you before you reach your own country, you would stay here, live with me, and let me make you immortal, no matter how anxious you are to see your wife, whom you think about constantly day and night. Yet I believe I'm every bit as tall and beautiful as she is, for it's not right to expect a mortal woman to compare in beauty with an immortal goddess."

"Goddess," replied Odysseus, "please don't be angry with me about this. I know perfectly well that my wife Penelope is nothing like as tall or beautiful as you. She's only a human, while you're immortal. But still, I want to go home, and I can think of nothing else. If some god wrecks me when I'm on the sea, I'll bear it and make the best of it. I've already had endless trouble both on land and sea, so let this be added to the rest."
Soon the sun set and darkness fell, and the pair went into the inner part of the cave and went to bed.

When Dawn appeared with her rosy fingers, Odysseus put on his shirt and cloak, while the goddess wore a dress of light, delicate fabric, very fine and graceful, with a beautiful golden belt around her waist and a veil over her head. She immediately began thinking about how to help Odysseus on his way. She gave him a great bronze ax that fit his hands perfectly. It was sharp on both sides and had a beautiful olive wood handle fitted firmly to it. She also gave him a sharp adze, then led him to the far end of the island where the largest trees grew—alder, poplar, and pine that reached toward the sky. These were very dry and well-seasoned, perfect for building a light raft for the water. After showing him where the best trees grew, Calypso went home, leaving him to cut them down, which he quickly finished. He cut down twenty trees in all and smoothed them with his adze, shaping them properly like a skilled craftsman. Meanwhile, Calypso returned with drilling tools, so he bored holes and fitted the timbers together with bolts and rivets. He made the raft as wide as a skilled shipbuilder makes the deck of a large vessel. He built a deck on top of the frame and put a rail around it. He also made a mast with a crossbeam, and a rudder to steer with. He surrounded the raft with woven barriers to protect against the waves, then threw on a quantity of wood. Soon Calypso brought him linen to make sails, and he made these too, excellently, fastening them with ropes. Finally, using levers, he dragged the raft down into the water.

In four days he had completed the entire job, and on the fifth day Calypso sent him away from the island after bathing him and giving him clean clothes. She gave him a goatskin bag full of dark wine and another larger one of water. She also gave him a bag full of food, including much good meat. Moreover, she made the wind favorable and warm for him, and Odysseus gladly spread his sail before it while he sat and skillfully guided the raft with the rudder. He never closed his eyes but kept them fixed on the Pleiades (a cluster of stars), on late-setting Bootes (a constellation), and on the Great Bear—which people also call the Big Dipper, and which turns round and round in one place, facing the constellation Orion, and alone never sinks into the ocean—for Calypso had told him to keep this constellation on his left side. For seventeen days he sailed over the sea, and on the eighteenth day the dim outlines of mountains on the nearest part of the Phaeacian coast appeared, rising like a shield on the horizon.

But King Poseidon, god of the sea, was returning from visiting the Ethiopians when he spotted Odysseus far away from the mountains of Solymi. He could see him sailing on the sea, and it made him furious. He shook his head and muttered to himself, "Good heavens! So the gods have changed their minds about Odysseus while I was away in Ethiopia, and now he's close to the land of the Phaeacians, where it's decreed that he'll escape from all his troubles. Still, he'll have plenty of hardship before he's finished!"

Then Poseidon gathered his clouds together, grasped his three-pronged trident, stirred up the sea, and awakened every wind that blows until earth, sea, and sky were hidden in clouds, and night burst out of the heavens. Winds from east, south, north, and west struck him all at once, and a tremendous storm arose, so that Odysseus's heart began to fail him. "Oh no!" he said to himself in dismay. "What will become of me? I'm afraid Calypso was right when she said I would have trouble at sea before I got home. It's all coming true! How dark Zeus is making heaven with his clouds, and what a sea the winds are raising from every direction at once! Now I'm sure to die. Lucky were those Greeks who died before Troy fighting for the sons of Atreus! I wish I had been killed on the day when the Trojans were attacking me so fiercely around Achilles's dead body, for then I would have had a proper burial and the Greeks would have honored my name. But now it seems I'll come to a most pitiful end."

As he spoke, a huge wave broke over him with such terrible force that the raft spun around, and he was thrown far overboard. He let go of the steering oar, and the hurricane was so strong that it broke the mast in half, sending both sail and crossbeam into the sea. For a long time Odysseus was underwater, and it was all he could do to rise to the surface again, because the clothes Calypso had given him weighed him down. But at last he got his head above water and spat out the bitter seawater streaming down his face. Despite all this, he didn't lose sight of his raft. He swam as fast as he could toward it, grabbed hold of it, and climbed back on board to avoid drowning. The sea tossed the raft around like autumn winds whirl thistledown round and round on a road. It was as if the south, north, east, and west winds were all playing a game of catch with it at once.

While he was in this terrible situation, Ino, daughter of Cadmus (also called Leucothea), saw him. She had once been a mortal woman but had since become a sea goddess. Seeing Odysseus in such great distress, she felt sorry for him and rose like a seagull from the waves to sit on his raft.

"My poor man," she said, "why is Poseidon so furiously angry with you? He's giving you a great deal of trouble, but despite all his raging, he won't kill you. You seem sensible, so do as I tell you. Take off your clothes, leave your raft to drift with the wind, and swim to the Phaeacian shore, where better luck awaits you. Here, take my veil and wrap it around your chest. It's magic, and you can't be harmed as long as you wear it. As soon as you touch land, take it off, throw it back as far as you can into the sea, and then walk away." With these words, she took off her veil and gave it to him. Then she dove down again like a seagull and vanished beneath the dark blue waters.

But Odysseus didn't know what to think. "Oh no," he said to himself in dismay, "this is probably just another god trying to trick me into destruction by telling me to leave my raft. I won't do it right now, because the land where she said I'd be safe from all troubles still seems far away. I know what I'll do—I'm sure it's best. No matter what happens, I'll stick to the raft as long as its timbers hold together. But when the sea breaks it apart, I'll swim for it. I don't see how I can do any better than this."

While he was torn between these choices, Poseidon sent a terrible, enormous wave that seemed to tower above his head until it crashed right over the raft, which then broke apart like a pile of dry straw tossed about by a whirlwind. Odysseus grabbed one plank and rode it like a horse. Then he took off the clothes Calypso had given him, tied Ino's magic veil under his arms, and dove into the sea, planning to swim to shore. King Poseidon watched him do this and shook his head, muttering to himself, "There now! Swim around as best you can until you meet some civilized people. I don't think you'll be able to say I've been too easy on you!" With that, he whipped his horses and drove to his underwater palace at Aegae.

But Athena decided to help Odysseus, so she stopped all the winds except one and made them lie completely still. She stirred up a good strong breeze from the north that would calm the waters until Odysseus reached the land of the Phaeacians, where he would be safe.

Then he floated for two nights and two days in the water, with heavy swells on the sea and death staring him in the face. But when the third day dawned, the wind died down and there was complete calm, without even a breath of air stirring. As he rose on a swell, he looked eagerly ahead and could see land quite near. Then, just as children rejoice when their dear father begins to recover after suffering for a long time from a terrible illness sent by some angry spirit, but the gods deliver him from evil, so Odysseus was thankful when he saw land and trees again. He swam on with all his strength to set foot on dry ground once more. But when he got close enough to hear the surf, he began to hear waves thundering against the rocks, for the swells still crashed against them with a terrifying roar. Everything was covered in spray. There were no harbors where a ship could anchor, no shelter of any kind—only headlands, slippery rocks, and mountain peaks.

Odysseus's heart began to fail him, and he said despairingly to himself, "Oh no! Zeus has let me see land after swimming so far that I had given up all hope, but I can find no place to land. The coast is rocky and beaten by surf. The rocks are smooth and rise straight up from the sea, with deep water right beneath them, so I can't climb out because there's nowhere to put my feet. I'm afraid some huge wave will lift me up and smash me against the rocks as I try to leave the water—which would be a terrible way to land! If I swim farther looking for some sloping beach or harbor, a hurricane might carry me back out to sea against my will, or heaven might send some great sea monster to attack me, for Amphitrite (Poseidon's wife) breeds many such creatures, and I know Poseidon is very angry with me."

While he was torn between these choices, a wave caught him and hurled him with such force against the rocks that he would have been smashed and torn to pieces if Athena hadn't shown him what to do. He grabbed the rock with both hands and clung to it, groaning with pain until the wave pulled back, so he was saved that time. But immediately the wave returned and carried him back out with it far into the sea, tearing his hands just as the suckers of an octopus are torn when someone pulls it from its rocky home, and stones come up with it. In the same way, the rocks tore the skin from his strong hands, and then the wave dragged him deep underwater.

Here poor Odysseus would certainly have died, even despite his destined fate, if Athena hadn't helped him keep his wits about him. He swam back out to sea, beyond the reach of the surf pounding against the land. At the same time, he kept looking toward the shore to see if he could find some bay or a sandbar that would break the waves sideways. Soon, as he swam on, he came to the mouth of a river, and he thought this would be the best place because there were no rocks, and it provided shelter from the wind. He felt there was a current, so he prayed silently:

"Hear me, O king, whoever you may be, and save me from the anger of Poseidon, for I come to you as a humble beggar. Anyone who has lost his way has a claim on the gods at all times, so in my distress I approach your stream and beg for your mercy. Have pity on me, O king, for I declare myself your humble suppliant."

Then the river god stopped his current and calmed the waves, making everything peaceful before Odysseus and bringing him safely into the river's mouth. Here at last, Odysseus's knees and strong hands gave out, for the sea had completely exhausted him. His body was swollen all over, and seawater poured from his mouth and nose like a river, so he could neither breathe nor speak. He lay unconscious from complete exhaustion. Soon, when he had caught his breath and come to himself again, he took off the scarf that Ino had given him and threw it back into the salty river, where Ino received it in her hands from the wave that carried it to her. Then he left the river, lay down among the rushes, and kissed the life-giving earth.

"Oh no," he cried to himself in dismay, "what will become of me, and how will this all end? If I stay here by the riverbank through the long hours of the night, I'm so exhausted that the bitter cold and dampness might kill me—for toward sunrise there will be a sharp wind blowing off the river. But if I climb the hillside, find shelter in the woods, and sleep in some thicket, I might escape the cold and get a good night's rest. But some wild beast might take advantage of me and devour me."

In the end, he decided it would be best to go to the woods, and he found some on high ground not far from the water. There he crawled beneath two olive shoots that grew from a single trunk—one wild and ungrafted, the other carefully cultivated. No wind, however strong, could break through the cover they provided. The sun's rays couldn't pierce them, nor could rain get through, so closely did they grow together. Odysseus crept under these and began to make himself a bed to lie on, for there was a thick layer of dead leaves lying about—enough to keep two or three men warm even in the hardest winter weather. He was glad to see this, so he lay down and heaped the leaves all around him. Then, just as someone who lives alone in the countryside, far from any neighbor, buries a glowing coal in ashes to preserve the fire and avoid having to get light from somewhere else, so Odysseus covered himself with leaves. And Athena poured sweet sleep upon his eyes, closed his eyelids, and made him forget all his sorrows.

chapters.title: Book VI — The meeting between nausicaa and ulysses.
paragraphs: While Ulysses slept deeply on the beach, exhausted from his journey, the goddess Minerva traveled to the land of the Phaeacians. These seafaring people once lived near the dangerous one-eyed giants called Cyclopes, but their wise king moved them to a safe island called Scheria. Now King Alcinous ruled them, and Minerva had a plan to help Ulysses get home.

Minerva slipped into the beautiful palace and found Princess Nausicaa sleeping in her fancy bedroom. Two pretty servant girls slept by her door. The clever goddess disguised herself as one of Nausicaa's best friends and floated over the princess like a gentle breeze. Then she spoke to the sleeping girl.

"Nausicaa, how can you be so lazy?" the disguised goddess whispered. "Your clothes are scattered everywhere! You'll be getting married soon, and you need to look your best. All the handsome young men want to marry you. Let's do the washing tomorrow at dawn. I'll help you get everything clean and ready. Ask your father for a wagon and mules to carry the heavy clothes down to the washing pools by the sea."

After giving these instructions, Minerva flew back to Mount Olympus, the magical mountain where the gods live forever. No storms ever reach that peaceful place—just endless sunshine and perfect calm. The blessed gods never worry about wind or rain there.

When morning came, Nausicaa woke up wondering about her strange dream. She hurried to find her parents in their room. Her mother sat by the fire, spinning beautiful purple thread with her maids around her. She caught her father just as he was leaving for an important meeting with the town leaders.

"Papa dear," she said sweetly, "could I please borrow a big wagon today? I want to take all our dirty clothes to the river for washing. You're the most important man in town, so you should have clean shirts for your meetings. And my five brothers need fresh clothes too—especially the unmarried ones who like to look good when they go dancing!"

She didn't mention anything about her own wedding plans, feeling too shy. But her father understood and smiled. "Of course, my dear! You can have the mules and whatever else you need. The servants will prepare a strong wagon with plenty of room for all the clothes."

The king called his servants, who quickly prepared the wagon and harnessed the mules. Nausicaa gathered armfuls of dirty clothes from the storage room. Her mother packed a basket full of delicious food and a leather bottle of wine. She also gave her daughter a golden jar of olive oil for washing. Then Nausicaa climbed into the wagon, took the reins, and urged the mules forward with her servant girls following behind.

They traveled to the washing pools by the seashore, where fresh spring water bubbled up constantly—perfect for cleaning even the dirtiest clothes. The girls unhitched the mules and let them graze on the sweet grass nearby. Then they pulled the clothes from the wagon and began the hard work of washing, trampling the fabric in the stone pools to get all the dirt out. After everything was clean, they spread the wet clothes on the rocky beach to dry in the sun. Then they bathed themselves, rubbed olive oil on their skin, and enjoyed their lunch by the stream. When the clothes were nearly dry, they removed their head scarves and started playing catch with a ball. Nausicaa sang beautifully while they played, standing out among her servants like the moon goddess Diana among her woodland companions.

As they prepared to fold the dry clothes and load the wagon, Minerva decided it was time for Ulysses to wake up and meet the princess. She caused Nausicaa to throw the ball too hard—it missed her target and splashed into deep water. All the girls shrieked with laughter, and their loud voices woke Ulysses from his deep sleep.

"Oh no," Ulysses said to himself, sitting up in his leafy bed. "What kind of people live here? Are they cruel savages who might hurt me, or kind folks who welcome strangers? Those sound like young women's voices—maybe they're nymphs, those magical spirits who live in forests and rivers. Well, I need to find out. Let me try to get a look at them."

Ulysses crawled out from under his bush and broke off a leafy branch to cover himself, since he had no clothes. He looked like a fierce, hungry lion prowling for food—wild, powerful, and desperate. When the servant girls saw this rough, salt-stained stranger emerging from the bushes, they screamed and ran away. But Princess Nausicaa stood her ground, because Minerva filled her heart with courage. Ulysses wondered whether he should rush up and beg for help by grasping her knees (as was the custom), or speak to her politely from a distance so she wouldn't be frightened. He decided to stay back and use gentle words.

"Oh princess," he said in his most respectful voice, "please help me! Are you a goddess or a mortal woman? If you're a goddess, you must be Diana, daughter of great Jupiter, because you're so beautiful. If you're human, then your parents and brothers are the luckiest people alive to have such a lovely daughter and sister. And the man who marries you will be the happiest of all! I once saw a young palm tree growing by Apollo's temple on the island of Delos that was so magnificent it took my breath away—just like you do now. I don't dare come closer, but I desperately need help. For twenty days I've been tossed about on the stormy sea, and the waves finally threw me onto your shore. I fear the gods still have more troubles planned for me."

"Please take pity on me, your majesty! You're the first person I've met here, and I know no one else. Show me the way to your town and give me something to cover myself with. May the gods bless you with everything your heart desires—a loving husband, a happy home, and perfect harmony in your marriage. Nothing is more wonderful than when husband and wife live together in complete agreement, bringing joy to their friends and frustration to their enemies."

Princess Nausicaa replied thoughtfully, "Stranger, you seem like an intelligent and decent person. The gods give good fortune and bad luck as they choose, so you must accept whatever Jupiter sends you and make the best of it. Since you've come to our country, you won't lack for clothes or anything else a lost traveler needs. I'll show you to our town and tell you about us. We're called Phaeacians, and my father Alcinous is our king."

Then she called to her frightened maids: "Come back here, girls! Why are you running from this poor man? Do you think he's a dangerous robber or murderer? No enemy can harm us Phaeacians, because we're protected by the gods and live on this remote island, far from other peoples. This is just some unfortunate man who's lost his way. We must be kind to him, because Jupiter watches over all strangers and foreigners in need. So give this poor fellow some food and drink, and let him wash himself in the stream at a spot sheltered from the wind."

The servant girls stopped running and came back, calling to each other nervously. They set up a sheltered spot for Ulysses as Nausicaa had ordered, bringing him a clean shirt and cloak. They also gave him the little golden jar of oil and told him to bathe in the stream. But Ulysses said politely, "Young ladies, please stand aside while I wash the salt from my body and rub oil on my skin—it's been so long since I've been able to clean myself properly. I can't bathe while you're all watching. I'd be too embarrassed to undress in front of you."

So the girls moved away and told their mistress what was happening. Meanwhile, Ulysses washed himself thoroughly in the fresh stream, scrubbing away all the dried salt and seaweed. After rubbing oil into his skin, he put on the clean clothes the princess had given him. Then Minerva worked her magic—she made him look taller, stronger, and more handsome than before. His hair grew thick and curly like flower petals, and he seemed to glow with divine beauty, like a masterpiece crafted by the finest artist. When he finished and sat down on the beach, he looked young and godlike. The princess stared at him in amazement.

"Listen, girls," Nausicaa whispered to her maids, "I think the gods who live in heaven have sent this man to us Phaeacians. At first he looked rough and plain, but now he's as handsome as a god! I wish my future husband could be just like him—if only he would stay here instead of wanting to leave. But give him food and drink right away."

The servant girls obeyed and brought Ulysses a meal. He ate and drank hungrily—he hadn't tasted food in days! While he ate, Nausicaa folded the clean laundry and loaded it into the wagon. She hitched up the mules and called to the stranger.

"Get up, stranger, and let's head back to town. I'll take you to my father's palace, where you'll meet all the important Phaeacian leaders. But listen carefully and do exactly as I say, since you seem like a wise person. While we're passing through the countryside, walk quickly behind our wagon with my maids, and I'll lead the way. But when we reach the city walls—which are very high and strong, with harbors on both sides—we'll have to be more careful. You'll see the marketplace with Neptune's temple in the center, all paved with huge stones. The Phaeacians sell ship supplies there—ropes, sails, and oars. We're not a nation of warriors with bows and arrows, but sailors who love our ships and take pride in crossing the wide seas.

"I'm worried about what people might say if they see us together. The folks here love to gossip, and some nasty person might say, 'Who's that handsome stranger with Princess Nausicaa? Where did she find him? I bet she plans to marry him! Maybe he's some homeless sailor from a foreign ship, or perhaps a god came down from heaven to answer her prayers.' It would be terrible if people thought I was running around with strange men while my parents are still alive and before I'm properly married.

"So if you want my father to help you get home, do this: You'll see a beautiful grove of poplar trees dedicated to the goddess Minerva, with a spring and meadow around it. My father owns a garden nearby, about as far from town as you can shout. Wait there until we've had time to reach the palace. Then come into the city and ask anyone for directions to King Alcinous's house—even a child can point it out, because no other house is nearly so grand. Go through the gates and courtyards straight to my mother. You'll find her sitting by the fire, spinning purple wool by the firelight—a beautiful sight as she leans against a pillar with all her maids behind her. My father's throne sits nearby, where he drinks wine like an immortal god. Ignore him and go straight to my mother. Clasp her knees and beg for her help (this was the proper way to ask for protection in ancient times). If you win her over, she'll make sure you get home safely, no matter how far away your country is."

With these words, Nausicaa cracked her whip and the mules began their steady trot homeward, their hooves clattering on the stone road. She was careful not to go too fast, so Ulysses and the walking maids could keep up with the wagon. As the sun began to set, they reached Minerva's sacred grove, where Ulysses sat down and prayed to the mighty goddess.

"Hear me, great daughter of Jupiter!" he cried. "You didn't help me when Neptune was trying to drown me, but please listen now! Grant that I may find friends among these Phaeacians and receive the hospitality I desperately need."

Minerva heard his prayer and wanted to help him, but she didn't appear to him directly. She was still being careful around her uncle Neptune, who remained furiously determined to keep Ulysses from reaching home.

chapters.title: Book VII — Reception of ulysses at the palace of king alcinous.
paragraphs: Odysseus waited and prayed while the princess drove her wagon to town. When she reached her father's house, she stopped at the gate. Her handsome brothers gathered around her, unhitched the mules from the wagon, and carried the clean clothes inside. Meanwhile, she went to her room, where an old servant named Eurymedusa lit a fire for her. This elderly woman had been brought from across the sea and given to King Alcinous as a gift because he ruled the Phaeacians so well that his people obeyed him like a god. She had been Nausicaa's nurse and now brought her dinner to her room.

Soon Odysseus got up to head toward the city. Athena, the goddess of wisdom, wrapped a thick mist around him to hide him from any proud Phaeacians who might be rude or ask too many questions. As he entered the town, she appeared before him disguised as a young girl carrying a water jug. She stood right in his path, and Odysseus spoke to her.
"My dear child, would you kindly show me the way to King Alcinous's house? I'm a stranger from far away, in great trouble, and I don't know anyone in your town."

Athena replied, "Of course, kind sir! I'll show you the house you seek—King Alcinous lives very close to my own father's home. I'll lead the way, but don't speak to anyone as we walk, and don't stare or ask questions. The people here don't like strangers and aren't friendly to visitors from other lands. They're seafaring people who sail the oceans with ships blessed by Poseidon, god of the sea. Their vessels glide as swift as thought itself, like birds flying through the air."

She led the way, and Odysseus followed closely behind. Not one of the Phaeacians could see him as he walked through their city, because the great goddess Athena had hidden him in a magical cloud. He marveled at their harbors full of ships, their meeting places, and the city's high walls topped with wooden spikes. When they reached the king's palace, Athena said to him:

"Here's the house you wanted me to show you, good stranger. You'll find many important people dining inside, but don't be afraid—walk straight in boldly. The braver you are, the better your chances of success, even as a stranger. Look for the queen first. Her name is Arete, and she comes from the same royal family as her husband Alcinous. They both descend from Poseidon, god of the sea, who had a son named Nausithous with a beautiful woman called Periboea. She was the youngest daughter of Eurymedon, who once ruled over the giants, but he destroyed his people and himself through his foolish actions."

"Poseidon had a son with Periboea—the great Nausithous, who became king of the Phaeacians. Nausithous had two sons, Rhexenor and Alcinous. Apollo, god of light and music, killed Rhexenor while he was still a young bridegroom before he could have sons. But Rhexenor left behind a daughter named Arete, whom Alcinous married. He honors her more than any other woman honors her husband in the world."

"She is respected beyond measure by her children, by Alcinous himself, and by all the people, who treat her almost like a goddess. They greet her with reverence whenever she walks through the city, for she is wise and good-hearted. When women come to her for help, she also helps their husbands settle their disagreements. If you can win her favor, you'll have every hope of seeing your friends again and returning safely to your homeland."

Then Athena left the island of Scheria and flew away over the sea. She traveled to Marathon and the wide streets of Athens, where she entered her temple. But Odysseus continued toward Alcinous's house, stopping in wonder before the bronze threshold. The palace blazed with splendor like the sun or moon! Bronze walls stretched from end to end, topped with a blue enamel border. Golden doors hung on silver pillars rising from a bronze floor, with a silver doorframe and a golden door handle.

On either side of the entrance stood golden and silver watchdogs that Hephaestus, the god of metalworking, had crafted with his amazing skill to guard King Alcinous's palace forever. These magical dogs would never age or die. Along the walls stood seats covered with beautiful cloth woven by the women of the house. Here the Phaeacian nobles sat to eat and drink—there was always plenty of food. Golden statues of young men holding blazing torches stood on pedestals to light the hall at night. Fifty servant women worked in the house—some grinding golden grain at mills, others weaving at looms or spinning thread. Their shuttles moved back and forth like fluttering leaves, and they wove linen so fine it would shed water like oil. Just as the Phaeacians were the world's best sailors, their women were the finest weavers, taught by Athena herself.

Outside the courtyard lay a magnificent garden covering four acres, surrounded by a wall. It bloomed with beautiful trees—pears, pomegranates, and the most delicious apples. There were sweet figs and olive trees heavy with fruit. The fruit never rotted or failed, growing year-round in the mild climate. New crops ripened as old ones were picked—pear after pear, apple after apple, fig after fig. The vineyard was equally amazing: in one section, grapes dried into raisins; in another, workers gathered fresh grapes; some were being pressed in wine vats while others were just beginning to ripen. At the far end grew flower beds that bloomed all year long. Two streams flowed through the garden—one watering the plants through channels, the other flowing underground to the palace and the town's well. These were the wonderful gifts the gods had given to King Alcinous's house.

Odysseus stood there gazing at these marvels, but when he had seen enough, he crossed the threshold and entered the palace. Inside he found all the Phaeacian nobles making their final offerings to Hermes, messenger of the gods—something they always did before going to bed each night. Still hidden by Athena's magic darkness, he walked straight through the great hall until he reached Queen Arete and King Alcinous. Then he grasped the queen's knees in the traditional gesture of a desperate person asking for help. At that moment, the miraculous darkness fell away and he became visible to all. Everyone gasped in amazement at seeing this stranger appear from nowhere, but Odysseus immediately began his plea.

"Queen Arete, daughter of great Rhexenor, I come to you in my despair, humbly begging you, your husband, and all these guests—may the gods bless them with long, happy lives and let them pass their wealth to their children along with the honors they've earned—please help me return to my own country as quickly as possible. I have been far from my friends and in terrible trouble for so long."

Then he sat down among the ashes by the hearth, and everyone fell silent. Finally an old hero named Echeneus, who was known for his wisdom and fine speaking among the Phaeacians, addressed them honestly:

"Alcinous," he said, "it's not right for a stranger to sit among the ashes at your hearth while we all wait to hear what you'll say. Tell him to get up and take a proper seat on a silver-studded stool. Have your servants mix wine and water so we can make an offering to Zeus, lord of thunder, who protects all humble visitors. And let the housekeeper give him dinner from whatever food we have."

When Alcinous heard this, he took Odysseus by the hand and helped him up from the hearth. He gave him the seat of his favorite son, Laodamas, who had been sitting beside him. A servant brought beautiful golden pitcher and poured water into a silver basin for Odysseus to wash his hands. She set a clean table beside him, and the head servant brought bread and offered him the best food in the house. Odysseus ate and drank gratefully. Then Alcinous called to a servant, "Pontonous, mix wine and water and serve everyone, so we can make drink-offerings to Zeus the thunderer, who protects all respectful visitors."
Pontonous mixed the wine and water, giving each person their portion for the offering. After they had poured out their offerings and drunk as much as they wanted, Alcinous spoke:

"Leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, listen to me. You've had your dinner, so now go home to bed. Tomorrow morning I'll invite even more nobles and hold a great feast in our guest's honor. Then we can discuss his journey home and figure out how to send him back to his own country quickly and safely, no matter how far away it might be. We must make sure no harm comes to him on his voyage, but once he reaches home, he'll have to face whatever fate the gods planned for him from birth, like everyone else. However, it's possible that this stranger is one of the immortal gods who has come down from heaven to visit us. If so, the gods are acting differently than usual, because they've always appeared openly to us when we sacrifice to them. They come and feast with us just like ordinary people, and if any lone traveler happens to meet one of them, they don't hide their identity—after all, we're closely related to the gods, just like the Cyclopes and the savage giants are."

Odysseus replied: "Please, Alcinous, don't think such a thing about me. I'm nothing like the immortal gods, neither in body nor mind. In fact, I'm more like the most unfortunate people among you. If I told you everything that heaven has made me suffer, you'd say I'm even worse off than they are. But let me eat despite my sorrow, because an empty stomach is a demanding thing that forces itself on a person's attention no matter how terrible their troubles are. I'm in great distress, yet my stomach insists that I eat and drink, making me forget my sorrows and think only of filling it up. As for you, please do as you suggest and at dawn help me get home. I'd be content to die if I could just see my property, my servants, and my great house one more time."

Everyone approved of his words and agreed he should have safe passage home since he had spoken so reasonably. After making their final drink offerings and drinking their fill, they all went home to their own houses. This left Odysseus in the courtyard with Arete and Alcinous while the servants cleared away the dinner things. Queen Arete spoke first, because she recognized the shirt, cloak, and fine clothes that Odysseus wore as the work of herself and her maids. She said, "Stranger, before we go any further, I want to ask you something. Who are you and where do you come from? Who gave you those clothes? Didn't you say you came here from across the sea?"

Odysseus answered, "It would take a very long time, Your Majesty, to tell you the full story of my misfortunes, because the gods have made me suffer greatly. But to answer your question—far away in the sea lies an island called Ogygia. There lives the clever and powerful goddess Calypso, daughter of Atlas the Titan. She lives all alone, far from any neighbors, human or divine. But fate brought me to her shores, desolate and alone, when Zeus struck my ship with his thunderbolts and smashed it in the middle of the ocean. All my brave companions drowned, but I clung to the broken keel and drifted for nine days. On the tenth night, during the darkness, the gods brought me to Ogygia, where great Calypso lives. She rescued me and treated me with the greatest kindness. She even wanted to make me immortal so I would never grow old, but she couldn't convince me to agree."

"I stayed with Calypso for seven long years, and the whole time I wept tears that soaked the fine clothes she gave me. But when the eighth year came, she told me to leave of her own free will—either because Zeus had commanded it, or because she had changed her mind. She sent me away from her island on a raft loaded with plenty of bread and wine. She also gave me sturdy clothes and sent a warm, fair wind. For seventeen days I sailed across the sea, and on the eighteenth day I saw the mountains of your coast—how glad I was to see them! But I still had much trouble ahead, because Poseidon wouldn't let me go any further. He raised a terrible storm against me. The waves were so enormous that my raft broke apart under the fury of the gale, and I had to swim until the wind and current brought me to your shores."

"I tried to land there, but I couldn't because it was a dangerous place where waves crashed against the rocks. So I swam on until I found a river that looked like a good landing spot—there were no rocks and it was sheltered from the wind. I crawled out of the water and collected myself. Night was falling, so I left the river and went into a thicket, where I buried myself under a pile of leaves. Then heaven blessed me with deep sleep. Sick and miserable as I was, I slept among the leaves all night and through the next day until afternoon. I woke as the sun was setting and saw your daughter's servant girls playing on the beach, with your daughter among them, looking like a goddess. I begged for her help, and she showed an excellent character—much better than you'd expect from someone so young, since young people are often thoughtless. She gave me plenty of bread and wine, had me wash in the river, and gave me these clothes you see me wearing. So there, though it pains me to do so, I've told you the complete truth."
Then Alcinous said, "Stranger, my daughter did wrong by not bringing you straight to our house with the maids, since you asked her for help first."

"Please don't scold her," Odysseus replied. "She's not to blame. She did tell me to follow along with the maids, but I was too ashamed and afraid. I thought you might be angry if you saw me with them. Every human being can be a little suspicious and quick to anger sometimes."

"Stranger," Alcinous replied, "I'm not the kind of person who gets angry over nothing—it's always better to be reasonable. But I swear by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, seeing what kind of person you are and how similarly we think, I wish you would stay here, marry my daughter, and become my son-in-law! If you stayed, I'd give you a house and property. But no one could ever keep you here against your will—may the gods forbid such a thing! And to prove this to you, I'll arrange your escort tomorrow. You can sleep during the entire voyage if you want, while my men sail you over calm seas to your own home, or wherever you wish to go, even if it's much farther than Euboea. My people who have been there say it's the most distant place they know—they went there when they took golden-haired Rhadamanthus to visit Tityus, son of Earth. Yet they completed the whole voyage in a single day without getting tired and returned home afterward. You'll see for yourself how much my ships surpass all others, and what magnificent rowers my sailors are."
Odysseus was overjoyed and prayed aloud: "Father Zeus, grant that Alcinous may do everything he has promised! Then his name will live forever among all people, and I will return to my country."

While they talked, Queen Arete told her maids to set up a bed in the entrance hall and make it with fine red blankets, spreading coverlets on top with woolen cloaks for Odysseus to wear. The maids went out carrying torches, and when they had prepared the bed, they returned to Odysseus and said, "Rise, sir stranger, and come with us—your bed is ready." He was very glad indeed to go to his rest.
So Odysseus slept in a bed placed in a room above the echoing gateway, while Alcinous lay in the inner part of the house with the queen his wife beside him.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Banquet in the house of alcinous—the games.
paragraphs: When the rosy-fingered Dawn appeared in the morning sky, King Alcinous and Ulysses both woke up. Alcinous led the way to the Phaeacian meeting place, which was built near their ships by the harbor. They sat down together on seats made of smooth, polished stone. Meanwhile, Minerva (the goddess of wisdom) disguised herself as one of the king's servants and walked through the town to help Ulysses get home. She went to each citizen and said, "Town leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, come to the assembly! Listen to this stranger who just arrived after a long sea voyage to King Alcinous's house. He looks as magnificent as an immortal god!"

With these words, she made everyone eager to come see Ulysses. They flocked to the assembly until every seat was taken and people were standing wherever they could find room. Everyone stared in amazement at Ulysses, because Minerva had made him look more handsome and impressive—taller and stronger than he really was. She wanted the Phaeacians to think well of him and to do well in any contests they might challenge him to try. When everyone had gathered together, King Alcinous stood up to speak.

"Listen to me," he said, "town leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians. This stranger, whoever he may be, has somehow found his way to my house from either the East or West. He needs safe passage home and wants us to help him. Let's prepare a ship for him, just as we've done for others before. No one who has ever come to my house has been able to complain that I didn't help them get home quickly enough. Let's launch a ship that has never sailed before and crew it with fifty-two of our best young sailors. After you've fastened your oars properly to the ship, come to my house for a feast. I'll provide everything we need. These are my orders for the young men who will be the crew. As for you councilors, you'll join me in entertaining our guest in the palace courtyards. I won't accept any excuses, and we'll have Demodocus sing for us—there's no bard like him, no matter what he chooses to sing about."

King Alcinous then led the way, with everyone following behind him, while a servant went to fetch Demodocus the bard. The fifty-two chosen oarsmen went down to the seashore as they'd been told. When they got there, they dragged the ship into the water, put the mast and sails inside, tied the oars to the rowing pins with twisted leather straps (just as it should be done), and raised the white sails. They anchored the ship a little way from shore, then came back to land and went to King Alcinous's house. The courtyards, gardens, and all the surrounding areas were packed with crowds of people, both young and old. For the feast, Alcinous had twelve sheep, eight full-grown pigs, and two oxen killed and prepared, creating a magnificent banquet.

A servant then brought in the famous bard Demodocus, whom the Muse (the goddess of music and poetry) had dearly loved. But she had given him both a gift and a curse—though she blessed him with the divine ability to sing beautifully, she had taken away his eyesight. Pontonous set up a chair for him among the guests, leaning it against a pillar. He hung Demodocus's lyre on a peg above his head and showed him how to reach for it with his hands. He also placed a table with food beside him and a cup of wine he could drink from whenever he wanted.

Everyone then began eating the delicious food in front of them. But as soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, the Muse inspired Demodocus to sing about the great deeds of heroes. He chose to sing about something that was famous everywhere at the time—the quarrel between Ulysses and Achilles, and the angry words they threw at each other during a feast. But King Agamemnon was actually glad to hear about his two greatest warriors arguing, because Apollo (the god of prophecy) had told him at his oracle at Pytho that this would happen. This was the beginning of all the trouble that Jupiter (the king of the gods) would bring upon both the Greeks and Trojans in the great war.

The bard sang this tale, but Ulysses pulled his purple cloak over his head and covered his face because he was ashamed to let the Phaeacians see him crying. When the bard finished singing, Ulysses wiped away his tears, uncovered his face, and lifted his cup to make an offering to the gods. But when the Phaeacians asked Demodocus to sing more (because they loved his songs), Ulysses again pulled his cloak over his head and wept bitterly. No one noticed how upset he was except King Alcinous, who was sitting close to him and could hear the heavy sighs he was making. So the king immediately said, "Town leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, we've had enough feasting and music for now. Let's move on to athletic contests, so our guest can tell his friends back home how much we excel all other nations in boxing, wrestling, jumping, and running."

With these words, he led the way out, and everyone followed. A servant hung Demodocus's lyre on its peg, helped him out of the courtyard, and guided him along the same path the Phaeacian nobles were taking to watch the games. A crowd of several thousand people followed them, and there were many excellent competitors ready to try for all the prizes. The athletes included Acroneos, Ocyalus, Elatreus, Nauteus, Prymneus, Anchialus, Eretmeus, Ponteus, Proreus, Thoon, Anabesineus, and Amphialus (son of Polyneus, son of Tecton). There was also Euryalus, son of Naubolus, who looked like Mars himself and was the most handsome man among the Phaeacians except for Laodamas. Three of King Alcinous's own sons also competed: Laodamas, Halios, and Clytoneus.
