The foot races came first. They marked out the course from the starting line, and all the runners kicked up a cloud of dust as they shot forward at the same moment. Clytoneus won by a huge margin—he left everyone else behind by the length of furrow that two mules could plow in an empty field. Next came wrestling, where Euryalus proved to be the best. Amphialus beat everyone at jumping, while no one could come close to Elatreus in throwing the discus (a heavy stone disk used in athletic contests). King Alcinous's son Laodamas was the best boxer. After everyone had enjoyed watching the games, Laodamas said, "Let's ask our stranger if he's good at any of these sports. He looks incredibly strong—his thighs, calves, hands, and neck show tremendous power. He's not old either, but he's clearly suffered a lot lately. Nothing wears a man down like the sea, no matter how strong he is."
"You're absolutely right, Laodamas," replied Euryalus. "Go talk to him about it yourself."

When Laodamas heard this, he walked into the middle of the crowd and said to Ulysses, "Sir, I hope you'll enter one of our competitions if you're skilled at any of them. You must have competed in many contests before. Nothing brings a man more honor throughout his life than showing he's skilled with his hands and feet. Why don't you try something and forget your worries? Your journey home won't be delayed much longer—the ship is already in the water and the crew is ready."

Ulysses answered, "Laodamas, why do you mock me this way? My mind is focused on my troubles, not contests. I've been through endless hardship and have come to you as someone begging for help, asking your king and people to help me get home."

Then Euryalus insulted him openly and said, "I can tell you're not skilled at any of the sports that men usually enjoy. I suppose you're one of those greedy traders who sail around as ship captains or merchants, thinking only about their cargo and profits. You don't look like much of an athlete to me."

"Shame on you!" Ulysses replied angrily. "You're a rude fellow! It's true that the gods don't bless all men equally with good looks, speaking ability, and intelligence. One man might not look impressive, but heaven has given him such excellent conversation skills that he charms everyone who meets him. His smooth words win people over so completely that he becomes a leader among his peers, and wherever he goes, people look up to him. Another man might be as handsome as a god, but his good looks aren't matched by good sense. That's your case. No god could make anyone better-looking than you, but you're a fool. Your thoughtless remarks have made me extremely angry, and you're completely wrong about me. I excel at many athletic activities! When I was young and strong, I was among the best athletes of my time. Now I'm worn out by hard work and sorrow—I've endured much both in battle and on the dangerous seas. Still, despite all this, I'll compete, because your taunts have stung me deeply."

Without even taking off his cloak, he hurried forward and grabbed a discus that was larger, heavier, and more massive than the ones the Phaeacians used in their own competitions. Swinging it back, he hurled it with his powerful arm, and it made a humming sound as it flew through the air. The Phaeacians ducked as it whooshed overhead, flying gracefully from his hand and landing far beyond any mark that had been made yet. Minerva, disguised as a man, came and marked where it had landed. "Even a blind man could find your mark by feeling around for it, sir," she said. "It's so far ahead of all the others! You can stop worrying about this contest—no Phaeacian can come close to a throw like yours."

Ulysses was happy to find he had a friend among the spectators, so he began speaking more cheerfully. "Young men," he said, "try to match that throw if you can, and I'll throw another discus just as heavy or even heavier! If anyone wants to compete with me, let him come forward—I'm extremely angry now, and I'll box, wrestle, or run with any of you, except for Laodamas. I won't compete with him because I'm his guest, and it's not right to challenge your host's family to contests, especially in a foreign country. That would be cutting off the branch you're sitting on! But I'll make no exceptions for anyone else, because I want to settle this matter and prove who's the best. I'm excellent at every kind of athletic sport known to mankind. I'm a superb archer—in battle, I'm always the first to bring down an enemy with my arrow, no matter how many others are aiming at the same target. Only Philoctetes could shoot better than me when we Greeks were fighting at Troy. I'm far better than everyone else alive today who still eats bread on this earth, though I wouldn't want to compete against the mighty dead heroes like Hercules or Eurytus the Oechalian—men who could even challenge the gods themselves with their bows. That's actually how Eurytus died too early—Apollo got angry with him and killed him for challenging the god to an archery contest. I can throw a spear farther than anyone else can shoot an arrow. Running is the only thing I'm worried about—some of you Phaeacians might beat me there, because the sea has worn me down terribly. My food ran out, so I'm still weak."

Everyone stayed quiet except King Alcinous, who said, "Sir, we've enjoyed hearing everything you've told us. I understand that you want to show your abilities because you were offended by some rude remarks from one of our athletes—words that should never have been spoken by anyone who knows how to speak properly. I hope you understand what I mean, and I want you to be able to explain to your family and friends back home that we Phaeacians have natural talent for all kinds of skills. We're not particularly famous for boxing or wrestling, but we're incredibly fast runners and excellent sailors. We especially love good food, music, and dancing. We also enjoy having plenty of clean clothes, warm baths, and comfortable beds. So now, please, let our best dancers perform, so our guest can tell his friends back home how much we surpass all other nations as sailors, runners, dancers, and musicians. Someone run and get Demodocus's lyre from my house."

A servant hurried off to bring the lyre from the king's house, while nine men who had been chosen as event organizers stepped forward. Their job was to manage everything connected with the sports, so they smoothed the ground and marked out a wide space for the dancers. Soon the servant returned with Demodocus's lyre. The bard took his place in the center, and the best young dancers in town began to dance so skillfully that Ulysses was delighted watching their feet move so nimbly.

Meanwhile, the bard began singing about the love affair between Mars (the god of war) and Venus (the goddess of love), and how they first began their secret romance in the house of Vulcan (the god of fire and metalworking, who was Venus's husband). Mars gave Venus many gifts and dishonored King Vulcan's marriage bed. The Sun, who sees everything, told Vulcan what they were doing. Vulcan became furious when he heard this terrible news, so he went to his workshop planning revenge. He set up his great anvil and began forging chains that no one could break or untie, so the lovers would be trapped there. When he finished making his trap, he went to his bedroom and draped chains all over the bed posts like spider webs. He also hung many chains from the ceiling beam. Not even a god could see them, they were so fine and delicate. After spreading the chains all over the bed, he pretended to leave for the island of Lemnos, which was his favorite place in the world. But Mars was keeping a sharp lookout, and as soon as he saw Vulcan leave, he hurried to the house, burning with love for Venus.

Venus had just returned from visiting her father Jupiter and was about to sit down when Mars came into the house. Taking her hand in his, he said, "Let's go to Vulcan's bed. He's not home—he's gone to Lemnos to visit the Sintians, whose language is strange and foreign."

She was more than willing, so they went to the bed to rest together. But they were immediately caught in the clever trap that Vulcan had set for them and couldn't get up or move their hands or feet. Too late, they realized they were trapped! Then Vulcan returned—he had turned back before reaching Lemnos when his scout the Sun told him what was happening. He was absolutely furious and stood in the entrance making a terrible noise as he shouted to all the gods.

"Father Jupiter," he cried, "and all you other blessed gods who live forever, come here and see this ridiculous and shameful sight I'll show you! Jupiter's daughter Venus is always dishonoring me because I'm lame. She's in love with Mars, who's handsome and well-built, while I'm a cripple—but my parents are to blame for that, not me! They never should have had me. Come and see the pair of them sleeping together on my bed! It makes me furious to look at them. They're very fond of each other, but I don't think they'll want to lie there much longer, and I don't think they'll be getting much sleep! There they'll stay until her father pays me back the bride-price I gave him for his worthless daughter, who may be beautiful but certainly isn't faithful."

At this, the gods gathered at Vulcan's house. Earth-shaking Neptune came, and Mercury the messenger god, and King Apollo. But the goddesses all stayed home out of embarrassment. The gods who give all good things stood in the doorway, and they burst into uncontrollable laughter when they saw how cleverly Vulcan had caught the lovers. One would turn to his neighbor saying:

"Evil deeds don't pay, and sometimes the weak can outsmart the strong. Look how limping Vulcan, lame as he is, has caught Mars, who's the fastest god in heaven! Now Mars will have to pay heavy damages."
That's how they talked, but King Apollo said to Mercury, "Messenger Mercury, bringer of good things, you wouldn't care how strong those chains were if you could sleep with Venus, would you?"

"King Apollo," Mercury answered, "I only wish I could get the chance, even if there were three times as many chains—and all of you gods and goddesses could watch, but I'd still sleep with her if I could!"

The immortal gods burst out laughing when they heard him, but Neptune took it all seriously and kept begging Vulcan to free Mars. "Let him go," he cried, "and I promise you, as you require, that he'll pay you all the damages that are considered fair among the immortal gods."
"Don't ask me to do this," Vulcan replied. "A bad man's promise is worthless security. What could I do to you if Mars ran away and left his debts behind along with his chains?"
"Vulcan," said Neptune, "if Mars leaves without paying his damages, I'll pay you myself." So Vulcan answered, "In that case, I cannot and must not refuse you."

Then he released the bonds that held them. As soon as they were free, they ran off—Mars to Thrace and laughter-loving Venus to Cyprus and to Paphos, where her sacred grove and altar fragrant with offerings were located. There the Graces (goddesses of beauty and charm) bathed her and rubbed her with ambrosial oil that the immortal gods use, and they dressed her in the most enchantingly beautiful clothes.
The bard sang this tale, and both Ulysses and the seafaring Phaeacians were charmed as they listened.

Then King Alcinous told his sons Laodamas and Halius to dance by themselves, since no one could compete with them. They took a red ball that Polybus had made for them. One brother bent backward and threw it high up toward the clouds, while the other jumped from the ground and caught it easily before it came back down. After throwing the ball straight up into the air, they began to dance while continuing to throw it back and forth to each other. All the young men in the circle applauded and stamped their feet loudly. Then Ulysses said:
"King Alcinous, you said your people were the nimblest dancers in the world, and they've certainly proved it! I was amazed watching them."

The king was delighted and called out to the Phaeacians, "Town leaders and councilors! Our guest seems to be a person of excellent judgment. Let's give him the kind of hospitality he deserves. There are twelve chief men among you, and counting myself, thirteen. Each of you contribute a clean cloak, a shirt, and a talent of fine gold (a talent was a large amount of money). Let's give him all of this right now, so when he eats dinner, he can do so with a happy heart. As for Euryalus, he'll need to make a formal apology and give a gift too, since he was rude."

Everyone applauded the king's words and sent their servants to fetch the presents. Then Euryalus said, "King Alcinous, I'll give the stranger all the satisfaction you require. He shall have my sword, which is made of bronze except for the silver hilt. I'll also give him the scabbard of freshly carved ivory that it fits into. It will be worth a great deal to him."

As he spoke, he placed the sword in Ulysses' hands and said, "Good luck to you, father stranger! If anything rude has been said, may the winds blow it away, and may heaven grant you a safe return home. I understand you've been away from home for a long time and have suffered much hardship."
Ulysses answered, "Good luck to you too, my friend, and may the gods grant you every happiness. I hope you won't miss the sword you've given me along with your apology."

With these words, he strapped the sword around his shoulders. As the sun began to set, the presents started arriving as servants brought them to King Alcinous's house. The king's sons received them and placed them in their mother's care. Then Alcinous led everyone to the house and had his guests take their seats.

"Wife," he said, turning to Queen Arete, "go get our best chest and put a clean cloak and shirt in it. Also, put a copper pot on the fire and heat some water—our guest will have a warm bath. See that the presents the noble Phaeacians have given him are packed carefully. This way he'll better enjoy both his dinner and the singing that will follow. I'll give him this golden goblet myself—it's beautifully crafted—so he'll be reminded of me for the rest of his life whenever he makes an offering to Jupiter or any of the other gods."

Queen Arete told her maids to put a large three-legged pot on the fire as quickly as they could. They set a pot full of bath water over a bright fire, threw on sticks to make it blaze, and the water grew hot as the flames played around the bottom of the pot. Meanwhile, Arete brought a magnificent chest from her own room and packed all the beautiful presents of gold and clothing that the Phaeacians had brought. Finally, she added a cloak and a fine shirt from Alcinous and said to Ulysses:
"Look after the lid yourself and tie the whole thing securely, in case anyone tries to rob you while you're sleeping on your ship."

When Ulysses heard this, he put the lid on the chest and tied it with a special knot that the sorceress Circe had taught him. He had barely finished when a servant told him to come to the bath and wash himself. He was very glad to have a warm bath, since no one had waited on him like this since he left the house of the sea-nymph Calypso, who had taken care of him as if he were a god while he stayed with her. After the servants finished washing and rubbing him with oil and gave him clean clothes, he left the bathroom and joined the guests who were sitting with their wine. Lovely Nausicaa (the princess who had found him on the beach) stood by one of the pillars supporting the courtyard roof and admired him as she saw him pass. "Farewell, stranger," she said, "don't forget me when you're safely home again, because you owe me your life for saving you first."

Ulysses replied, "Nausicaa, daughter of great Alcinous, may Jupiter, Juno's mighty husband, grant that I reach my home safely! If so, I'll bless you as my guardian angel all my days, for you were the one who saved me."

After saying this, he sat down beside King Alcinous. Dinner was then served, and wine was mixed for drinking. A servant led in the favorite bard Demodocus and seated him in the middle of the company, near one of the pillars so he could lean against it. Then Ulysses cut off a piece of roast pork with plenty of fat (there was still plenty left on the joint) and told a servant, "Take this piece of pork to Demodocus and tell him to eat it. Despite any pain his songs might cause me, I'll honor him just the same. Bards are honored and respected throughout the world because the Muse teaches them their songs and loves them."

The servant carried the pork over to Demodocus, who accepted it and was very pleased. Everyone then began eating the good food in front of them. When they had finished eating and drinking, Ulysses said to Demodocus, "Demodocus, I admire you more than anyone in the world! You must have learned from the Muse, Jupiter's daughter, and from Apollo, because you sing so accurately about the Greeks' return home with all their sufferings and adventures. If you weren't there yourself, you must have heard it all from someone who was. Now, though, change your song and tell us about the wooden horse that Epeus built with Minerva's help, and which Ulysses used his cleverness to get inside Troy's fortress after filling it with the warriors who later destroyed the city. If you sing this story well, I'll tell the whole world how magnificently heaven has gifted you."

The heaven-inspired bard picked up the story where some of the Greeks set fire to their tents and sailed away, while others hid inside the wooden horse, waiting with Ulysses in Troy's main square. The Trojans themselves had dragged the horse into their fortress, and it stood there while they held a council meeting around it. They couldn't decide what to do—some wanted to break it apart right then and there, others wanted to drag it to the top of the cliff their fortress stood on and push it over the edge, while still others thought they should leave it as an offering to please the gods. In the end, they decided to keep it, and this sealed the city's doom. Once Troy accepted that horse, with all the bravest Greeks hiding inside it ready to bring death and destruction to the Trojans, the city was finished. The bard sang how the Greeks burst out of the horse and attacked the city, spreading out everywhere and destroying it. He sang how Ulysses went rampaging through the city like the god Mars, along with Menelaus, heading for Deiphobus's house, where the fiercest fighting took place. But with Minerva's help, Ulysses was victorious.

The bard told all of this, but Ulysses was overcome with emotion as he listened, and tears ran down his cheeks. He wept like a woman who throws herself on her husband's body after he's fallen defending his city and people, fighting bravely to protect his home and children. She screams and wraps her arms around him as he gasps for breath and dies, but her enemies beat her on the back and shoulders and drag her away into slavery, to a life of hard work and sorrow, and the beauty fades from her cheeks. Just as pitifully did Ulysses weep, but none of the guests noticed his tears except King Alcinous, who was sitting near him and could hear the sobs and sighs he was making. The king immediately stood up and said:

"Town leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus stop his song, because there are people here who don't seem to enjoy it. From the moment we finished dinner and Demodocus began singing, our guest has been groaning and crying the whole time. He's obviously very upset, so let the bard stop so we can all enjoy ourselves—hosts and guest alike. This would be much better, since all these festivities, the escort home, and the presents we're giving so generously are entirely in his honor. Anyone with even basic good manners knows you should treat a guest and someone asking for help as if he were your own brother.

"Therefore, sir, don't hide anything or be secretive about what I'm going to ask you. It would be more polite to give me a straight answer. Tell me the name your father and mother called you back home, and what your neighbors and fellow citizens knew you by. No one in the world, rich or poor, is completely without a name, because people's parents give them names as soon as they're born. Tell me also about your country, your people, and your city, so our ships can plan their route accordingly and take you there. You see, the Phaeacians don't have pilots or steering wheels like other nations' ships do. Our ships understand what we're thinking and wanting. They know all the cities and countries in the whole world and can cross the sea even when it's covered with mist and clouds, so there's no danger of being wrecked or harmed. Still, I remember my father saying that Neptune was angry with us for being too helpful in giving people rides home. He said that one day the sea god would wreck one of our ships as it returned from escorting someone, and bury our city under a high mountain. That's what my father used to say, but whether the god will carry out his threat is up to him to decide.

"Now, tell me the truth. Where have you been wandering, and what countries have you traveled through? Tell us about the peoples and their cities—who were hostile, savage, and uncivilized, and who, on the other hand, were welcoming and kind. Tell us also why hearing about the Greek warriors' return from Troy makes you so sad. The gods arranged all of this and sent them their misfortunes so that future generations would have something to sing about. Did you lose some brave relative of yours or your wife's family when you were fighting at Troy? A son-in-law or father-in-law—who are a man's closest relations outside his own blood? Or was it some brave and kind-hearted friend? A good friend is as dear to a man as his own brother."

chapters.title: Book IX — Ulysses declares himself and begins his story—-the cicons, lotophagi, and cyclopes.
paragraphs: Ulysses answered, "King Alcinous, it's wonderful to hear a singer with such a heavenly voice. There's nothing better than when all the people celebrate together, with guests sitting properly to listen, while tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the cup-bearer pours wine for everyone. This is truly the finest sight a person can see. But now, since you want to hear about my troubles and bring back my sad memories, I don't know how to begin or continue or end my story, because the gods have made me suffer terribly.

"First, I'll tell you my name so you'll know it, and someday, if I survive these sorrows, you might visit me even though I live far from all of you. I am Ulysses, son of Laertes, famous among all people for my cleverness, so that my reputation reaches to heaven itself. I live on Ithaca, where there's a high mountain called Neritum, covered with forests. Near it are other islands close together—Dulichium, Same, and wooded Zacynthus. My island sits low on the horizon, farthest toward the sunset, while the others lie toward the sunrise. It's a rocky island, but it raises brave men, and my eyes have never seen any land they love better. The goddess Calypso kept me prisoner in her cave and wanted to marry me, as did the cunning witch-goddess Circe. But neither could persuade me, because nothing is dearer to a person than their own country and parents. No matter how splendid a home you might have in a foreign land, if it's far from your family, you don't truly care about it. Now I'll tell you about the many dangerous adventures that Zeus sent me on my way home from Troy."

"When I sailed from Troy, the wind first carried me to Ismarus, the city of the Cicones people. There I attacked the town and killed the people with swords. We took their wives and much treasure, which we shared equally so no one could complain. I said we should leave immediately, but my men foolishly wouldn't obey me. They stayed there drinking lots of wine and killing many sheep and cattle on the shore. Meanwhile, the Cicones called for help from other Cicones who lived inland. These reinforcements were greater in number and stronger, and better at fighting—they could battle from horse-drawn chariots or on foot as needed. In the morning they came as thick as leaves in summer, and heaven was against us, so we were in serious trouble. They arranged their battle line near our ships, and both sides threw bronze-tipped spears at each other. As long as it was morning, we held our own against them, though they outnumbered us. But as the sun went down, around the time when farmers bring in their oxen, the Cicones defeated us. We lost six men from each ship, but we escaped with those who survived."

"We sailed away with heavy hearts, glad to have escaped death though we'd lost our comrades. We didn't leave until we'd called out three times to each poor fellow who had died at the hands of the Cicones. Then Zeus sent the North wind against us until it blew like a hurricane, hiding both land and sky in thick clouds, and darkness fell from the heavens. We let our ships run before the storm, but the wind's force tore our sails to pieces, so we took them down to avoid shipwreck and rowed as hard as we could toward land. There we lay for two days and nights, suffering from both exhaustion and worry. But on the morning of the third day, we raised our masts again, set sail, and took our positions, letting the wind and helmsmen guide our ship. I should have reached home safely then, but the North wind and sea currents fought against me as I was rounding Cape Malea, pushing me off course toward the island of Cythera."

"Bad winds drove me from there for nine days across the sea, but on the tenth day we reached the land of the Lotus-eaters, people who live on food that comes from a special flower. We landed here to get fresh water, and our crews ate their midday meal on the shore near the ships. After they'd eaten and drunk, I sent two of my men to see what kind of people lived there, with a third man to help them. They started out immediately and mixed with the Lotus-eaters, who didn't hurt them but gave them lotus flowers to eat. The lotus was so delicious that those who ate it stopped caring about home and didn't even want to return to tell us what had happened. They just wanted to stay and keep eating lotus with the Lotus-eaters, forgetting all about going home. Even though they cried bitterly, I forced them back to the ships and tied them down under the rowing benches. Then I told the rest of my men to board quickly, in case any of them should taste the lotus and lose their desire to get home. So they took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars."

"We sailed from there, still in great distress, until we came to the land of the lawless and savage Cyclopes. These Cyclopes don't plant crops or plow fields, but trust in the gods and live on wheat, barley, and grapes that grow wild without any farming. Their wild grapes give them wine as the sun and rain help them grow. They have no laws or town meetings, but live in caves on high mountaintops. Each one rules his own family like a king, and they don't care about their neighbors."

"Near their harbor lies a wooded and fertile island, not too close to the land of the Cyclopes but not far either. It's overrun with wild goats that breed there in great numbers and are never disturbed by humans. Hunters—who usually endure great hardships in forests or mountain cliffs—don't go there, and it's never plowed or grazed. It lies as an empty wilderness year after year, with no living creatures except goats. The Cyclopes have no ships, and no shipbuilders who could make ships for them. So they can't travel from city to city or sail across the sea to visit each other like people with ships can do. If they had ships, they would have settled this island, because it's excellent land that would produce everything in its proper season. There are meadows that reach right down to the seashore, well-watered and full of rich grass. Grapes would grow excellently there, and there's level land for plowing that would always yield heavy harvests, because the soil is deep. There's a good harbor where no ropes or anchors are needed—you just beach your ship and stay until the wind is right for sailing again. At the head of the harbor, clear water flows from a spring in a cave, and poplar trees grow all around it."

"We entered this harbor, but the night was so dark that some god must have guided us in, because we couldn't see anything. Thick mist surrounded our ships, and the moon was hidden behind clouds, so no one could have seen the island even if they'd looked for it. There were no waves breaking to warn us we were near shore before we found ourselves on land. When we'd beached our ships, we took down the sails, went ashore, and camped on the beach until dawn."

"When morning came with rosy-fingered Dawn (as the Greeks called the sunrise), we admired the island and explored it. The nymphs, who were Zeus's daughters and spirits of nature, stirred up the wild goats so we could hunt them for dinner. We fetched our spears, bows, and arrows from the ships and divided into three groups to hunt the goats. Heaven sent us excellent hunting—I had twelve ships with me, and each ship got nine goats, while my own ship got ten. So all day long until sunset we ate and drank our fill, and we still had plenty of wine left from what we'd taken when we raided the Cicones' city. While we feasted, we kept looking toward the land of the Cyclopes nearby and saw smoke from their fires. We could almost hear their voices and the bleating of their sheep and goats. When the sun set and darkness came, we camped on the beach, and the next morning I called a meeting."

"'Stay here, my brave friends,' I said, 'all of you except those who'll come with me in my ship to explore these people. I want to see if they're uncivilized savages or a friendly and civilized people.'"

"I went aboard, telling my men to do the same and untie the ropes. They took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars. When we reached the land, which wasn't far, we saw a great cave on a cliff face near the sea, overhung with laurel trees. It was clearly a shelter for many sheep and goats, and outside was a large yard surrounded by a high wall made of stones set deep in the ground, plus pine and oak trees. This was the home of a huge monster who was away tending his flocks. He had nothing to do with other people but lived like an outlaw. He was a horrible creature, not like a human being at all, but more like a rocky cliff that stands boldly against the sky on a high mountain."

"I told my men to pull the ship ashore and stay there, all except the twelve best, who would come with me. I also took a goatskin full of sweet black wine that had been given to me by Maron, son of Euanthes. Maron was a priest of Apollo (the god of music, prophecy, and the sun) who protected the city of Ismarus, and he lived within the sacred temple grounds. When we were attacking the city, we respected him and spared his life, along with his wife and child. So he gave me valuable gifts—seven talents of fine gold, a silver bowl, and twelve jars of sweet wine, unmixed with water and perfectly aged. No one in his house knew about this wine except himself, his wife, and one housekeeper. When he drank it, he mixed twenty parts water to one part wine, yet the smell from the mixing bowl was so wonderful that no one could resist drinking it. I filled a large wineskin with this wine and took a bag full of food with me, because I suspected I might have to deal with some savage of great strength who wouldn't respect what's right or lawful."

"We soon reached the cave, but the Cyclops was out shepherding, so we went inside and looked at everything we could see. His cheese racks were loaded with cheeses, and he had more lambs and young goats than his pens could hold. They were kept in separate flocks—first the year-old animals, then the older young lambs, and finally the very young ones, all kept apart from each other. As for his dairy equipment, all the bowls and milk pails he used for milking were swimming in whey (the watery part of milk). When my men saw all this, they begged me to let them steal some cheeses first and escape to the ship with them. Then they wanted to return, drive down the lambs and young goats, put them aboard, and sail away. It would have been much better if we'd done that, but I wouldn't listen to them because I wanted to see the owner himself, hoping he might give me a guest-gift. But when we saw him, my poor men found him terrible to deal with."

"We lit a fire, offered some of the cheeses as a sacrifice to the gods, ate others, and then sat waiting for the Cyclops to return with his sheep. When he came, he brought a huge load of dry firewood to light his fire for supper, and he threw it down on the cave floor with such a crash that we hid in fear at the far end of the cave. Meanwhile, he drove all the female sheep inside, along with the female goats he was going to milk, but left the males—both rams and male goats—outside in the yards. Then he rolled a huge stone to the mouth of the cave—so huge that twenty-two strong four-wheeled wagons couldn't move it from the doorway. After doing this, he sat down and milked his sheep and goats in proper order, then let each have her young one to nurse. He turned half the milk into cheese and put it aside in wicker baskets, but poured the other half into bowls to drink for his supper. When he'd finished all his work, he lit the fire and caught sight of us. Then he said:"
"'Strangers, who are you? Where do you sail from? Are you merchants, or do you roam the sea as pirates, risking your lives and bringing trouble to others?'"

"We were terrified by his loud voice and monstrous appearance, but I managed to say, 'We are Greeks on our way home from Troy, but Zeus's will and bad weather have driven us far off course. We are the people of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, who has won great fame throughout the world by conquering such a great city and killing so many people. So we humbly ask you to show us hospitality and give us the gifts that visitors can reasonably expect. Please respect the gods' anger, because we are your guests asking for help, and Zeus protects all respectable travelers—he punishes those who harm guests and foreigners in need.'"

"But he gave me a heartless answer. 'Stranger,' he said, 'you're either a fool or you know nothing about this country. Don't talk to me about fearing the gods or avoiding their anger! We Cyclopes don't care about Zeus or any of your blessed gods, because we're much stronger than they are. I won't spare you or your companions out of any respect for Zeus, unless I feel like it. Now tell me where you left your ship when you came ashore. Was it around the point, or is it lying straight offshore?'"

"He said this to trick me into revealing information, but I was too clever to be caught that way, so I answered with a lie. 'Poseidon (the sea god),' I said, 'smashed my ship against the rocks at the far end of your country and wrecked it. We were driven onto them from the open sea, but I and these men with me escaped death.'"

"The cruel monster didn't answer me with even one word. Instead, he suddenly grabbed two of my men at once and smashed them on the ground like puppies. Their brains splattered on the floor, and the earth was wet with their blood. Then he tore them apart and ate them. He devoured them like a lion in the wilderness—flesh, bones, marrow, and organs—leaving nothing uneaten. We wept and raised our hands to heaven at such a horrible sight, not knowing what else to do. After the Cyclops had filled his huge belly and washed down his meal of human flesh with plain milk, he stretched out full-length on the ground among his sheep and went to sleep. At first I wanted to draw my sword and drive it into his heart, but I realized that if I did, we'd all certainly die, because we could never move the stone he'd put in front of the door. So we stayed there sobbing and sighing until morning came."

"When morning came with rosy-fingered dawn, he lit his fire again, milked his goats and sheep properly, and let each have her young one. As soon as he'd finished all his work, he grabbed two more of my men and ate them for his morning meal. Then, with the greatest ease, he rolled the stone away from the door and drove out his sheep, but immediately put it back again—as easily as putting a lid on a quiver full of arrows. After doing this, he shouted and called 'Shoo, shoo!' to drive his sheep toward the mountain. So I was left to plan some way of getting revenge and winning glory for myself."

"Finally I decided the best plan would be this: The Cyclops had a great club lying near one of the sheep pens. It was made of green olive wood, and he'd cut it planning to use it as a walking stick once it dried. It was so huge that we could only compare it to the mast of a twenty-oared merchant ship, big enough to venture into the open sea. I went to this club and cut off about six feet of it. I gave this piece to my men and told them to smooth it evenly at one end, which they did. Then I sharpened it to a point myself, hardening the tip in the fire. When I'd finished, I hid it under the dung that was scattered all over the cave, and told the men to draw lots to see which four would help me lift it and bore it into the monster's eye while he slept. The lot fell on the very four men I would have chosen, and I made the fifth. In the evening the monster returned from shepherding and drove his flocks into the cave—this time bringing them all inside instead of leaving any in the yards. I suppose some whim struck him, or a god prompted him to do it. As soon as he'd put the stone back in place at the door, he sat down, milked his sheep and goats properly, then let each have her young one. When he'd finished all this work, he grabbed two more of my men and made his supper from them. Then I approached him with an ivy-wood bowl of black wine in my hands:"

"'Look here, Cyclops,' I said, 'you've been eating a lot of human flesh, so drink some wine and see what kind of drink we had on our ship. I was bringing it to you as an offering, hoping you'd take pity on me and help me get home. But all you do is rage and act terribly. You should be ashamed of yourself—how can you expect anyone to visit you if you treat them this way?'"

"He took the cup and drank. He was so delighted with the wine's taste that he asked me for another bowl. 'Please be so kind,' he said, 'as to give me more, and tell me your name right now. I want to give you a gift you'll be happy to have. We have wine in this country too, because our soil grows grapes and the sun ripens them, but this tastes like nectar and ambrosia combined!' (Nectar and ambrosia were the food and drink of the gods.)"

"I gave him more wine. Three times I filled the bowl for him, and three times he drained it without thinking. When I saw the wine had gone to his head, I said as smoothly as I could: 'Cyclops, you asked my name and I'll tell you. Give me the gift you promised. My name is Noman—that's what my father, mother, and friends have always called me.'"
"But the cruel monster said, 'Then I'll eat all of Noman's companions before Noman himself, and save Noman for last. That's the gift I'll give him.'"

"As he spoke, he swayed and fell sprawling face-up on the ground. His great neck fell backward heavily, and deep sleep overcame him. Soon he felt sick and vomited up both wine and chunks of human flesh he'd been gorging on, because he was very drunk. Then I thrust the wooden beam deep into the fire's coals to heat it, and encouraged my men so none would lose courage. When the wood, though still green, was about to burst into flame, I pulled it from the fire glowing with heat. My men gathered around me, because heaven had filled their hearts with courage. We drove the sharp end of the beam into the monster's eye, and I put all my weight behind it, turning it round and round like boring a hole in a ship's plank with a drill that two men can keep turning with a wheel and strap. We bored the red-hot beam into his eye until the boiling blood bubbled around it as we twisted it. The steam from the burning eyeball scalded his eyelids and eyebrows, and the eye's roots sizzled in the fire. Like when a blacksmith dips a hot axe or hatchet into cold water to strengthen the iron—and it makes a great hissing sound—that's how the Cyclops's eye hissed around the olive wood beam. His horrible screams made the cave ring with echoes. We ran away in terror, but he pulled the gore-covered beam from his eye and hurled it away in a frenzy of rage and pain, shouting to the other Cyclopes who lived on the rocky cliffs nearby. They gathered from all directions around his cave when they heard him crying and asked what was wrong."

"'What's the matter, Polyphemus?' they said. 'Why are you making such noise, breaking the night's silence and keeping us from sleeping? Is someone stealing your sheep? Is someone trying to kill you by trickery or force?'"
"But Polyphemus shouted to them from inside the cave, 'Noman is killing me by trickery! Noman is killing me by force!'"

"'Well then,' they said, 'if no man is attacking you, you must be sick. When Zeus makes people ill, there's no help for it, so you'd better pray to your father Poseidon.' (Poseidon was the god of the sea and earthquakes, and Polyphemus's father.)"

"Then they went away, and I laughed silently at how well my clever trick had worked. But the Cyclops, groaning in agony, felt around with his hands until he found the stone and removed it from the door. Then he sat in the doorway and stretched his hands across it to catch anyone trying to leave with the sheep, thinking I might be foolish enough to try this."

"I kept thinking about how to save my own life and those of my companions. I planned and schemed, knowing my life depended on it, because we were in great danger. Finally I decided this plan was best: The male sheep were fully grown and had thick black wool, so I quietly tied them together in groups of three with the flexible branches the wicked monster used for bedding. There would be a man under the middle sheep, with the two on either side covering him, so three sheep protected each man. As for myself, there was a ram finer than all the others, so I grabbed him by the back, tucked myself into the thick wool under his belly, and hung on patiently to his fleece, face up, keeping a firm grip the whole time."

"So we waited in great fear until morning came. When dawn appeared with rosy fingers, the male sheep hurried out to graze, while the females stayed bleating around the pens, waiting to be milked because their udders were painfully full. But their master, despite all his pain, felt the backs of all the sheep as they walked upright past him. He wasn't clever enough to discover that men were hiding underneath their bellies. As the ram—last of all, heavy with wool and my crafty weight—was going out, Polyphemus grabbed it and said:"

"'My good ram, why are you the last to leave my cave this morning? You don't usually let the female sheep go before you, but lead the flock running to flowery meadows or bubbling springs, and you're the first to come home at night. But now you're last of all. Are you sad because you know your master has lost his eye, blinded by that wicked Noman and his horrible crew when they got me drunk? But I'll have his life yet! If you could understand and speak, you'd tell me where that wretch is hiding, and I'd smash his brains against the ground until they splattered all over the cave. That would give me some satisfaction for the harm this no-good Noman has done me.'"

"As he spoke, he let the ram go outside. When we were a little way from the cave and yards, I first freed myself from under the ram's belly, then untied my companions. As for the sheep, which were very fat, we kept heading them in the right direction and managed to drive them down to our ship. The crew was overjoyed to see those of us who had escaped death, but they wept for the others the Cyclops had killed. However, I gestured by nodding and frowning for them to stop crying, and told them to get all the sheep aboard at once and put out to sea. So they went aboard, took their places, and struck the gray sea with their oars. When I'd gotten far enough out that my voice would carry, I began to taunt the Cyclops."

"'Cyclops!' I said, 'you should have been more careful about who you were dealing with before eating his companions in your cave! You monster, devouring visitors in your own home! You might have known your evil deeds would catch up with you, and now Zeus and the other gods have punished you.'"

"He became more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top off a high mountain and hurled it just in front of my ship, almost hitting the tip of the rudder. The sea shook as the rock fell into it, and the wave it created washed us back toward the mainland, forcing us toward shore. But I grabbed a long pole and pushed the ship away, signaling to my men by nodding that they must row for their lives. They rowed with all their strength. When we'd gotten twice as far as before, I was ready to taunt the Cyclops again, but my men begged and pleaded with me to keep quiet."

"'Don't,' they cried, 'be crazy enough to make this savage creature even angrier! He's already thrown one rock that drove us back to the mainland, and we thought it would kill us. If he hears any more voices, he'll pound our heads and our ship's wood to pieces with the jagged rocks he can throw, because he can hurl them a long way.'"

"But I wouldn't listen to them, and shouted to him in my anger, 'Cyclops, if anyone asks who put out your eye and ruined your looks, tell them it was the brave warrior Ulysses, son of Laertes, who lives on Ithaca.'"

"At this he groaned and cried out, 'Oh no! The old prophecy about me is coming true. There was a prophet here once, a man both brave and tall, named Telemus, son of Eurymus. He was an excellent fortune-teller who did all the prophesying for the Cyclopes until he grew old. He told me this would happen someday—that I'd lose my sight at the hands of Ulysses. I've been expecting someone impressive and superhuman in strength, but he turns out to be a little, insignificant weakling who managed to blind my eye by getting me drunk! Come here then, Ulysses, so I can give you gifts to show my hospitality, and ask Poseidon to help you on your journey—for Poseidon and I are father and son. He can heal me if he chooses, which no one else, neither god nor human, can do.'"
"Then I said, 'I wish I could be as sure of killing you completely and sending you down to Hades' realm of the dead, as I am that it will take more than Poseidon to heal that eye of yours.'"

"At this he raised his hands to the starry heavens and prayed, saying, 'Hear me, great Poseidon! If I'm truly your son, grant that Ulysses may never reach his home alive. Or if he must return to his friends at last, let him arrive late and in terrible condition after losing all his men. Let him reach home in someone else's ship and find trouble in his house.'"

"So he prayed, and Poseidon heard his prayer. Then he picked up a rock much larger than the first, swung it high, and hurled it with tremendous force. It fell just short of the ship but came close to hitting the end of the rudder. The sea shook as the rock crashed into it, and the wave it raised drove us forward on our way toward the island where our other ships waited."

"When we finally reached the island where we'd left the rest of our ships, we found our companions mourning us and anxiously waiting for our return. We ran our ship onto the sand and got out onto the shore. We also brought the Cyclops's sheep to land and divided them equally among us so no one could complain. As for the ram, my companions agreed I should have it as an extra share. So I sacrificed it on the seashore and burned its thigh bones to Zeus, who rules over all. But he ignored my sacrifice and only thought about how he might destroy both my ships and my men."

"So all day long until sunset we feasted on meat and drink. When the sun went down and darkness came, we camped on the beach. When morning came with rosy-fingered dawn, I ordered my men aboard and told them to untie the ropes. They took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars. We sailed on with sadness in our hearts, but glad to have escaped death even though we'd lost our companions."

chapters.title: Book X — Aeolus, the laestrygones, circe.
paragraphs: From there we sailed to the floating island of Aeolus, son of Hippotas, who was beloved by the immortal gods. His island seemed to drift on the sea itself, surrounded by high bronze walls. Aeolus had six daughters and six strong sons, and he had arranged for the sons to marry their own sisters—which was acceptable to the gods in those ancient times. They all lived together as one big family with their parents, feasting every day on the most delicious foods you could imagine. The smell of roasting meat filled their palace from morning till night, and at nighttime each couple slept in their own beautiful beds. This was the household that welcomed us.

Aeolus was a wonderful host who entertained me for a whole month, asking endless questions about the war at Troy, the Greek ships, and how the other heroes were getting home. I told him everything that had happened. When I finally said I needed to leave, he was happy to help. He did something amazing—he skinned a huge ox and made the hide into a bag, then trapped all the storm winds inside it! You see, Zeus had made Aeolus the master of all winds, so he could control each one as he pleased. He sealed the bag tight with a silver cord so not even the tiniest breeze could escape. The only wind he left free was the gentle West Wind, which would blow us straight home. But our good fortune was ruined by my men's foolishness.

For nine days and nine nights we sailed smoothly toward home. On the tenth day, we could actually see Ithaca! We were so close I could make out the cooking fires on the beach. I was exhausted because I had steered the ship the entire time, never letting anyone else take the wheel—I wanted to get us home as quickly as possible. Finally, I fell into a light sleep. That's when my men started whispering among themselves. They were convinced I was hiding treasure in Aeolus's bag. "Look how lucky he always is!" they grumbled. "Everywhere he goes, people shower him with gifts. He's probably got gold and silver from Troy in that bag, while we're going home empty-handed. And now Aeolus has given him even more! Let's see what's really inside!"

Their jealousy got the better of them, and they untied the bag. Instantly, all the imprisoned winds burst out with a terrible howling! A fierce storm exploded around us, carrying our weeping crew far back out to sea, away from our beloved homeland. I woke up to this disaster and didn't know whether to throw myself overboard or keep trying to survive. I chose to endure it, pulling my cloak over my head and lying down while my men wailed in despair as the wild winds carried us all the way back to Aeolus's island.

When we reached the island again, we went ashore to get fresh water and eat near our ships. Right after our meal, I took a herald and one of my men and went straight to Aeolus's palace. We found him dining with his wife and children, so we sat down as beggars at his doorway. They were shocked to see us. "Odysseus!" they exclaimed. "What brings you back here? What angry god has been tormenting you? We took such care to help you get home to Ithaca or wherever you wanted to go!"
I answered them sadly, "My men have ruined me! They and cruel sleep have destroyed everything. My friends, please fix this disaster—you have the power to do it if you choose."

I spoke as persuasively as I could, but everyone stayed silent until Aeolus himself answered harshly: "Get off this island immediately, you most cursed of men! The gods clearly hate you, and I will not help someone the heavens despise. Leave now—you come here as one rejected by the gods!" With those bitter words, he threw me out of his house.

We sailed away sadly, and my men grew tired from rowing without any wind to help us. For six long days and nights we struggled with the oars, and on the seventh day we reached the rocky fortress of the Laestrygonians—a place called Telepylus, ruled by King Lamus. In that strange land, the days and nights were almost the same length, so a man who never slept could work double shifts—one herding cattle, another tending sheep—because it stayed light so long.

When we reached their harbor, we found it surrounded by towering cliffs with only a narrow entrance between two rocky points. All my other captains sailed their ships inside and tied them close together in the calm, sheltered water. But something made me keep my ship outside, moored to a rock at the very tip of the point. I climbed up high to scout the area but saw no signs of people or animals—only some smoke rising from the ground. So I sent two of my men with a messenger to find out what kind of people lived there.

When my scouts went ashore, they followed a wide road that the locals used to haul firewood from the mountains to their town. Soon they met a young woman coming to fetch water from a spring called Artacia. She was the daughter of a Laestrygonian named Antiphates. When my men asked her who ruled this land and what the people were like, she directed them to her father's house. But when they got there, they found his wife—and she was a giantess as tall as a mountain! The sight of her filled them with terror.

The giant woman immediately called for her husband Antiphates from the town meeting place. As soon as he arrived, he grabbed one of my men and started eating him alive! The other two ran back to the ships as fast as their legs could carry them. But Antiphates raised the alarm, and thousands of enormous Laestrygonians came running from everywhere—not men, but giants! They hurled huge boulders down at us from the cliffs like they were throwing pebbles. I heard the horrible sounds of ships being crushed together and my men screaming as the giants speared them like fish and carried them off to eat. While this massacre was happening in the harbor, I drew my sword, cut my ship's anchor rope, and shouted for my crew to row for their lives! We escaped into open water, but every other ship and all those brave men were lost.

We sailed on with heavy hearts, glad to be alive but grieving for our lost friends. Eventually we reached the island of Aeaea, home of the powerful goddess Circe. She was the sister of Aeetes the magician—both were children of the Sun god and the ocean nymph Perse. Some god guided us into a safe harbor without any effort on our part. We were so exhausted in body and spirit that we just lay on the beach for two whole days and nights. On the morning of the third day, I took my spear and sword and climbed to a high lookout point to see if there were any signs of people living on the island. From the mountaintop, I spotted smoke rising from Circe's house through a thick forest. I thought about investigating right away, but decided it was better to return to the ship, feed my men, and send a scouting party instead of going alone.

As I was heading back to the ship, some merciful god took pity on me and sent a magnificent stag with huge antlers right into my path. The deer was coming down from his grazing ground to drink from the river—the heat was driving all the animals to water. When he passed by, I struck him in the middle of his back with my bronze spear point, which went clean through him. He collapsed, groaning, until his life left him. I stood over him, pulled out my spear, and gathered tough grass and reeds to twist into a strong rope about six feet long. With this I tied the stag's four feet together, slung him around my neck, and walked back to the ship leaning on my spear for support—the deer was far too heavy to carry on my shoulder. When I dropped him in front of the ship, I called to my men cheerfully, "Look here, my friends! We're not going to die before our time after all. At least we won't starve as long as we have food and drink aboard!" At this, they uncovered their heads and stared in wonder at the stag—he truly was a magnificent beast. After admiring him, they washed their hands and prepared him for dinner.

All day long until sunset we feasted on the delicious meat and wine. When the sun went down and darkness fell, we made camp on the seashore. When Dawn with her rosy fingers appeared, I called everyone together and said, "My friends, we're in serious trouble. Listen carefully. We have no idea which direction is which—we can't even tell where the sun rises or sets, so we don't know east from west. I can't see any way out of our situation, but we must try to find one. I know for certain we're on an island because I climbed high this morning and saw water all around us to the horizon. The land is low and flat, but I did see smoke rising from the middle of a thick forest."

Their hearts sank when they heard this, remembering how cruelly the giant Antiphates and the savage Cyclops Polyphemus had treated us. They wept bitterly, but crying wouldn't help, so I divided them into two groups with a captain for each. I put Eurylochus in charge of one group while I led the other. Then we drew lots from a helmet, and Eurylochus's name came up. So he set out with twenty-two men, and both groups wept—those who left and those who stayed behind.

When they reached Circe's house, they found it built of polished stone in a clearing that could be seen from far away, right in the middle of the forest. Wild mountain wolves and lions prowled all around it—but these were actually bewitched men whom Circe had transformed and tamed with her magic potions. Instead of attacking my men, these creatures wagged their tails, rubbed against them affectionately, and acted like friendly dogs greeting their master. But my men were terrified to see such strange beasts acting so tame. Soon they reached the gates of the goddess's palace, and they could hear Circe inside, singing beautifully as she worked at her loom, weaving cloth so fine and colorful that only a goddess could make it. Polites, one of my most trusted men, said, "Someone inside is weaving and singing most beautifully—the whole place echoes with it. Let's call to her and see if she's a woman or a goddess."

They called out, and Circe came down, opened the door wide, and invited them in. Not suspecting any danger, they all followed her inside—all except Eurylochus, who smelled trouble and stayed outside. Once she had them in her house, she seated them on benches and chairs and mixed them a drink of cheese, honey, barley, and special wine. But she drugged it with evil magic to make them forget their homeland. When they drank it down, she struck them with her wand and transformed them into pigs! They had pigs' heads, bodies, bristles, and voices—they grunted just like pigs. But their minds stayed human, and they remembered everything that had happened to them.

So there they were, locked up squealing in the pig pens while Circe threw them acorns and nuts to eat, just like regular pigs. Meanwhile, Eurylochus hurried back to tell me about our comrades' terrible fate. He was so shocked and upset that even though he tried to speak, no words would come out. His eyes filled with tears and he could only sob and sigh until we finally forced the story out of him.

"We went through the forest as you ordered," he said, "and in the middle we found a beautiful house made of cut stone that could be seen from far away. There we found a woman—or maybe she was a goddess—working at her loom and singing sweetly. The men shouted and called to her, and she immediately came down, opened the door, and invited us in. The others didn't suspect any trickery, so they followed her into the house, but I stayed where I was because I thought there might be treachery. From that moment I never saw them again—not one of them ever came back out, though I waited and watched for a long time."

Then I strapped on my bronze sword and slung my bow over my shoulder, telling Eurylochus to come back with me and show me the way. But he grabbed me with both hands and begged pitifully, "Sir, please don't force me to go with you! Let me stay here, because I know you won't bring any of them back, and you won't even return alive yourself. Let's see if we can escape with the few men we have left—we might still save our lives."
"Stay here then," I answered, "eating and drinking at the ship. But I must go—I'm absolutely bound to do this."

With that, I left the ship and headed inland. When I got through the enchanted grove and was near Circe's great house, I met Mercury (the messenger of the gods) carrying his golden wand. He looked like a handsome young man in the prime of life, with the first soft beard just appearing on his face. He came up to me, took my hand in his, and said, "My poor unfortunate man, where are you going over this mountain alone, not knowing the way? Your men are shut up in Circe's pig pens like wild boars in their cages. You don't really think you can free them, do you? I can tell you that you'll never get back and will have to stay there with the rest. But don't worry—I'll protect you and get you out of trouble. Take this herb, which has great power, and keep it with you when you go to Circe's house. It will protect you from all kinds of harm.

"I'll tell you about all the wicked magic Circe will try to use on you. She'll mix a drink for you and drug the food in it, but she won't be able to enchant you because this herb I'm giving you will block her spells. Listen carefully: when Circe strikes you with her wand, draw your sword and rush at her as if you're going to kill her. She'll be frightened and will ask you to come to bed with her. Don't refuse completely, because you want her to free your companions and take care of you too. But make her swear a solemn oath by all the blessed gods that she won't plot any more harm against you, or when she has you defenseless, she'll steal your strength and courage."

As he spoke, he pulled an herb from the ground and showed me what it looked like. The root was black, but the flower was white as milk. The gods call it Moly, and ordinary humans can't uproot it, but the gods can do whatever they please.

Then Mercury returned to high Mount Olympus, flying over the wooded island, while I continued toward Circe's house with a worried heart. When I reached her gates, I stood there and called to the goddess. As soon as she heard me, she came down, opened the door, and asked me to come in. I followed her, deeply troubled. She seated me on a beautiful chair decorated with silver, with a footstool under my feet, and mixed me a drink in a golden cup. But she drugged it, planning to harm me. When she gave it to me and I had drunk it without being enchanted, she struck me with her wand and cried, "There! Now go to the pig pen and lie down with the rest of them!"

But I rushed at her with my drawn sword as though I meant to kill her. She fell back with a loud scream, grabbed my knees, and spoke desperately: "Who are you and where do you come from? What city and family? How can it be that my drugs have no power over you? No man has ever been able to resist even a taste of the herb I gave you before! You must be protected by magic. Surely you can only be the great hero Odysseus, whom Mercury always said would come here someday in his ship while returning home from Troy. If that's true, put away your sword and let's go to bed together, so we can learn to trust each other."

I answered, "Circe, how can you expect me to be friendly when you've just turned all my men into pigs? And now that you have me here, you're planning more mischief by asking me to bed, where you'll steal my strength and courage. I certainly won't sleep with you unless you first swear a solemn oath not to plot any more harm against me."
So she immediately swore the oath I demanded, and when she had completed it, I went to bed with her.

Meanwhile, her four servants, who take care of the household, went about their duties. These servants are the spirits of groves, springs, and the sacred rivers that flow down to the sea. One spread a beautiful purple cloth over a chair and laid a carpet beneath it. Another brought silver tables to the seats and set golden baskets on them. A third mixed sweet wine with water in a silver bowl and placed golden cups on the tables, while the fourth brought water and set it to heat in a large cauldron over a good fire. When the water was warm, she mixed it with cold water until it was just the right temperature, then had me sit in a bathtub and began washing me from head to shoulders to take away my weariness and stiffness. After bathing and rubbing me with olive oil, she dressed me in a fine cloak and tunic and led me to the beautifully decorated silver chair with the footstool. A servant brought me water in a lovely golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin so I could wash my hands. She set a polished table beside me, and the head servant brought bread and offered me many delicious foods from the house. Then Circe told me to eat, but I wouldn't touch anything. I sat there ignoring the food, still gloomy and suspicious.

When Circe saw me sitting there without eating, looking deeply sad, she came to me and said, "Odysseus, why do you sit there like a mute person, eating your heart out with grief and refusing both food and drink? Are you still suspicious? You shouldn't be—I've already sworn solemnly that I won't hurt you."

I replied, "Circe, no decent man would think of eating or drinking in your house until you free his friends and let him see them. If you want me to eat and drink, release my men and bring them to me so I can see them with my own eyes."

When I said this, she went straight through the courtyard with her wand and opened the pig pen doors. My men came out looking like fat pigs, but she went among them and rubbed each one with a different drug. Immediately, all the bristles that her evil potion had given them fell off, and they became men again—but younger than before, and much taller and more handsome! They recognized me at once, each one grabbing my hand and weeping with joy until the whole house echoed with their happy shouting. Even Circe felt sorry for them and came up to me saying, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, go back to the seashore where you left your ship. First, pull it up onto the beach, then hide all your ship's equipment and treasure in some cave, and come back here with the rest of your men."

I agreed to this plan, so I returned to the seashore and found the remaining crew weeping and wailing pitifully by the ship. When they saw me, the dear fellows began dancing around me like calves frisking around their mothers when the cows come home to be milked after grazing all day, making the farmyard ring with their joyful lowing. They seemed as happy to see me as if they had reached their own rocky Ithaca where they were born and raised. "Sir," said these loyal men, "we're as glad to see you back as if we had gotten safely home to Ithaca! But tell us what happened to our other companions."

I spoke comfortingly to them: "We must pull our ship onto the beach and hide all our gear and treasure in some cave. Then come with me quickly to Circe's house, where you'll find your comrades eating and drinking surrounded by great abundance."

The men would have come with me immediately, but Eurylochus tried to stop them: "You poor fools, what will become of us? Don't rush toward your doom by going to Circe's house, where she'll turn us all into pigs, wolves, or lions, and we'll have to guard her palace! Remember how the Cyclops treated us when our comrades went into his cave with Odysseus. It was all because of his reckless foolishness that those men died."

When I heard this, I was tempted to draw the sharp sword from my side and cut off his head, even though he was my relative. But the men intervened: "Sir, if you agree, let this fellow stay here and guard the ship, but take the rest of us with you to Circe's house."
So we all went inland, and Eurylochus wasn't left behind after all—he came too, because he was frightened by the harsh scolding I had given him.

Meanwhile, Circe had been taking care of the men who had been left behind. She had them washed and rubbed with olive oil, and gave them wool cloaks and tunics. When we arrived, we found them all dining comfortably in her house. As soon as the men saw each other face to face and recognized one another, they wept for joy and cried out so loudly that the whole palace rang with the sound. Then Circe came up to me and said, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, tell your men to stop weeping. I know how much you've all suffered at sea and how badly cruel savages on the mainland have treated you. But that's over now, so stay here and eat and drink until you're as strong and healthy as when you left Ithaca. Right now you're worn out in both body and spirit, constantly thinking about the hardships of your travels, so that you have no joy left in you."

We agreed with her words and stayed with Circe for a whole year, feasting on endless quantities of meat and wine. But when the year had passed and the seasons had come full circle, my men took me aside and said, "Sir, it's time you started thinking about going home, if you're destined to be saved and see your house and native country again."

They spoke truly, and I agreed. So all that day until sunset we feasted on meat and wine, but when the sun went down and darkness came, the men lay down to sleep in the covered halls. But I went to bed with Circe and begged her by her knees to keep her promise. The goddess listened to my request. "Circe," I said, "please keep the promise you made about helping me get home. I want to return, and so do my men—they're always complaining to me about it whenever you're not around."

The goddess answered, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, you don't have to stay here any longer if you don't want to. But there's another journey you must make before you can sail home. You have to go to the house of Hades and dread Persephone (goddess of the dead) to consult the spirit of the blind prophet Tiresias of Thebes, whose mind is still sharp. Persephone has left him his understanding even in death, while the other ghosts drift around mindlessly."

I was horrified when I heard this. I sat up in bed and wept, wishing I could die rather than face such a journey. But when I was tired of weeping and thrashing about, I said, "Who will guide me on this voyage? The realm of the dead is not a port that any ship can reach."

"You won't need a guide," she answered. "Raise your mast, set your white sails, sit quietly, and the North Wind will carry you there by itself. When your ship has crossed the waters of Ocean, you'll reach the fertile shore of Persephone's land with its groves of tall poplars and willows that drop their fruit before it ripens. Beach your ship on the shore of Ocean and go straight to the dark realm of Hades. You'll find it where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus (which is a branch of the river Styx) flow into the river Acheron. There's a rock there, right where the two roaring rivers join together.

"When you reach that spot, dig a trench about three feet long, wide, and deep. Pour into it offerings to all the dead: first honey mixed with milk, then wine, and third, water—sprinkling white barley meal over everything. Also, you must pray earnestly to the weak spirits of the dead, promising that when you return to Ithaca you'll sacrifice your best cow to them and pile the altar with good things. Most importantly, promise that Tiresias will have a black sheep all to himself, the finest in your flock.

"After you've made these prayers and promises to the spirits, sacrifice a ram and a black ewe, pointing their heads toward Erebus (the entrance to the underworld) while you turn away as if heading toward the river. Then many ghosts of the dead will come to you, and you must tell your men to skin the two sheep you've killed and burn them with prayers to Hades and Persephone. Draw your sword and sit there, preventing any other spirits from coming near the spilled blood until Tiresias has answered your questions. The prophet will come to you soon and tell you about your journey—what route to take and how to sail the sea to reach your home."

It was daybreak by the time she finished speaking, so she dressed me in my tunic and cloak. She put on a beautiful, light, silvery robe, fastened with a golden belt around her waist, and covered her head with a veil. Then I went throughout the house, speaking kindly to each man: "You can't stay here sleeping any longer," I told them. "We must leave, for Circe has explained everything to me." They did as I commanded.

Even so, I didn't get them all away without trouble. We had with us a young man named Elpenor, who wasn't particularly smart or brave. He had gotten drunk and was sleeping on the roof, away from the other men, trying to sleep off his wine in the cool air. When he heard the noise of the men getting ready to leave, he jumped up suddenly and forgot to use the main staircase. Instead, he fell right off the roof, broke his neck, and his soul went down to the house of Hades.

When I had gathered the men together, I said to them, "You think you're about to start home, but Circe has told me that instead, we must go to the house of Hades and Persephone to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias."

The men were heartbroken when they heard this, and threw themselves on the ground, groaning and tearing their hair. But their crying didn't help anything. When we reached the seashore, still weeping and lamenting our fate, Circe brought the ram and ewe and tied them near the ship. She passed among us without our seeing her—for who can watch the comings and goings of a god when the god doesn't wish to be seen?

chapters.title: Book XI — The visit to the dead.
paragraphs: We drew our black ship down to the seashore and loaded our mast and sails. We put the sheep aboard and climbed in ourselves, tears streaming down our faces. Our hearts felt heavy with dread. But Circe, the powerful goddess with her magic spells, sent us a perfect wind that filled our sails and stayed with us all day. We sailed over the dark sea until the sun disappeared and night covered the world. Then we reached the deep waters of the river Oceanus, where the mysterious land of the Cimmerians lies hidden. These poor people live forever wrapped in mist and darkness—the sun never shines on them, whether it's rising or setting. They exist in endless, gloomy night. When we arrived, we beached our ship, unloaded the sheep, and walked along the riverbank until we found the special place Circe had told us about.

Here my two men, Perimedes and Eurylochus, held the sheep while I drew my sharp sword and dug a trench in the ground—one foot wide and one foot long. I poured offerings to all the dead spirits: first honey mixed with milk, then wine, and finally water. I sprinkled white barley flour over everything, praying desperately to the powerless ghosts. I promised them that when I returned home to Ithaca, I would sacrifice my best cow for them and pile the funeral fire high with treasures. I especially promised the prophet Teiresias the finest black sheep from my flocks. After my prayers, I slit the throats of both sheep and let their blood flow into the trench. Suddenly, ghosts came swarming up from Erebus—the dark underworld where the dead live. There were young brides, unmarried men, tired old grandfathers, girls who had died broken-hearted, and brave warriors still wearing their blood-stained armor. They came from everywhere, fluttering around the trench with horrible screaming sounds that made my face turn white with terror. When I saw them approaching, I ordered my men to quickly skin the dead sheep and burn them as offerings, while praying to Hades, king of the underworld, and his wife Proserpine. But I sat with my sword drawn, refusing to let any ghost near the blood until Teiresias answered my questions.

The first ghost to appear was my companion Elpenor—we had left his body unburied in Circe's house because we'd been in such a hurry to leave. My heart broke when I saw him. "Elpenor!" I cried, "How did you get down here to this land of gloom and darkness? You got here on foot faster than I did with my ship!"

"Captain," he said with a deep groan, "bad luck and too much wine killed me. I fell asleep on Circe's roof and forgot about the stairs. I tumbled right off the roof and broke my neck, so my soul came down here to Hades' realm. Now I beg you—by your wife, by your father who raised you, and by your son Telemachus who is your family's only hope—please do what I'm about to ask. I know that when you leave this place of the dead, you'll sail back to Circe's island. Don't leave me there unburied and unmourned, or I might bring the gods' anger down on you. Burn my body with whatever armor I have, build me a grave mound by the seashore so people will remember me, and plant the oar I used to row with on top of my grave." And I promised him, "My poor friend, I'll do everything you've asked."

So we sat there having this sad conversation—me on one side of the blood-filled trench with my sword ready, and my dead companion's ghost speaking to me from the other side. Then came my dear mother's ghost, Anticlea, daughter of Autolycus. I had left her alive when I sailed to Troy, and seeing her now made tears pour down my face. But even though my heart was breaking, I wouldn't let her approach the blood until I had spoken with Teiresias.

Then came the ghost of Teiresias from the city of Thebes, holding his golden staff. He recognized me immediately and said, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, why have you left the world of the living to visit us dead in this sad place? Step back from the trench and put away your sword so I can drink the blood and give you true answers."
So I moved back and sheathed my sword. After he drank the blood, he began to prophesy.

"You want to know about your journey home," he said, "but the gods will make it very difficult. I don't think you'll escape the anger of Poseidon, god of the sea, who still holds a bitter grudge against you for blinding his son, the Cyclops. Still, after much suffering, you may reach home—if you can control yourself and your men when you reach the island of Thrinacia. There you'll find the sacred cattle and sheep that belong to Helios, the sun god who sees everything. If you leave those animals alone and focus only on getting home, you may eventually reach Ithaca after great hardship. But if you harm them, I warn you that your ship and crew will be destroyed. Even if you survive, you'll return home alone in someone else's ship, and you'll find trouble waiting—arrogant men taking over your house, eating your food, and trying to marry your wife.

"When you get home, you'll take revenge on these suitors. After you've killed them in your own house, you must take a well-made oar and travel inland until you reach a country where people have never seen the sea. They don't even put salt on their food, and they know nothing about ships or oars.
