Here's how you'll know you've found the right place: someone will meet you and ask why you're carrying a winnowing fan on your shoulder. (A winnowing fan is a tool used to separate grain from chaff—they'll mistake your oar for this farm tool because they've never seen ships.) When this happens, plant the oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Poseidon. Then return home and offer grand sacrifices to all the gods. As for your own death, it will come to you from the sea, but it will be gentle when you're old and at peace, surrounded by prosperous people. Everything I've told you will come true."

"This must happen as the gods will," I answered, "but tell me truly—I see my poor mother's ghost sitting by the blood without speaking. Even though I'm her own son, she doesn't seem to recognize me. How can I make her know who I am?"
"That's easy," he replied. "Any ghost that tastes the blood will talk to you like a normal person, but those who don't drink it will drift away again."

With that, Teiresias's ghost returned to the house of Hades, his prophecies complete. I stayed where I was until my mother came forward and tasted the blood. Immediately she knew me and spoke lovingly: "My son, how did you come to this dark realm while you're still alive? It's incredibly difficult for the living to reach these places—there are terrible waters and great Oceanus between our worlds, which no one can cross on foot without a strong ship. Have you been wandering all this time trying to get home from Troy? Haven't you reached Ithaca yet or seen your wife?"

"Mother," I said, "I was forced to come here to consult the ghost of the prophet Teiresias. I've never been near Greece or set foot in my homeland—I've had nothing but trouble since the day I sailed with King Agamemnon to fight at Troy. But tell me truly, how did you die? Did you suffer a long illness, or did the gods grant you a peaceful death? Tell me about my father and the son I left behind—do they still control my property, or has someone else taken it, thinking I'll never return? And what about my wife? What are her plans? Does she stay with my son and protect our home, or has she remarried someone else?"

My mother answered, "Your wife Penelope remains in your house, but she lives in constant sorrow, crying day and night. No one has taken your property yet—Telemachus still controls your lands safely. He has to host many feasts, as is expected of someone in his position as a leader, and everyone invites him to their gatherings. Your father stays at his old farm in the country and never comes to town. He doesn't have a comfortable bed—in winter he sleeps on the floor by the fire with the servants, dressed in rags. But in summer, when the weather's warm, he lies outside in the vineyard on a pile of grape leaves scattered on the ground. He grieves constantly about your absence and suffers more as he grows older. As for my own death, it wasn't a disease that killed me, nor did I die peacefully in my home. It was my desperate longing to know what had happened to you, and my overwhelming love for you—that's what killed me."

Then I tried to embrace my dear mother's ghost. Three times I reached out to hold her, but each time she slipped through my arms like a dream or shadow. My heart aching, I said to her, "Mother, why don't you stay still so I can hug you? Even here in Hades, we could comfort each other by sharing our grief. Is Proserpine, queen of the underworld, just tormenting me with a fake image?"

"My son," she replied, "unluckiest of all people, Proserpine isn't deceiving you. This is simply how all dead people are. Once we die, our muscles and bones no longer hold together—the fierce fire of death destroys them, and the soul flits away like a dream. Now hurry back to the world of light, and remember everything you've learned here so you can tell your wife about it later."

As we talked, Proserpine sent up the ghosts of many famous women—wives and daughters of great heroes. They crowded around the blood, and I wondered how to question them one by one. Finally, I decided to draw my sharp sword again and keep them from all drinking at once. So they came forward one at a time, and each told me her story and family history.

First I saw Tyro, daughter of King Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus. She fell in love with the beautiful river Enipeus, the most gorgeous river in the world. One day while she was walking by its banks, Poseidon disguised himself as the river god and made love to her at the river's mouth. A huge wave arched over them like a mountain to hide both woman and god. Afterward, Poseidon took her hand and said, "Tyro, be happy! The love of gods is never wasted—in twelve months you'll have fine twin sons. Take good care of them. I am Poseidon, so go home now, but don't tell anyone what happened."

Then he dove back into the sea, and she later gave birth to Pelias and Neleus, who both served Zeus faithfully. Pelias became a great sheep herder in Iolcus, while Neleus ruled in Pylos. Her other children were by her husband Cretheus: Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon, who became a mighty warrior and chariot driver.

Next I saw Antiope, daughter of the river god Asopus, who could boast that she had slept with Zeus himself. She bore him two sons, Amphion and Zethus, who founded the great city of Thebes with its seven gates and built walls around it—for even though they were strong, they couldn't defend Thebes without walls.
Then I saw Alcmena, wife of Amphitryon, who also bore a son to Zeus—the mighty hero Hercules. I also saw Megara, daughter of great King Creon, who married Hercules.

I saw fair Jocasta, mother of King Oedipus, whose terrible fate was to unknowingly marry her own son. He had married her after killing his father, not knowing who either of them really were. When the gods revealed the horrible truth to everyone, Oedipus remained king of Thebes but lived in great misery. Jocasta hanged herself in grief, and the avenging spirits tormented Oedipus for the rest of his life.

Then I saw Chloris, whom Neleus married for her beauty after giving priceless gifts for her hand. She was the youngest daughter of King Amphion and became Queen of Pylos. She bore the famous Nestor, Chromius, and Periclymenus, and also the incredibly beautiful Pero. Every man in the country wanted to marry Pero, but Neleus said he'd only give her to whoever could steal the cattle of Iphicles from the fields of Phylace—a nearly impossible task. Only one excellent prophet was brave enough to attempt it, but heaven was against him. The cattle guards caught him and threw him in prison. However, after a full year passed, Iphicles freed him after he had correctly interpreted all the gods' prophecies. This was how Zeus's will was fulfilled.

I saw Leda, wife of King Tyndarus, who bore him two famous sons: Castor the horse-tamer and Pollux the mighty boxer. Both heroes lie under the earth, yet they're still alive in a way—by Zeus's special gift, they die and come back to life on alternating days throughout all time, and they have the rank of gods.

After her I saw Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, who claimed that Poseidon had embraced her. She bore two sons, Otus and Ephialtes, but both died young. They were the finest and most handsome children ever born (except for the great hunter Orion). At only nine years old, they were already nine fathoms tall and nine cubits around the chest! They threatened to make war against the gods on Mount Olympus and tried to pile Mount Ossa on top of Mount Olympus, and Mount Pelion on top of Ossa, so they could climb to heaven itself. They would have succeeded too, if they'd lived to grow up, but Apollo killed both of them before they even had whiskers on their faces.

Then I saw Phaedra, Procris, and beautiful Ariadne, daughter of the magical King Minos. Theseus was carrying Ariadne from Crete to Athens, but he never got to enjoy her company because Diana killed her on the island of Dia, acting on something Bacchus had said against her.

I also saw Maera, Clymene, and the hateful Eriphyle, who sold her own husband's life for gold. But it would take me all night to name every single wife and daughter of heroes that I saw, and it's time for me to sleep, either here with you or on my ship with my crew. I'll leave the details of my journey home to you and the gods.
Here Odysseus finished his tale, and all the Phaeacian guests sat in complete, amazed silence throughout the covered hall. Then Queen Arete spoke:

"What do you think of this man, Phaeacians? Isn't he tall and handsome and clever? He's my guest, but you all share in the honor of hosting him. Don't be in a hurry to send him away, and don't be stingy with your gifts to someone who needs them so badly—the gods have blessed all of you with great wealth."

Then the elderly hero Echeneus, one of the oldest men among them, spoke: "Friends, what our respected queen has just said is both wise and appropriate—we should follow her advice. But the final decision, whether in words or actions, belongs to King Alcinous."

"It will be done!" declared Alcinous. "As surely as I live and rule the Phaeacians, it will be done. Our guest is eager to get home, but we must persuade him to stay until tomorrow, when I can gather all the gifts I plan to give him. As for getting him home, that's a matter for all of us, but especially for me as your king."

Odysseus answered, "King Alcinous, if you asked me to stay here for a whole year and then sent me home loaded with your noble gifts, I'd gladly obey. It would be greatly to my advantage—I'd return to my people with full hands and be more respected and beloved by everyone when I reach Ithaca."

Alcinous replied, "Odysseus, none of us who see you think you're a liar or trickster. I know there are many people who tell such believable lies that it's hard to see through them, but there's something about the way you speak that proves your good character. Moreover, you've told the story of your own misfortunes and those of the Greeks as skillfully as a trained bard. But tell me truly—did you see any of the mighty heroes who went to Troy with you and died there? The evenings are still long, and it's not yet bedtime. Continue with your amazing story—I could stay here listening until dawn, as long as you keep telling us about your adventures."

"Alcinous," Odysseus answered, "there's a time for storytelling and a time for sleep. But since you want to hear more, I won't refuse to tell you the even sadder tale of my comrades who didn't die fighting the Trojans, but were killed on their way home by a wicked woman's treachery.

When Proserpine had sent away all the female ghosts, the spirit of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, came sadly toward me, surrounded by those who had died with him in Aegisthus's house. As soon as he tasted the blood, he recognized me and wept bitterly, stretching out his arms to embrace me. But he had no strength or substance anymore. I wept too, pitying him. 'How did you die, King Agamemnon?' I asked. 'Did Poseidon sink you in a storm at sea, or did enemies kill you on land while you were raiding their cattle or sheep, or fighting to defend their women and city?'

'Odysseus, noble son of Laertes,' he answered, 'I wasn't lost at sea in any storm, nor did enemies kill me in battle. Aegisthus and my evil wife murdered me together. He invited me to his house, fed me a feast, then butchered me like a cow in a slaughterhouse. All around me, my companions were slain like sheep or pigs being prepared for a wedding feast or banquet. You've probably seen many men killed in battle or single combat, but you never saw anything as horrible as the way we fell in that hall, with the wine bowl and loaded tables all around us, and the ground soaked with our blood. I heard Cassandra, daughter of King Priam, scream as my wife Clytemnestra killed her right beside me. I lay dying with the sword in my body, raising my hands to strike the murderous witch, but she slipped away from me. She wouldn't even close my eyes or mouth when I was dying—there's nothing in this world as cruel and shameless as a woman who commits such crimes. Imagine murdering her own husband! I thought I'd be welcomed home by my children and servants, but her horrible crime has brought disgrace on herself and all women who will come after—even the good ones.'

'Truly,' I said, 'Zeus has hated the house of Atreus from the beginning because of their women's evil schemes. Look how many of us died for Helen's sake, and now it seems Clytemnestra plotted against you while you were away.'

'Therefore,' Agamemnon continued, 'don't be too trusting, even with your own wife. Don't tell her everything you know. Tell her only part of it and keep the rest to yourself. Not that your wife Penelope is likely to murder you—she's a very good woman with an excellent character. We left her as a young bride with a baby at her breast when we sailed for Troy. That child is surely grown to manhood now, and he and his father will have a joyful reunion and embrace each other as they should. But my wicked wife didn't even let me see my son before she killed me. I'll give you one more piece of advice—take it to heart: don't announce yourself when you bring your ship to Ithaca. Sneak in secretly, because after all this, you can't trust women. But tell me truly, do you have any news of my son Orestes? Is he in Orchomenus, or Pylos, or Sparta with Menelaus? I assume he's still alive.'
'Agamemnon,' I said, 'why do you ask me? I don't know if your son is alive or dead, and it's wrong to speak about things I don't know.'

As we sat weeping and talking sadly together, the ghost of Achilles approached us, along with Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax—who was the finest and most handsome of all the Greeks after Achilles himself. The swift descendant of Aeacus recognized me and spoke mournfully: 'Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, what daring deed will you attempt next? How did you dare to come down to Hades among us silly dead, who are just shadows of our former selves?'

'Achilles, son of Peleus, greatest champion of the Greeks,' I replied, 'I came to consult Teiresias, hoping he could advise me about my return to Ithaca. I've never been able to get near Greece or set foot in my own country—I've been in trouble the whole time. As for you, Achilles, no one was ever as fortunate as you, nor ever will be. We all honored you like a god while you lived, and now you're a great prince among the dead. Don't be so upset about being dead.'

'Don't try to comfort me about death,' he answered. 'I'd rather be a poor man's servant in the world above than king of all the dead down here. But give me news about my son—has he gone to war, and will he be a great soldier? Tell me also if you've heard anything about my father Peleus. Does he still rule the Myrmidons, or do they disrespect him throughout Greece now that he's old and weak? If only I could stand beside him in the sunlight with the same strength I had when I killed the bravest Trojans on the battlefield—if I could be as I was then and go even briefly to my father's house, anyone who tried to harm him or overthrow him would regret it!'

'I've heard nothing about Peleus,' I answered, 'but I can tell you all about your son Neoptolemus—I brought him from Scyros in my own ship to join the Greeks. In our war councils before Troy, he always spoke first, and his judgment was perfect. Only Nestor and I could match his wisdom. When it came to fighting on the plains of Troy, he never stayed with the main group of soldiers but charged far ahead, bravest of them all. He killed many men in battle—I can't name everyone he slew fighting for the Greeks, but I'll mention how he killed the valiant hero Eurypylus, son of Telephus, who was the handsomest man I ever saw except for Memnon. Many other warriors fell around Eurypylus because of a woman's bribes. When all the bravest Greeks climbed inside the wooden horse that Epeus built, and I had to decide when we should open our hiding place or stay hidden, all the other leaders were crying and shaking with fear. But I never once saw your son turn pale or wipe away a tear. He kept urging me to break out of the horse, gripping his sword handle and bronze-tipped spear, breathing fury against our enemies. When we finally captured Priam's city, he got his fair share of the treasure and boarded his ship unwounded—not a scratch from a thrown spear or close combat, for the god of war's favor is unpredictable.'
When I told him this, Achilles's ghost strode away across a meadow full of asphodel flowers, rejoicing over what I'd said about his son's courage.

The ghosts of other dead men came near and each told me his own sad story. But Ajax, son of Telamon, stayed away—still angry with me for winning our dispute over Achilles's armor. The sea-goddess Thetis had offered it as a prize, and the Trojan prisoners and the goddess Athena were the judges. I wish I had never won that contest, because it cost Ajax his life. He was the finest of all the Greeks after Achilles in both size and skill.

When I saw him, I tried to make peace and said, 'Ajax, won't you forget and forgive even in death? Must your anger about that cursed armor still burn in you? That armor cost us Greeks dearly when we lost a tower of strength like you. We mourned you as much as we mourned Achilles himself. The blame lies only with Zeus's hatred for the Greek army—that's what caused your destruction. Come here, control your proud anger, and listen to what I have to say.'

But he wouldn't answer. He turned away toward Erebus and the other ghosts. Still, I might have made him talk to me despite his anger, or I might have kept talking to him, but there were other dead I wanted to see.
Then I saw Minos, son of Zeus, holding his golden scepter and judging the dead. The ghosts sat and stood around him in the spacious halls of Hades, waiting to learn their fate.
After him I saw huge Orion in a meadow full of asphodel flowers, herding the ghosts of wild beasts he had killed on the mountains. He carried a great bronze club in his hands, unbreakable forever.

I saw Tityus, son of Earth, stretched across the plain and covering nine acres of ground. Two vultures sat on either side of him, digging their beaks into his liver, and he kept trying to beat them off with his hands but couldn't. This was his punishment for attacking Leto, Zeus's lover, as she traveled through Panopeus on her way to Pytho.

I also saw the dreadful punishment of Tantalus, who stood in a lake that reached his chin. He was dying of thirst but could never reach the water—whenever the poor man stooped to drink, it dried up and vanished, leaving nothing but parched ground. Tall trees hung their fruit over his head—pears, pomegranates, apples, sweet figs, and juicy olives—but whenever he reached up to grab some, the wind tossed the branches back up to the clouds.

And I saw Sisyphus at his endless task, pushing his enormous stone with both hands. He strained with hands and feet to roll it up the hill, but always, just as he was about to push it over the top, its weight became too much for him, and the pitiless stone came thundering back down to the plain. Then he'd start trying to push it uphill again, sweat pouring off him and steam rising from his body.

After him I saw mighty Hercules—though it was only his ghost, since his real self feasts forever with the immortal gods and is married to lovely Hebe, daughter of Zeus and Hera. The ghosts were screaming around him like frightened birds flying everywhere. He looked black as night with his bow in his hands and an arrow on the string, glaring around as if always ready to shoot. Around his chest was a marvelous golden belt decorated with bears, wild boars, and lions with gleaming eyes, plus scenes of war, battle, and death. Whoever made that belt could never make another like it. Hercules recognized me immediately and spoke sadly: 'Poor Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, are you also living the same miserable kind of life I lived when I was above ground? I was Zeus's son, but I went through endless suffering because I became a slave to someone far beneath me—a worthless man who gave me impossible tasks. He once sent me here to bring back the hell-hound Cerberus, thinking he couldn't find anything harder for me than that. But I got the hound out of Hades and brought it to him, because Mercury and Athena helped me.'

With that, Hercules went back into the house of Hades, but I stayed where I was in case other mighty dead heroes came to me. I would have seen others from long ago that I wanted to meet—Theseus and Pirithous, glorious sons of gods—but thousands of ghosts swarmed around me with such horrible cries that I panicked, terrified that Proserpine might send up the head of the awful monster Gorgon from Hades. So I hurried back to my ship and ordered my men to get aboard immediately and untie the ropes. They climbed in and took their places, and the ship sailed down the stream of the river Oceanus. At first we had to row, but soon a fair wind sprang up.

chapters.title: Book XII — The sirens, scylla and charybdis, the cattle of the sun.
paragraphs: After we sailed away from the river Oceanus and reached the open sea, we traveled until we came to Aeaea island, where the goddess Circe lived. This was where dawn and sunrise happened just like everywhere else. We pulled our ship onto the sandy beach and climbed out onto the shore, where we fell asleep and waited for morning to come.

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared in the morning sky, I sent some of my men to Circe's house to get the body of Elpenor, one of our crew who had died there. We cut firewood from the forest near the cliff that stuck out into the sea. After we cried over him and mourned our lost friend, we held his funeral ceremony. When his body and armor had been burned to ashes, we built a pile of stones over the spot, placed a marker stone on top, and stuck his rowing oar at the very top of the pile—the same oar he had used when he was alive.

While we were doing all this, Circe knew we had returned from the land of the dead. She dressed herself and hurried to us as fast as she could, bringing her servant girls with bread, meat, and wine. She stood among us and said, "You have done something incredibly brave by going down alive to the house of Hades, the land of the dead. You will have died twice while other people die only once. Now stay here for the rest of today, eat and drink your fill, and continue your voyage tomorrow morning at dawn. Meanwhile, I will tell Odysseus about the dangers ahead and explain everything so you won't suffer disaster on land or sea."

We agreed to do what she suggested and feasted all day long until the sun went down. When darkness came, my men lay down to sleep by the ropes that held our ship. Then Circe took me by the hand and led me away from the others. She sat down beside me and asked me to tell her about all our adventures in the underworld.

"Good," she said when I finished my story. "Now listen carefully to what I'm about to tell you—the gods themselves will help you remember these warnings. First, you will come to the Sirens, magical creatures who enchant everyone who comes near them. If anyone foolishly sails too close and hears the Sirens singing, his wife and children will never welcome him home again. The Sirens sit in a green meadow and sing so sweetly that they lure sailors to their death. Around them lies a huge pile of dead men's bones with rotting flesh still clinging to them. So sail past these Sirens quickly, and plug your men's ears with soft wax so none of them can hear. But if you want to listen yourself, have your men tie you tightly to the mast as you stand upright. They must bind the ropes firmly to the mast itself so you can enjoy listening safely. If you beg and plead with them to untie you, they must bind you even tighter."

"After your crew takes you past the Sirens, I can't give you clear directions about which path to choose next. I'll describe both dangers, and you must decide for yourself. One route leads past some towering rocks where the dark blue waves crash with terrible fury. Even the blessed gods call these rocks the Wandering Rocks. Not even birds can fly past them safely—not even the gentle doves that carry ambrosia (the food of the gods) to mighty Zeus. The jagged rocks always snatch one of them, and Zeus has to send another dove to replace it. No ship that has ever approached these rocks has escaped. The waves carry away wreckage and dead bodies in whirlwinds of fire. Only one ship ever made it through—the famous Argo carrying Jason and his heroes. Even that ship would have crashed, except that the goddess Hera guided it past because she loved Jason."

"Of the two towering rocks on the other route, one reaches up to heaven with its peak lost in dark clouds. The clouds never leave it, so the top is never clear, not even in summer or early fall. No person, even with twenty hands and twenty feet, could get a grip on it and climb up, because it's as smooth as polished stone and completely straight up. Halfway up is a large cave facing west toward the land of darkness. You must steer your ship past this way, but the cave is so high that even the strongest archer couldn't shoot an arrow into it. Inside lives Scylla, who barks with a voice like a young dog, but she's actually a horrible monster. No one—not even a god—could look at her without being terrified. She has twelve misshapen feet and six enormously long necks. At the end of each neck is a frightful head with three rows of sharp teeth packed tightly together, ready to crunch anyone to death instantly. She sits deep in her shadowy cave, sticking out her heads and looking all around the rock, fishing for dolphins, sharks, or any bigger sea monster she can catch. No ship has ever sailed past without losing some men, because she shoots out all six heads at once and grabs a man in each mouth."

"The other rock sits lower in the water, and they're so close together there's barely an arrow's shot between them. A large fig tree with thick leaves grows on top of it, and underneath lies the deadly whirlpool of Charybdis. Three times each day she spits up the seawater, and three times she sucks it back down. Make sure you're not there when she's sucking it down, because not even Neptune, god of the sea, could save you then. You must hug the side with Scylla and sail past as fast as possible. It's better to lose six men than your entire crew."
"Isn't there any way," I asked, "to escape Charybdis while also fighting off Scylla when she tries to harm my men?"

"You daredevil!" the goddess replied. "You always want to fight someone or something! You won't let yourself be beaten even by immortal beings. Scylla isn't mortal—she's savage, wild, cruel, and unbeatable. There's no fighting her. Your best chance is to sail past her rock as quickly as possible. If you waste time putting on your armor, she might strike again with all six heads and snatch up another half-dozen of your men. So drive your ship past at full speed, and shout loudly to Crataiis, who is Scylla's mother—curse her! Then she'll stop Scylla from attacking you a second time."

"Next you'll come to the island of Thrinacia, where you'll see many herds of cattle and flocks of sheep belonging to the sun-god. There are seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep, with fifty animals in each group. These animals never breed or die, and they're tended by the goddesses Phaethusa and Lampetie, daughters of the sun-god Hyperion. When their mother finished nursing them, she sent them to this distant island to watch over their father's flocks and herds. If you leave these animals alone and think only of getting home, you may still reach Ithaca after much hardship. But if you harm them, I warn you that both your ship and your companions will be destroyed. Even if you yourself escape, you'll return home late, in terrible condition, after losing all your men."

Here Circe finished speaking, and golden Dawn began to show in the sky. The goddess went back inland, and I returned to the ship and told my men to untie the moorings. They quickly climbed aboard, took their places, and began to strike the gray sea with their oars. Soon the great and clever goddess Circe sent us a fair wind that blew steadily from behind, filling our sails perfectly. So we took care of the ship's equipment and let her sail as the wind and helmsman directed.

Then, feeling very worried, I spoke to my men: "Friends, it's not right for only one or two of us to know the prophecies Circe gave me. I'll tell you everything, so whether we live or die, we'll face it with our eyes open. First, she said we must stay away from the Sirens, who sit and sing beautifully in a field of flowers. She said I could listen to them myself as long as no one else did. So take me and tie me to the crosspiece halfway up the mast. Bind me as I stand upright with ropes so tight I can't possibly break free, and tie the rope ends to the mast itself. If I beg and pray for you to set me free, then tie me even tighter."

I had barely finished explaining everything to my men when we reached the island of the two Sirens, helped by favorable wind. Suddenly the wind died completely—there wasn't a breath of air or a ripple on the water. The men rolled up the sails and stored them, then took up their oars and made the water white with foam from their rowing. Meanwhile, I took a large wheel of wax and cut it into small pieces with my sword. Then I kneaded the wax in my strong hands until it became soft from the squeezing and the rays of the sun. I plugged the ears of all my men with the wax, and they tied me hand and foot to the mast as I stood upright on the crosspiece. Then they kept rowing. When we got close enough to shore for the ship to be heard, the Sirens saw us approaching and began their song.

"Come here," they sang, "famous Odysseus, pride of the Greeks, and listen to our voices. No one has ever sailed past us without stopping to hear the enchanting sweetness of our song—and whoever listens goes away not only charmed but wiser. We know all the suffering the gods brought upon the Greeks and Trojans at Troy, and we can tell you everything that will happen in the world."

They sang these words so beautifully that I desperately wanted to hear more. I made signs by frowning at my men to untie me, but instead they rowed harder. Eurylochus and Perimedes bound me with even stronger ropes until we were out of hearing range of the Sirens' voices. Only then did my men take the wax from their ears and untie me.

Right after we passed the island, I saw a huge wave with spray shooting up from it, and I heard a loud roaring sound. The men were so frightened they let go of their oars, and the whole sea echoed with the rushing waters. But the ship stopped moving because the men had stopped rowing. I went around encouraging each man not to lose heart.

"Friends," I said, "this isn't the first time we've been in danger. We're not in nearly as bad a situation as when the Cyclops trapped us in his cave. Even then, my courage and wise planning saved us, and we'll live to look back on this too. Now do as I say: trust in Zeus and row with all your strength. Helmsman, these are your orders—pay attention because the ship is in your hands. Steer away from those foaming rapids and stay close to the rock, or the current will catch us and sweep us over there before you know it, and that will be the death of us all."

They did as I commanded, but I said nothing about the terrible monster Scylla. I knew the men would stop rowing if I told them and would huddle together in the ship's hold instead. I disobeyed Circe's strict instructions in one thing only—I put on my armor. Then, grabbing two strong spears, I took my position at the front of the ship, because that's where I expected to first see the monster who would harm my men so badly. But I couldn't spot her anywhere, though I strained my eyes searching every part of the gloomy rock.

We entered the narrow strait in great fear, because on one side was Scylla, and on the other side terrible Charybdis kept sucking up the salt water. When she vomited it back up, it was like water in a huge pot boiling over a great fire, and the spray reached the tops of the rocks on both sides. When she began to suck it down again, we could see all the water inside swirling around and around. It made a deafening noise as it crashed against the rocks. We could see the bottom of the whirlpool, all black with sand and mud, and the men were terrified out of their wits. While we were distracted by this, expecting every moment to die, Scylla suddenly pounced down on us and snatched up my six best men. I looked back at both the ship and my crew, and in an instant I saw their hands and feet high above me, struggling in the air as Scylla carried them off. I heard them call out my name in one final, despairing cry. Just like when a fisherman sits on a jutting rock with his spear, throws bait into the water to trick little fish, then spears them and throws them gasping onto the land—that's exactly how Scylla brought these struggling men to her rock and crunched them up at the entrance to her den while they screamed and reached out their hands to me in their death agony. This was the most horrible sight I saw in all my travels.

After we passed the Wandering Rocks with Scylla and terrible Charybdis, we reached the noble island of the sun-god, where the beautiful cattle and sheep of Hyperion lived. While still at sea, I could hear the cattle lowing as they returned home to their pens and the sheep bleating. Then I remembered what the blind prophet Tiresias had told me, and how carefully Circe had warned me to avoid the island of the blessed sun-god. Feeling very troubled, I said to my men, "Friends, I know you're exhausted, but listen while I tell you the prophecy Tiresias gave me, and how carefully Circe warned me to stay away from the island of the blessed sun-god. She said this is where our worst danger lies. So steer the ship away from this island."

The men were dismayed by this, and Eurylochus immediately gave me a defiant answer. "Odysseus," he said, "you're being cruel. You're very strong yourself and never get tired—you seem to be made of iron. Now, even though your men are exhausted from hard work and lack of sleep, you won't let them land and cook a good meal on this island. Instead, you tell us to sail out to sea and wander aimlessly through the night. It's during the night that dangerous winds blow hardest and wreck ships. How can we escape if one of those sudden storms comes up from the south or west, the kind that often destroy vessels when the gods are angry? Let's obey the commands of night and prepare our supper here by the ship. Tomorrow morning we'll board again and sail out to sea."

Eurylochus spoke this way, and all the men agreed with him. I could see that the gods meant trouble for us, and I said, "You force me to give in because you're many against one. But each of you must swear a solemn oath that if you find a herd of cattle or a large flock of sheep, you won't be so foolish as to kill even one animal. You'll be satisfied with the food Circe gave us."

They all swore the oath as I demanded. When they finished, we anchored the ship in a harbor near a freshwater stream. The men went ashore and cooked their dinners. After they had eaten and drunk enough, they began talking about their poor companions whom Scylla had grabbed and eaten. This made them start crying, and they wept until they fell into a deep sleep.

During the third watch of the night, when the stars had moved to different positions, Zeus sent a powerful gale that blew like a hurricane. Land and sea were covered with thick clouds, and darkness poured down from the heavens. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared in the morning, we brought the ship to shore and pulled her into a cave where sea-nymphs held their meetings and dances. I called the men together for a council.

"Friends," I said, "we have food and drink on the ship, so let's be careful not to touch the cattle, or we'll suffer for it. These cattle and sheep belong to the mighty sun-god, who sees and hears everything." Again they promised they would obey.

For a whole month the wind blew steadily from the south—there was no other wind except south and east. As long as bread and wine lasted, the men didn't touch the cattle when they were hungry. But when they had eaten everything on the ship, they were forced to hunt further away with hooks and fishing lines, catching birds and taking whatever they could find, because they were starving. One day I went up into the island's interior to pray to heaven to show me some way to escape. When I had gone far enough to be away from all my men and found a place sheltered from the wind, I washed my hands and prayed to all the gods on Mount Olympus. Before long, they sent me into a deep sleep.

Meanwhile, Eurylochus was giving bad advice to the men. "Listen to me, my poor friends," he said. "All ways of dying are terrible, but there's none worse than starving to death. Why don't we take the best of these cattle and sacrifice them to the immortal gods? If we ever get back to Ithaca, we can build a beautiful temple to the sun-god and fill it with wonderful offerings. But if he's determined to sink our ship in revenge for these cattle, and the other gods agree with him, I'd rather drink seawater once and be done with it than slowly starve to death on this deserted island."

Eurylochus spoke this way, and the men agreed with him. The beautiful, healthy cattle were grazing not far from the ship. The men drove in the best ones and stood around them saying prayers. Since they had no barley meal for the sacrifice, they used tender oak leaves instead. After praying, they killed the cattle and prepared the meat. They cut out the thigh bones, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and placed pieces of raw meat on top. They had no wine to pour over the sacrifice while it cooked, so they kept sprinkling water on it while the inner parts grilled. When the thigh bones were burned and they had tasted the organs, they cut up the rest and put the pieces on spits to roast.

By this time my deep sleep had ended, and I headed back toward the ship and seashore. As I got closer, I began to smell roasting meat, so I cried out in prayer to the immortal gods. "Father Zeus," I exclaimed, "and all you other gods who live in eternal happiness, you've played a cruel trick on me by sending me that sleep. Look what terrible things my men have done while I was gone!"

Meanwhile, Lampetie went straight to the sun-god and told him we had been killing his cattle. He flew into a great rage and said to the immortals, "Father Zeus and all you other gods who live in eternal happiness, I demand revenge on Odysseus's crew! They had the nerve to kill my cattle, which were the one thing I loved to see whether I was traveling up to heaven or back down again. If they don't pay me back for my cattle, I'll go down to Hades and shine among the dead instead."
"Sun-god," said Zeus, "keep on shining for us gods and for people on the fertile earth. I'll smash their ship into tiny pieces with a white lightning bolt as soon as they sail out to sea."
Calypso told me all this later. She said she had heard it directly from Hermes, the messenger god.

As soon as I reached my ship and the seashore, I scolded each man separately, but we couldn't undo what was done—the cattle were already dead. And indeed, the gods immediately began showing strange signs among us. The cattle hides crawled around by themselves, and the meat on the spits began to moo like living cows. The meat, whether cooked or raw, kept making noises just like cattle do.

For six days my men kept slaughtering the best cattle and feasting on them. But when Zeus added a seventh day, the fury of the storm calmed down. We went on board, raised our masts, spread the sails, and sailed out to sea. As soon as we were far from the island with nothing visible but sky and sea, Zeus raised a black cloud over our ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it. We didn't travel much further before we were hit by a terrific squall from the west that snapped the ropes holding our mast, so it fell backward. All the ship's equipment tumbled around in the bottom of the vessel. The mast struck the helmsman in the stern, crushing his skull to pieces. He fell overboard as if diving, with no life left in him.

Then Zeus hurled his thunderbolts, and the ship spun around and around, filled with fire and the smell of sulfur as lightning struck it. All the men fell into the sea and were carried around in the water near the ship, looking like seagulls. But the god took away any chance of them ever getting home again.

I held onto the ship until the sea knocked her sides away from the keel, which floated by itself. The waves also broke the mast away from the ship in the direction of the keel. But there was still a strong leather strap hanging from the mast, and I used this to tie the mast and keel together. Sitting astride them like riding a horse, I was carried wherever the winds wanted to take me.

The western gale had spent its force, and the wind shifted to the south again, which frightened me because I might be carried back to the terrible whirlpool of Charybdis. This is exactly what happened—I was carried along by the waves all night, and by sunrise I had reached Scylla's rock and the whirlpool. Charybdis was sucking down the salt seawater, but I was lifted up toward the fig tree. I grabbed onto it and clung like a bat. I couldn't plant my feet anywhere to stand securely because the roots were far below and the branches that shaded the whole pool were too high, too huge, and too spread out for me to reach. So I hung there patiently, waiting for the whirlpool to spit out my mast and keel again—and it seemed like a very long time. A judge isn't more happy to go home for dinner after being stuck in court all day with difficult cases than I was to see my makeshift raft beginning to work its way out of the whirlpool again. Finally, I let go with my hands and feet and fell heavily into the sea, right next to my raft. I climbed onto it and began rowing with my hands. As for Scylla, the father of gods and men wouldn't let her see me again—otherwise I certainly would have died.

I was carried along like this for nine days, until on the tenth night the gods washed me ashore on the island of Ogygia, where the great and powerful goddess Calypso lived. She took me in and was kind to me, but I don't need to say more about that because I told you and your noble wife all about it yesterday, and I hate repeating the same story over and over again.

chapters.title: Book XIII — Ulysses leaves scheria and returns to ithaca.
paragraphs: Ulysses finished his amazing story, and everyone in the great hall sat perfectly still, completely spellbound by his adventures. Finally, King Alcinous broke the silence.

"Ulysses," said the king, "now that you've reached my palace, I'm sure you'll make it home safely, no matter how much you've suffered before. But listen, all you nobles who come here each night to drink my finest wine and hear my singers—our guest has already packed the clothes, gold, and other treasures you've given him. Let's each give him one more gift: a large bronze tripod and a cooking pot. We'll collect money from everyone later to pay for these expensive presents, since no one person should bear such a cost alone."

Everyone agreed this was a good idea, then went home to sleep. When Dawn appeared with her rosy fingers, they hurried to the ship carrying their bronze pots. King Alcinous went aboard and made sure everything was safely stored under the benches so nothing would slide around and hurt the rowers. Then they returned to the palace for dinner. The king sacrificed a bull to Zeus, the king of all gods. They grilled the meat and had a wonderful feast. The famous singer Demodocus entertained them with songs, but Ulysses kept looking at the sun, eager for it to set so he could begin his journey home. He felt like a farmer who has plowed all day with his oxen and can barely stand, desperate for sunset so he can go eat dinner. When the sun finally went down, Ulysses immediately spoke to the Phaeacians, especially King Alcinous:

"Your majesty, and all of you, farewell! Pour your wine offerings to the gods and send me on my way with joy. You have given me everything I hoped for—an escort home and wonderful gifts. May the gods help me use them well! I pray I'll find my dear wife safe at home with loyal friends, and may heaven bless all of you with happiness for your wives and children. May no evil ever come to your people."

Everyone agreed he had spoken well and that he deserved safe passage home. So King Alcinous called to his servant, "Pontonous, mix the wine and serve everyone, so we can pray to Father Zeus and speed our guest on his journey."

Pontonous mixed the wine and served it to everyone. Each person poured some wine from their seat as an offering to the blessed gods in heaven, but Ulysses stood up and placed his cup in the hands of Queen Arete.
"Farewell, Queen," he said, "from now until old age and death come to you, as they do to all people. I'm leaving now. Be happy in this house with your children, your people, and King Alcinous."

With those words, he crossed the doorway, and King Alcinous sent a man to escort him to the ship. Queen Arete also sent servants—one carrying a clean shirt and cloak, another with his treasure chest, and a third with food and wine. When they reached the shore, the crew loaded everything aboard, including all the food and drink. They spread a soft rug and linen sheet on the deck for Ulysses to sleep comfortably in the back of the ship. He climbed aboard and lay down without a word, while the crew took their places at the oars and untied the rope from the stone post. As soon as they started rowing out to sea, Ulysses fell into a deep, peaceful sleep—almost like death itself.

The ship flew forward like a four-horse chariot racing across a track when the horses feel the whip. Her front end rose and fell like a stallion's neck, and a huge wave of dark blue water foamed behind her. She held steady on course, and even a falcon—the fastest of all birds—couldn't have kept up with her. So she cut through the water, carrying a man as clever as the gods themselves, who now slept peacefully, forgetting all his suffering in war and on the stormy seas.

When the bright morning star appeared, announcing dawn's approach, the ship neared land. Now there's a harbor in Ithaca that belongs to old Phorcys, a sea god. Two rocky points jut out like arms, protecting the harbor from outside storms. Once ships get inside, they can rest safely without even being tied up. At the head of this harbor grows a huge olive tree, and nearby there's a beautiful cave sacred to water nymphs called Naiads. Inside the cave are stone bowls and jars where bees make their honey. The nymphs weave sea-purple robes on great stone looms—an amazing sight! Fresh water always flows there. The cave has two entrances: one facing north where humans can enter, and one facing south that's more mysterious—only gods can use that entrance.

The Phaeacian sailors knew this harbor well and steered their ship straight in. The ship had so much speed that it ran halfway up onto the beach! After landing, they first lifted Ulysses out with his rug and sheet, still fast asleep, and laid him on the sand. Then they unloaded all the gifts that Athena (the goddess of wisdom) had convinced the Phaeacians to give him. They piled everything by the olive tree, away from the road so no passing thief would steal them before Ulysses woke up. Then they sailed for home.

But Neptune, god of the sea, hadn't forgotten his threats against Ulysses, so he spoke with Zeus. "Father Zeus," he said, "the other gods won't respect me anymore if mortals like the Phaeacians—my own relatives—ignore me so completely. I said I'd let Ulysses reach home after suffering enough. I didn't say he'd never get there, since you'd already nodded your head and promised he would. But now they've brought him home in a ship while he slept, and loaded him with more magnificent gifts of bronze, gold, and clothing than he would ever have brought back from Troy with his fair share of the treasure!"

Zeus answered, "What are you talking about, Lord of Earthquakes? The gods certainly respect you. It would be terrible if they insulted someone as old and honored as you. As for mortals, if any are being rude and disrespectful to you, you can always deal with them however you think best. Do whatever you want."

"I would have acted immediately," Neptune replied, "but I didn't want to displease you. Now I'd like to wreck the Phaeacian ship as it returns home. This will stop them from escorting people in the future. I'd also like to bury their city under a huge mountain."

"My friend," Zeus answered, "here's what I suggest: right when the people are watching their ship return to harbor, turn it into a rock that looks like a ship near the shore. This will amaze everyone. Then you can bury their city under the mountain."

When Neptune heard this, he traveled to Scheria where the Phaeacians lived and waited until their fast ship approached the harbor. Then he went up to it, turned it to stone, and slammed it down with his hand, rooting it to the sea floor. After this, he left.

The Phaeacians began talking excitedly to each other. One would turn to his neighbor and say, "Good heavens! Who could have turned our ship to stone just as it was entering port? We could see the whole ship clearly just a moment ago!"

That's how they talked, but they didn't understand what had happened. Then King Alcinous said, "Now I remember my father's old prophecy. He said Neptune would be angry with us for safely escorting everyone across the sea, and would someday wreck a Phaeacian ship returning from an escort and bury our city under a high mountain. This is what my old father used to say, and now it's all coming true! So here's what we must do: first, we must stop giving people escorts when they come here. Second, we must sacrifice twelve of our best bulls to Neptune so he'll have mercy on us and not bury our city under that mountain." When the people heard this, they were terrified and prepared the bulls for sacrifice.

So the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians prayed to King Neptune, standing around his altar. At the same time, Ulysses woke up on his own homeland. He'd been away so long that he didn't recognize it. Also, Athena, Zeus's daughter, had made the day foggy so people wouldn't know he'd returned, giving her time to tell him everything without his wife, citizens, or friends recognizing him until he could get revenge on the wicked suitors (men trying to marry his wife). Everything looked completely different to him—the long paths, the harbors, the cliffs, and the beautiful trees all seemed changed as he stood up and looked at his native land. He slapped his thighs with his hands and cried out in despair.

"Oh no!" he exclaimed. "What kind of people have I ended up with? Are they savage and uncivilized, or kind and welcoming? Where will I put all this treasure, and which way should I go? I wish I'd stayed with the Phaeacians, or gone to some other great chief who would have been good to me and given me an escort. Now I don't know where to put my treasure, and I can't leave it here in case someone steals it. The Phaeacian chiefs and rulers haven't been fair to me—they've left me in the wrong country! They promised to take me back to Ithaca and they haven't done it. May Zeus, who protects travelers, punish them, since he watches over everyone and punishes wrongdoers. Still, I should count my belongings and see if the crew took any of them."

He counted his beautiful bronze pots and cauldrons, his gold, and all his clothes, but nothing was missing. Still, he kept grieving about not being in his own country and wandered up and down the shore of the roaring sea, crying about his terrible situation. Then Athena came to him disguised as a young shepherd with a delicate, royal appearance. She wore a fine cloak folded double over her shoulders, had sandals on her lovely feet, and carried a spear. Ulysses was happy to see her and walked straight over.

"My friend," he said, "you're the first person I've met in this country. I greet you and ask you to be kind to me. Protect my belongings and me too, for I kneel before you and pray to you as if you were a god. Tell me truly—what land and country is this? Who lives here? Am I on an island, or is this the coast of some continent?"

Athena answered, "Stranger, you must be very simple, or come from somewhere far away, not to know what country this is. It's a very famous place that everyone knows, both east and west. It's rocky and not good for driving horses, but it's not a bad island for what it is. It grows plenty of grain and wine grapes, since it gets both rain and dew. It raises cattle and goats, has all kinds of trees, and has springs that never run dry. So, sir, the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy, which I understand is very far from this Greek land."
Ulysses was thrilled to find himself, as Athena told him, in his own country. But he didn't tell the truth and made up a lying story from his naturally cunning heart.

"I heard of Ithaca when I was in Crete across the sea," he said, "and now it seems I've reached it with all these treasures. I left just as much behind for my children, but I'm fleeing because I killed Orsilochus, son of King Idomeneus—the fastest runner in Crete. I killed him because he tried to rob me of the treasure I'd earned from Troy with so much trouble and danger, both in battle and on the dangerous seas. He claimed I hadn't served his father loyally at Troy as a vassal, but had acted like an independent ruler. So I hid by the roadside with one of my followers and speared him as he came into town from the countryside. It was a very dark night and nobody saw us, so no one knew I'd killed him. As soon as I did it, I went to a ship and begged the owners, who were Phoenicians, to take me aboard and bring me to Pylos or Elis, where the Epeans rule. I gave them plenty of treasure to satisfy them. They meant no harm, but the wind blew them off course, and we sailed until we came here by night. We could barely get into the harbor, and none of us mentioned supper though we badly wanted it. We all went ashore and lay down just as we were. I was exhausted and fell asleep immediately, so they took my goods from the ship and placed them beside me where I lay on the sand. Then they sailed away to Sidonia, leaving me here in great distress."

That was his story, but Athena smiled and touched him with her hand. Then she took the form of a beautiful, tall, wise woman. "Anyone who could beat you in tricks and lies would have to be very clever indeed," she said, "even if they were a god! You rascal, full of cunning, never tired of deception—can't you stop your tricks and natural dishonesty even now that you're in your own country? Let's say no more about this, since we can both be deceptive when we need to be. You're the most skilled counselor and speaker among all humans, while I have no equal among the gods for cleverness and subtlety. Didn't you recognize me—Zeus's daughter Athena? I've always been with you, watching over you in all your troubles, and I made the Phaeacians like you so much. Now I've come here again to discuss things with you and help you hide the treasure I made the Phaeacians give you. I want to tell you about the troubles waiting for you in your own house. You'll have to face them, but don't tell anyone—man or woman—that you've come home. Bear everything and put up with everyone's rudeness without saying a word."

Ulysses answered, "A man may know a great deal, goddess, but you're always changing your appearance, so when he meets you it's hard to know if it's really you. But I know this very well: you were very kind to me while we Greeks fought at Troy. But from the day we boarded ships after destroying Priam's city and heaven scattered us—from that day, Athena, I saw no more of you and don't remember you coming to my ship to help me when I was in trouble. I had to wander around sick and miserable until the gods saved me from evil and I reached the Phaeacians' city, where you encouraged me and brought me into town. Now I beg you, by your father's name, tell me the truth. I don't believe I'm really back in Ithaca. I must be in some other country, and you're mocking me and deceiving me with everything you've said. Tell me truly—have I really returned to my own country?"

"You're always thinking like that," Athena replied, "and that's why I can't abandon you in your troubles. You're so clever, shrewd, and cunning. Anyone else returning from such a long voyage would immediately rush home to see his wife and children, but you don't seem to care about asking after them or hearing news about them until you've tested your wife, who stays home constantly grieving for you, having no peace day or night because of the tears she sheds for you. As for my not coming near you, I was never worried about you because I was certain you'd get home safely, though you'd lose all your men. I didn't want to quarrel with my uncle Neptune, who never forgave you for blinding his son, the Cyclops. Now I'll show you the layout of the land, and then you'll believe me. This is the harbor of old Phorcys the sea-god, and here's the olive tree that grows at its head. Near it is the cave sacred to the water nymphs. Here's the overarching cavern where you've offered many acceptable sacrifices to the nymphs, and this is the wooded mountain Neritum."

As she spoke, the goddess cleared away the mist and the land appeared clearly. Then Ulysses rejoiced at finding himself in his own land again and kissed the generous soil. He raised his hands and prayed to the nymphs, saying, "Naiad nymphs, daughters of Zeus, I was sure I'd never see you again, so now I greet you with all my loving prayers, and I'll bring you offerings as in the old days, if Zeus's mighty daughter grants me life and lets my son grow to manhood."

"Take heart and don't worry about that," Athena replied. "Let's focus on storing your belongings right away in the cave, where they'll be completely safe. Let's figure out the best way to manage everything."

Then she went down into the cave to look for the safest hiding places, while Ulysses brought up all the treasure of gold, bronze, and fine clothing the Phaeacians had given him. They stored everything carefully, and Athena placed a stone against the cave's entrance. Then the two sat down by the great olive tree's roots and planned how to destroy the wicked suitors.

"Ulysses," said Athena, "noble son of Laertes, think about how you can deal with these disgraceful men who've been ruling your house for three years, courting your wife and bringing her wedding gifts, while she does nothing but mourn your absence. She gives hope and sends encouraging messages to each of them, but means the complete opposite of what she says."

Ulysses answered, "Truly, goddess, it seems I would have met the same terrible end in my own house as Agamemnon did, if you hadn't given me this timely information. Tell me how I can best get my revenge. Stand beside me and fill my heart with courage, as you did when we destroyed Troy's beautiful crown. Help me now as you did then, and I'll fight three hundred men if you, goddess, will be with me."

"Count on me for that," she said. "I won't lose sight of you once we begin, and I imagine some of those men who are devouring your wealth will splatter the floor with their blood and brains. I'll start by disguising you so no human will recognize you. I'll cover your body with wrinkles and make you lose all your golden hair. I'll dress you in clothes that will make everyone who sees you feel disgusted. I'll make your bright eyes dim and turn you into an ugly sight for the suitors, your wife, and the son you left behind. Then go immediately to the swineherd who takes care of your pigs. He's always been loyal to you and devoted to Penelope and your son. You'll find him feeding his pigs near the rock called Raven by the spring Arethusa, where they're getting fat on acorns and spring water. Stay with him and learn how things are going, while I travel to Sparta to see your son, who's with Menelaus at Lacedaemon. He went there to try to find out if you're still alive."
"But why," asked Ulysses, "didn't you tell him, since you knew everything? Did you want him to go sailing around facing all kinds of hardship while others eat up his inheritance?"

Athena answered, "Don't worry about him. I sent him so he'd gain a good reputation for having made the journey. He's not in any trouble but is staying comfortably with Menelaus, surrounded by every kind of luxury. The suitors have gone out to sea and are lying in wait for him, planning to kill him before he can get home. I don't think they'll succeed. Instead, some of those men who are now eating up your estate will find graves first."

As she spoke, Athena touched him with her wand and covered him with wrinkles. She took away all his golden hair and withered the flesh all over his body. She made his naturally beautiful eyes dim and changed his clothes, throwing an old, ragged wrap around him and a torn, filthy, smoke-stained tunic. She also gave him an untanned deerskin as an outer garment and provided him with a staff and a torn wallet with a twisted strap to sling over his shoulder.
After making these plans together, they parted, and the goddess went straight to Lacedaemon to find Telemachus.

chapters.title: Book XIV — Ulysses in the hut with eumaeus.
paragraphs: Odysseus now left the harbor and took the rocky path up through the woods and over the mountain top until he reached the place where Athena (the goddess of wisdom) had told him he would find the swineherd. This man was the most faithful and hardworking servant Odysseus had. He found him sitting in front of his hut, which was near the pig yards he had built on high ground where you could see far in all directions. He had made the yards large and well-built, with plenty of room for the pigs to run around. He had built them while his master was away, using stones he gathered from the ground, without telling Penelope or Laertes. He had topped the walls with thorn bushes to keep the pigs safe. Outside the yard, he had built a strong fence of split oak posts, placed close together. Inside, he had built twelve separate pens for the mother pigs to sleep in. There were fifty pigs wallowing in each pen, all breeding females. But the male boars slept outside and were much fewer in number, because the suitors kept eating them. The swineherd had to keep sending them the best pigs for their feasts. There were three hundred and sixty boar pigs, and the herdsman's four dogs, which were as fierce as wolves, always slept with them. At that moment, the swineherd was cutting out a pair of sandals from good thick ox hide. Three of his men were out watching the pigs in different places, and he had sent the fourth to town with a boar that he was forced to send to the suitors so they could sacrifice it and feast on it.

When the dogs saw Odysseus, they started barking furiously and rushed at him. But Odysseus was clever enough to sit down and drop the stick he was carrying. Even so, he would have been torn apart by them right there in his own homeland if the swineherd hadn't dropped his ox hide and rushed through the gate at full speed, driving the dogs off by shouting and throwing stones at them. Then he said to Odysseus, "Old man, the dogs nearly made short work of you, and then you would have gotten me in trouble. The gods have given me quite enough worries without that, for I have lost the best of masters, and I'm constantly sad about it. I have to take care of pigs for other people to eat, while he, if he's still alive to see the light of day, is starving in some distant land. But come inside, and when you've had your fill of bread and wine, tell me where you come from and all about your troubles."

With that, the swineherd led the way into the hut and told him to sit down. He spread a thick bed of rushes on the floor, and on top of this he threw a shaggy chamois skin—a great thick one—that he used to sleep on at night. Odysseus was pleased at being welcomed so kindly, and said, "May Zeus, sir, and the rest of the gods grant you your heart's desire in return for the kind way you have received me."

To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus, "Stranger, even if a poorer man than you came here, it would not be right for me to insult him, for all strangers and beggars are protected by Zeus (the king of the gods). You must take what you can get and be thankful, for servants live in fear when they have young lords for their masters. And this is my misfortune now, for heaven has prevented the return of him who would have always been good to me and given me something of my own—a house, a piece of land, a good-looking wife, and all else that a generous master gives a servant who has worked hard for him, and whose work the gods have blessed as they have mine in the job I hold. If my master had grown old here, he would have done great things for me, but he is gone. I wish that Helen's whole family were completely destroyed, for she has been the death of many a good man. It was this matter that took my master to Troy, the land of fine horses, to fight the Trojans for King Agamemnon." (Helen was the beautiful queen whose kidnapping started the Trojan War.)

As he spoke, he tied his belt around him and went to the pens where the young suckling pigs were kept. He picked out two which he brought back and sacrificed. He burned off their hair, cut them up, and put them on spits. When the meat was cooked, he brought it all in and set it before Odysseus, hot and still on the spit. Odysseus sprinkled it with white barley meal. The swineherd then mixed wine in a bowl made of ivy-wood, and taking a seat across from Odysseus, told him to begin eating.

"Dig in, stranger," he said, "to a dish of servant's pork. The fat pigs have to go to the suitors, who eat them up without shame or worry. But the blessed gods do not love such shameful behavior, and they respect those who do what is lawful and right. Even fierce pirates who go raiding other people's lands, and Zeus gives them their treasure—even they, when they have filled their ships and returned home, feel guilty and fearfully await punishment. But some god seems to have told these people that Odysseus is dead and gone. They will not, therefore, go back to their own homes and propose marriage in the proper way, but waste his property by force, without fear or limit. Not a day or night passes but they sacrifice not just one victim or two, and they drink up his wine freely, for he was extremely rich. No other great man either in Ithaca or on the mainland is as rich as he was. He had as much as twenty men put together. I will tell you what he had. There are twelve herds of cattle on the mainland, and as many flocks of sheep. There are also twelve droves of pigs, while his own men and hired strangers tend twelve widely scattered herds of goats. Here in Ithaca he runs eleven large flocks of goats on the far end of the island, and they are watched by excellent goat herds. Each one of these sends the suitors the best goat in the flock every day. As for myself, I'm in charge of the pigs that you see here, and I have to keep picking out the best I have and sending them to the suitors."

This was his story, but Odysseus went on eating and drinking hungrily without a word, planning his revenge. When he had eaten enough and was satisfied, the swineherd took the bowl from which he usually drank, filled it with wine, and gave it to Odysseus, who was pleased and said as he took it in his hands, "My friend, who was this master of yours who bought you and paid for you, so rich and so powerful as you tell me? You say he died in the cause of King Agamemnon. Tell me who he was, in case I may have met such a person. Zeus and the other gods know, but I may be able to give you news of him, for I have traveled much."

Eumaeus answered, "Old man, no traveler who comes here with news will get Odysseus's wife and son to believe his story. Nevertheless, tramps looking for a place to stay keep coming with their mouths full of lies, and not a word of truth. Everyone who finds his way to Ithaca goes to my mistress and tells her falsehoods, and she takes them in, treats them well, and asks them all kinds of questions, crying all the time as women do when they have lost their husbands. And you too, old man, would doubtless make up a very pretty story for a shirt and a cloak. But the wolves and birds of prey have long since torn Odysseus to pieces, or the fish of the sea have eaten him, and his bones are lying buried deep in sand on some foreign shore. He is dead and gone, and it's a bad business for all his friends—especially for me. Go where I may, I shall never find so good a master, not even if I were to go home to my mother and father where I was born and raised. I don't care so much about my parents now, though I would dearly like to see them again in my own country. It is the loss of Odysseus that grieves me most. I cannot speak of him without respect, though he is no longer here, for he was very fond of me and took such care of me that wherever he may be, I shall always honor his memory."

"My friend," replied Odysseus, "you are very stubborn and very hard to convince about your master's coming home again. Nevertheless, I will not merely say, but will swear, that he is coming. Do not give me anything for my news until he has actually come. Then you may give me a shirt and cloak of good quality if you will. I am in great need, but I will not take anything at all until then, for I hate a man, as much as I hate the fires of hell, who lets his poverty tempt him into lying. I swear by King Zeus, by the sacred laws of hospitality, and by that hearth of Odysseus to which I have now come, that all will surely happen as I have said it will. Odysseus will return in this very same year. With the end of this moon and the beginning of the next, he will be here to punish all those who are mistreating his wife and son."

To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus, "Old man, you will neither get paid for bringing good news, nor will Odysseus ever come home. Drink your wine in peace, and let us talk about something else. Do not keep reminding me of all this. It always pains me when anyone speaks about my honored master. As for your oath, we will forget about it, but I only wish he may come, as do Penelope, his old father Laertes, and his son Telemachus. I am terribly unhappy too about this same boy of his. He was growing up fast into manhood and promised to be no worse a man, in face and figure, than his father. But someone, either god or man, has been unsettling his mind, so he has gone off to Pylos to try and get news of his father, and the suitors are lying in wait for him as he comes home, hoping to leave the house of Arceisius without an heir in Ithaca. But let us say no more about him, and leave him to be captured, or else to escape if Zeus holds his hand over him to protect him. And now, old man, tell me your own story. Tell me also, for I want to know, who you are and where you come from. Tell me of your town and parents, what kind of ship you came in, how your crew brought you to Ithaca, and from what country they said they came—for you cannot have come by land."

And Odysseus answered, "I will tell you all about it. If there were meat and wine enough, and we could stay here in the hut with nothing to do but eat and drink while the others go to their work, I could easily talk on for a whole twelve months without ever finishing the story of the sorrows with which it has pleased heaven to visit me.

"I am by birth a Cretan. My father was a well-to-do man who had many sons born in marriage, whereas I was the son of a slave woman he had bought as a mistress. Nevertheless, my father Castor, son of Hylax (whose family line I claim, and who was held in the highest honor among the Cretans for his wealth, success, and the courage of his sons) put me on the same level with my brothers who had been born in wedlock. When death took him to the house of Hades (the underworld), his sons divided his property and cast lots for their shares, but to me they gave only a small holding and little else. Nevertheless, my courage enabled me to marry into a rich family, for I was not given to bragging or shirking on the battlefield. It is all over now, but still, if you look at the straw you can see what the grain was like, for I have had trouble enough and to spare. The gods of war made me strong in battle. When I had picked my men to surprise the enemy with an ambush, I never gave death so much as a thought, but was the first to leap forward and spear all whom I could catch. Such was I in battle, but I did not care about farm work or the quiet home life of those who would raise children. My delight was in ships, fighting, javelins, and arrows—things that most men shudder to think of. But one man likes one thing and another likes another, and this was what I was most naturally drawn to. Before the Greeks went to Troy, nine times was I in command of men and ships on foreign missions, and I gathered much wealth. I had my pick of the treasure at first, and much more was given to me later on.

"My house grew quickly and I became a great man among the Cretans, but when Zeus decided on that terrible expedition in which so many died, the people required me and Idomeneus to lead their ships to Troy, and there was no way out of it, for they insisted on our doing so. There we fought for nine whole years, but in the tenth we captured the city of Priam and sailed home again as heaven scattered us. Then it was that Zeus planned evil against me. I spent only one month happily with my children, wife, and property, and then I got the idea of attacking Egypt, so I fitted out a fine fleet and manned it. I had nine ships, and the people flocked to fill them. For six days my men and I feasted, and I provided them many animals both for sacrifice to the gods and for themselves, but on the seventh day we went on board and set sail from Crete with a fair north wind behind us, going as smoothly as if we were sailing down a river. Nothing went wrong with any of our ships, and we had no sickness on board, but sat where we were and let the ships go as the wind and helmsmen took them. On the fifth day we reached the river of Egypt. There I stationed my ships in the river, telling my men to stay by them and keep guard over them while I sent out scouts to look around from every high point.

"But the men disobeyed my orders, followed their own ideas, and attacked the land of the Egyptians, killing the men and taking their wives and children captive. The alarm was soon carried to the city, and when they heard the war cry, the people came out at daybreak until the plain was filled with horsemen and foot soldiers and with the gleam of armor. Then Zeus spread panic among my men, and they would no longer face the enemy, for they found themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive to do forced labor for them. Zeus, however, put it in my mind to do this—and I wish I had died then and there in Egypt instead, for there was much sorrow in store for me—I took off my helmet and shield and dropped my spear from my hand. Then I went straight up to the king's chariot, grabbed his knees and kissed them, and he spared my life, told me to get into his chariot, and took me weeping to his own home. Many attacked me with their ash spears and tried to kill me in their fury, but the king protected me, for he feared the anger of Zeus, the protector of strangers, who punishes those who do evil.

"I stayed there for seven years and gathered much money among the Egyptians, for they all gave me something. But when it was going on for eight years, there came a certain Phoenician, a cunning scoundrel who had already committed all sorts of crimes, and this man talked me into going with him to Phoenicia, where his house and possessions were. I stayed there for a whole twelve months, but at the end of that time when months and days had gone by until the same season had come round again, he put me on board a ship bound for Libya, pretending that I was to take a cargo along with him to that place, but really so that he might sell me as a slave and take the money I would bring. I suspected his plan, but went on board with him, for I could not help it.

"The ship ran before a fresh north wind until we had reached the sea that lies between Crete and Libya. There, however, Zeus planned their destruction, for as soon as we were well out from Crete and could see nothing but sea and sky, he raised a black cloud over our ship and the sea grew dark beneath it. Then Zeus let fly with his thunderbolts and the ship spun round and round and was filled with fire and sulfur as the lightning struck it. The men all fell into the sea. They were carried about in the water around the ship looking like so many seagulls, but the god took away all chance of them getting home again. I was terrified. Zeus, however, sent the ship's mast within my reach, which saved my life, for I clung to it and drifted before the fury of the gale. Nine days did I drift, but in the darkness of the tenth night a great wave carried me to the Thesprotian coast. There Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, entertained me hospitably without charging me anything at all—for his son found me when I was nearly dead with cold and exhaustion, and he raised me by the hand, took me to his father's house, and gave me clothes to wear.

"There it was that I heard news of Odysseus, for the king told me he had entertained him and shown him much hospitality while he was on his homeward journey. He showed me also the treasure of gold and wrought iron that Odysseus had gathered. There was enough to keep his family for ten generations, so much had he left in the house of King Pheidon. But the king said Odysseus had gone to Dodona so that he might learn Zeus's mind from the god's high oak tree, and know whether after so long an absence he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret. Moreover, the king swore in my presence, making drink-offerings in his own house as he did so, that the ship was by the water side and the crew found that should take him to his own country. He sent me off, however, before Odysseus returned, for there happened to be a Thesprotian ship sailing for the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, and he told those in charge of her to be sure and take me safely to King Acastus.

"These men hatched a plot against me that would have reduced me to extreme misery, for when the ship had gotten some way out from land, they decided to sell me as a slave. They stripped me of the shirt and cloak that I was wearing and gave me instead the tattered old rags in which you now see me. Then, toward nightfall, they reached the cultivated lands of Ithaca, and there they tied me up with a strong rope in the ship, while they went on shore to get supper by the seaside.
