But the gods soon undid my bonds for me, and having drawn my rags over my head, I slid down the rudder into the sea, where I struck out and swam until I was well clear of them and came ashore near a thick wood in which I lay hidden. They were very angry at my having escaped and went searching about for me, until at last they thought it was no use and went back to their ship. The gods, having hidden me so easily, then took me to a good man's door—for it seems that I am not to die yet."

To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus, "Poor unhappy stranger, I have found the story of your misfortunes very interesting, but that part about Odysseus is not right, and you will never get me to believe it. Why should a man like you go about telling lies in this way? I know all about my master's return. The gods, one and all of them, hate him, or they would have taken him before Troy, or let him die with friends around him when the days of his fighting were done. For then the Greeks would have built a mound over his ashes and his son would have inherited his fame, but now the storm winds have carried him away we know not where.

"As for me, I live out of the way here with the pigs and never go to town unless Penelope sends for me when some news about Odysseus arrives. Then they all sit around and ask questions, both those who grieve over the king's absence and those who rejoice at it because they can eat up his property without paying for it. For my own part, I have never cared about asking anyone else since the time when I was fooled by an Aetolian who had killed a man and come a long way until at last he reached my station, and I was very kind to him. He said he had seen Odysseus with Idomeneus among the Cretans, repairing his ships which had been damaged in a storm. He said Odysseus would return in the following summer or autumn with his men, and that he would bring back much wealth. And now you, you unfortunate old man, since fate has brought you to my door, do not try to flatter me in this way with false hopes. It is not for any such reason that I shall treat you kindly, but only out of respect for Zeus, the god of hospitality, fearing him and pitying you."

Odysseus answered, "I see that you are of an unbelieving mind. I have given you my oath, and yet you will not believe me. Let us then make a bargain and call all the gods in heaven to witness it. If your master comes home, give me a cloak and shirt of good quality and send me to Dulichium where I want to go. But if he does not come as I say he will, set your men on me and tell them to throw me from that cliff, as a warning to tramps not to go about the country telling lies."

"And a pretty figure I should cut then," replied Eumaeus, "both now and hereafter, if I were to kill you after receiving you into my hut and showing you hospitality. I should have to say my prayers very earnestly if I did. But it is just supper time and I hope my men will come in soon, so that we may cook something tasty for supper."

Thus they talked, and presently the swineherds came up with the pigs, which were then shut up for the night in their pens, making a tremendous squealing as they were being driven into them. But Eumaeus called to his men and said, "Bring in the best pig you have, so that I may sacrifice him for this stranger, and we will enjoy him ourselves. We have had trouble enough all this time feeding pigs while others reap the benefit of our work."

With this he began chopping firewood, while the others brought in a fine fat five-year-old boar pig and set it at the altar. Eumaeus did not forget the gods, for he was a man of good principles, so the first thing he did was to cut bristles from the pig's face and throw them into the fire, praying to all the gods as he did so that Odysseus might return home again. Then he clubbed the pig with a piece of oak which he had kept back when he was chopping the firewood and stunned it, while the others killed and singed it. Then they cut it up, and Eumaeus began by putting raw pieces from each joint on some of the fat. These he sprinkled with barley meal and laid upon the embers. They cut the rest of the meat up small, put the pieces on spits and roasted them until they were done. When they had taken them off the spits, they threw them on the serving board in a heap. The swineherd, who was a very fair man, then stood up to give everyone his share. He made seven portions. One of these he set apart for Hermes, the son of Maia, and the nymphs (nature spirits), praying to them as he did so. The others he gave out to each man. He gave Odysseus some slices cut lengthways down the loin as a mark of special honor, and Odysseus was very pleased. "I hope, Eumaeus," said he, "that Zeus will be as well disposed toward you as I am, for the respect you are showing to an outcast like myself."
To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus, "Eat, my good fellow, and enjoy your supper, such as it is. God gives this and withholds that, just as he thinks right, for he can do whatever he chooses."

As he spoke, he cut off the first piece and offered it as a burnt sacrifice to the immortal gods. Then he poured out wine as an offering, put the cup in the hands of Odysseus, and sat down to his own portion. Mesaulius brought them their bread. The swineherd had bought this man on his own from among the Taphians during his master's absence, and had paid for him with his own money without saying anything either to his mistress or Laertes. They then put their hands on the good things that were before them, and when they had had enough to eat and drink, Mesaulius took away what was left of the bread, and they all went to bed after having made a hearty supper.

Now the night came on stormy and very dark, for there was no moon. It poured without stopping, and the wind blew strong from the west, which brings rain, so Odysseus thought he would see whether Eumaeus, in the excellent care he took of him, would take off his own cloak and give it to him, or make one of his men give him one. "Listen to me," said he, "Eumaeus and the rest of you. When I have said a prayer, I will tell you something. It is the wine that makes me talk in this way. Wine will make even a wise man start singing, make him chuckle and dance and say many words that he had better leave unspoken. Still, as I have begun, I will go on. Would that I were still young and strong as when we set up an ambush before Troy. Menelaus and Odysseus were the leaders, but I was in command also, for the other two wanted it so. When we had come up to the wall of the city, we crouched down beneath our armor and lay there under cover of the reeds and thick brushwood that grew about the swamp. It started to freeze with a north wind blowing. The snow fell small and fine like frost, and our shields were coated thick with ice. The others had all gotten cloaks and shirts and slept comfortably enough with their shields around their shoulders, but I had carelessly left my cloak behind me, not thinking that I should be too cold, and had gone off in nothing but my shirt and shield. When the night was two-thirds through and the stars had shifted their places, I nudged Odysseus who was close to me with my elbow, and he immediately listened.
"'Odysseus,' said I, 'this cold will be the death of me, for I have no cloak. Some god fooled me into setting off with nothing on but my shirt, and I do not know what to do.'
"Odysseus, who was as crafty as he was brave, came up with the following plan:
"'Keep still,' said he in a low voice, 'or the others will hear you.' Then he raised his head on his elbow.
"'My friends,' said he, 'I have had a dream from heaven in my sleep. We are a long way from the ships. I wish someone would go down and tell Agamemnon to send us up more men at once.'

"At this, Thoas, son of Andraemon, threw off his cloak and set out running to the ships, and I took the cloak and lay in it comfortably enough until morning. Would that I were still young and strong as I was in those days, for then some one of you swineherds would give me a cloak both out of good will and for the respect due to a brave soldier. But now people look down on me because my clothes are shabby."

And Eumaeus answered, "Old man, you have told us an excellent story and have said nothing so far but what is quite satisfactory. For the present, therefore, you shall want neither clothing nor anything else that a stranger in distress may reasonably expect, but tomorrow morning you will have to wrap your own old rags about your body again, for we do not have many spare cloaks or shirts up here. Every man has only one. When Odysseus's son comes home again, he will give you both cloak and shirt and send you wherever you may want to go."

With this he got up and made a bed for Odysseus by throwing some goatskins and sheepskins on the ground in front of the fire. Here Odysseus lay down, and Eumaeus covered him over with a great heavy cloak that he kept for a change in case of extremely bad weather.

Thus did Odysseus sleep, and the young men slept beside him. But the swineherd did not like sleeping away from his pigs, so he got ready to go outside, and Odysseus was glad to see that he looked after his property during his master's absence. First he slung his sword over his strong shoulders and put on a thick cloak to keep out the wind. He also took the skin of a large and well-fed goat, and a javelin in case of attack from men or dogs. Thus equipped, he went to his rest where the pigs were camping under an overhanging rock that gave them shelter from the north wind.

chapters.title: Book XV — Minerva summons telemachus from lacedaemon—he meets with theoclymenus at pylos and brings him to ithaca—on landing he goes to the hut of eumaeus.
paragraphs: But Athena, goddess of wisdom, went to the beautiful city of Sparta to find Odysseus's son and tell him it was time to come home. She found Telemachus and his friend Pisistratus sleeping in the palace courtyard of King Menelaus. Pisistratus was sound asleep, but Telemachus tossed and turned all night, worried about his missing father. Athena came close to him and spoke:

"Telemachus, you shouldn't stay so far from home any longer! You've left your house full of dangerous men who want to steal everything you own. Ask Menelaus to send you home right away, or you might find that your wonderful mother is no longer there when you return. Her father and brothers are already pushing her to marry Eurymachus, who has given her more gifts than any of the other suitors and keeps bringing more wedding presents. I hope nothing valuable has been stolen from your house while you've been gone, but you know how it is—women often think they should do what's best for the man who marries them, and they forget about the children from their first marriage. Go home now and put your most trusted woman servant in charge of everything until the gods send you a wife of your own. But listen carefully—there's something else you need to know. The worst of the suitors are hiding in the narrow waters between Ithaca and the island of Samos, planning to kill you before you can reach home. I don't think they'll succeed. It's more likely that some of these men who are eating up your property will find their own graves first. Sail day and night, and keep your ship away from the islands. The god who watches over you will send you good winds. When you reach Ithaca, send your ship and crew to town, but you go straight to the swineherd who takes care of your pigs. He's loyal to you—stay with him for the night, then send him to tell your mother Penelope that you've returned safely from Pylos."

Then Athena returned to Mount Olympus, where the gods live. But Telemachus nudged Pisistratus with his foot to wake him up. "Wake up, Pisistratus! Hitch the horses to the chariot—we need to leave for home right now."

But Pisistratus said, "No matter how much of a hurry we're in, we can't drive in the dark. Morning will come soon. Let's wait until Menelaus brings his farewell gifts and puts them in our chariot, and let him say goodbye to us properly. A guest should never forget a host who has been kind to him."

As he spoke, dawn began to break, and Menelaus, who had already gotten up (leaving his wife Helen still in bed), came toward them. When Telemachus saw him, he quickly put on his shirt, threw a large cloak over his shoulders, and went to meet him. "Menelaus," he said, "please let me return to my own country now. I really want to get home."

Menelaus replied, "Telemachus, if you insist on going, I won't keep you here. I don't like hosts who hold onto their guests too tightly or who are rude to them. Balance is best in everything—not letting someone go when they want to leave is just as bad as telling them to go when they'd rather stay. A host should treat a guest well while he's in the house and help him when he wants to leave. Wait, though, until I can load your beautiful gifts into your chariot so you can see them yourself. I'll tell the servants to prepare a good meal from what we have in the house. It will be proper and practical for you to eat before starting such a long journey. And if you'd like to tour Greece, I'll hitch up my horses and guide you through all our important cities myself. No one will send us away empty-handed—everyone will give us something: a bronze tripod, a pair of mules, or a golden cup."

"Menelaus," Telemachus replied, "I want to go home immediately. When I left, I had no one protecting my property, and I'm afraid that while searching for my father, I might lose everything myself, or discover that something valuable has been stolen while I was away."

When Menelaus heard this, he immediately told his wife and servants to prepare a good meal from whatever was in the house. At that moment, a servant named Eteoneus joined them—he lived nearby and had just woken up. Menelaus told him to light the fire and cook some meat, which he did right away. Then Menelaus went down to his treasure room, which smelled sweet with perfumes. He didn't go alone—Helen came too, along with his son Megapenthes. When he reached the place where his house's treasures were kept, he chose a beautiful double cup and told Megapenthes to bring a silver mixing bowl as well. Meanwhile, Helen went to the chest where she kept the lovely dresses she had made with her own hands. She took out the largest and most beautifully embroidered one—it sparkled like a star and had been lying at the very bottom of the chest. Then they all returned through the house to where Telemachus waited. Menelaus said, "Telemachus, may Zeus, the mighty king of the gods, bring you safely home as you wish. I want to give you the finest and most precious piece in all my house. It's a mixing bowl made of pure silver, except for the rim, which is decorated with gold. It's the work of Hephaestus, the god of metalworking. King Phaedimus of the Sidonians gave it to me when I visited him on my way home from Troy. I'd like you to have it."

With these words, he placed the double cup in Telemachus's hands, while Megapenthes brought the beautiful mixing bowl and set it before him. Lovely Helen stood nearby, holding the robe ready in her hands.

"I also have something for you, my son," she said. "It's a keepsake from Helen's own hands—a robe for your bride to wear on her wedding day. Until then, ask your dear mother to keep it safe for you. May you return home rejoicing to your own country and house."

She gave him the robe, and he accepted it gladly. Then Pisistratus put all the presents into the chariot, admiring each one as he did. Soon Menelaus brought Telemachus and Pisistratus into the house, and they sat down at the table. A servant brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver bowl so they could wash their hands. She placed a clean table beside them, and another servant brought bread and offered them many good things from the house. Eteoneus carved the meat and gave each person their portion, while Megapenthes poured the wine. They ate and drank until they were satisfied. Then Telemachus and Pisistratus hitched up the horses and climbed into the chariot. They drove out through the inner courtyard and under the echoing gateway. Menelaus followed them with a golden cup of wine in his right hand so they could pour an offering to the gods before leaving. He stood in front of the horses and raised his cup, saying, "Farewell to both of you, and be sure to tell Nestor how well I've treated you, for he was like a father to me when we Greeks were fighting at Troy."

"We'll certainly tell him everything as soon as we see him, sir," answered Telemachus. "I wish I could be as sure of finding Odysseus back home when I reach Ithaca, so I could tell him about your great kindness and all the beautiful presents I'm taking with me."

Just as he was speaking, a bird flew by on their right side—a huge eagle carrying a white goose in its claws that it had snatched from a farmyard. Men and women were running after it, shouting. The eagle flew quite close to them, then soared away on their right, ahead of the horses. When they saw this, they felt happy and hopeful. Pisistratus said, "Tell me, Menelaus, has heaven sent this sign for us or for you?"

Menelaus was thinking about the best way to answer, but Helen spoke first. "I'll explain what this means, just as the gods have put it in my heart, and I'm sure it will come true. The eagle came from the mountain where it was born and has its nest, and in the same way, Odysseus will return home after traveling far and suffering much, and he'll take his revenge—if he isn't already back, planning trouble for the suitors."
"May Zeus make it so," replied Telemachus. "If that happens, I'll pray to you as if you were a goddess, even when I'm back home."

As he spoke, he urged his horses forward, and they raced at full speed through the town toward the open countryside. All day long they traveled, the harness swaying on the horses' necks, until the sun set and darkness covered the land. They reached the town of Pherae, where Diocles lived. He was the son of Ortilochus, whose father was Alpheus. There they spent the night and were treated as honored guests. When Dawn appeared, painting the sky pink with her rosy fingers, they hitched up their horses again and took their places in the chariot. They drove out through the courtyard and under the echoing gateway. Pisistratus whipped his horses, and they flew forward eagerly. Before long they reached Pylos, and then Telemachus said:

"Pisistratus, I hope you'll promise to do what I'm about to ask. You know our fathers were old friends, and we're about the same age. This journey has made us even closer friends. Please don't take me past my ship—leave me there. If I go to your father's house, he'll try to keep me because of his warm feelings toward me, but I must go home at once."

Pisistratus thought about how to do as his friend asked, and finally decided it would be best to turn his horses toward the ship. He put Menelaus's beautiful gifts of gold and clothing in the back of the vessel. Then he said, "Get on board quickly and tell your men to do the same, before I can get home to tell my father. I know how stubborn he is, and I'm sure he won't let you go. He'll come down here to fetch you himself, and he won't go back without you. He'll be very angry with me."

With that, he drove his fine horses back to the city of Pylos and soon reached home. Meanwhile, Telemachus called his men together and gave his orders. "Men, get everything ready on the ship. We're setting sail for home."

His crew obeyed and boarded the ship as he commanded. While Telemachus was busy preparing and praying to Athena at the ship's stern, a stranger approached him. This man came from a distant land and was a prophet, fleeing from the city of Argos because he had killed someone. He came from the famous family of Melampus, who used to live in Pylos, the land of many sheep. Melampus had been wealthy and owned a great house, but the powerful King Neleus forced him into exile. Neleus took all his property and held it for a whole year, during which Melampus was imprisoned in King Phylacus's house. He suffered greatly, both because of a curse and because he was trying to win Neleus's daughter for his brother. Eventually, he escaped, stole cattle from Phylace, brought them to Pylos, got his revenge, and gave Neleus's daughter to his brother as promised. Then he left the country and went to Argos, where he was destined to rule over many people. There he married and settled down, having two famous sons: Antiphates and Mantius. Antiphates became the father of Oicleus, and Oicleus became the father of Amphiaraus, who was dearly loved by both Zeus and Apollo. But he didn't live to old age because he was killed at Thebes because of a woman's greed. His sons were Alcmaeon and Amphilochus. Mantius, the other son of Melampus, was the father of Polypheides and Cleitus. The goddess Dawn carried off Cleitus because of his beauty, so he could live among the immortal gods. But Apollo made Polypheides the greatest prophet in the whole world after Amphiaraus died. He quarreled with his father and went to live in Hyperesia, where he stayed and told the future for everyone who asked.

It was Polypheides's son, Theoclymenus, who now approached Telemachus as he was making offerings and praying on his ship. "Friend," he said, "since I find you making sacrifices in this place, I beg you by your sacrifices and by the god you're honoring, and by your own life and the lives of your followers—tell me the truth and nothing but the truth. Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me about your city and parents."

Telemachus answered honestly: "I'll tell you the complete truth. I'm from Ithaca, and my father is Odysseus—if he's still alive. But something terrible has happened to him. That's why I took this ship and gathered my crew—to see if I can learn any news about him, because he's been gone for a very long time."

"I too am an exile," replied Theoclymenus, "because I killed a man from my own people. He has many brothers and relatives in Argos, and they're very powerful among the Argives. I'm running away to escape death at their hands, so I'm doomed to wander the earth. I'm begging you—please take me aboard your ship so they won't kill me, because I know they're chasing me."
"I won't refuse you," replied Telemachus. "If you want to join us, come aboard. When we reach Ithaca, we'll treat you as an honored guest with whatever we have."

Telemachus took Theoclymenus's spear and laid it on the ship's deck. He climbed aboard and sat in the stern, telling Theoclymenus to sit beside him. Then the crew untied the ropes. Telemachus told them to grab the rigging, and they hurried to obey. They set the mast in its socket, raised it up, and secured it with ropes. They hoisted their white sails made of ox-hide. Athena sent them a fair wind that blew fresh and strong, carrying the ship forward as fast as possible. They sailed past the towns of Crouni and Chalcis.

Soon the sun set and darkness covered the land. The ship made quick progress to Pheae and then to Elis, where the Epeans rule. From there, Telemachus steered toward some small islands, wondering whether he would escape death or be captured by his enemies.

Meanwhile, Odysseus and the swineherd were eating their evening meal in the hut, along with the other workers. After they finished eating and drinking, Odysseus decided to test the swineherd to see if he would continue treating him kindly and ask him to stay, or send him away to the city. So he said:

"Eumaeus, and all of you, tomorrow I want to leave and start begging around the town, so I won't be a burden to you or your men anymore. Give me your advice and provide a good guide to show me the way. I'll go around the city begging, as I must, to see if anyone will give me something to drink and a piece of bread. I'd also like to go to Odysseus's house and bring news to Queen Penelope about her husband. I could also visit the suitors and see if they'll give me dinner from all their plenty. I could quickly become an excellent servant in many ways. Listen and believe me when I tell you that with Mercury's blessing—he's the god who brings success to all men's work—no one alive could be a more useful servant than I would be. I could put fresh wood on the fire, chop fuel, carve meat, cook, pour wine, and do all the jobs that poor men do for their masters."

The swineherd was very upset when he heard this. "Heaven help me!" he exclaimed. "What could have put such an idea in your head? If you go near the suitors, you'll certainly be destroyed, because their pride and cruelty reach to the sky itself. They would never think of taking someone like you as a servant. Their servants are all young men, well-dressed, wearing fine cloaks and shirts, with good-looking faces and neatly combed hair. Their tables are kept spotless and loaded with bread, meat, and wine. Stay here where you are—you're not bothering anyone. I don't mind you being here, and neither do the others. When Telemachus comes home, he'll give you a shirt and cloak and send you wherever you want to go."

Odysseus replied, "I hope you'll be as dear to the gods as you are to me, for saving me from wandering around and getting into trouble. There's nothing worse than being homeless and always on the move. Still, when people have fallen on hard times, they'll endure a lot for the sake of their empty stomachs. But since you're encouraging me to stay here and wait for Telemachus to return, tell me about Odysseus's mother and his father, whom he left on the edge of old age when he sailed for Troy. Are they still alive, or have they already died and gone to the land of the dead?"

"I'll tell you everything about them," replied Eumaeus. "Laertes is still alive, but he prays to heaven every day to let him die peacefully in his own home, because he's terribly distressed about his missing son and also about his wife's death, which grieved him greatly and aged him more than anything else. She died unhappily from sorrow over her son—may no friend or neighbor who has been kind to me ever suffer such an end. As long as she was still living, even though she was always grieving, I enjoyed seeing her and asking how she was, because she raised me along with her daughter Ctimene, the youngest of her children. We grew up together as boy and girl, and she treated us almost the same. When we both became adults, they sent Ctimene to the island of Same and received a wonderful dowry for her. As for me, my mistress gave me a good shirt and cloak with sandals for my feet, and sent me to work in the countryside, but she was just as fond of me as ever. All that is over now. Still, heaven has blessed my work in my current position. I have enough to eat and drink, and I can provide for any decent stranger who comes here. But there's no getting a kind word or deed from my current mistress, because the house has fallen into the hands of wicked people. Servants sometimes want to see their mistress and talk with her—they like to eat and drink at the main house and take something back with them to the countryside. This is what keeps servants happy."

Odysseus said, "Then you must have been very young, Eumaeus, when you were taken so far from your home and parents. Tell me truthfully—was the city where your father and mother lived attacked and destroyed, or did enemies capture you when you were alone watching sheep or cattle, then ship you here and sell you to whoever paid your master's price?"

"Stranger," replied Eumaeus, "since you ask about this: sit comfortably, drink your wine, and listen to me. The nights are very long now—there's plenty of time for both sleeping and staying up talking together. You shouldn't go to bed too early; too much sleep is as bad as too little. If any of the others want to sleep, they can leave us and do so. In the morning, after breakfast, they can take my master's pigs out to pasture. We'll sit here in the hut, eating and drinking and telling each other stories about our troubles. When someone has suffered much and been tossed around in the world, they find comfort in remembering sorrows from long ago. So regarding your question, here's my story:

"You may have heard of an island called Syria that lies beyond Ortygia, where the sun turns around. It's not very populated, but the soil is good, with plenty of pasture for cattle and sheep, and it produces excellent wine and wheat. Famine never comes there, and the people aren't plagued by diseases. When they grow old, Apollo comes with his sister Diana and kills them painlessly with his arrows. The island has two cities, and my father Ctesius, son of Ormenus, ruled over both. He was a man who seemed almost godlike.

"One day some clever traders from Phoenicia came to our island. The Phoenicians are great sailors, and they brought a ship loaded with all kinds of beautiful trinkets. Now, there happened to be a Phoenician woman working in my father's house—she was tall and beautiful and an excellent servant. These scoundrels got hold of her one day when she was washing clothes near their ship. They seduced her and sweet-talked her in ways that no woman can resist, no matter how good she might be. The man who had seduced her asked who she was and where she came from. 'I'm from Sidon,' she told him, 'and I'm the daughter of Arybas, a very wealthy man. One day when I was walking from the country into town, some Taphian pirates grabbed me and brought me here across the sea, where they sold me to the man who owns this house. He paid their price for me.'
"The man who had seduced her then said, 'Would you like to come with us to see your parents' house and your parents themselves? They're both still alive and are said to be wealthy.'
"'I'd be happy to do that,' she answered, 'if you men will first swear a solemn oath that you won't harm me on the way.'

"They all swore the oath as she requested. When they finished swearing, the woman said, 'Keep quiet about this! And if any of your men see me in the street or at the well, don't let them talk to me, in case someone tells my master. He might become suspicious, put me in chains, and have all of you killed. Keep this secret, buy your goods as quickly as possible, and send me word when you're finished loading your ship. I'll bring as much gold as I can get my hands on, and there's something else I can do to pay for my passage. I'm the nurse to my master's son, a cute little boy who's just learning to walk. I'll bring him with me on your ship, and you'll get a lot of money for him if you take him and sell him in foreign lands.'

"Then she returned to the house. The Phoenicians stayed for a whole year, loading their ship with valuable goods. When they had enough cargo, they sent a messenger to the woman. This very cunning fellow came to my father's house with a golden necklace strung with amber beads. While my mother and the servants were holding it, admiring it, and bargaining over it, he quietly signaled to the woman, then went back to the ship. She took me by the hand and led me out of the house. In the front hall, she saw tables set with cups from guests who had been dining with my father in his role as their leader. These guests had now gone to a public meeting, so she quickly grabbed three cups and hid them in her dress, while I followed her innocently. The sun had set and darkness covered the land, so we hurried as fast as we could until we reached the harbor where the Phoenician ship was waiting. When they got on board, they sailed away across the sea, taking us with them, and Zeus sent them a favorable wind. We sailed day and night for six days, but on the seventh day, Diana struck the woman down, and she fell heavily into the ship's hold like a seabird diving into the water. They threw her overboard to the seals and fish, leaving me all alone and heartbroken. Eventually the winds and waves carried the ship to Ithaca, where Laertes traded some of his possessions for me. That's how I came to see this land."

Odysseus replied, "Eumaeus, I've listened to your story of misfortune with great interest and sympathy, but Zeus has given you good things as well as bad. Despite everything, you have a good master who makes sure you always have enough to eat and drink, and you live a good life. Meanwhile, I'm still wandering from city to city, begging for my food."

They talked like this, and they had very little time left for sleep because dawn was approaching. Meanwhile, Telemachus and his crew were nearing land, so they lowered the sails, took down the mast, and rowed the ship into the harbor. They dropped their anchor stones and tied up the mooring ropes. Then they got out on the beach, mixed their wine with water, and prepared their meal. After they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus said, "Take the ship to the town, but leave me here. I want to check on the herdsmen at one of my farms. This evening, after I've seen everything I need to see, I'll come down to the city. Tomorrow morning, to thank you for your hard work, I'll give you all a fine dinner with meat and wine."
Then Theoclymenus asked, "And what should I do, my dear young friend? To whose house among all your nobles should I go? Or should I go straight to your own house and your mother?"

"At any other time," replied Telemachus, "I would invite you to come to my own house, where you'd find no lack of hospitality. Right now, however, you wouldn't be comfortable there, because I'll be away, and my mother won't see you. She doesn't often show herself even to the suitors, but sits in an upstairs room, weaving at her loom, staying out of their way. But I can tell you about someone whose house you can visit—Eurymachus, the son of Polybus. Everyone in Ithaca respects him highly. He's the best man and the most determined suitor among all those courting my mother and trying to take Odysseus's place. However, only Zeus in heaven knows whether they'll meet a bad end before any marriage takes place."

As he was speaking, a bird flew by on his right side—a hawk, which is Apollo's messenger. It was holding a dove in its claws, and as it tore at the smaller bird, feathers fell to the ground between Telemachus and the ship. Theoclymenus called him aside and took his hand. "Telemachus," he said, "that bird didn't fly on your right side by accident—some god sent it there. As soon as I saw it, I knew it was a sign from heaven. It means that your family will remain powerful and that no house in Ithaca will be more royal than yours."
"I hope that proves to be true," answered Telemachus. "If it does, I'll show you such kindness and give you so many gifts that everyone who meets you will say how fortunate you are."

Then he spoke to his friend Piraeus: "Piraeus, son of Clytius, throughout this journey you've been the most willing to help me of all those who came with me to Pylos. I'd like you to take this stranger to your house and entertain him as an honored guest until I can come for him."
Piraeus answered, "Telemachus, you can stay away as long as you need to. I'll take good care of him, and he'll find no lack of hospitality."

As he spoke, Piraeus boarded the ship and told the others to do the same and untie the ropes. They took their places in the vessel. But Telemachus put on his sandals and picked up a long, strong spear with a sharp bronze point from the ship's deck. The crew untied the mooring ropes, pushed the ship away from land, and headed toward the city as they'd been instructed. Meanwhile, Telemachus walked as quickly as he could until he reached the farm where his countless herds of pigs were kept, and where lived the excellent swineherd who was so devoted and loyal to his master.

chapters.title: Book XVI — Ulysses reveals himself to telemachus.
paragraphs: Meanwhile Odysseus and the pig keeper had built a fire in their small hut. They were making breakfast at sunrise, having already sent the workers out with the pigs. When Telemachus walked up to the hut, the dogs didn't bark at him—instead they wagged their tails happily. Odysseus heard footsteps and noticed the dogs weren't barking, so he said to Eumaeus:
"Eumaeus, I hear someone walking. I think it must be one of your men or someone you know coming here, because the dogs are being friendly instead of barking."

Before he finished speaking, his son appeared at the door. Eumaeus jumped up so quickly that the bowls he was using to mix wine crashed to the ground. He rushed to his young master, kissing his head and eyes, crying with joy. A father couldn't have been happier to see his only son return home—a son he loved dearly—after ten years away in a foreign land, having suffered many hardships. He hugged him and kissed him all over, as if Telemachus had come back from the dead, speaking lovingly:

"You've come back, Telemachus! You're the light of my eyes! When I heard you had sailed to Pylos, I was sure I'd never see you again. Come inside, my dear boy, and sit down so I can get a good look at you now that you're home. You don't visit us country folk very often—you usually stay in town. I suppose you think it's better to keep watch on what those suitors are doing."

"You're right, old friend," answered Telemachus. "But I've come now because I want to see you and find out if my mother is still at home, or if she's married someone else. I need to know if my father's bed lies empty and covered with spider webs."
"She's still at the house," replied Eumaeus, "crying and breaking her heart. She does nothing but weep, day and night."

As he spoke, he took Telemachus's spear. The young prince stepped across the stone doorway and came inside. Odysseus started to get up to give him his seat, but Telemachus stopped him. "Stay seated, stranger," he said. "I can easily find another place to sit, and Eumaeus will set it up for me."

Odysseus sat back down, and Eumaeus spread fresh green branches on the floor, then threw a sheepskin on top for Telemachus to sit on. The pig keeper brought them plates of cold meat left over from the day before, and filled baskets with bread as quickly as he could. He mixed wine in wooden bowls and sat down facing Odysseus. They all ate the good food before them, and when they had finished eating and drinking, Telemachus said to Eumaeus, "Old friend, where does this stranger come from? How did sailors bring him to Ithaca, and who were they? He certainly didn't walk here!"

The pig keeper Eumaeus answered, "My boy, I'll tell you the truth. He says he's from Crete and has traveled far and wide. Right now he's escaping from a ship from Thesprotia and came to my farm for help. I'm putting him in your care. Do whatever you think is best—just remember he's asking for your protection." (In ancient times, people who asked for help and protection were called suppliants, and it was considered sacred to help them.)

"I'm very worried by what you've told me," said Telemachus. "How can I take this stranger to my house? I'm still young and not strong enough to defend myself if someone attacks me. My mother can't decide whether to stay home and take care of the house to honor my father's memory, or whether it's time to marry the best of her suitors—the one who offers the most. Still, since this stranger has come to your farm, I'll get him a good cloak and tunic, plus a sword and sandals, and send him wherever he wants to go. Or you can keep him here, and I'll send clothes and food so he won't be a burden to you and your men. But I won't let him go near the suitors—they're too rude and would surely mistreat him in ways that would upset me greatly. No matter how brave a man is, he can't fight so many enemies alone."

Then Odysseus said, "Sir, I should speak up here. I'm shocked by what you've said about how rudely the suitors are behaving, despite having such a fine young man as you around. Tell me, do you put up with this treatment quietly, or has some god turned your people against you? Can't you count on your relatives for help? That's usually who a man turns to for support, no matter how big the fight. I wish I were as young as you and felt as angry as I do now. If I were Odysseus's son—or even Odysseus himself—I'd rather have someone cut off my head than not go to that house and punish every single one of those men! Even if there were too many for me to handle alone, I'd rather die fighting in my own home than watch such shameful things happen every day—strangers treated badly, servant women dragged around improperly, wine wasted, and food thrown away for no good reason."

Telemachus answered, "I'll tell you the whole truth. My people aren't angry with me, and I can't complain about not having brothers to help me—that's usually who a man can count on in a big fight. Zeus has made our family line have only one son each generation. Laertes was Arceisius's only son, Odysseus was Laertes's only son, and I'm Odysseus's only son. He left me behind when he went away, so I've never been any help to him. That's why my house is full of enemies. Chiefs from all the nearby islands—Dulichium, Same, and Zacynthus—plus all the important men from Ithaca itself are eating up my inheritance while pretending to court my mother. She won't say clearly that she won't marry them, but she won't end the situation either. So they're destroying my property, and soon they'll destroy me too. But the outcome is in heaven's hands. Old friend Eumaeus, go right now and tell Penelope that I'm safe and have returned from Pylos. Tell only her, then come straight back without letting anyone else know, because many people are plotting against me."

"I understand completely," replied Eumaeus. "You don't need to explain further. But since I'm going that way anyway, should I let poor Laertes know you're back? He used to manage the farm work despite his terrible sadness about Odysseus, and he would eat and drink normally with his servants. But I hear that since you left for Pylos, he hasn't been eating or drinking properly, and he doesn't look after the farm. He just sits there weeping, getting thinner and thinner."

"That's very sad," answered Telemachus, "and I'm sorry for him. But we have to leave him alone for now. If people could have whatever they wanted, the first thing I'd choose would be my father's return. But go give your message, then hurry back. Don't go out of your way to tell Laertes. Tell my mother to send one of her servant women secretly with the news right away—let him hear it from her."

So he urged the pig keeper on his way. Eumaeus put on his sandals, tied them tight, and headed for town. Athena watched him leave the farm, then came to visit in the form of a beautiful, tall, and wise woman. (Athena was the goddess of wisdom and warfare.) She appeared beside the entrance where Odysseus could see her, but Telemachus couldn't see her and didn't know she was there—the gods only let themselves be seen by certain people. Odysseus saw her, and so did the dogs, who didn't bark but whimpered and slunk away to the other side of the yard. She nodded and signaled to Odysseus with her eyebrows, so he left the hut and stood before her outside the main fence. Then she said:

"Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, it's time to tell your son the truth. Don't keep him in the dark any longer. Make your plans for destroying the suitors, then head to town. I won't be long in joining you—I'm eager for the fight too."

As she spoke, she touched him with her golden wand. First she put a clean, fine shirt and cloak on him. Then she made him look younger and more impressive—she brought back his healthy color, filled out his cheeks, and made his beard dark again. Then she left, and Odysseus went back inside the hut. His son was amazed when he saw him and turned away, afraid he might be looking at a god.

"Stranger," he said, "you've suddenly changed completely from what you looked like just moments ago! You're dressed differently and your skin looks different. Are you one of the gods who live in heaven? If so, please be kind to me until I can make proper sacrifices and offerings of gold to you. Have mercy on me."
Odysseus said, "I'm not a god—why do you think I am? I'm your father, the one you've grieved for and suffered so much because of these lawless men."
As he spoke, he kissed his son, and a tear rolled down his cheek—he had held back his tears until now. But Telemachus still couldn't believe it was really his father, and said:

"You're not my father! Some god is giving me false hope just to make me sadder later. No ordinary person could do what you just did—make yourself old and young in an instant—unless a god was helping him. A moment ago you were old and wearing rags, and now you look like a god who came down from heaven."

Odysseus answered, "Telemachus, you shouldn't be so amazed that I'm really here. No other Odysseus will come after me. I am who I am—after twenty years of wandering and hardship, I've finally made it home to my own country. What amazes you is the work of the powerful goddess Athena, who can do whatever she wants with me. She can make me look like a beggar one moment and like a well-dressed young man the next. It's easy for the gods in heaven to make any person look rich or poor."

As he finished speaking, he sat down. Telemachus threw his arms around his father and cried. They were both so overcome with emotion that they wept loudly, like eagles or hawks whose babies have been stolen from their nest. They would have kept crying until sunset, but Telemachus suddenly said, "What ship brought you home, dear father? What crew did they say they were? You couldn't have come by land."

"I'll tell you the truth, my son," replied Odysseus. "The Phaeacians brought me here. They're excellent sailors who help anyone who reaches their shores. They carried me across the sea while I was fast asleep and landed me in Ithaca, giving me many gifts of bronze, gold, and clothing. By heaven's blessing, these treasures are hidden in a cave. I came here because Athena suggested we meet to plan how to kill our enemies. First, give me a list of the suitors and their numbers, so I can think about whether the two of us can fight them all by ourselves, or if we need to find others to help us."

Telemachus answered, "Father, I've always heard about your fame both as a warrior and a wise counselor, but what you're talking about is huge—I'm awed just thinking about it! Two men can't stand against so many brave enemies. There aren't just ten suitors, or even twenty, but many times more than that. Let me tell you their numbers right now: fifty-two chosen young men from Dulichium with six servants; twenty-four from Same; twenty young men from Zacynthus; and twelve from Ithaca itself, all from good families. They also have a servant named Medon, a singing poet, and two men who serve at meals. If we face numbers like these, you might have bitter reason to regret coming here for revenge. See if you can think of anyone who might be willing to help us."
"Listen to me," replied Odysseus, "and think about whether Athena and her father Zeus might be enough help, or if I should try to find someone else too."
"The ones you've named," answered Telemachus, "are two powerful allies! Even though they live high up in the clouds, they have power over both gods and humans."

"Those two," continued Odysseus, "won't stay out of the fight for long when the suitors and we clash in my house. Now, go home early tomorrow morning and mingle with the suitors as usual. Later, the pig keeper will bring me to the city disguised as a miserable old beggar. If you see them treating me badly, steel your heart against my suffering. Even if they drag me out of the house by my feet or throw things at me, just watch and do nothing except gently try to make them behave better. But they won't listen to you—their day of reckoning is coming. Also, remember this important point: when Athena puts the idea in my mind, I'll nod my head at you. When you see me do this, collect all the weapons in the house and hide them in the strong storage room. When the suitors ask why you're moving them, make up an excuse. Say you're taking them away from the smoke because they're no longer as bright as when Odysseus left—they've become dirty and stained with soot. Add that you're worried Zeus might make them fight over their wine, and they might hurt each other, which would ruin both the feast and the courting. The sight of weapons sometimes makes people want to use them. But leave a sword and spear for each of us, plus two leather shields so we can grab them quickly when needed. Zeus and Athena will take care of these people then. There's one more thing: if you're really my son with my blood in your veins, don't let anyone know that Odysseus is in the house—not Laertes, not the pig keeper, not any of the servants, not even Penelope herself. Let's figure out which women we can trust, and let's also test some of the male servants to see who's on our side and who's against us."

"Father," replied Telemachus, "you'll get to know my character soon enough, and you'll find I can keep secrets. But I don't think your plan will work well for either of us. Think about it—it will take us a long time to go around to all the farms and test the workers, and meanwhile the suitors will keep wasting your property without any guilt or hesitation. By all means test the women to see who's disloyal and who's innocent, but I don't want to go around testing all the men. We can deal with that later, if you really have some sign from Zeus that he'll support you."

While they talked, the ship that had brought Telemachus and his crew from Pylos reached Ithaca's harbor. After sailing inside the harbor, they pulled the ship onto the beach. Servants came and took their weapons, and they left all the gifts at Clytius's house. Then they sent a messenger to tell Penelope that Telemachus had gone to the countryside but had sent the ship to town so she wouldn't worry. This messenger and Eumaeus happened to meet while they were both heading to tell Penelope the same news. When they reached the house, the messenger stood up and announced to the queen in front of all the servant women, "Your son has returned from Pylos, ma'am." But Eumaeus went close to Penelope and privately told her everything her son had asked him to say. After delivering his message, he left the house and grounds and went back to his pigs.

The suitors were shocked and angry about what had happened, so they went outside the great wall around the outer courtyard and held a meeting near the main entrance. Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke first.

"Friends," he said, "this trip of Telemachus is a serious problem. We were sure it would come to nothing. Now let's get a ship ready with a crew to send after the others and tell them to come back as fast as they can."

He had barely finished speaking when Amphinomus turned around and saw the ship in the harbor with the crew lowering the sails and putting away the oars. He laughed and said to the others, "We don't need to send any message—they're already here! Some god must have told them, or they saw the ship go by and couldn't catch up."

They got up and went to the waterfront. The crew pulled the ship ashore, servants took their weapons, and they all went to the assembly area. They wouldn't let anyone old or young join them, and Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke first.

"Good heavens," he said, "see how the gods have saved this man from death! We kept scouts watching from the cliffs all day long, and when the sun set we didn't go ashore to sleep. Instead we waited in our ship all night until morning, hoping to capture and kill him. But some god brought him home despite our efforts. Let's figure out how to finish him off. He must not escape us—we'll never succeed in our plans while he's alive, because he's very clever and public opinion isn't entirely on our side. We must act quickly before he can call the people to an assembly. He won't waste time doing that because he'll be furious with us, and he'll tell everyone how we plotted to kill him but failed. People won't like hearing this—they might hurt us or drive us out of our own country into exile. Let's try to catch him either at his farm away from town or on the road. Then we can divide up his property among ourselves and let his mother and whoever marries her keep the house. If this doesn't appeal to you and you want Telemachus to live and keep his father's property, then we shouldn't gather here eating up his wealth this way. Instead, each of us should court Penelope from his own house, and she can marry whoever offers the most and is destined to win her."

Everyone stayed quiet until Amphinomus stood up to speak. He was the son of Nisus, who was the son of King Aretias, and he was the leading suitor from the wheat-growing, grassy island of Dulichium. His conversation pleased Penelope more than any other suitor's because he was naturally good-hearted. "My friends," he said, speaking honestly and plainly, "I don't favor killing Telemachus. It would be a terrible crime to kill someone of noble blood. Let's ask the gods for guidance first, and if Zeus's signs encourage it, I'll help kill him myself and urge everyone else to do the same. But if the gods advise against it, I think we should hold back."
His words pleased them, so they got up right away and went to Odysseus's house, where they took their usual seats.

Then Penelope decided to show herself to the suitors. She knew about the plot against Telemachus because the servant Medon had overheard their plans and told her. She went down to the courtyard with her servant women, and when she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the columns supporting the roof. She held a veil over her face and scolded Antinous, saying:

"Antinous, you rude and wicked schemer! People say you're the best speaker and advisor of anyone your age in Ithaca, but you're nothing like that at all! You madman, why are you trying to kill Telemachus and ignoring the rights of suppliants, which Zeus himself protects? It's wrong for you to plot against each other like this. Don't you remember how your father fled to this house in fear when the people were furious with him for joining Taphian pirates and raiding the Thesprotians, who were at peace with us? They wanted to tear him apart and take everything he owned, but Odysseus protected him even though they were enraged. Now you're consuming Odysseus's property without paying, breaking my heart by courting his wife and trying to kill his son. Stop doing this and make the others stop too!"

Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered, "Don't worry, Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, and don't trouble yourself about these matters. The man who would lay hands on your son Telemachus isn't born yet and never will be, as long as I live and can see. I promise you—and it will surely happen—that my spear will be stained with his blood! Many times Odysseus held me on his knees, gave me wine to drink, and put pieces of meat in my hands. Therefore Telemachus is my dearest friend, and he has nothing to fear from us suitors. Of course, if death comes to him from the gods, he can't escape that." He said this to calm her, but actually he was plotting against Telemachus.

Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband until Athena made her fall asleep. In the evening, Eumaeus returned to Odysseus and his son, who had just sacrificed a one-year-old pig and were preparing supper together. So Athena came to Odysseus, touched him with her wand to make him look like an old man again, and dressed him in his raggedy clothes, in case the pig keeper might recognize him and not keep the secret but go tell Penelope.
Telemachus spoke first. "So you're back, Eumaeus," he said. "What's the news from town? Have the suitors returned, or are they still waiting somewhere to ambush me on my way home?"

"I didn't think to ask about that," replied Eumaeus, "when I was in town. I just wanted to deliver my message and get back as quickly as I could. I did meet a messenger sent by the men who sailed with you to Pylos, and he was first to tell your mother the news. But I can tell you what I saw with my own eyes: I had just reached the top of Mercury's hill above the town when I saw a ship entering the harbor with many men aboard. They had lots of shields and spears, and I thought it was the suitors, but I can't be sure."
Hearing this, Telemachus smiled at his father, but made sure Eumaeus couldn't see him.

When they finished their work and the meal was ready, they ate it. Everyone had a full portion and was satisfied. After they had eaten and drunk enough, they lay down to rest and enjoyed the gift of sleep.

chapters.title: Book XVII — Telemachus and his mother meet—ulysses and eumaeus come down to the town, and ulysses is insulted by melanthius—he is recognised by the dog argos—he is insulted and presently struck by antinous with a stool—penelope desires that he shall be sent to her.
paragraphs: When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared in the morning sky, Telemachus tied on his sandals and picked up a strong spear that felt good in his hands. He wanted to go into the city. "Old friend," he said to the swineherd, "I must go to town now and show myself to my mother. She won't stop worrying and crying until she sees me with her own eyes. Take this poor stranger to town with you and let him beg there. Anyone who wants to can give him some food and drink. I have enough troubles of my own without taking on other people's problems. If this makes him angry, that's too bad for him. I believe in speaking plainly."

Then Ulysses said, "Sir, I don't want to stay here anyway. A beggar can always do better in town than in the countryside, because more people can help him there. I'm too old to stay here doing whatever a master tells me to do. So let this man do as you just said and take me to town. But first let me warm up by the fire until the day gets warmer. My clothes are terribly thin, and this cold morning will freeze me to death. Besides, you said the city is quite far away."

With that, Telemachus strode off through the farmyard, his mind full of plans for revenge against the suitors. When he reached his home, he leaned his spear against one of the columns, crossed the stone courtyard, and went inside.

Old Nurse Eurycleia saw him long before anyone else did. She was putting soft sheepskins on the chairs when she burst into tears and ran to him. All the other servant women rushed up too, covering his head and shoulders with kisses. Penelope came out of her room looking as beautiful as the goddess Diana or Venus. She wept as she threw her arms around her son, kissing his forehead and both his handsome eyes. "Light of my eyes," she cried tenderly, "you've come home! I was sure I would never see you again. How could you go off to Pylos without telling me or asking my permission? But come now, tell me what you saw."

"Don't scold me, mother," answered Telemachus, "or make me feel bad when I've just barely escaped danger. But wash your face, put on clean clothes, go upstairs with your maids, and promise great sacrifices to all the gods if Zeus will only help us get our revenge on the suitors. I must go now to the town square to invite a stranger who came back with me from Pylos. I sent him ahead with my crew and told Piraeus to take him home and look after him until I could come get him myself." (In ancient Greece, offering sacrifices to the gods was a way of asking for their help and showing respect.)
She listened to her son's words, washed her face, changed her dress, and promised great sacrifices to all the gods if they would help her get revenge on the suitors.

Telemachus walked through and out of the courtyard with his spear in hand. He wasn't alone—his two swift dogs went with him. The goddess Athena made him look so handsome and godly that everyone stared at him in wonder as he passed by. The suitors gathered around him with friendly words on their lips, but evil thoughts in their hearts. He avoided them and went to sit with Mentor, Antiphus, and Halitherses—old friends of his father's family. They made him tell them everything that had happened to him. Then Piraeus came up with Theoclymenus, whom he had brought through the town to the meeting place. Telemachus immediately joined them. Piraeus spoke first: "Telemachus," he said, "I wish you would send some of your women servants to my house to collect the gifts that Menelaus gave you."

"We don't know what might happen, Piraeus," answered Telemachus. "If the suitors kill me in my own house and divide up my property among themselves, I'd rather you kept those presents than let any of those men get their hands on them. But if I manage to kill them instead, I'll be very grateful if you bring me my presents."

With these words, he took Theoclymenus to his own house. When they arrived, they laid their cloaks on the benches and seats, went to the baths, and washed themselves. After the servant women had washed and rubbed them with olive oil, and given them clean cloaks and shirts, they sat down at the table. A maid brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver bowl so they could wash their hands. She set up a clean table beside them. Another servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from the household stores. Across from them sat Penelope, leaning against one of the pillars and spinning thread. They ate and drank their fill, and then Penelope said:

"Telemachus, I'm going upstairs to lie down on that sad bed of mine, which I haven't stopped watering with my tears since the day Ulysses left for Troy with the other Greek kings. But you failed to tell me clearly, before the suitors came back to the house, whether you heard anything about your father's return."

"I'll tell you the whole truth," replied her son. "We went to Pylos and saw old King Nestor, who welcomed me to his house and treated me as kindly as if I were his own son returning after a long journey. His sons did the same. But he said he hadn't heard a word from any person about Ulysses, whether he was alive or dead. So he sent me with a chariot and horses to visit Menelaus. There I saw Helen—the woman whose beauty caused so many Greeks and Trojans to die in the war that the gods had planned. Menelaus asked me why I had come to his kingdom, and I told him everything. Then he said, 'So these cowards want to take over a brave man's home and wife! They're like a deer trying to lay her newborn babies in a lion's den, then wandering off to graze in the meadows. When the lion comes back to his lair, he'll make quick work of both the deer and her young—and that's exactly what Ulysses will do to these suitors. By Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, if Ulysses is still the same man who once wrestled with Philomeleides on the island of Lesbos and threw him so hard that all the Greeks cheered—if he's still that strong and came near these suitors, they'd have very short lives and a sorry wedding indeed. As for your question, I won't lie to you or keep anything back. The Old Man of the Sea told me he could see Ulysses on an island, crying bitterly in the house of the sea-nymph Calypso, who was keeping him prisoner. He couldn't get home because he had no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea.' That's what Menelaus told me. When I heard his story, I left, and the gods gave me fair winds that brought me safely home." (The Old Man of the Sea was Proteus, a sea god who could see the future.)
These words touched Penelope's heart deeply. Then Theoclymenus said to her:

"Madam, wife of Ulysses, Telemachus doesn't understand the signs, so listen to me. I can read them clearly and will hide nothing from you. I swear by Zeus, king of heaven, and by the laws of hospitality, and by Ulysses' own hearth that I now approach—Ulysses himself is here in Ithaca right now! Either he's traveling around the island or staying in one place, learning about all these evil deeds and planning a day of punishment for the suitors. I saw a sign when I was on the ship that meant exactly this, and I told Telemachus about it."
"May it be just as you say," answered Penelope. "If your words come true, you'll receive such gifts and friendship from me that everyone who sees you will call you blessed."

While they talked, the suitors were outside throwing discuses and hurling spears at targets on the level ground in front of the house, acting as rude and arrogant as always. But when dinnertime came, and the flocks of sheep and goats arrived in town from all the surrounding countryside with their shepherds as usual, then Medon, their favorite servant who waited on them at meals, called out, "Now then, young masters, you've had enough sport for now. Come inside so we can prepare dinner. There's nothing wrong with eating dinner at dinnertime!"

They stopped their games as he told them and went inside the house. They hung their cloaks on the benches and seats, then sacrificed some sheep, goats, pigs, and a young cow—all of them fat and well-fed. This is how they prepared for their meal. Meanwhile, Ulysses and the swineherd were getting ready to leave for town. The swineherd said, "Stranger, I suppose you still want to go to town today, as my master told you to do. I would have preferred you to stay here as a farm worker, but I must do what my master commands, or he'll scold me later. And being scolded by your master is no small matter. So let's go now, since it's broad daylight. It will be evening soon, and then you'll find it even colder."
"I know and understand," replied Ulysses. "You don't need to say more. Let's go, but if you have a walking stick ready, let me use it, since you say the road is very rough."

As he spoke, he slung his shabby, torn old bag over his shoulders by its cord, and Eumaeus gave him a walking stick that felt right in his hands. The two men started off, leaving the farm in care of the dogs and shepherds who stayed behind. The swineherd led the way, and his master followed, looking like some broken-down old tramp leaning on his staff, with his clothes all in tatters. When they had climbed over the rough, steep ground and were getting close to the city, they reached the fountain where the citizens got their water. This fountain had been built by three men: Ithacus, Neritus, and Polyctor. Around it grew a circle of water-loving poplar trees, and clear cold water flowed down to it from a high rock. Above the fountain stood an altar to the water nymphs, where all travelers stopped to make offerings. Here Melanthius, son of Dolius, caught up with them as he drove down some of the best goats from his flock for the suitors' dinner. Two other shepherds were with him. When he saw Eumaeus and Ulysses, he insulted them with terrible, shameful language that made Ulysses very angry.

"Well, look at this!" cried Melanthius. "What a perfect pair you make! See how heaven brings birds of the same feather together. Where are you taking this miserable wretch, master swineherd? The sight of such a creature at the dinner table would make anyone sick. A fellow like this has never won a prize for anything in his life. He'll just go around rubbing his shoulders against everyone's doorposts, begging—not for swords and fine metal bowls like a real man, but just for a few scraps not worth begging for. If you gave him to me to work at my station, he might be able to clean out the animal pens or bring some feed to the young goats. He could build up his skinny legs as much as he wanted on whey. But he's gotten into bad habits and won't do any real work. He'll do nothing but beg for food all over town to feed his greedy belly. Mark my words—and this will surely happen—if he goes near Ulysses' house, they'll break his head with the stools they throw at him until they drive him out."

As he passed by, he gave Ulysses a kick in the hip just out of meanness, but Ulysses stood firm as a rock and didn't move from the path. For a moment he wondered whether to attack Melanthius and kill him with his staff, or grab him and beat his brains out. But he decided to control himself and wait. The swineherd, however, looked straight at Melanthius and scolded him, raising his hands and praying to heaven:

"Fountain nymphs," he cried, "daughters of Zeus, if Ulysses ever burned offerings of fat lamb and goat thighbones for you, grant my prayer that heaven will send him home. He would soon put an end to the swaggering threats that men like you make while insulting people—wandering all over town while your flocks are ruined because you're such a bad shepherd."

Then Melanthius the goatherd answered, "Listen to this worthless dog bark! What are you talking about? Someday I'll put you on a ship and take you to a foreign country where I can sell you and pocket the money. I wish I could be as sure that Apollo would strike Telemachus dead this very day, or that the suitors would kill him, as I am that Ulysses will never come home again."

With that, he left them to follow at their own pace while he hurried ahead and soon reached his master's house. When he got there, he went inside and sat down among the suitors across from Eurymachus, who liked him better than any of the others. The servants brought him his portion of meat, and a head servant woman set bread before him. Soon Ulysses and the swineherd came up to the house and stopped outside it. They could hear music, for the bard Phemius was just beginning to sing for the suitors. Then Ulysses took the swineherd's hand and said:

"Eumaeus, this house of Ulysses is truly magnificent. No matter how far you travel, you'll find few like it. One building connects to another. The outer courtyard has a wall with battlements all around it. The doors are double and well-made. It would be very hard to capture this place by force. I can tell there are many people feasting inside, because I smell roast meat and hear music, which the gods made to go along with feasting."

Then Eumaeus said, "You've observed correctly, as you usually do. But let's think about what we should do. Will you go inside first and join the suitors while I wait out here? Or will you wait here and let me go in first? But don't wait long, or someone might see you hanging around outside and throw something at you. Think about this, please."

And Ulysses answered, "I understand and will be careful. Go in first and leave me here. I'm quite used to being beaten and having things thrown at me. I've been knocked around so much in war and at sea that I'm tough as leather, and this would just be more of the same. But a man can't hide the demands of a hungry stomach. Hunger is an enemy that causes much trouble for everyone. It's because of hunger that ships are built to sail the seas and make war on other people."

As they were talking, a dog that had been lying asleep raised his head and pricked up his ears. This was Argos, whom Ulysses had raised as a puppy before leaving for Troy, but he had never gotten to use him for hunting. In the old days, the young men used to take him out when they hunted wild goats, deer, or rabbits. But now that his master was gone, he lay neglected on the piles of mule and cow dung in front of the stable doors, waiting for the workers to cart it away to fertilize the big field. He was covered with fleas. As soon as he saw Ulysses standing there, he lowered his ears and wagged his tail, but he was too weak to get up and go to his master. When Ulysses saw the dog on the other side of the yard, he secretly wiped a tear from his eyes without letting Eumaeus see, and said:

"Eumaeus, what a noble dog that is over there on the manure pile. He's beautifully built. Is he as good as he looks, or is he just one of those dogs that hang around the table begging for scraps and are kept just for show?"

"This dog," answered Eumaeus, "belonged to my master who died in a far country. If he were what he was when Ulysses left for Troy, he would quickly show you what he could do. No wild animal in the forest could escape him once he got on its trail. But now he's fallen on hard times because his master is dead and gone, and the women don't take care of him. Servants never do their work properly when their master isn't there to watch them, because Zeus takes away half a person's worth when he becomes a slave."
As he spoke, he went inside the buildings to the courtyard where the suitors were feasting. But Argos died as soon as he had recognized his master.

Telemachus saw Eumaeus long before anyone else did and motioned for him to come sit beside him. Eumaeus looked around and found a stool near where the carver was serving portions to the suitors. He picked it up, brought it to Telemachus's table, and sat down across from him. A servant brought him his portion of food and gave him bread from the bread basket.

Right after that, Ulysses came inside, looking like a poor, miserable old beggar, leaning on his staff with his clothes all in rags. He sat down on the threshold made of ash wood, just inside the doors that led from the outer courtyard to the inner one, leaning against a cypress-wood pillar that the carpenter had skillfully planed and fitted perfectly with his tools. Telemachus took a whole loaf from the bread basket, along with as much meat as he could hold in both hands, and said to Eumaeus, "Take this to the stranger and tell him to go around to all the suitors and beg from them. A beggar shouldn't be too proud to ask for help."
So Eumaeus went up to him and said, "Stranger, Telemachus sends you this food and says you should go around to all the suitors begging, because beggars shouldn't be too proud."
Ulysses answered, "May King Zeus grant all happiness to Telemachus and fulfill the desire of his heart."

Then he took what Telemachus had sent him with both hands and laid it on his dirty old bag at his feet. He ate while the bard was singing, and he had just finished his meal when the song ended. The suitors clapped for the bard, and then Athena came to Ulysses and urged him to beg for pieces of bread from each of the suitors. She wanted him to see what kind of people they were and tell the good ones from the bad—though she wasn't planning to save a single one of them no matter what. So Ulysses went around the room from left to right, stretching out his hands to beg as if he were a real beggar. Some of them felt sorry for him and were curious about him, asking each other who he was and where he came from. Then the goatherd Melanthius said, "Suitors of my noble mistress, I can tell you something about this man, because I've seen him before. The swineherd brought him here, but I don't know anything about the man himself or where he comes from."

When he heard this, Antinous began insulting the swineherd. "You stupid fool," he shouted, "why did you bring this man to town? Don't we have enough tramps and beggars already to bother us while we're eating? Do you think it's nothing that such people gather here to waste your master's property—and now you have to bring this man too?"

And Eumaeus answered, "Antinous, you come from a good family, but your words are evil. It wasn't my idea for him to come here. Who would invite a stranger from a foreign country unless he was someone useful—like a prophet, a doctor, a carpenter, or a bard who can entertain us with his singing? Such people are welcome everywhere, but no one is likely to invite a beggar who will just be trouble. You are always harder on Ulysses' servants than any of the other suitors, and especially hard on me. But I don't care as long as Telemachus and Penelope are alive and well."
But Telemachus said, "Quiet! Don't answer him. Antinous has the meanest tongue of all the suitors, and he makes the others act worse too."

Then, turning to Antinous, he said, "Antinous, you act like you care about my welfare as much as a father would. Why do you want to see this stranger thrown out of the house? Heaven forbid! Take something and give it to him yourself. I don't mind—I'm telling you to do it. Don't worry about my mother or any of the other servants in the house. But I know you won't do what I say, because you prefer to eat things yourself rather than give them to other people."
"What do you mean by this big talk, Telemachus?" replied Antinous. "If all the suitors gave him as much as I'm about to give him, he wouldn't come back here for another three months."

As he spoke, he pulled out the footstool he had been resting his fancy feet on from under the table and raised it as if to throw it at Ulysses. But all the other suitors gave him something and filled his bag with bread and meat. He was about to go back to the threshold to eat what the suitors had given him, but first he went up to Antinous and said:

"Sir, give me something. You're surely not the poorest man here—you look like a chief, the most important of them all. Therefore you should give more generously, and I will spread word of your kindness far and wide. I too was once a rich man with a fine house of my own. In those days I gave freely to many a wanderer like I am now, no matter who he was or what he needed. I had countless servants and everything else that people have when they live well and are considered wealthy. But it pleased Zeus to take it all away from me. He sent me with a band of wandering pirates to Egypt—it was a long voyage that ruined me. I anchored my ships in the Nile River and ordered my men to stay with them and guard them while I sent out scouts to look around from every high point."

"But my men disobeyed my orders, followed their own desires, and attacked the Egyptian people, killing the men and taking their wives and children as prisoners. The alarm quickly reached the city, and when the Egyptians heard the war cry, they came out at sunrise until the plain was filled with soldiers on foot and horseback, and with the gleam of armor. Then Zeus made my men panic, and they no longer wanted to fight the enemy because they found themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive to work as slaves. As for me, they gave me to a friend they met, to take to Cyprus. His name was Dmetor, son of Iasus, who was a powerful man in Cyprus. From there I have come here in great misery."

Then Antinous said, "What god could have sent such a plague to ruin our dinner? Get out into the open part of the courtyard, or I'll give you another taste of Egypt and Cyprus for your boldness and begging! You've begged from all the others, and they've given you plenty, because they have abundance around them and it's easy to be generous with other people's property when there's lots of it."

At this, Ulysses began to back away and said, "My fine sir, your looks are better than your manners. If you were in your own house, you wouldn't give a poor man so much as a pinch of salt. Even though you're in someone else's house, surrounded by plenty, you can't find it in yourself to give him even a piece of bread."

This made Antinous very angry, and he glared at Ulysses, saying, "You'll pay for this before you get out of this courtyard." With these words he threw the footstool at him and hit him on the right shoulder blade near the top of his back. Ulysses stood firm as a rock, and the blow didn't even make him stagger. He just shook his head silently as he planned his revenge. Then he went back to the threshold and sat down there, setting his well-filled bag at his feet.

"Listen to me," he called out, "you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. A man feels no pain or hurt when he gets hit while fighting for his money, his sheep, or his cattle.
