And Antinous has hit me while I was serving my miserable belly, which is always getting people into trouble. But if poor people have gods and avenging spirits to protect them, I pray that Antinous will die before his wedding day."

"Sit there and eat your food in silence, or get out!" shouted Antinous. "If you say another word, I'll have you dragged by your hands and feet through the courtyards, and the servants will strip the skin off you."

The other suitors were very displeased with this, and one of the young men said, "Antinous, you did wrong to hit that poor tramp. It will be worse for you if he turns out to be some god—because we know the gods disguise themselves as people from foreign countries and travel around the world to see who does wrong and who does right." (In Greek mythology, gods often disguised themselves as beggars or travelers to test people's kindness.)

The suitors said this, but Antinous paid them no attention. Meanwhile, Telemachus was furious about the blow that had been given to his father. Though no tear fell from his eyes, he shook his head in silence and brooded on his revenge.

When Penelope heard that the beggar had been struck in the dining hall, she said to her maids, "I wish Apollo would strike you the same way, Antinous." And her waiting woman Eurynome answered, "If our prayers were answered, not one of the suitors would ever see another sunrise." Then Penelope said, "Nurse, I hate every single one of them because they mean nothing but trouble, but I hate Antinous like death itself. A poor unfortunate tramp came here begging because he was truly needy. Everyone else gave him something to put in his bag, but Antinous hit him on the right shoulder with a footstool."

She talked this way with her maids as she sat in her room, while Ulysses was eating his meal. Then she called for the swineherd and said, "Eumaeus, go tell the stranger to come here. I want to see him and ask him some questions. He seems to have traveled widely, and he might have seen or heard something about my poor husband."

To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus, "If these Greeks would only keep quiet, madam, you would be enchanted by the story of his adventures. I had him with me for three days and three nights in my hut, which was the first place he reached after escaping from his ship. Even then he hadn't finished telling the story of his misfortunes. If he had been the most gifted storyteller in the whole world, someone whose words hold all listeners spellbound, I couldn't have been more charmed as I sat in my hut listening to him. He says there's an old friendship between his family and that of Ulysses, and that he comes from Crete, where the descendants of King Minos live. He's been driven here and there by every kind of misfortune. He also says that he has heard of Ulysses being alive and nearby among the Thesprotians, and that he's bringing great treasure home with him." (The Thesprotians were a people who lived in northwestern Greece.)

"Bring him here then," said Penelope, "so I can hear his story too. As for the suitors, let them enjoy themselves indoors or outside as they wish, since they have nothing to worry about. Their grain and wine stay unused in their houses with only servants to consume them, while they keep hanging around our house day after day, killing our oxen, sheep, and fat goats for their feasts, and never giving a thought to how much wine they drink. No estate can survive such recklessness, because we no longer have Ulysses to protect us. If he were to return, he and his son would quickly get their revenge."

As she spoke, Telemachus sneezed so loudly that the whole house echoed with it. Penelope laughed when she heard this and said to Eumaeus, "Go and call the stranger. Didn't you hear how my son sneezed just as I was speaking? This can only mean that all the suitors are going to die, and not one of them will escape. Furthermore, I tell you this, and take it to heart: if I'm satisfied that the stranger is telling the truth, I'll give him a shirt and cloak of good quality." (In ancient Greece, sneezing at the right moment was considered a good omen, a sign that the gods approved of what was being said.)

When Eumaeus heard this, he went straight to Ulysses and said, "Father stranger, my mistress Penelope, Telemachus's mother, has sent for you. She's in great sorrow, but she wants to hear anything you can tell her about her husband. If she's satisfied that you're telling the truth, she'll give you a shirt and cloak, which are exactly what you need most. As for food, you can get enough to fill your belly by begging around town from those who are willing to give."

"I will tell Penelope," answered Ulysses, "nothing but the strict truth. I know all about her husband and have shared troubles with him. But I'm afraid to pass through this crowd of cruel suitors, because their pride and violence reach to heaven. Just now, as I was walking harmlessly around the house, a man hit me hard, but neither Telemachus nor anyone else defended me. Tell Penelope, therefore, to be patient and wait until sunset. Let her give me a seat close to the fire, because my clothes are very thin—you know they are, since you've seen them ever since I first asked for your help. Then she can ask me about her husband's return."

The swineherd went back when he heard this, and Penelope said as she saw him cross the threshold, "Why aren't you bringing him here, Eumaeus? Is he afraid that someone will mistreat him, or is he too shy to come inside the house at all? Beggars shouldn't be bashful."

To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus, "The stranger is being quite sensible. He's avoiding the suitors, and he's only doing what anyone else would do. He asks you to wait until sunset, and it will be much better, madam, for you to have him all to yourself when you can listen to him and talk with him privately."
"The man is no fool," answered Penelope. "It would very likely be just as he says, because there are no more terrible people in the whole world than these men."

When she finished speaking, Eumaeus went back to the suitors, having explained everything. Then he went up to Telemachus and whispered in his ear so no one else could hear him, "My dear sir, I'll go back to the pigs now to look after your property and my own work. You take care of what's happening here, but above all, be careful to stay out of danger, because there are many who wish you harm. May Zeus destroy them before they hurt us."
"Very well," replied Telemachus. "Go home after you've had your dinner, and in the morning come back here with the animals we need to sacrifice for the day. Leave everything else to heaven and me."

At this, Eumaeus sat down again, and when he had finished his dinner, he left the courtyards and the dining hall with the men still at their tables, and went back to his pigs. As for the suitors, they soon began to entertain themselves with singing and dancing, since it was now getting on toward evening.

chapters.title: Book XVIII — The fight with irus—ulysses warns amphinomus—penelope gets presents from the suitors—the braziers—ulysses rebukes eurymachus.
paragraphs: A dirty beggar came to Odysseus's home in Ithaca. Everyone knew this man as a greedy drunk who would do anything for food. His real name was Arnaeus, but people called him Irus because he ran messages for coins. When he saw Odysseus sitting by the door, he got angry and tried to push him away.

"Get out of here, old man!" Irus shouted. "Move away from this doorway or I'll drag you out! Can't you see everyone wants me to throw you out? I'm being nice by not doing it yet. Get up and leave, or we'll have to fight!"

Odysseus glared at him. "Friend, I'm not hurting anyone. People give you plenty, and I'm not jealous. This doorway is big enough for both of us. You don't own the things people give away. You seem like just another beggar like me. Maybe the gods will give us better luck someday. But don't talk about fighting, or you'll make me angry. Even though I'm old, I'll make you bleed. Then I'll have peace tomorrow because you won't come back here again."

Irus became furious. "You dirty pig! You talk too much like an old fish seller. I should knock all your teeth out like a wild boar's tusks. Get ready to fight! Let all these people watch. You can't beat someone so much younger than you!"

The two ragged beggars argued loudly on the stone floor by the doorway. When Antinous (one of the suitors trying to marry Odysseus's wife) saw this, he laughed. "This is the best entertainment we've ever had! The gods sent us great fun today. The stranger and Irus want to fight. Let's make them do it!"

All the suitors gathered around, laughing at the two beggars. "Listen," said Antinous. "We have some goat stomachs filled with blood and fat cooking by the fire for dinner. Whoever wins this fight gets first choice of the food. He can eat at our table, and we won't let any other beggar in the house."

Everyone agreed. But Odysseus, pretending to be weak, said, "Sirs, an old man like me, worn out by suffering, can't fight a young man. But my hungry belly forces me to try, even though I know I'll get beaten. You must promise that none of you will cheat by helping Irus win."

They swore they would be fair. Then Telemachus (Odysseus's son, though no one knew the beggar was really his father) spoke up. "Stranger, if you want to fight this man, don't worry about anyone here. If someone hits you, they'll have to fight more than one person. I'm the host, and Antinous and Eurymachus agree with me."

Everyone nodded. Odysseus tied his old rags around his waist, showing his strong thighs, broad chest and shoulders, and powerful arms. Minerva (the goddess of wisdom, called Athena by the Greeks) came and made his muscles even stronger. The suitors were amazed. One whispered to another, "Look at those muscles under his rags! There won't be anything left of Irus!"

Irus became terrified when he heard this. The servants had to force him into the courtyard because he was shaking with fear. Antinous scolded him: "You big bully! You shouldn't have been born if you're afraid of this old broken-down beggar. Listen—if he beats you, I'll put you on a ship and send you to King Echetus on the mainland. He kills everyone who comes near him and will cut off your nose and ears and feed your insides to the dogs!"

This scared Irus even more, but they dragged him to fight. Odysseus thought about whether to hit him hard enough to kill him or just knock him down. He decided to hit lightly so the Greeks wouldn't guess who he really was. They began fighting. Irus punched Odysseus in the right shoulder, but Odysseus hit Irus in the neck under his ear, breaking the bones in his skull. Blood poured from Irus's mouth as he fell, groaning and grinding his teeth in the dust. The suitors laughed so hard they nearly died as Odysseus dragged Irus by the foot to the gate and propped him against the wall with his staff. "Sit here and keep the dogs and pigs away," Odysseus said. "You're pathetic. If you try to be king of the beggars again, you'll get worse treatment."

Odysseus threw his torn old bag over his shoulder and went back to sit by the doorway. The suitors went inside the covered walkway, laughing and congratulating him. "May Zeus and all the gods give you whatever you want for stopping that greedy tramp's begging! We'll send him to King Echetus on the mainland—he kills everyone."

Odysseus took this as a good sign. Antinous brought him a big goat's stomach filled with blood and fat. Amphinomus gave him two loaves of bread and a golden cup of wine. "Good luck, father stranger," he said. "You're having hard times now, but I hope things get better for you."

Odysseus answered, "Amphinomus, you seem wise, as you should be since you're the son of Nisus of Dulichium, a brave and wealthy man. Listen carefully to what I'm saying. Humans are the most foolish creatures on earth. When the gods give them health and strength, they think nothing bad will happen to them. Even when the gods bring sorrow, they bear it and make the best of it, because God gives people their daily thoughts each day. I know this because I was once rich and did wrong things because of my pride, trusting that my father and brothers would protect me. So a person should always respect God and accept good fortune without boasting. Look at the terrible things these suitors are doing! See how they're wasting the estate and dishonoring the wife of a man who will certainly return soon. He'll be here before long. May heaven send you home safely before you meet him when he comes, because once he's here, the suitors and he won't part without bloodshed."

After saying this, Odysseus poured a drink offering to the gods. When he finished drinking, he gave the golden cup back to Amphinomus, who walked away sadly, shaking his head because he sensed trouble coming. But even this wouldn't save him, because Minerva had decided he would die by Telemachus's hand in the coming battle. So he sat back down where he had been before.

Then Minerva put an idea in Penelope's mind to show herself to the suitors. This would make them love her even more and bring more honor from her son and husband. Penelope laughed mockingly and said to her servant Eurynome, "I've changed my mind and want to appear before the suitors, even though I hate them. I should also warn my son not to spend time with them anymore. They speak nicely but plan evil things."

"My dear child," answered Eurynome, "everything you say is true. Go tell your son, but first wash and put oils on your face. Don't go around with your cheeks covered in tears. It's not right to grieve so constantly. Telemachus, whom you always prayed you'd live to see grow a beard, is already a man."

"I know you mean well, Eurynome," replied Penelope, "but don't try to make me wash and oil myself. Heaven took away all my beauty the day my husband sailed away. But call Autonoe and Hippodamia to come with me. They must be with me when I'm in the main hall. I won't go among the men alone—that wouldn't be proper."

The old woman left to get the maids. Meanwhile, Minerva had another idea and made Penelope fall into a sweet sleep on her couch. Then the goddess gave her grace and beauty so all the Greeks would admire her. She washed Penelope's face with the divine loveliness that Venus wears when she dances with the Graces (goddesses of beauty and charm). She made her taller and more commanding, and her skin became whiter than carved ivory. When Minerva finished, she left, and the maids came in and woke Penelope with their talking.

"What a wonderfully peaceful sleep I had," Penelope said, touching her face, "despite all my sadness. I wish Diana (goddess of the hunt) would let me die so peacefully right now, so I wouldn't have to keep wasting away in despair for my dear husband. He had every good quality and was the most outstanding man among all the Greeks."

With these words, she came down from her upstairs room with two maids. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars that supported the covered walkway roof, holding a veil over her face with a loyal maid on each side. When the suitors saw her, they were overwhelmed and fell desperately in love with her. Each one prayed he could win her as his wife.

"Telemachus," she said to her son, "I'm afraid you're not as wise and well-behaved as you used to be. When you were younger, you had better manners. Now that you're grown up, though a stranger would think you're the son of a wealthy father based on your size and good looks, your behavior isn't what it should be. What was all that fighting about? How could you let a stranger be treated so badly? What if he had been seriously hurt while seeking help in our house? That would have been very shameful for you."

"I'm not surprised you're displeased, dear mother," replied Telemachus. "I understand everything and know when things are wrong, which I couldn't do when I was younger. But I can't behave perfectly all the time. These wicked people keep driving me crazy, and I have no one to help me. But this fight between Irus and the stranger didn't go the way the suitors wanted—the stranger won. I wish Father Zeus, Minerva, and Apollo would break the necks of every one of your suitors, both inside and outside the house. I wish they'd all be as weak as Irus is now by the gate. Look how his head droops like a drunk man's! He got such a beating he can't stand up or get home because he has no strength left."

As they talked, Eurymachus came up and said, "Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, if all the Greeks in Argos could see you right now, you'd have even more suitors here tomorrow morning. You're the most wonderful woman in the world for both beauty and intelligence."

Penelope replied, "Eurymachus, heaven took away all my beauty when the Greeks sailed for Troy with my dear husband. If he returned to take care of our affairs, I'd be more respected and look better to the world. As it is, I'm weighed down with worry and the troubles heaven has given me. My husband saw this coming. When he was leaving home, he took my right hand and said, 'Wife, we won't all come home safely from Troy because the Trojans fight well with bows, spears, and from chariots—and nothing decides a battle faster than chariot fighting. I don't know if heaven will send me back to you or if I'll die at Troy. Meanwhile, take care of things here. Look after my father and mother as you do now, or even more while I'm gone. But when you see our son growing a beard, marry whoever you want and leave this house.' That's what he said, and now it's all coming true. A night will come when I'll have to accept a marriage I hate, because Zeus has taken away all my hope of happiness. And here's another grief that cuts my heart. You suitors aren't courting me the proper way. When men court a woman they think will be a good wife and who comes from a noble family, they usually bring cattle and sheep to feast the lady's friends, and they give her magnificent gifts instead of eating up other people's property without paying for it."
When Odysseus heard this, he was glad because she was cleverly getting presents from the suitors while flattering them with sweet words that she didn't mean.

Then Antinous said, "Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, take as many presents as you want from anyone who will give them to you. It's not right to refuse a gift. But we won't leave or go about our business until you marry the best man among us, whoever that may be."

The others agreed with what Antinous said, and each sent his servant to bring gifts. Antinous's servant returned with a large, beautiful dress covered in exquisite embroidery and twelve beautifully made golden pins to fasten it. Eurymachus immediately brought her a magnificent gold and amber necklace that gleamed like sunlight. Eurydamas's two men brought earrings shaped like three brilliant hanging ornaments that sparkled beautifully. King Pisander, son of Polyctor, gave her a necklace of the finest craftsmanship. Everyone else brought her a beautiful present too.

Then the queen went back upstairs to her room, and her maids carried the presents after her. Meanwhile, the suitors began singing and dancing until evening came. They danced and sang until it grew dark. Then they brought in three metal fire baskets to give light and filled them with chopped firewood that was very old and dry. They lit torches from the fires, and the maids held them up, taking turns. Then Odysseus said:

"Maids, servants of Odysseus who has been away so long, go to the queen inside the house. Sit with her and entertain her, or spin thread and pick wool. I'll hold the light for all these people. They can stay until morning, but they won't defeat me because I can endure a great deal."

The maids looked at each other and laughed. Pretty Melantho began mocking him rudely. She was the daughter of Dolius but had been raised by Penelope, who gave her toys and cared for her as a child. But despite this kindness, she showed no consideration for her mistress's sorrows and was having a love affair with Eurymachus.

"You crazy fool," she said, "have you lost your mind completely? Go sleep in a blacksmith's shop or some public meeting place instead of chattering here. Aren't you ashamed to open your mouth in front of your betters—so many of them? Has wine gotten to your head, or do you always babble like this? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus. Be careful that a better man doesn't come and beat you bloody and throw you out of the house."
"You witch," replied Odysseus, scowling at her, "I'll go tell Telemachus what you've been saying, and he'll have you torn apart."

His words frightened the women, and they hurried away into the house. They trembled all over because they thought he would do what he threatened. But Odysseus stood near the burning fire baskets, holding up torches and watching the people—thinking all the while about things that would surely happen.

But Minerva wouldn't let the suitors stop being rude even for a moment because she wanted Odysseus to become even angrier with them. So she made Eurymachus, son of Polybus, mock him, which made the others laugh. "Listen," he said, "you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. This man didn't come to Odysseus's house for nothing. I think the light isn't coming from the torches but from his own head—because he's completely bald!"

Then turning to Odysseus, he said, "Stranger, would you work as my servant if I sent you to the countryside and paid you well? Can you build stone walls or plant trees? I'd feed you all year and give you shoes and clothes. Will you do it? No, you won't, because you've gotten into bad habits and don't want to work. You'd rather fill your belly by begging around the country."

"Eurymachus," answered Odysseus, "if you and I were to work against each other in early summer when the days are longest—give me a good scythe and take one yourself—let's see which of us can last longer or cut stronger, from dawn until dark when we're mowing grass. Or if you want to plow against me, let's each take a pair of strong, well-matched oxen and work a four-acre field to see who can plow a straighter furrow. If war broke out today, give me a shield, two spears, and a helmet that fits my head—you'd find me at the front of the battle and would stop your jokes about my belly. You're rude and cruel and think you're important because you live in a small, bad world. If Odysseus returns to his home, his doors are wide now, but you'll find them narrow when you try to escape through them."

Eurymachus became furious at all this. He glared and cried, "You wretch! I'll make you pay for daring to say such things to me, and in public too! Has wine gotten to your head, or do you always babble like this? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus." He grabbed a footstool, but Odysseus quickly moved to the knees of Amphinomus of Dulichium for protection. The stool hit the wine server on his right hand and knocked him down. The man fell flat on his back with a cry, and his wine jug fell ringing to the ground. The suitors in the covered walkway were now in an uproar. One turned to his neighbor saying, "I wish the stranger had gone somewhere else—bad luck to him for all the trouble he causes us. We can't have such disturbance over a beggar. If such bad ideas win out, we'll have no more pleasure at our feast."

Then Telemachus stepped forward and said, "Sirs, are you crazy? Can't you eat your food and drink properly? Some evil spirit has taken control of you. I don't want to drive any of you away, but you've had your dinner, and the sooner you all go home to bed, the better."

The suitors bit their lips and were amazed at how boldly he spoke. But Amphinomus, son of Nisus, who was son of Aretias, said, "Let's not take offense. That's reasonable, so let's not argue back. And let's not hurt the stranger or any of Odysseus's servants. Let the wine server make drink offerings to the gods so we can make our offerings and go home to rest. As for the stranger, let's leave Telemachus to deal with him, since this is his house."

Everyone liked what he said. So Mulius of Dulichium, Amphinomus's servant, mixed them a bowl of wine and water and passed it around to each man. They made their drink offerings to the blessed gods. Then, after they had made their offerings and each had drunk as much as he wanted, they went their separate ways to their own homes.

chapters.title: Book XIX — Telemachus and ulysses remove the armour—ulysses interviews penelope—euryclea washes his feet and recognises the scar on his leg—penelope tells her dream to ulysses.
paragraphs: Ulysses sat alone in the courtyard, thinking hard about how he and the goddess Minerva could defeat the suitors. He turned to his son and said, "Telemachus, we need to gather all the weapons and hide them away. When the suitors ask why you've moved them, tell them you're protecting the armor from smoke damage. Say that the weapons have gotten dirty and blackened from sitting out so long. Also tell them you're worried that if they drink too much wine and start fighting, they might grab the weapons and hurt each other. Sometimes just seeing weapons makes people want to use them."

Telemachus agreed with his father's plan. He called for Euryclea, his old nurse, and said, "Nurse, please lock the servant women in their rooms while I move my father's armor to the storage room. No one has taken care of it since he left, and it's gotten covered with soot during my childhood. I want to store it somewhere safe from the smoke."

"I wish you would take charge of the whole household, child," Euryclea replied. "You should manage all the property yourself. But who will carry a torch to light your way to the storage room? The maids could help you, but you won't let them."
"The stranger will hold the light for me," said Telemachus. "Anyone who eats my food must earn it, no matter where they come from."

Euryclea did as she was told and locked the women in their room. Then Ulysses and his son quickly gathered all the helmets, shields, and spears. Minerva walked ahead of them carrying a golden lamp that cast a brilliant, magical glow. Telemachus gasped, "Father, this is amazing! The walls, ceiling beams, and wooden supports are all glowing like they're on fire. Surely one of the gods has come down from heaven!"

"Quiet," Ulysses whispered. "Don't ask questions about this. This is just how the gods work. Go to bed now and leave me here to talk with your mother and the servants. Your mother will want to ask me many questions in her grief."

So Telemachus took his torch and went to his bedroom on the other side of the inner courtyard, where he always slept. There he lay until morning, while Ulysses remained in the courtyard, still planning with Minerva's help how to destroy the suitors.

Then Penelope came down from her room, beautiful as the goddesses Venus or Diana. The servants brought her favorite chair, decorated with silver and ivory scrollwork, near the fire where she always sat. A craftsman named Icmalius had made this special chair with a built-in footstool, and it was covered with a thick fleece. As she sat down, the maids came from the women's quarters to join her. They began clearing away the tables where the greedy suitors had been eating and drinking. They emptied the coals from the fire baskets and piled on fresh wood for light and warmth. But Melantho, a rude servant girl, started insulting Ulysses again. "Stranger, are you planning to bother us all night, hanging around the house and spying on the women? Get out, you wretch! Go eat your dinner outside, or we'll drive you out with a burning stick!"

Ulysses glared at her angrily. "Woman, why are you so mean to me? Is it because I'm dirty and my clothes are torn, and because I have to beg for food like other homeless people? I was once a rich man with a fine house of my own. In those days, I gave food to many beggars just like I am now, no matter who they were or what they needed. I had many servants and everything that wealthy people have. But the god Jupiter decided to take it all away from me. So woman, be careful that you don't lose your own comfortable position! Watch out that you don't fall out of favor with your mistress, and that Ulysses doesn't come home - because there's still a chance he might return. And even if he's dead as you think, he left behind a son, Telemachus, who notices when servants behave badly. He's no longer a child."

Penelope heard what the stranger said and scolded the maid harshly. "You rude girl! I see exactly how terribly you're behaving, and you'll be punished for it. You knew perfectly well - because I told you myself - that I planned to speak with this stranger and ask him about my husband, for whom I grieve constantly."

Then she spoke to Eurynome, her head servant. "Bring a chair with a soft fleece covering so the stranger can sit comfortably while he tells his story and listens to what I have to say. I want to ask him some questions."

Eurynome quickly brought the seat and placed a fleece on it. As soon as Ulysses sat down, Penelope began. "Stranger, first I must ask - who are you and where do you come from? Tell me about your city and your parents."

"My lady," Ulysses replied, "who in all the world would dare to criticize you? Your fame reaches to the heavens! You're like a perfect king who rules with justice over a great and brave nation. Because of his goodness, the earth produces wheat and barley, trees bear fruit, sheep have lambs, the sea is full of fish, and his people do good deeds. But please, as I sit here in your house, ask me something else. Don't ask about my family and background, or you'll bring back sad memories that will make me even more sorrowful. I'm already full of sadness, and I shouldn't sit here weeping in someone else's house. It's not right to keep grieving like this. One of your servants - or even you - might complain that my eyes are full of tears because I've had too much wine."

Penelope answered, "Stranger, heaven took away all my beauty when the Greek armies sailed for Troy, taking my dear husband with them. If he were to return and take care of our affairs, I would be more respected and present a better face to the world. Instead, I'm overwhelmed with worry and troubles that heaven has piled upon me. Chiefs from all the nearby islands - Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, and even from Ithaca itself - are trying to force me to marry them, and they're destroying my property. So I can't properly welcome strangers, visitors, or skilled craftsmen, because I'm constantly heartbroken about Ulysses. The suitors want me to remarry immediately, so I have to think of tricks to fool them. First, heaven gave me the idea to set up a large weaving frame in my room and begin working on an enormous piece of fine fabric. Then I told them, 'Young men, Ulysses is indeed dead, but please don't pressure me to marry right away. Wait until I finish weaving a burial shroud for the hero Laertes, to be ready when death takes him. He's very wealthy, and the women here will gossip if he's buried without a proper shroud.' This is what I said, and they agreed. So every day I worked on my great weaving, but every night I secretly unraveled what I had done by torchlight. I fooled them this way for three years without them discovering my trick. But in the fourth year, as time passed and many days went by, those good-for-nothing servant girls betrayed me to the suitors. They caught me unraveling the work and were very angry. So I was forced to finish the shroud whether I wanted to or not. Now I don't see how I can avoid this marriage any longer. My parents are pressuring me greatly, and my son is upset about how the suitors are wasting his inheritance. He's now old enough to understand everything and perfectly able to manage his own affairs - heaven has blessed him with an excellent character. Still, despite all this, tell me who you are and where you come from. You must have had parents of some kind - you can't be the son of a tree or a rock!" (In ancient Greece, asking about someone's parentage was very important, as family lines determined social status.)

Ulysses replied, "My lady, wife of Ulysses, since you keep asking about my family, I'll answer, no matter how much it hurts me. People who have been exiles as long as I have, suffering among so many different peoples, must expect to feel pain when talking about home. But I'll tell you what you want to know. There's a beautiful, fertile island in the middle of the sea called Crete. It's heavily populated with ninety cities, and the people speak many overlapping languages - there are Achaeans, brave Eteocretans, three tribes of Dorians, and noble Pelasgi. The great city there is Cnossus, where King Minos ruled. Every nine years he would meet with Jupiter himself." (Minos was a legendary king of Crete who was said to receive laws directly from Jupiter.) "Minos was the father of Deucalion, and I am Deucalion's son. Deucalion had two sons - Idomeneus and myself. I'm the younger one, called Aethon, while my brother was both older and braver. That's how I came to see Ulysses in Crete and show him hospitality when the winds blew his ship off course on his way to Troy. The storm carried him past Cape Malea and left him at Amnisus, near the cave of Ilithuia, where the harbors are dangerous and he could barely find shelter. As soon as he reached land, he went into town asking for Idomeneus, claiming to be his old friend. But Idomeneus had already sailed for Troy ten or twelve days earlier. So I took Ulysses to my own house and showed him every kindness, for I had plenty of everything. I also fed his men with barley from the public storehouse and got donations of wine and cattle for them to sacrifice. They stayed with me twelve days because a fierce north wind was blowing - so strong you could hardly stand up on land. I think some unfriendly god had stirred it up. But on the thirteenth day, the wind died down and they sailed away."

Ulysses told many more believable stories, and Penelope wept as she listened, her heart melting with emotion. Just as snow melts on mountaintops when warm winds from the southeast and west blow on it, causing rivers to overflow with water, so her cheeks overflowed with tears for her husband who was sitting right beside her the whole time. Ulysses felt sorry for her and pitied her, but he kept his eyes as hard as horn or iron, not letting them even quiver. He cleverly held back his tears. When she had finished crying, she wiped her eyes and said, "Now, stranger, I'm going to test you to see whether you really did welcome my husband and his men as you claim. Tell me how he was dressed, what he looked like, and describe his companions too."

"My lady," Ulysses answered, "it was so long ago that I can barely remember. Twenty years have come and gone since he left my home. But I'll tell you as well as I can recall. Ulysses wore a purple wool cloak, double-lined, fastened with a gold brooch that had two pins. On the front was a design showing a dog holding a spotted fawn between its front paws, watching as the fawn lay panting on the ground. Everyone marveled at how skillfully these figures were made in gold - the dog looking at the fawn and strangling it, while the fawn struggled desperately to escape. The shirt he wore next to his skin was so soft it fit him like an onion's skin and gleamed in the sunlight, amazing all the women who saw it. I should mention that I don't know if Ulysses was wearing these clothes when he left home, or if one of his companions gave them to him during the voyage, or perhaps someone he stayed with made them as gifts. He was a man with many friends and few equals among the Greeks. I myself gave him a bronze sword and a beautiful purple cloak, double-lined, with a shirt that reached his feet, and I sent him off with every honor. He had a servant with him, a little older than himself, and I can describe him too: he had hunched shoulders, dark skin, and thick curly hair. His name was Eurybates, and Ulysses treated him with more familiarity than any of the others because they thought alike."

Penelope was moved even more deeply when she heard these unmistakable proofs, and after crying again, she said to him, "Stranger, I was already inclined to pity you, but from now on you'll be honored and welcomed in my house. I was the one who gave Ulysses those clothes you describe. I took them from the storage room and folded them myself, and I gave him that gold brooch as well. Alas! I'll never welcome him home again. It was terrible luck that he ever set sail for that hateful city whose name I can't even bear to speak!" (She means Troy.)

Then Ulysses answered, "My lady, wife of Ulysses, don't make yourself suffer more by grieving so bitterly, though I can hardly blame you. Any woman who has loved her husband and had children with him would naturally grieve at losing him, even if he were a worse man than Ulysses, who they say was like a god. But stop your tears and listen to what I can tell you. I'll hide nothing and can say truthfully that I recently heard news of Ulysses - he's alive and on his way home! He's among the Thesprotians, bringing back valuable treasures he's collected from various people. But his ship and all his crew were lost when they left the island of Thrinacia, because Jupiter and the sun-god were angry that his men had killed the sun-god's sacred cattle. Everyone drowned except Ulysses, who clung to the ship's keel and drifted to the land of the Phaeacians. These people are related to the immortal gods, and they treated him like a god himself, giving him many gifts and wanting to escort him home safely. In fact, Ulysses would have been here long ago, but he decided it was better to travel from land to land gathering wealth - no living man is as clever as he is! King Pheidon of the Thesprotians told me all this and swore to me, making sacred drink offerings in his house, that a ship was ready at the harbor with a crew to take Ulysses home. He sent me away first on a Thesprotian ship sailing to the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, but he showed me all the treasure Ulysses had collected - enough to support his family for ten generations! The king said Ulysses had gone to Dodona to learn Jupiter's will from the sacred oak tree there, to find out whether he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret after such a long absence." (Dodona was a famous oracle site where people believed Jupiter spoke through a sacred oak tree.) "So you can be sure he's safe and will be here soon. He's close by and can't stay away from home much longer. I'll swear an oath and call mighty Jupiter to witness, and by this hearth of Ulysses where I now sit, that everything I've said will come true. Ulysses will return this very year - between the end of this month and the beginning of the next!"

"I hope it happens just as you say," Penelope replied. "If your words come true, you'll receive such gifts and friendship from me that everyone who sees you will congratulate you. But I know very well how it will really be. Ulysses won't return, and you won't get safe passage from here either. There are no longer any masters in this house like Ulysses was, to properly receive honored guests or help them on their way home. Now, you maids, wash his feet and prepare a bed with blankets so he'll be warm and comfortable until morning. Then at daybreak, wash and oil him again so he can sit in the courtyard and eat with Telemachus. It will go badly for any of these hateful suitors who treats him rudely - they'll have no more business in this house. For how else, sir, will you be able to judge whether I'm better than other women in kindness and wisdom, if I let you dine in my halls dirty and poorly dressed? People don't live very long - if they're cruel and treat others badly, people curse them while they're alive and speak badly of them when they're dead. But those who are good and treat others fairly are praised throughout all lands, and many call them blessed."

Ulysses answered, "My lady, I've given up soft blankets and beds since the day I left the snowy mountains of Crete to go to sea. I'll sleep as I have on many sleepless nights before, in rough places, waiting for morning. Also, I don't like having my feet washed - I won't let any of the young servant girls in your house touch my feet. But if you have an old, respectable woman who has gone through as much trouble as I have, I'll let her wash them."

Penelope replied, "My dear sir, of all the guests who have ever come to my house, none has spoken with such perfect manners as you do. It happens that there's a very respectable old woman in the house - the same one who received my poor dear husband in her arms the night he was born and nursed him as a baby. She's very frail now, but she'll wash your feet. Come here, Euryclea, and wash your master's contemporary. I suppose Ulysses' hands and feet look much the same as this man's do now, since trouble ages us all terribly fast."

When she heard these words, the old woman covered her face with her hands and began to weep and wail, saying, "My dear child, I don't know what to do about you! I'm certain no one was ever more god-fearing than yourself, yet Jupiter seems to hate you. No one in the whole world ever burned more offerings to him or gave him finer sacrifices when you prayed to live to old age and see your son grow up to be like you. Yet see how he's prevented you alone from returning to your home! I'm sure the women in whatever foreign palace Ulysses has reached are mocking him, just as all these worthless girls here have been mocking you. I don't blame you for not wanting them to wash you after how they've insulted you. I'll gladly wash your feet myself, as Penelope has asked me to do. I'll do it both for Penelope's sake and for your own, because you've stirred such deep compassion in my heart. Let me say this too - please pay attention - we've had all kinds of strangers in need come here before, but I dare say no one ever came who was so much like Ulysses in appearance, voice, and feet as you are."
"Those who have seen us both," Ulysses replied, "have always said we looked remarkably alike, and now you've noticed it too."

Then the old woman took the basin she was going to use to wash his feet and poured in plenty of cold water, adding hot water until the bath was warm enough. Ulysses sat by the fire, but soon he turned away from the light. It occurred to him that when the old woman held his leg, she would recognize a certain scar it bore, and then the whole truth would come out. And indeed, as soon as she began washing her master, she immediately recognized the scar - one that had been given to him by a wild boar when he was hunting on Mount Parnassus with his excellent grandfather Autolycus. Autolycus was the most accomplished thief and liar in the whole world, and the god Mercury had given him this gift because Autolycus used to burn thigh bones of goats and kids as offerings to him, so Mercury enjoyed his friendship. It happened once that Autolycus had come to Ithaca and found his daughter's child just born. As soon as he finished dinner, Euryclea placed the baby on his knees and said, "Autolycus, you must choose a name for your grandson - you really wanted to have one."

"Son-in-law and daughter," Autolycus replied, "name the child as I tell you. I'm very angry with many people in various places, both men and women, so call the child 'Ulysses' - the child of anger. When he grows up and comes to visit his mother's family on Mount Parnassus, where my wealth is stored, I'll give him presents and send him home happy."

So Ulysses went to Mount Parnassus to receive the gifts from Autolycus, who welcomed him warmly along with his sons. His grandmother Amphithea threw her arms around him and kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes, while Autolycus told his sons to prepare dinner, which they did. They brought in a five-year-old bull, skinned it, prepared it, and cut it into pieces. Then they carefully sliced these into smaller portions and cooked them on spits, roasting them perfectly and serving everyone their share. All day long until sunset they feasted, and everyone ate their fill. When the sun set and darkness came, they went to bed and enjoyed restful sleep.

When Dawn appeared with rosy fingers, Autolycus's sons went out hunting with their dogs, and Ulysses went with them. They climbed the wooded slopes of Parnassus and soon reached its windy mountain valleys. As the sun began to warm the fields, rising fresh from the slow currents of Ocean (the Greeks believed the sun rose from a great river that circled the earth), they came to a mountain valley. The dogs were ahead, searching for tracks of their prey, followed by Autolycus's sons and Ulysses, who carried a long spear. Here in some thick bushes was the den of a huge boar - so dense that wind and rain couldn't get through, nor could the sun's rays penetrate it. The ground underneath was thick with fallen leaves. The boar heard the sound of men's feet and dogs barking on all sides as the hunters approached. He rushed from his lair, bristles raised on his neck, and stood ready to fight with fire flashing in his eyes. Ulysses was first to raise his spear and try to drive it into the beast, but the boar was too quick and charged sideways, ripping him above the knee with a deep gash that didn't reach the bone. As for the boar, Ulysses hit him in the right shoulder, and his spear point went right through, so the boar fell groaning in the dust until he died. Autolycus's sons took care of the boar's carcass and bandaged Ulysses' wound. After saying a magic spell to stop the bleeding, they went home as fast as they could. When Autolycus and his sons had completely healed Ulysses, they gave him splendid presents and sent him back to Ithaca with great mutual friendship. When he returned home, his father and mother were overjoyed to see him and asked all about his adventure and how he got hurt. So he told them how the boar had wounded him while hunting with Autolycus and his sons on Mount Parnassus.

As soon as Euryclea got hold of the scarred leg and felt it carefully, she recognized it and immediately dropped his foot. His leg fell into the bath with a loud clang, overturning the basin so that all the water spilled on the ground. Euryclea's eyes filled with tears of joy and grief, and she couldn't speak. She grabbed Ulysses by the beard and said, "My dear child, I'm sure you must be Ulysses himself! I just didn't recognize you until I actually touched and felt you."

As she spoke, she looked toward Penelope, wanting to tell her that her dear husband was in the house. But Penelope couldn't look in that direction or see what was happening because Minerva had distracted her attention. So Ulysses grabbed Euryclea by the throat with his right hand and pulled her close with his left, saying, "Nurse, do you want to destroy me? You nursed me at your own breast, and now after twenty years of wandering, I've finally come to my own home. Since heaven has made you recognize me, keep quiet and don't say a word about it to anyone else in the house. If you do, I tell you - and this will surely happen - that even though you're my own nurse, I won't spare you when I kill the other women, if heaven grants me victory over these suitors."

"My child," Euryclea answered, "what are you saying? You know very well that nothing can bend or break me. I'll keep silent as stone or iron. Furthermore, let me tell you this - when heaven has delivered the suitors into your hands, I'll give you a list of the women in the house who have misbehaved and those who are innocent."
Ulysses replied, "Nurse, you don't need to talk that way. I'm perfectly capable of judging them all for myself. Keep quiet and leave everything to heaven."

As he said this, Euryclea left the courtyard to get more water, since the first had all spilled. When she had washed him and rubbed him with oil, Ulysses moved his seat closer to the fire to warm himself and hid the scar under his rags. Then Penelope began talking to him again:

"Stranger, I'd like to speak with you briefly about one more thing. It's almost bedtime - at least for those who can sleep despite their sorrows. As for me, heaven has given me a life of such terrible grief that even during the day, when I'm doing my duties and managing the servants, I'm still weeping and mourning the whole time. Then when night comes and we all go to bed, I lie awake thinking, and my heart becomes prey to constant, cruel torture. Like the brown nightingale, daughter of Pandareus, who sings in early spring from her hidden perch in the shadows, pouring out her sad song about how she accidentally killed her own child Itylus, son of King Zethus - just so my mind tosses and turns, uncertain whether I should stay here with my son and protect my property, my servants, and my household's reputation out of respect for public opinion and my late husband's memory, or whether it's now time to go with the best of these suitors who are courting me and offering such magnificent gifts. As long as my son was young and couldn't understand, he wouldn't hear of my leaving my husband's house. But now that he's grown up, he begs and pleads with me to do so, being angry about how the suitors are consuming his inheritance. Listen to a dream I had and interpret it for me if you can. I have twenty geese around the house that eat mash from a trough, and I'm very fond of them. I dreamed that a great eagle swooped down from a mountain and stuck his curved beak into each of their necks until he had killed them all. Then he soared off into the sky, leaving them lying dead in the yard. I wept in my dream until all my maids gathered around me, I was grieving so pitifully because the eagle had killed my geese. Then he came back and perched on a projecting roof beam, speaking to me in a human voice. He told me to stop crying. 'Be brave,' he said, 'daughter of Icarius. This is no dream, but a vision of good fortune that will surely come true. The geese are the suitors, and I am no longer an eagle, but your own husband, returned to you, and I will bring these suitors to a disgraceful end.' At this I woke up, and when I looked outside, I saw my geese at the trough eating their food as usual."

"This dream, my lady," Ulysses replied, "can have only one meaning, since Ulysses himself has told you how it will be fulfilled. The death of the suitors is foretold, and not a single one of them will escape."

Penelope answered, "Stranger, dreams are very strange and puzzling things, and they don't always come true. There are two gates through which these shadowy fantasies come - one made of horn, and the other of ivory. Dreams that come through the ivory gate are false, but those from the horn gate have real meaning for those who see them. I don't think my own dream came through the horn gate, though my son and I would be very grateful if it did. I'll tell you something else - and take this to heart - tomorrow's dawn will bring the cursed day that will separate me from Ulysses' house forever. I'm going to hold a contest with axes. My husband used to set up twelve axes in the courtyard, one behind the other, like the supports used in shipbuilding. Then he would stand back and shoot an arrow through all twelve. I'll make the suitors try to do the same thing. Whoever can string the bow most easily and send his arrow through all twelve axes - him I will marry, leaving this house of my lawful husband, so beautiful and full of wealth. Even so, I'm sure I'll remember it in my dreams."

Then Ulysses answered, "My lady, wife of Ulysses, don't delay your contest, because Ulysses will return before any of them can string the bow, handle it however they try, and send their arrows through the iron."

Penelope said, "As long as you sit here and talk with me, sir, I have no desire to go to bed. But people can't go without sleep forever, and heaven has appointed a time for all things for us who live on earth. So I'll go upstairs and lie on that bed which I've never stopped flooding with tears since the day Ulysses left for the city with the hateful name." (Again, she means Troy.)
Then she went upstairs to her room, not alone but accompanied by her servant women. There she mourned for her dear husband until Minerva gently closed her eyes with sweet sleep.

chapters.title: Book XX — Ulysses cannot sleep—penelope’s prayer to diana—the two signs from heaven—eumaeus and philoetius arrive—the suitors dine—ctesippus throws an ox’s foot at ulysses—theoclymenus foretells disaster and leaves the house.
paragraphs: Ulysses lay down to sleep in the courtyard on a raw cowhide, covered with sheepskins from the animals the suitors had eaten. Eurynome the housekeeper threw a cloak over him. But Ulysses couldn't sleep. He lay there awake, planning how to defeat the suitors. Soon he heard the servant women who had been sneaking around with the suitors, giggling as they left the house. This made Ulysses furious. He thought about jumping up and killing them all right then and there, but he held back. His heart growled with anger like a mother dog protecting her puppies when a stranger approaches. But he forced himself to be patient, remembering worse times he'd survived—like when the terrible one-eyed giant Cyclops ate his friends. "Heart, be still," he told himself. "You've endured worse than this and lived to tell about it."

He tossed and turned like meat cooking over a fire, thinking about how one man could possibly defeat so many enemies. Then Athena, the wise goddess who had always helped him, came down from Mount Olympus (the home of the gods). She appeared as a woman and hovered over his head. "My poor, troubled friend," she said gently, "why can't you sleep? This is your own house. Your wife is safe inside, and so is your son—a young man any father would be proud of."

"Goddess," Ulysses replied, "everything you say is true. But I'm worried about how I can possibly defeat all these wicked suitors by myself. There are so many of them! And even if Zeus and you help me kill them, where will I hide from their families when they come seeking revenge?"

"Shame on you!" Athena scolded. "Anyone else would trust a weaker ally than me, even just a regular person with less wisdom. I'm a goddess! Haven't I protected you through all your troubles? I tell you, even if fifty armies surrounded us, wanting to kill us, you would still drive away their cattle and sheep as your prize. Now go to sleep. Staying awake all night won't help anything, and your troubles will be over soon."
As she spoke, she made his eyes grow heavy with sleep, then returned to Mount Olympus.

While Ulysses finally slept deeply, his wonderful wife Penelope woke up in her bedroom. She sat up and began to cry. When her tears were spent, she prayed to Diana, the goddess of the hunt. "Great goddess Diana, daughter of Zeus, please shoot an arrow through my heart and end my misery! Or let a whirlwind carry me away into darkness and drop me into the deep ocean, like what happened to the daughters of Pandareus long ago." She told the story of those poor girls who lost their parents when the gods killed them. The goddesses tried to care for the orphans—Venus fed them honey and wine, Juno made them beautiful and smart, Diana made them tall and graceful, and Athena taught them many skills. But when Venus went to ask Zeus about finding them husbands, storm winds snatched them away to serve the Furies (terrifying goddesses of revenge). "I wish the same would happen to me," Penelope wept, "rather than marry someone worse than my dear Ulysses. At least during the day I can bear my grief, but at night even my dreams torment me. Just now I dreamed he was lying beside me, looking exactly as he did when he left for war. I was so happy, thinking it was real—but it was only a dream."

Dawn was breaking, and Ulysses heard his wife crying. For a moment, it seemed like she recognized him and was right there beside him. He gathered up his bedding and put it on a chair in the courtyard, then took the cowhide outside. He raised his hands to the sky and prayed: "Father Zeus, you've brought me home across land and sea after so much suffering. Now give me a sign from someone inside the house who's awake, and another sign from outside."

Zeus heard his prayer and immediately sent thunder rolling across the clear sky from Mount Olympus. Ulysses smiled with joy when he heard it. At the same time, a servant woman working at the grain mill nearby gave him another sign. Twelve women worked the mills, grinding wheat and barley to make bread. Eleven had finished their work and gone to rest, but one weak old woman was still grinding. When she heard the thunder from the clear sky, she stopped her work and called out: "Father Zeus, ruler of gods and men! You've made thunder without a single cloud—this must be a sign for someone. Please answer the prayer of your poor servant: let this be the very last day these suitors eat in Ulysses' house! They've worn me out making me grind grain for their endless feasts. I hope they never eat another meal anywhere!"
Ulysses was delighted to hear these omens—the woman's words and the thunder—because he knew they meant he would have his revenge on the suitors.

The other servants woke up and lit the fire. Telemachus got up too, putting on his clothes, strapping on his sword, tying his sandals, and picking up a sharp bronze-tipped spear. He went to the doorway and asked Euryclea, his old nurse: "Did you take good care of the stranger—give him a proper bed and food? Or did you leave him to fend for himself? My mother is good-hearted, but sometimes she pays attention to the wrong people and ignores those who deserve better treatment."

"Don't blame anyone when there's nothing to blame, child," said Euryclea. "The stranger sat drinking wine as long as he wanted. Your mother offered him more food, but he said no thank you. When bedtime came, she told us servants to make him a proper bed, but he refused. He said he was just a poor wanderer who wouldn't sleep on a real bed with blankets. He insisted on sleeping right here in the courtyard on that raw cowhide with some sheepskins, and I covered him with a cloak myself."

Telemachus left the courtyard to join the other young men of Ithaca for their morning meeting, carrying his spear and followed by his two dogs. Meanwhile, Euryclea called to the servant women: "Come on, wake up! Start sweeping the courtyards and sprinkling water to keep the dust down. Put covers on the chairs, wipe the tables with wet sponges, clean the wine cups and mixing bowls, and fetch fresh water from the spring. The suitors will arrive early today—it's a feast day."

The women did exactly as she ordered. Twenty went to fetch water from the spring while others busied themselves around the house. The men who served the suitors arrived and started chopping firewood. Soon the women returned with water, and Eumaeus the swineherd arrived with three of his finest pigs for the feast. He let them root around the yard, then spoke cheerfully to Ulysses: "Stranger, are the suitors treating you any better now, or are they still as rude as ever?"
"May heaven pay them back," Ulysses replied, "for the shameful way they act in another man's house!"

While they talked, Melanthius the goatherd arrived with his best goats for the suitors' dinner, along with two other shepherds. They tied up the goats under the gateway, and then Melanthius began mocking Ulysses again. "Are you still here, stranger, bothering everyone with your begging? Why don't you go somewhere else? You and I are going to come to blows before this is over. You have no shame in your begging—aren't there other houses where you could get food?"

Ulysses said nothing, just bowed his head and kept his thoughts to himself. Then a third man arrived—Philoetius the cattle herder, bringing a young cow and some goats. The ferryman had brought them across the water (there was a ferry service for travelers). After securing his animals under the gateway, Philoetius walked up to the swineherd. "Who is this new stranger?" he asked. "What family does he come from? Where is his home? Poor man, he looks like he might have been someone important once. The gods can bring sorrow to anyone—even kings—when they choose to."

He walked over to Ulysses and held out his right hand in greeting. "Good day, old stranger," he said kindly. "You seem to be having hard times now, but I hope things get better for you soon. Father Zeus, you are the cruelest of all gods! We are your own children, yet you show us no mercy in our suffering. I started sweating when I saw this man, and my eyes filled with tears, because he reminds me of Ulysses. I fear my master might be wandering somewhere in rags just like these—if he's even still alive. If he's dead and gone to Hades' realm, then alas for my good master! He made me his head cattleman when I was just a young man, and now his herds have grown beyond counting. No one could have done better with them—they've multiplied like grain in a field. But now I have to keep bringing the best cattle for these other men to eat. They don't care about his son, even though he's right here in the house, and they don't fear the gods' anger. They're already eager to divide up Ulysses' property since he's been gone so long. I've often thought about taking the cattle and leaving for some foreign land—but that wouldn't be right while his son is still alive. Still, it's hard to stay here and watch strangers abuse what belongs to my master. I would have run away long ago to serve some other chief, but I keep believing my poor master will return and chase all these suitors from his house."

"Cattle herder," Ulysses answered, "you seem like a good and sensible man. So I'll tell you something and swear an oath to prove it. I swear by Zeus, the greatest of gods, and by this hearth of Ulysses where I now stand: Ulysses will return before you leave this place. If you want, you'll see him killing these suitors who now act like masters here."
"If Zeus would make that happen," replied the cattle herder, "you'd see how hard I'd fight to help him!"
Eumaeus the swineherd said the same prayer—that Ulysses would come home.

While they talked, the suitors were plotting to murder Telemachus. But suddenly a bird appeared on their left—an eagle holding a dove in its claws. This was considered a bad omen. Amphinomus saw it and said, "Friends, this plan to kill Telemachus won't work out. Let's just go eat dinner instead."

The others agreed, so they went inside and hung their cloaks on chairs and benches. They sacrificed sheep, goats, pigs, and the young cow, and when the meat was cooked, they served it around. They mixed wine in large bowls, and the swineherd gave everyone cups while Philoetius passed around bread in baskets and Melanthius poured the wine. Then they all began to eat and drink.

Telemachus deliberately seated Ulysses in the stone-paved part of the courtyard, giving him a shabby chair at a small table by himself. But he made sure Ulysses got his fair share of meat and gave him wine in a gold cup. "Sit here," he announced, "and drink your wine with these important men. I'll put a stop to any insults or violence from the suitors. This isn't a public inn—it's Ulysses' house, passed down to me. So, suitors, keep your hands and nasty comments to yourselves, or there'll be trouble."

The suitors were amazed by his bold words. Antinous, their leader, said, "We don't like this kind of talk, but we'll put up with it since Telemachus is making serious threats. If Zeus had allowed it, we would have silenced his brave words by now."
Antinous spoke, but Telemachus ignored him. Meanwhile, heralds were leading a special sacrifice through the city, and the people of Ithaca gathered in Apollo's sacred grove.

Back at the house, they roasted the meat, pulled it off the spits, and everyone got their portion. The servers made sure Ulysses received exactly the same amount as everyone else, just as Telemachus had ordered.

But Athena wouldn't let the suitors stop their insulting behavior—she wanted Ulysses to become even more angry with them. Among the suitors was a particularly nasty man named Ctesippus from the island of Same. He was very wealthy and was trying to marry Penelope. He stood up and said to the others, "Listen, everyone! The stranger has already gotten his fair share of food, which is proper—we shouldn't mistreat any guest of Telemachus. But I want to give him a special present of my own, so he'll have something to tip the bath-woman or other servants with."

As he spoke, he grabbed a cow's foot from the meat basket and hurled it at Ulysses. But Ulysses quickly ducked his head to one side, avoiding it with a grim smile (the kind of bitter smile people from Sardinia were known for). The cow's foot hit the wall instead. Telemachus was furious and shouted at Ctesippus: "You're lucky the stranger dodged, or you would have missed him! If you had hit him, I would have run you through with my spear, and your father would be planning your funeral instead of your wedding. I won't tolerate any more of this disgusting behavior from any of you! I'm grown up now and understand the difference between right and wrong, instead of being the child I used to be. I've watched you killing my sheep and wasting my grain and wine for too long. I've put up with it because one person can't fight many, but don't push me further! If you want to kill me, then do it—I'd rather die than watch these shameful scenes every day, seeing guests insulted and servant women dragged around the house!"

Everyone fell silent until Agelaus, son of Damastor, finally spoke: "No one should be offended by what Telemachus just said—it's perfectly reasonable. Stop mistreating the stranger and the other servants. But let me offer some friendly advice to Telemachus and his mother. As long as you had hope that Ulysses might return, no one could blame you for waiting and letting the suitors stay in your house. It would have been wonderful if he had come back, but now it's clear he never will. So talk this over quietly with your mother and convince her to marry the best man who makes the most generous offer. Then you'll be able to manage your inheritance and eat and drink in peace, while your mother takes care of some other man's household, not yours."

Telemachus replied, "I swear by Zeus and by my poor father's sufferings—whether he's dead or wandering in some distant land—I'm not preventing my mother's remarriage! I encourage her to choose whoever she wants, and I'll give her countless gifts besides. But I can't force her to leave this house against her will. Heaven forbid I should do such a thing!"

Then Athena made the suitors burst into uncontrollable laughter, but it was a strange, forced laughter that made no sense. Their food became smeared with blood, their eyes filled with tears, and their hearts grew heavy with dark feelings. Theoclymenus the prophet saw this and cried out: "Miserable men, what's happening to you? Darkness covers you from head to foot! I hear the sound of weeping! Your cheeks are wet with tears! The walls and ceiling are dripping blood! The courtyard and gateway are full of ghosts heading down to the underworld! The sun has vanished from the sky, and evil darkness spreads over everything!"
The suitors all laughed at his words. Eurymachus said, "This stranger who just arrived has lost his mind. Servants, throw him out into the street, since he thinks it's so dark in here."

But Theoclymenus replied, "Eurymachus, I don't need anyone to escort me. I have my own eyes, ears, feet, and brain. I'll take myself out of here, because I can see disaster coming for all of you. Not one of you men who are insulting people and plotting evil in Ulysses' house will escape what's coming."

He left the house and went back to Piraeus, who welcomed him kindly. But the suitors kept looking at each other and provoking Telemachus by mocking the strangers. One arrogant young man said, "Telemachus, you're really unlucky with your guests! First you have this annoying beggar who wants food and wine but can't work or fight—completely useless! And now here's another one pretending to be a prophet. Let me convince you—it would be much better to put them both on a ship and sell them to the Sicilians for whatever they'd bring."
Telemachus paid no attention to him. He sat quietly, watching his father and waiting for the moment when he would begin his attack on the suitors.

Meanwhile, wise Penelope had a special chair placed where she could see into the courtyard and hear everything being said. The dinner had been prepared with much celebration—it was both delicious and plentiful, since they had sacrificed many animals. But the evening meal was still to come, and nothing could be more horrible than the feast that a goddess and a brave hero were about to serve them—for the suitors had brought their doom upon themselves.

chapters.title: Book XXI — The trial of the axes, during which ulysses reveals himself to eumaeus and philoetius
paragraphs: Minerva (also called Athena, the goddess of wisdom) now gave Penelope an idea. She would make the suitors compete with Ulysses' bow and iron axes. This contest would lead to their doom. Penelope climbed the stairs and took the bronze key with its ivory handle. With her servants, she went to the treasure room at the far end of the house. Here lay her husband's riches - gold, bronze, and fine metalwork. Here too was his mighty bow and quiver full of deadly arrows. These had been a gift from a friend he met long ago in Lacedaemon - Iphitus, son of Eurytus. The two men had met in Messene at Ortilochus's house. Ulysses was there trying to get back a debt the whole Messenian people owed him. They had stolen three hundred sheep from Ithaca and sailed away with them and their shepherds. Ulysses made this long journey while still young, sent by his father and other chiefs to recover the stolen flock. Iphitus had come there too, seeking twelve valuable mares he had lost, along with their mule foals. Sadly, these same mares would cause his death. When he went to mighty Hercules' house (Hercules was Zeus's son, famous for his incredible strength), Hercules shamefully killed his guest. He feared no punishment from the gods and showed no respect for his own table where Iphitus had eaten. He murdered Iphitus and kept the mares for himself. It was while searching for these mares that Iphitus met Ulysses and gave him the bow that great Eurytus used to carry, which Eurytus had left to his son when he died. Ulysses gave Iphitus a sword and spear in return, starting a close friendship. But they never visited each other's homes again, for Hercules killed Iphitus before they could. This bow, given by Iphitus, had stayed home when Ulysses sailed to Troy. He had used it for hunting on Ithaca but left it behind as a treasured keepsake from his dear friend.

Penelope reached the oak doorway of the treasure room. A skilled carpenter had planed the wood smooth and drawn a straight line to guide his work. He had set the doorposts perfectly and hung the heavy doors. She untied the leather strap from the handle, put in the key, and pushed it home to shoot back the iron bolts that held the doors shut. The doors flew open with a sound like a bull bellowing in a meadow. Penelope stepped onto the raised wooden platform where chests held fine linens and clothes, stored with sweet-smelling herbs. From there, she lifted down the bow in its leather case from the peg where it hung. She sat with it on her knees, weeping bitter tears as she took the bow from its case. When her tears had given her some relief, she walked to the great hall where the suitors waited. She carried the bow and quiver filled with many deadly arrows. Her servants came with her, carrying a chest full of iron and bronze prizes her husband had won long ago. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars that held up the roof. She held a veil before her face, with a maid on each side. Then she spoke:

"Listen to me, you suitors who keep abusing the hospitality of this house while its master has been gone so long. You have no excuse except that you want to marry me. Well then, since I am the prize you're fighting for, I will bring out mighty Ulysses' bow. Whoever can string it most easily and shoot an arrow through all twelve axes - him I will follow. I will leave this house of my true husband, so beautiful and full of wealth. Even so, I know I will remember it always in my dreams."

As she spoke, she told Eumaeus the swineherd to set the bow and iron axes before the suitors. Eumaeus wept as he obeyed her command. Nearby, Philoetius the cattle herder also wept when he saw his master's bow. But Antinous scolded them both. "You country fools!" he said. "Silly simpletons! Why do you add to your mistress's sorrow by crying like this? She has enough grief losing her husband. Sit quietly and eat your dinner in silence, or go outside if you want to cry. Leave the bow here with us. We suitors will have to fight hard for it - this will be no easy contest. Stringing this bow will be incredibly difficult. There's not one of us who can match Ulysses. I've seen him and remember him, though I was just a child then."

This is what Antinous said, but secretly he expected to string the bow and shoot through the iron axes himself. In truth, he would be the first to taste arrows from Ulysses' hands - the same Ulysses he was dishonoring in his own house, while encouraging others to do the same.

Then Telemachus spoke up. "Great heavens!" he exclaimed. "Zeus must have stolen my wits! Here's my dear, wonderful mother saying she'll leave this house and marry again, yet I'm laughing and having fun as if nothing's happening. But suitors, since we've agreed on this contest, let's get on with it. The prize is a woman whose equal can't be found in Pylos, Argos, Mycenae, Ithaca, or anywhere on the mainland. You know this as well as I do - why should I need to praise my mother? Come on then, make no excuses for delay. Let's see if you can string the bow or not. I'll try it too. If I can string it and shoot through the iron, then my mother won't have to leave this house with a stranger, at least not if I can win the same contests my father won before me."

As he spoke, he jumped up from his seat, threw off his red cloak, and took his sword from his shoulder. First he set up the axes in a long, straight row. He had dug a groove for them and made it perfectly straight with a measuring line. Then he stamped the earth tight around them. Everyone was amazed to see him set them up so neatly, though he had never seen anything like this before. When this was done, he stepped onto the platform to try the bow. Three times he pulled at it, using all his strength to draw the string. Three times he had to stop, though he hoped desperately to string the bow and shoot through the iron. He was trying for the fourth time and might have succeeded, but Ulysses signaled him to stop, despite his eagerness. So Telemachus said:

"Oh no! Either I'll always be weak and useless, or I'm too young and haven't reached my full strength yet to defend myself if anyone attacks me. You others who are stronger than me, try the bow and settle this contest."
With these words, he put the bow down, leaning it against the door that led into the house, with the arrow standing against the bow's tip. Then he sat back down, and Antinous said:
"Come on, each of you take a turn, going from right to left, starting where the wine server begins when he pours the drinks."

Everyone agreed, and Leiodes, son of Oenops, was first to stand. He was the priest who performed sacrifices for the suitors and always sat in the corner near the wine-mixing bowl. He was the only one who hated their evil deeds and was angry with the others. Now he was first to take the bow and arrow. He went to the platform to try, but he could not string the bow. His hands were soft and weak from never doing hard work, so they quickly grew tired. He said to the suitors, "My friends, I cannot string it. Let someone else try. This bow will take the life and soul from many chiefs among us. It's better to die than to live having failed at the prize we've worked for so long, which has kept us together here so long. Some of us are hoping and praying right now to marry Penelope. But when he has seen this bow and tried it, let him court some other woman instead. Let Penelope marry whoever offers her the most and whose fate it is to win her."
With that, he put the bow down, leaning it against the door with the arrow standing against the bow's tip. Then he sat back down, and Antinous scolded him:

"Leiodes, what are you saying? Your words are terrible and unbearable! It makes me angry to listen to you. Should this bow kill many chiefs among us just because you can't bend it yourself? True, you weren't born to be an archer, but there are others here who will string it soon enough."

Then he called to Melanthius the goat herder: "Quick! Light a fire in the courtyard and set up a chair with a sheepskin on it. Bring us a big ball of fat from the house stores. We'll warm the bow and grease it - then we'll try again and finish this contest."

Melanthius lit the fire and set up a chair covered with sheepskins beside it. He also brought a large ball of fat from the house stores. The suitors warmed the bow and tried again, but none of them was nearly strong enough to string it. Only Antinous and Eurymachus remained - the leaders of the suitors and by far the strongest among them.
Then the swineherd and cattle herder left the great hall together, and Ulysses followed them. When they had gotten outside the gates and outer courtyard, Ulysses spoke to them quietly:

"Cattle herder, and you, swineherd, I have something on my mind. I'm not sure whether to say it, but I think I will. What kind of men would you be to fight for Ulysses if some god brought him back here suddenly? Tell me honestly - would you side with the suitors or with Ulysses?"
"Father Zeus," answered the cattle herder, "if only you would make it so! If some god would just bring Ulysses back, you'd see with what strength and determination I would fight for him!"

Eumaeus prayed the same way to all the gods that Ulysses might return. When Ulysses saw for certain what they truly felt, he said, "I am here - I am Ulysses! I have suffered greatly, but finally, after twenty years, I've returned to my own country. I see that you two alone among all my servants are glad I've come back. I haven't heard any of the others praying for my return. So to you two I will tell the truth of what will happen. If heaven puts the suitors in my power, I will find wives for both of you. I'll give you houses and land close to my own, and you'll be like brothers and friends to Telemachus. Now I'll give you proof so you'll know me and be certain. Look - here's the scar from the wild boar's tusk that ripped me when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus with Autolycus's sons." (Autolycus was Ulysses' grandfather, famous for his cleverness.)

As he spoke, he pulled his rags away from the great scar. When they had examined it carefully, both men wept and threw their arms around Ulysses, kissing his head and shoulders. Ulysses kissed their hands and faces in return. The sun would have set on their joyful reunion if Ulysses hadn't stopped them:
