"Stop weeping, in case someone comes outside and sees us, then tells those inside. When you go back in, go separately, not together. I'll go first, and you follow after. Here's our signal: the suitors will all try to stop me from getting the bow and quiver. So Eumaeus, when you're carrying it around, put it in my hands. Tell the women to lock the doors of their rooms. If they hear groaning or fighting sounds from men battling in the house, they must not come out. They must stay quiet and keep working. And Philoetius, I order you to lock the doors of the outer courtyard and tie them securely right away."
After saying this, he went back to the house and took the same seat he had left. Soon after, his two faithful servants followed him inside.

At that moment, Eurymachus held the bow, warming it by the fire, but even then he could not string it. He was deeply frustrated and sighed heavily. "I'm upset for myself and all of us! I'm sad that I'll have to give up this marriage, but I don't care so much about that - there are plenty of other women in Ithaca and other places. What bothers me most is that we're so much weaker than Ulysses that we can't even string his bow. This will shame us in the eyes of future generations."

"That won't happen, Eurymachus," said Antinous, "and you know it. Today is Apollo's feast day throughout all the land. Who can string a bow on such a holy day? Put it aside - the axes can stay where they are, since no one will come to the house and steal them. Let the wine server go around with cups so we can pour drink offerings to the gods and forget about the bow. Tomorrow we'll tell Melanthius to bring the best goats he has. We can offer the thigh bones to mighty Apollo the archer, then try the bow again and finish the contest."

Everyone agreed with his words. Servants poured water over the guests' hands, while young men filled the mixing bowls with wine and water, serving everyone after each person made their offering to the gods. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as they wanted, Ulysses spoke cleverly:

"Suitors of the famous queen, listen while I speak my mind. I appeal especially to Eurymachus and to Antinous, who just spoke so wisely. Stop shooting for now and leave the matter to the gods. In the morning, let heaven give victory to whoever it chooses. But for now, give me the bow so I can test the strength of my hands among you all. Let me see if I still have the power I used to have, or if travel and hardship have destroyed it."

This made them all very angry, because they feared he might actually string the bow. So Antinous scolded him harshly: "Wretched creature! You don't have a grain of sense in your whole body! You should consider yourself lucky to eat safely among your betters, getting the same portions we do, and to hear our conversation. No other beggar or stranger has been allowed to hear what we say among ourselves. The wine must be harming you, as it does everyone who drinks too much. It was wine that drove the Centaur Eurytion mad when he was staying with King Peirithous among the Lapiths." (Centaurs were mythical creatures - half man, half horse, known for their wild behavior.) "When wine went to his head, he went crazy and did terrible things in Peirithous's house. This angered the heroes gathered there, so they attacked him and cut off his ears and nose. Then they dragged him out the door, so he left in madness, carrying the burden of his crime and his lost wits. From then on, there was war between humans and centaurs, but he brought it on himself through drunkenness. I tell you it will go badly for you if you string that bow. You'll find no mercy from anyone here. We'll ship you off to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him. You'll never escape alive, so drink quietly and don't pick fights with men younger than yourself."

Then Penelope spoke to him: "Antinous, it's not right for you to mistreat any guest of Telemachus who comes to this house. If this stranger proves strong enough to string mighty Ulysses' bow, do you really think he would take me home and make me his wife? Even he can't have such an idea! None of you should let that thought disturb your feasting - it would be completely unreasonable."

"Queen Penelope," answered Eurymachus, "we don't think this man will take you away - that's impossible! But we're afraid some of the common people, men or women among the Greeks, will gossip and say, 'These suitors are weaklings! They're courting the wife of a brave man whose bow none of them could string, yet some ragged tramp who came to the house strung it easily and shot an arrow through the iron.' That's what people will say, and it will bring shame on us."

"Eurymachus," Penelope replied, "people who keep eating up a great chief's estate and dishonoring his house can't expect others to think well of them. So why should you care if people talk the way you think they will? This stranger is strong and well-built, and he says he's of noble birth. Give him the bow and let's see whether he can string it or not. I promise you this - and it will surely happen - if Apollo grants him the glory of stringing it, I'll give him a fine cloak and shirt, a spear to keep off dogs and robbers, and a sharp sword. I'll also give him sandals and help him travel safely wherever he wants to go."

Then Telemachus said, "Mother, I'm the only one in Ithaca or in all the islands near Elis who has the right to give anyone this bow or refuse it. No one can force me either way, not even if I choose to give the bow to this stranger outright and let him take it away. Go inside the house and busy yourself with your daily work - your weaving, your spinning, and managing the servants. This bow is men's business, and mine especially, since I am the master here."
She went back into the house, wondering, and took her son's words to heart. Going upstairs with her servants to her room, she mourned her dear husband until Minerva sent sweet sleep over her eyes.

The swineherd now picked up the bow to carry it to Ulysses, but the suitors shouted at him from all around the hall. One of them said, "You idiot! Where are you taking that bow? Are you out of your mind? If Apollo and the other gods answer our prayers, your own hunting dogs will drag you to some quiet place and tear you apart!"

Eumaeus was frightened by all their shouting, so he put the bow down right there. But Telemachus yelled at him from the other side of the hall, threatening him: "Father Eumaeus, bring the bow here despite what they say, or young as I am, I'll chase you back to the country with stones - I'm stronger than you! I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in this house as I am compared to you. I'd soon send some of them away sick and sorry, because they're planning evil!"

This made everyone laugh heartily, which put them in a better mood toward Telemachus. So Eumaeus brought the bow and placed it in Ulysses' hands. Then he called Euryclea the nurse aside and said to her, "Euryclea, Telemachus says you should lock the doors of the women's rooms. If they hear any groaning or sounds of men fighting in the house, they must not come out. They should stay quiet and keep working."
Euryclea did exactly as she was told and locked the doors of the women's rooms.

Meanwhile, Philoetius quietly slipped outside and secured the gates of the outer courtyard. There was a ship's rope made of papyrus fiber lying in the gatehouse, so he tied the gates shut with it. Then he came back in, returned to the seat he had left, and kept watching Ulysses. Ulysses now held the bow in his hands, turning it every way and examining it all over to see if worms had eaten into its two horn tips during his long absence. The suitors muttered to each other. One would say to his neighbor, "This guy's some kind of bow expert! Either he has one like this at home, or he wants to make one - look how skillfully the old beggar handles it!"
Another said, "I hope he's no more successful at other things than he'll be at stringing this bow!"

But Ulysses, when he had picked it up and examined it completely, strung it as easily as a skilled musician strings a new peg on his lyre and fastens the twisted gut string at both ends. Then he held it in his right hand to test the string, and it sang sweetly under his touch like a swallow's song. The suitors were shocked and their faces went pale when they heard it. At that very moment, Zeus thundered loudly as a sign, and Ulysses' heart rejoiced when he heard the omen that the son of crafty Cronus had sent him.

He took an arrow that lay on the table - the arrows that the Greeks would soon taste were all inside the quiver. He placed it on the center grip of the bow and drew back the arrow's notch and the string, still sitting in his seat. Taking careful aim, he let fly. His arrow pierced every single handle-hole of the axes, from first to last, and flew right through them into the outer courtyard. Then he said to Telemachus:

"Your guest has not embarrassed you, Telemachus. I didn't miss my target, and I wasn't slow in stringing my bow. I'm still strong, not weak as the suitors mock me for being. Now, however, it's time for the Greeks to prepare supper while there's still daylight, and then to enjoy themselves with song and dance - the perfect finishing touches for a feast."
As he spoke, he signaled with his eyebrows, and Telemachus strapped on his sword, gripped his spear, and stood armed beside his father's chair.

chapters.title: Book XXII — The killing of the suitors—the maids who have misconducted themselves are made to cleanse the cloisters and are then hanged.
paragraphs: Then Odysseus threw off his raggedy disguise and leaped onto the great stone floor with his bow and a quiver full of arrows. He poured the arrows out at his feet and shouted, "The contest is over! Now let's see if Apollo, the god of archery, will help me hit a target no one has ever hit before!"

He aimed a deadly arrow at Antinous, the worst of the suitors. Antinous was just lifting a golden cup to drink wine, with no thought of danger. Who would think that one man, no matter how brave, could stand alone against so many enemies? The arrow struck him in the throat and went straight through his neck. He toppled over, the cup falling from his hands as blood gushed from his nose. His legs kicked the table, sending bread and roasted meat crashing to the floor. The other suitors jumped up in panic when they saw a man had been killed. They looked wildly around the walls for shields and spears, but found none. They yelled angrily at Odysseus: "Stranger, you'll pay for shooting people! You're a dead man! The vultures will eat you for killing the finest young man in Ithaca!"
They thought he had killed Antinous by accident, not knowing that death was coming for all of them. But Odysseus glared at them fiercely and said:

"Dogs! Did you think I would never return from Troy? You've stolen my treasure, forced my servant women to sleep with you, and tried to marry my wife while I was still alive. You feared neither the gods nor justice. Now you will die!"
Their faces turned white with terror as he spoke. Every man looked around desperately for an escape route, but only Eurymachus dared to speak.

"If you really are Odysseus," he said, "then you're right to be angry. We have done terrible things in your lands and house. But Antinous, who led us in these crimes, is already dead. It was all his idea! He didn't really want to marry Penelope—he wanted something else entirely. Zeus didn't grant his wish—he wanted to kill your son and become king of Ithaca. Now that he's gotten what he deserved, spare the rest of us! We'll pay you back for everything we've eaten and drunk. Each of us will give you a treasure worth twenty oxen, and we'll keep giving you gold and bronze until you forgive us. No one could blame you for being angry until we make this right."

Odysseus glared at him again and said, "Even if you gave me everything you own now and everything you'll ever have, I won't stop until I've paid you all back in full. You must fight or run for your lives—and not one of you will escape!"
Their hearts sank when they heard this, but Eurymachus spoke again:

"Friends, this man will show us no mercy. He'll stand there and shoot us down until every one of us is dead. Let's fight back! Draw your swords and use the tables as shields against his arrows. Let's rush him together and drive him from the doorway. Then we can get to the town and raise an alarm to stop his shooting."

As he spoke, he drew his sharp bronze sword and charged at Odysseus with a loud war cry. But instantly, Odysseus shot an arrow that struck him in the chest, piercing his liver. Eurymachus dropped his sword and fell doubled over his table. Food and wine spilled everywhere as he hit the ground face-first in his death throes, kicking his stool until his eyes closed forever.

Then Amphinomus drew his sword and rushed straight at Odysseus, trying to force him away from the door. But Telemachus was faster—he hurled his spear from behind and struck Amphinomus between the shoulder blades. The spear went clean through his chest, and he crashed to the ground. Telemachus quickly ran away, leaving his spear in the body, afraid that if he stopped to pull it out, one of the suitors might attack him with a sword. He sprinted to his father's side and said:
"Father, let me bring you a shield, two spears, and a bronze helmet. I'll arm myself too, and bring weapons for the swineherd and cowherd. We need to be properly armed for battle."
"Go quickly and get them," Odysseus replied, "while I still have arrows. If I run out and I'm alone, they might drive me from the door."

Telemachus did as his father commanded and raced to the storeroom where the weapons were kept. He grabbed four shields, eight spears, and four bronze helmets decorated with horsehair plumes. He brought them back at top speed and armed himself first, while the loyal swineherd and cowherd also put on armor and took positions near Odysseus. Meanwhile, as long as his arrows lasted, Odysseus kept shooting the suitors one by one, and they fell in heaps. When his arrows ran out, he leaned his bow against the doorpost and hung a thick, four-layered shield on his shoulders. On his head he placed a well-made helmet with a horsehair crest that waved menacingly, and he gripped two powerful bronze-tipped spears.

Now there was a trap door in the wall, and at one end of the hall there was an exit leading to a narrow passage. This exit was closed by a strong door. Odysseus told Philoetius the cowherd to guard this door, since only one person could attack through it at a time. But Agelaus shouted out, "Can't someone go to the trap door and tell the people in town what's happening? Help would come quickly, and we'd soon put an end to this man's shooting!"

"That won't work, Agelaus," answered Melanthius the goatherd. "The narrow passage is too close to the main entrance. One brave man could stop any number from getting through. But I know what to do—I'll bring you weapons from the storeroom. I'm sure that's where Odysseus and his son put their extra armor."

The traitorous goatherd Melanthius crept through back passages to Odysseus's storeroom. There he selected twelve shields, helmets, and spears, and brought them back as fast as he could to arm the suitors. Odysseus's heart sank when he saw the suitors putting on armor and brandishing spears. He realized the great danger they were in and said to Telemachus, "Someone inside the house is helping the suitors against us. It must be Melanthius."

Telemachus answered, "The fault is mine, father! I left the storeroom door open, and they kept better watch than I did. Go, Eumaeus, close that door and see if it's one of the women helping them, or if it's Melanthius, as I suspect."

While they talked, Melanthius was going back to the storeroom for more weapons. The swineherd spotted him and said to Odysseus, "There's that villain Melanthius, just as we suspected, heading for the storeroom again. Should I kill him if I can overpower him, or bring him to you so you can take your own revenge for all the wrongs he's done in your house?"

Odysseus answered, "Telemachus and I will hold off these suitors, no matter what they do. You two go back and tie up Melanthius's hands and feet behind his back. Throw him in the storeroom and lock the door. Then put a rope around his body and hang him from a high beam so he suffers a long, painful death."

They did exactly as he said. They went to the storeroom and hid on either side of the door, waiting. Soon Melanthius came out carrying a helmet in one hand and an old, cracked shield in the other—one that had belonged to Odysseus's father Laertes when he was young, but had been stored away for years with broken straps. The two men grabbed Melanthius, dragged him back by his hair, and threw him struggling to the ground. They bound his hands and feet tightly behind his back with painful ropes, just as Odysseus had ordered. Then they put a noose around his body and strung him up from a high pillar until he hung near the rafters. The swineherd Eumaeus mocked him, saying, "Now you'll spend the night on a soft bed, as you deserve! You'll know when morning comes from the eastern sea, and it's time to drive your goats in for the suitors' feast."

They left him hanging in cruel bondage, put on their armor, closed the door, and returned to fight beside Odysseus. Now four men stood in the hall, fierce and ready for battle, while many brave enemies still faced them in the main court. Then Athena, the goddess of wisdom and war, came to them disguised as Mentor, an old friend. Odysseus was glad to see her and said, "Mentor, help me! Remember our old friendship and all the good things I've done for you."

But though he felt sure it was really Athena, the suitors shouted angrily when they saw her. Agelaus was first to threaten her: "Mentor, don't let Odysseus trick you into fighting alongside him against us! Here's what we'll do: after we kill this father and son, we'll kill you too. You'll pay with your life, and when you're dead, we'll take everything you own and add it to Odysseus's property. We won't let your sons live in your house, your daughters won't survive, and your wife won't be allowed to stay in Ithaca."

This made Athena even more furious, and she scolded Odysseus harshly. "Odysseus, your strength and courage aren't what they used to be when you fought for nine long years at Troy over beautiful Helen. You killed many men in those days, and it was your clever plan that brought down the city of Troy. How is it that you're so much weaker now that you're on your own land, facing the suitors in your own house? Come on, stand beside me and see how Mentor fights your enemies and repays your kindness!"
But she wouldn't give him complete victory yet—she wanted to test his courage and that of his brave son further. So she flew up to one of the roof beams and perched there in the form of a swallow.

Meanwhile, Agelaus, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander, and Polybus led the suitors' fight. Of all those still battling for their lives, these were by far the bravest, since the others had already fallen to Odysseus's arrows. Agelaus shouted to them, "Friends, he'll have to stop soon, since Mentor has left after doing nothing but boast. They're standing alone at the doors now. Don't all aim at him at once—let six of you throw your spears first. Maybe you can win glory by killing him. Once he falls, the others will be easy."

They threw their spears as he commanded, but Athena made them all miss their target. One hit the doorpost, another struck the door, and a third hit the wall. After dodging all the suitors' spears, Odysseus said to his men, "Friends, I think we should throw our spears right into the middle of them, or they'll add murder to all the other harm they've done us."

They aimed carefully and hurled their spears. Odysseus killed Demoptolemus, Telemachus killed Euryades, Eumaeus killed Elatus, and the cowherd killed Pisander. All four hit the dust, and as the other suitors retreated to a corner, Odysseus and his men rushed forward to pull their spears from the bodies of the dead.

The suitors threw their spears a second time, but again Athena made most of them harmless. One hit a pillar, another struck the door, and a third hit the wall. But Amphimedon managed to scrape the skin from Telemachus's wrist, and Ctesippus grazed Eumaeus's shoulder above his shield, though the spear passed by and fell to the ground. Then Odysseus and his men attacked the crowd of suitors again. Odysseus hit Eurydamas, Telemachus struck Amphimedon, and Eumaeus killed Polybus. The cowherd hit Ctesippus in the chest and taunted him: "Foul-mouthed son of Polytherses, don't be foolish enough to speak wickedly again! Let heaven guide your words, since the gods are far stronger than men. Take this as payment for the cow's hoof you threw at Odysseus when he was begging in his own house!"

The cowherd spoke these words as Odysseus speared the son of Damastor in close combat, and Telemachus struck Leocritus in the belly. The spear went straight through him, and he fell face-first to the ground. Then Athena held up her terrible aegis (a magical shield) from her perch on the rafter, and the suitors' hearts failed them with terror. They fled to the far end of the court like a herd of cattle maddened by stinging flies in early summer. Like eagles with curved beaks and hooked talons swooping down from the mountains to attack smaller birds that huddle helplessly on the ground—birds that cannot fight or fly while onlookers enjoy the spectacle—so Odysseus and his men fell upon the suitors and struck them down on every side. The suitors made horrible groaning sounds as their skulls were crushed, and the ground was soaked with blood.

Then Leiodes grabbed Odysseus's knees and begged, "Odysseus, have mercy on me and spare my life! I never wronged any woman in your house, either in word or deed, and I tried to stop the others. I saw their evil behavior, but they wouldn't listen, and now they're paying for their foolishness. I was their priest, offering sacrifices to the gods. If you kill me, I'll die without having done anything wrong, and I'll get no thanks for all the good I tried to do."

Odysseus looked at him sternly and answered, "If you were their priest, you must have prayed many times that I would never come home, and that you could marry my wife and have children with her. Therefore, you must die."
With these words, he picked up the sword that Agelaus had dropped when he died. Then he struck Leiodes on the back of the neck, so his head went rolling in the dust while he was still speaking.

The singer Phemius, son of Terpes—who had been forced by the suitors to perform for them—now tried to save his life. He stood near the trap door, holding his lyre. He didn't know whether to run outside and sit by the altar of Zeus in the courtyard, where both Laertes and Odysseus had made many sacrifices, or to go straight to Odysseus and beg for mercy. In the end, he decided to embrace Odysseus's knees in supplication. He set his lyre down between the wine bowl and a silver-studded chair, then went to Odysseus, grabbed his knees, and said, "Odysseus, have mercy and spare me! You'll regret it later if you kill a bard who can sing for both gods and men as I can. I compose all my own songs, and heaven fills me with inspiration. I would sing to you as if you were a god—don't be so quick to cut off my head! Your own son Telemachus will tell you that I didn't want to come to your house and sing for the suitors after their meals. They were too many and too strong for me, so they forced me to do it."

Telemachus heard him and quickly went to his father. "Stop!" he cried. "This man is innocent—don't hurt him! And let's spare Medon too, who was always kind to me when I was a child, unless Philoetius or Eumaeus has already killed him, or he got in your way during the fighting."
Medon heard Telemachus's words—he had been hiding under a chair, covered by a freshly skinned cowhide. He threw off the hide, went to Telemachus, and grabbed his knees.
"Here I am, dear sir," he said. "Hold back your hand and tell your father, or he'll kill me in his rage against the suitors who wasted his wealth and showed such disrespect to you."

Odysseus smiled at him and said, "Don't be afraid. Telemachus has saved your life, so you'll know and can tell others how much better good deeds turn out than evil ones. Go outside to the courtyard, away from this slaughter—you and the singer—while I finish my work here inside."

The two men hurried to the outer court as fast as they could and sat by Zeus's great altar, looking around fearfully and still expecting to be killed. Then Odysseus searched the entire hall carefully to see if anyone had managed to hide and was still alive, but he found them all lying in the dust, covered in blood. They looked like fish that fishermen have hauled from the sea in nets and thrown on the beach, where they lie gasping for water until the sun's heat kills them. That's how the suitors lay, all piled up against each other.
Then Odysseus said to Telemachus, "Call nurse Euryclea. I need to speak with her."
Telemachus went and knocked on the door of the women's quarters. "Hurry up," he said, "old woman who supervises all the other women in the house. Come outside—my father wants to speak with you."

When Euryclea heard this, she unbolted the door and came out, following Telemachus. She found Odysseus among the corpses, spattered with blood and gore like a lion that has just devoured an ox, with his chest and cheeks all bloody—a fearsome sight. That's how Odysseus looked, covered from head to foot with blood. When she saw all the bodies and the pools of blood, she started to cry out with joy, seeing that a great deed had been accomplished. But Odysseus stopped her: "Old woman, rejoice silently. Control yourself and don't make noise about it. It's wrong to boast over dead men. Heaven's judgment and their own evil deeds destroyed these men. They respected no one in the world, rich or poor, who came near them, and they've met a bad end as punishment for their wickedness and foolishness. Now tell me which women in the house have behaved badly, and which are innocent."

"I'll tell you the truth, my child," answered Euryclea. "There are fifty women in the house who we've taught to work—to card wool and do all kinds of household tasks. Of these, twelve have misbehaved and shown no respect to me or Penelope. They didn't disrespect Telemachus because he's only recently grown up, and his mother never let him give orders to the female servants. But let me go upstairs and tell your wife what's happened—some god has sent her to sleep."
"Don't wake her yet," Odysseus replied. "First, tell the women who have misbehaved to come to me."

Euryclea left the hall to get the guilty women and bring them to Odysseus. Meanwhile, he called Telemachus, the cowherd, and the swineherd. "Start removing the dead bodies," he said, "and make the women help you. Then get sponges and clean water to wash down the tables and chairs. When you've thoroughly cleaned the entire hall, take the women to the space between the round room and the outer wall, and run them through with your swords until they're dead and have forgotten all about the shameful way they secretly slept with the suitors."

The women came down together, weeping and wailing bitterly. First they carried out the dead bodies and propped them against each other in the gateway. Odysseus ordered them around and made them work quickly. When they finished this, they cleaned all the tables and chairs with sponges and water, while Telemachus and the two men shoveled up the blood and dirt from the floor. The women carried it all outside. After making the whole place clean and orderly, they took the guilty women out and trapped them in the narrow space between the wall of the round room and the outer courtyard, where they couldn't escape. Telemachus said to the other two, "I won't let these women die a clean death, since they insulted my mother and me and slept with the suitors."

He tied a ship's rope to one of the pillars that supported the roof of the round room and stretched it around the building at a good height so none of the women's feet would touch the ground. Like thrushes or doves caught in a net set in a thicket just as they were flying to their nest, meeting a terrible fate, the women had to put their heads in nooses one after another and die miserably. Their feet kicked for a little while, but not for long.

As for Melanthius, they dragged him through the hall into the inner courtyard. There they cut off his nose and ears, tore out his private parts and fed them raw to the dogs, then in their fury cut off his hands and feet.

When this was done, they washed their hands and feet and went back into the house, since all the work was finished. Odysseus said to dear old nurse Euryclea, "Bring me sulfur to purify the air of pollution, and bring fire so I can burn it and cleanse the hall. Also, go tell Penelope to come here with her attendants, and bring all the other maidservants in the house."
"Everything you've said is right," answered Euryclea, "but let me bring you clean clothes—a tunic and cloak. Don't keep wearing those rags any longer. It isn't proper."
"First light me a fire," Odysseus replied.

She brought fire and sulfur as he had asked, and Odysseus thoroughly purified the hall and both the inner and outer courtyards. Then she went inside to call the women and tell them what had happened. They came from their rooms carrying torches, crowding around Odysseus to embrace him, kissing his head and shoulders and taking his hands. It made him feel like weeping, because he remembered every one of them.

chapters.title: Book XXIII — Penelope eventually recognises her husband—early in the morning ulysses, telemachus, eumaeus, and philoetius leave the town.
paragraphs: Old Euryclea rushed upstairs, her heart bursting with joy. Her tired old legs felt young again as she hurried to wake her mistress. She bent over Penelope's bed and shook her gently. "Wake up, my dear child!" she cried. "Come and see what you've been praying for all these years! Odysseus has come home at last! He's killed all those greedy suitors who were ruining his house, eating his food, and treating his son so badly!"

"My dear nurse," Penelope said sleepily, "you must be going crazy. Sometimes the gods mess with people's minds - they make wise people act foolish, or foolish people suddenly smart. That's what must have happened to you! You've always been so sensible before. Why are you making fun of me when I already have enough troubles? You're talking nonsense and waking me from the best sleep I've had since my husband left for that cursed city of Troy. Go back to the women's rooms right now! If anyone else had woken me with such ridiculous news, I would have sent them away with a harsh scolding. Only your old age protects you from my anger."

"My dear child," Euryclea insisted, "I'm not making fun of you! It's absolutely true - Odysseus really has come home! He was that beggar everyone treated so horribly in the courtyard. Telemachus knew it was his father the whole time, but he kept the secret so they could get revenge on those wicked men."

Penelope jumped up from her bed, threw her arms around Euryclea, and burst into tears of joy. "But my dear nurse," she said, "explain this to me! If he really has returned as you say, how could he possibly defeat all those evil suitors by himself? There were so many of them!"

"I wasn't there to see it happen," Euryclea answered. "I only heard their groaning and screaming as they died. We servant women were hiding in our room with the doors locked tight, until your son came to get me because his father sent for me. When I came out, I found Odysseus standing among the dead bodies scattered all around him, one piled on top of another. You would have been amazed to see him there, covered in blood and dirt, looking fierce as a lion! But now all the corpses are stacked up in the gatehouse of the outer courtyard, and Odysseus has lit a great fire to cleanse the house with sulfur smoke. He sent me to bring you to him, so you can both be happy together at last! Your heart's greatest wish has come true - your husband is home, and he's found both his wife and son alive and well. He's taken his revenge on the suitors who treated him so terribly."

"My dear nurse," Penelope said carefully, "don't get too excited about all this. You know how thrilled everyone would be to see Odysseus come home - especially me and our son. But what you're telling me can't possibly be true. Some angry god must have destroyed the suitors because of their terrible wickedness. They showed no respect to anyone in the whole world, rich or poor, who came near them. Their evil deeds brought them to this bad end. But Odysseus is dead, far away from Greece. He'll never come home again."

"My child, what are you saying?" nurse Euryclea cried. "You've always been stubborn and have made up your mind that your husband will never return. But he's here right now, sitting by his own fireplace! And I can give you proof! When I was washing his feet, I saw the scar that wild boar gave him long ago. I wanted to tell you then, but he was too clever - he clamped his hand over my mouth to keep me quiet. Come with me, and I'll make you a deal - if I'm lying to you, you can have me killed in the cruelest way you can think of!"

"My dear nurse," Penelope replied, "no matter how wise you are, you can't understand the mysterious ways of the gods. But still, let's go find my son so I can see the dead suitors and the man who killed them."

So Penelope came down from her upstairs room. As she walked, she wondered whether she should keep her distance from this man and question him carefully, or run straight to him and throw her arms around him. When she reached the stone floor of the great hall, she sat down across from Odysseus by the fire, against the opposite wall. Odysseus sat near one of the wooden pillars that held up the roof, staring at the ground, waiting to see what his clever wife would say when she saw him. For a long time she sat in complete silence, absolutely amazed. One moment she would look right at his face, but then she would look away again, confused by his dirty, ragged clothes, unable to recognize him. Finally, Telemachus got frustrated and scolded her:

"Mother - though you're acting so cold I can hardly call you that - why are you staying away from my father like this? Why don't you sit beside him and talk to him and ask him questions? No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband after he'd been gone for twenty years and been through so much suffering! But your heart has always been as hard as stone."

Penelope answered, "My son, I'm so shocked that I can't find any words to ask questions or give answers. I can't even look him straight in the face. But if this really is Odysseus, back in his own home, we'll figure out the truth soon enough. There are secret signs that only we two know about, hidden from everyone else."

Odysseus smiled when he heard this, and said to Telemachus, "Let your mother test me however she wants. She'll make up her mind soon. Right now she's rejecting me because I'm covered with dirt and wearing these terrible clothes. But let's think about what we should do next. When someone kills another person - even if that person didn't have many friends to seek revenge - the killer still has to say goodbye to his friends and flee the country. But we've been killing the most important young men of our entire town, all the leading citizens of Ithaca. You need to think about this problem."

"You figure it out, father," Telemachus replied. "People say you're the wisest counselor in the world, and no other mortal man can match your intelligence. We'll follow you gladly, and you won't find us failing you as long as we have strength."

"I'll tell you what I think is best," Odysseus answered. "First, wash yourselves and put on clean clothes. Tell the servant women to go to their rooms and dress nicely too. Then Phemius the bard should play his lyre and strike up a happy dance tune. If people outside hear it, or neighbors, or someone walking down the street notices, they'll think there's a wedding celebration going on in the house. No rumors about the suitors' deaths will spread through town before we can escape to the woods on my land. Once we're there safely, we'll decide which plan the gods give us seems wisest."

They did exactly as he said. First they washed and put on clean shirts, while the women got dressed up nicely. Then Phemius took his lyre and filled everyone with the desire for beautiful music and graceful dancing. The house echoed with the sounds of men and women dancing, and people outside said, "I guess the queen finally got married again! She should be ashamed of herself for not protecting her husband's property better until he came home." (In ancient Greece, it was considered the wife's duty to guard the household and wealth while her husband was away.)

That's what they were saying, but they had no idea what had really happened inside. The head servant woman, Eurynome, washed Odysseus in his own house and rubbed him with olive oil, then gave him a clean tunic and cloak. The goddess Athena made him look taller and stronger than before. She made thick hair grow on his head and flow down in curls like hyacinth flowers. She made him glow with beauty around his head and shoulders, like a master craftsman who learned his art from the gods and decorates a piece of silver by covering it with gold. Odysseus came from his bath looking like one of the immortal gods and sat down across from his wife in the same chair he had left. "My dear," he said, "the gods have given you a heart more stubborn than any woman ever had. No other woman could bear to stay away from her husband when he came back after twenty years of absence and terrible suffering. Come on, nurse, make a bed for me. I'll sleep alone, since this woman's heart is as hard as iron."

"My dear," Penelope answered, "I'm not trying to act proud or look down on you. But I'm not impressed by your appearance, because I remember very well what kind of man you were when you sailed away from Ithaca. Still, Euryclea, take his bed outside the bedroom that he built himself. Move the bed out of that room and put blankets on it with soft fleeces, good coverlets, and warm blankets."

She said this to test him, but Odysseus became very angry and said, "Wife, I'm really upset by what you just said! Who has been moving my bed from where I left it? That would be an incredibly difficult job for even the most skilled worker, unless some god came to help him move it. No living man, no matter how strong or young, could move it from its place, because it's an amazing piece of work that I made with my own hands. There was a young olive tree growing inside our house's courtyard, healthy and thick as a support beam. I built our bedroom around this tree, with strong stone walls and a roof to cover them, and I made solid, well-fitted doors. Then I cut off the top branches of the olive tree, leaving the trunk standing. I smoothed it carefully from the roots up and worked it skillfully with carpenter's tools, making it perfectly straight and smooth, turning it into a bedpost. I drilled a hole down through the middle and made it the center post of our bed, decorating it with gold and silver inlay. Then I stretched a mattress of bright red ox-hide across the frame. So you see, I know all about it! Now I want to know whether it's still there, or if someone has cut down the olive tree at its roots and moved it."

When Penelope heard these unmistakable proofs that this really was Odysseus, she completely broke down. She ran to him weeping, flung her arms around his neck, and kissed him. "Don't be angry with me, Odysseus," she cried. "You're the wisest of all men! We've both suffered so much. The gods denied us the happiness of spending our youth together and growing old side by side. Don't be hurt or angry that I didn't embrace you as soon as I saw you. I've been trembling with fear this whole time that someone might come here and trick me with lies. There are so many evil people in the world. Even Helen, Zeus's daughter, wouldn't have run off with a foreign man if she had known that the Greeks would come after her and bring her back. The gods put it in her heart to do wrong, and she never thought about that terrible sin, which caused all our suffering. But now you've convinced me by showing that you know all about our bed, which no human being has ever seen except you and me and one servant girl, Actor's daughter, whom my father gave me when I married you - she guards our bedroom door. Even though I've been hard to convince, I can't doubt you any longer."

Then Odysseus melted with emotion and wept as he held his dear, faithful wife close. Just as the sight of land is welcome to swimmers struggling toward shore after Poseidon, god of the sea, has wrecked their ship with fierce winds and waves - only a few reach land, covered with salt water, grateful to find themselves on solid ground and out of danger - that's how welcome her husband was to her as she looked at him. She couldn't tear her arms from around his neck. Indeed, they would have kept crying tears of joy until rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, but the goddess Athena had other plans. She held back the night in the far west and wouldn't let Dawn leave the Ocean or harness her two horses, Lampus and Phaethon, who carry her forward to bring daylight to mankind.

Finally, Odysseus said, "Wife, we haven't reached the end of our troubles yet. I still have to complete a long and difficult task. I must go through with it, because the ghost of Tiresias the prophet told me about it when I went down to the Underworld to ask about my homecoming and that of my companions. But now let's go to bed so we can lie down and enjoy the blessed gift of sleep."

"You can go to bed whenever you want," Penelope replied, "now that the gods have brought you home to your own house and country. But since heaven has put it in your mind to mention it, tell me about this task ahead of you. I'll have to learn about it eventually, so it's better if you tell me now."

"My dear," Odysseus answered, "why do you insist on hearing this? Still, I won't hide it from you, though you won't like it. I don't like it myself. Tiresias told me I must travel far and wide, carrying an oar, until I reach a country where people have never heard of the sea and don't even use salt on their food. They know nothing about ships or oars that work like a ship's wings. He gave me a clear sign, which I won't hide from you. He said that when a traveler meets me and asks if that's a winnowing shovel I'm carrying on my shoulder, then I should stick my oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Poseidon. After that, I should go home and offer sacrifices to all the gods in heaven, one after another. As for my own death, he said it would come to me from the sea, and my life would slip away very peacefully when I'm full of years and peace of mind, with my people blessing me. All this, he said, will surely come to pass."
Penelope said, "If the gods are going to give you a happier time in your old age, then you can hope to have some relief from all this misfortune."

That's how they talked together. Meanwhile, Eurynome and the nurse brought torches and prepared the bed with soft covers. As soon as they had arranged everything, the old nurse went back to her own room to sleep, leaving Eurynome, the bedroom attendant, to guide Odysseus and Penelope to bed by torchlight. After she led them to their room, she left, and they joyfully returned to the ceremonies of their own marriage bed from long ago. Telemachus, Philoetius the cowherd, and Eumaeus the swineherd stopped their dancing and made the women stop too. Then they all lay down to sleep in the great hall.

When Odysseus and Penelope had satisfied their love, they lay talking with each other. She told him how much she had suffered watching the house filled with a crowd of wicked suitors who had slaughtered so many sheep and cattle because of her and had drunk so many jars of wine. Odysseus, in turn, told her about his own suffering and how much trouble he had caused other people. He told her everything, and she was so delighted to listen that she never fell asleep until he had finished his entire story.

He began with his victory over the Cicones people, and how he went from there to the fertile land of the Lotus-eaters (people who ate a magical plant that made them forget their homes). He told her all about the Cyclops and how he punished Polyphemus for so ruthlessly eating his brave companions. Then he told how he went to Aeolus, king of the winds, who welcomed him and helped him on his way - but even so, Odysseus couldn't reach home because a terrible storm carried him back out to sea. He told about the cannibal Laestrygonians at the city of Telepylos, where the people destroyed all his ships and crews except for his own ship. Then he told about clever Circe the witch and her magic, and how he sailed to the cold house of Hades, the Underworld, to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias. There he saw his old war companions and his mother who had given birth to him and raised him as a child. He told about hearing the wonderful singing of the Sirens, and going past the Wandering Rocks and terrible Charybdis the whirlpool and Scylla the six-headed monster, whom no man had ever passed safely before. He told how his men ate the cattle of the sun-god, and how Zeus struck their ship with thunderbolts as punishment, so all his men died together while he alone survived. Finally, he told how he reached Ogygia island and the nymph Calypso, who kept him in a cave and fed him and wanted to marry him - she even planned to make him immortal so he would never grow old, but she couldn't persuade him to agree. After much suffering, he found his way to the Phaeacians, who treated him like a god and sent him home in a ship, giving him gold, bronze, and clothes in great abundance. This was the last thing he told her about, because here deep sleep took hold of him and eased his burden of sorrows.

Then Athena thought of something else. When she decided that Odysseus had had enough time with his wife and enough rest, she commanded golden-throned Dawn to rise from the Ocean and shed light on mankind. At this, Odysseus got up from his comfortable bed and said to Penelope, "Wife, we've both had our full share of troubles - you here, crying over my absence, and me being prevented from getting home even though I was longing to do so the whole time. Now that we've finally come together, take care of the property in the house. As for the sheep and goats that the wicked suitors ate, I'll take many by force from other people, and I'll make the Greeks replace the rest until all my pens are full again. Now I'm going to the wooded countryside to see my father, who has been grieving for me so long. I'll give you these instructions, though you hardly need them: When the sun rises, word will quickly spread that I've been killing the suitors. So go upstairs and stay there with your women. Don't see anybody and don't ask any questions."

As he spoke, he put on his armor. Then he woke up Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus, and told them all to put on their armor too. They did this and armed themselves completely. When they were ready, they opened the gates and marched out, with Odysseus leading the way. It was now daylight, but Athena still concealed them in darkness and quickly led them out of the town.

chapters.title: Book XXIV — The ghosts of the suitors in hades—ulysses and his men go to the house of laertes—the people of ithaca come out to attack ulysses, but minerva concludes a peace.
paragraphs: Then Mercury, the messenger god with golden sandals, called forth the spirits of the dead suitors. In his hand he held a magical golden wand that could make people sleep or wake them up as he wished. He used this wand to gather the ghosts and lead them away, while they followed behind him, whimpering and wailing like bats. Just as bats squeak and flutter when they fall from their cluster in a dark cave, so did these spirits cry out as Mercury led them down to the shadowy land of the dead. They passed the great waters of Ocean and the white cliffs, until they reached the gates where the sun rises and the realm of dreams begins. Finally, they arrived at the meadow of pale flowers where the souls of the dead dwell forever.

In this ghostly place, they found the spirit of the great warrior Achilles, son of King Peleus, along with his dear friends Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax. Ajax had been the most handsome and finest warrior of all the Greeks, except for Achilles himself.

These heroic spirits gathered around Achilles, and soon the ghost of King Agamemnon joined them, his heart heavy with sorrow. Around Agamemnon were the spirits of those who had died with him in his own palace, murdered by the treacherous Aegisthus. Achilles' ghost spoke first.

"Son of Atreus," Achilles said, "we always believed that Zeus loved you more than any other hero, because you commanded so many brave warriors when we all fought together at Troy. Yet death, which no mortal can escape, took you far too soon. How much better it would have been if you had fallen at Troy in your moment of greatest glory! Then the Greeks would have built a magnificent tomb for you, and your son would have inherited your noble reputation. Instead, you met such a terrible end."

"Lucky son of Peleus," replied Agamemnon's ghost, "you were fortunate to die at Troy, far from home, while the bravest Trojans and Greeks fell around you, fighting over your body. There you lay in the swirling dust of battle, mighty and magnificent, no longer caring about earthly glory. We fought all day long for your body, and we never would have stopped if Zeus hadn't sent a great storm to end the battle. When we finally carried you back to our ships, we laid you on a bed and washed your noble body with warm water and oils. All the Greek warriors tore their hair and wept bitterly around you. When your mother Thetis heard the news, she came up from the sea with her immortal sea-nymphs, and such a great wailing arose over the waters that all the Greeks trembled with fear. They would have run in panic to their ships, but wise old Nestor, whose advice was always the best, stopped them saying, 'Hold fast, Greeks! Don't flee, sons of the Greeks! This is his mother coming from the sea with her immortal companions to see her son's body.'

"When Nestor spoke these words, the Greeks were no longer afraid. The daughters of the sea god surrounded you, weeping bitterly, and they dressed you in immortal robes. The nine Muses also came and lifted their sweet voices in a funeral song, calling and answering one another in beautiful harmony. There wasn't a single Greek warrior who didn't weep at the sadness of their song. For seventeen days and nights we mourned you, both mortals and immortals. On the eighteenth day, we gave your body to the flames, and we sacrificed many fat sheep and cattle around your funeral pyre. You were burned wearing the clothes of the gods, covered in rich perfumes and honey, while warriors on foot and horseback marched around the blazing fire, their armor clanging like thunder. When the heavenly flames had done their work, we gathered your white bones at dawn and placed them in oils and pure wine. Your mother brought a golden jar to hold them—a gift from Bacchus and crafted by Vulcan himself. In this jar we placed your bones along with those of Patroclus, who had died before you, and separately we placed the bones of Antilochus, who had been closer to you than any other friend after Patroclus was gone.

"Over these remains, the Greek army built a noble tomb on a cliff overlooking the wide sea, so that it could be seen from far away by those now living and by future generations. Your mother asked the gods for prizes, and offered them to be won by the greatest of the Greeks in funeral games. You must have seen the funeral games of many heroes, when young men prepare to compete for prizes when a great chief dies, but you never saw such magnificent prizes as silver-footed Thetis offered in your honor, for the gods loved you dearly. So even in death, Achilles, your fame lives on, and your name will be remembered forever by all people. But what comfort did I have when my fighting days were over? Zeus planned my destruction when I returned home, at the hands of Aegisthus and my evil wife."

As they were talking, Mercury appeared with the spirits of the suitors who had been killed by Odysseus. The ghosts of Agamemnon and Achilles were amazed to see them and went over to them right away. Agamemnon's spirit recognized Amphimedon, son of Melaneus, who had lived in Ithaca and had once been his host, so he began to speak with him.

"Amphimedon," Agamemnon said, "what happened to bring all you fine young men down here to the land of the dead—all of you the same age too? One couldn't pick a finer group of men from any city. Did Poseidon, god of the sea, sink your ships with winds and waves? Or did enemies kill you on land while you were stealing cattle or sheep, or while you were fighting to defend their wives and city? Answer me, for I was once your guest. Don't you remember when I came to your house with Menelaus to persuade Odysseus to join us with his ships against Troy? It took us a whole month before we could continue our journey, because we had such a hard time convincing Odysseus to come with us."

Amphimedon's ghost answered, "Agamemnon, son of Atreus, king of men, I remember everything you've said, and I'll tell you exactly how we met our end. Odysseus had been gone for a long time, and we were trying to court his wife Penelope. She wouldn't say no to marrying one of us, but she wouldn't say yes either, because she was planning our destruction. This was the trick she played on us: She set up a great weaving frame in her room and began working on an enormous piece of fine cloth. 'My suitors,' she said, 'Odysseus is indeed dead, but please don't pressure me to remarry right away. Wait until I finish this burial shroud for the hero Laertes, for when death takes him. He is very wealthy, and the women of this place will gossip if he's buried without a proper shroud.' This is what she told us, and we agreed. So we could see her working on her great web all day long, but at night she would secretly unravel her stitches by torchlight. She fooled us this way for three whole years without us finding out. But as time passed and she was in her fourth year, one of her maids who knew what she was doing told us, and we caught her undoing her work. So she had to finish the shroud whether she wanted to or not. When she showed us the robe after it was washed, it shone like the sun or moon.

"Then some spiteful god brought Odysseus to the mountain farm where his swineherd lives. Soon after, his son Telemachus arrived there too, returning from a voyage to Pylos, and the two of them planned our destruction. Telemachus came to town first, and then Odysseus followed, accompanied by the swineherd. He was dressed in rags and leaning on a walking stick, looking like a miserable old beggar. He came so unexpectedly that none of us recognized him, not even the older men among us, and we insulted him and threw things at him. He endured both the blows and the insults without saying a word, even though he was in his own house. But when Zeus inspired him to act, he and Telemachus gathered up all the weapons and hid them in an inner room, locking the doors. Then he cleverly had his wife offer his great bow and iron axes as prizes for us doomed suitors to compete for—and this was the beginning of our end. Not one of us could string that mighty bow, or even come close. When the bow was about to be given to Odysseus, we all shouted that he shouldn't have it, no matter what he said, but Telemachus insisted his father should try. When Odysseus got the bow in his hands, he strung it easily and shot his arrow straight through all the iron axes. Then he stood in the great hall and poured arrows on the ground, glaring fiercely around him. First he killed Antinous, then aiming carefully, he let fly his deadly arrows and they struck us one after another. It was clear that one of the gods was helping them, for they attacked us with incredible strength throughout the hall, and there was a horrible sound of screaming as our skulls were crushed, and the ground ran red with our blood. This is how we died, Agamemnon, and our bodies still lie unburied in Odysseus's house, because our families at home don't yet know what has happened, so they can't prepare our bodies and wash the dark blood from our wounds while mourning for us as is proper for the dead."

"Fortunate Odysseus, son of Laertes," replied Agamemnon's ghost, "you are truly blessed to have a wife with such excellent wisdom and faithfulness to her husband as Penelope, daughter of Icarius. Therefore, her reputation for goodness will never die, and the immortal gods will inspire a song that all people will love, honoring Penelope's loyalty. How different was the wickedness of the daughter of Tyndareus, who killed her lawful husband! Her song will be hateful among people, for she has brought shame on all womankind, even the good ones."

So they talked together in the house of Hades, deep within the earth. Meanwhile, Odysseus and his companions left the town and soon reached the beautiful, well-kept farm of Laertes, which the old man had cleared and cultivated with endless hard work. Here was his house, with a long shed running around it where his servants slept, ate, and rested. Inside the house lived an old Sicilian woman who took care of him on this country farm. When Odysseus arrived, he said to his son and the other two men:
"Go to the house and kill the best pig you can find for dinner. Meanwhile, I want to see whether my father will recognize me or fail to know me after such a long absence."

He then took off his armor and gave it to Eumaeus and Philoetius, who went straight to the house, while he turned toward the vineyard to test his father's reaction. As he walked down into the great orchard, he didn't see Dolius or any of his sons or other workers, because they were all gathering thorns to make a fence for the vineyard where the old man had told them to work. So he found his father alone, hoeing around a vine. Laertes wore a dirty old shirt, patched and very shabby. His legs were wrapped with leather strips to protect him from thorns, and he also wore leather sleeves. He had a goatskin cap on his head and looked very sad and worn down. When Odysseus saw him so tired, so old and full of sorrow, he stood still under a tall pear tree and began to cry. He wondered whether to embrace him, kiss him, and tell him everything about coming home, or whether he should first question him and see what he would say. In the end, he decided it would be better to test him with words first, so with this plan in mind, he approached his father, who was bending down and digging around a plant.

"I can see, sir," said Odysseus, "that you are an excellent gardener—what care you take with everything! There isn't a single plant, fig tree, vine, olive tree, pear tree, or flower bed that doesn't show your careful attention. However, I hope you won't be offended if I say that you take better care of your garden than of yourself. You are old, dirty, and very poorly dressed. It can't be because you're lazy that your master takes such poor care of you—indeed, your face and bearing show nothing of a slave about them, and prove you are of noble birth. I would have said you were someone who should eat well, dress well, and sleep comfortably at night, as old men have a right to do. But tell me truthfully—whose servant are you, and in whose garden are you working? Tell me also about another matter. Is this place I've come to really Ithaca? A man I met just now said it was, but he was a dull fellow who didn't have the patience to hear my whole story when I was asking about an old friend of mine—whether he was still alive or already dead and in Hades' realm. Believe me when I tell you that this man once came to my house when I was in my own country, and never did any stranger visit me whom I liked better. He said his family came from Ithaca and that his father was Laertes, son of Arcesius. I welcomed him warmly, sharing all the abundance of my house, and when he left I gave him all the customary gifts. I gave him seven talents of fine gold and a cup of solid silver decorated with flowers. I gave him twelve light cloaks and as many pieces of tapestry. I also gave him twelve cloaks, twelve rugs, twelve fine mantles, and the same number of shirts. To all this I added four beautiful women skilled in all useful crafts, and I let him choose which ones he wanted."

His father wept and answered, "Sir, you have indeed come to the country you named, but it has fallen into the hands of wicked people. All this wealth of gifts has been given for nothing. If you could have found your friend here alive in Ithaca, he would have welcomed you warmly and given you generous gifts in return when you left—as would have been only right considering what you had already given him. But tell me truthfully—how many years has it been since you entertained this guest, my unhappy son? Alas! He has died far from his own country. The fish of the sea have eaten him, or he has been killed by wild beasts on some distant land. Neither his mother nor I, his father, could hold him in our arms and wrap him in burial clothes, nor could his excellent and wealthy wife Penelope mourn her husband properly at his deathbed and close his eyes as is due to the departed. But now, tell me truly, for I want to know: Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me about your town and parents. Where is the ship that brought you and your men to Ithaca? Or were you a passenger on someone else's ship, and those who brought you here have gone away and left you?"

"I will tell you everything truthfully," answered Odysseus. "I come from Alybas, where I have a fine house. I am the son of King Apheidas, who is the son of Polypemon. My own name is Eperitus. Heaven drove me off course as I was leaving Sicily, and I have been brought here against my will. My ship is anchored over there, off the open coast outside town, and this is the fifth year since Odysseus left my country. Poor fellow, yet the omens were good for him when he departed. The birds all flew on our right side, and both he and I were happy to see them as we parted, for we had every hope that we would meet again as friends and exchange gifts."

A dark cloud of grief fell over Laertes as he listened. He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his gray head, groaning heavily as he did so. Odysseus's heart was deeply moved, and his nose tingled with emotion as he looked at his father. Then he sprang toward him, threw his arms around him and kissed him, saying, "I am he, father—the one you're asking about! I have returned after being away for twenty years. But stop your crying and mourning—we have no time to lose, for I must tell you that I have been killing the suitors in my house to punish them for their rudeness and crimes."
"If you really are my son Odysseus," replied Laertes, "and have truly come back, you must give me clear proof of your identity that will convince me."

"First, look at this scar," answered Odysseus, "which I got from a boar's tusk when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus. You and my mother had sent me to Autolycus, my mother's father, to receive the gifts he had promised to give me when he visited here. Furthermore, I will point out to you the trees in the vineyard that you gave me when I asked you about them as I followed you around the garden. We went over all of them, and you told me their names and what kind they were. You gave me thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees, and forty fig trees. You also promised me fifty rows of grapevines with corn planted between each row, and they bear grapes of every kind when the heat of summer ripens them."

Laertes felt his strength leave him when he heard these convincing proofs that his son had given him. He threw his arms around Odysseus, and Odysseus had to hold him up or he would have fainted. But as soon as Laertes recovered and began to regain his senses, he said, "O father Zeus, then you gods are still on Olympus after all, if the suitors have really been punished for their wickedness and foolishness! But I'm very worried that I'll have all the townspeople of Ithaca coming here soon, and they'll be sending messengers everywhere throughout all the nearby cities."

Odysseus answered, "Don't worry and don't trouble yourself about that. Let's go into the house near your garden. I've already told Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus to go there and prepare dinner as quickly as possible."

Talking together, the two made their way toward the house. When they arrived, they found Telemachus with the cowherd and swineherd cutting up meat and mixing wine with water. Then the old Sicilian woman took Laertes inside and washed him and rubbed him with oil. She dressed him in a fine cloak, and Athena came to him and made him look more impressive, making him taller and stronger than before. When he came back outside, his son was amazed to see him looking almost like a god, and said to him, "Dear father, one of the gods has been making you much taller and better-looking!"

Laertes answered, "I wish, by father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, that I were the man I was when I ruled among the island people and captured Nericum, that strong fortress on the coastland. If I were still what I was then and had been in our house yesterday with my armor on, I would have been able to stand by you and help you against the suitors. I would have killed many of them, and you would have been glad to see it!"

So they talked together. Meanwhile, the others finished their work and the feast was ready. They stopped working and took their proper places on the benches and seats, then began eating. Soon old Dolius and his sons finished their work and came up, for their mother—the Sicilian woman who looked after Laertes now that he was growing old—had gone to fetch them. When they saw Odysseus and were certain it was really him, they stood there amazed. But Odysseus spoke to them kindly and said, "Sit down to dinner, old man, and don't worry about your surprise. We've been wanting to begin eating for some time and have been waiting for you."

Then Dolius stretched out both his hands and went up to Odysseus. "Sir," he said, taking his master's hand and kissing it at the wrist, "we have been wishing for your return for so long, and now heaven has brought you back to us after we had given up hope! Welcome home, and may the gods bless you! But tell me—does Penelope already know you've returned, or should we send someone to tell her?"

"Old man," answered Odysseus, "she already knows, so you don't need to worry about that." Then he took his seat, and Dolius's sons gathered around Odysseus to greet him and embrace him one after another. Then they took their seats in proper order near their father Dolius.

While they were busy preparing their dinner, Rumor spread through the town, telling everyone about the terrible fate that had happened to the suitors. As soon as people heard about it, they gathered from every part of town, groaning and crying outside Odysseus's house. They took away their dead and buried each man in his own family plot. They put the bodies of those who came from other places on fishing boats, so the fishermen could take each one back to his own home. Then they met angrily in the town assembly, and when they were all gathered together, Eupeithes stood up to speak. He was overwhelmed with grief for his son Antinous, who had been the first man killed by Odysseus, so he said, weeping bitterly, "My friends, this man has done great wrong to our people. He took many of our best men away with him in his ships, and he lost both ships and men. Now, when he returns, he has been killing all the leading men among our island people. Let's act quickly before he can escape to Pylos or to Elis where the Epeans rule, or we'll be ashamed of ourselves forever. It will be an everlasting disgrace if we don't avenge the murder of our sons and brothers. For my part, I would have no pleasure in life and would rather die right now. Let's go after them before they can cross over to the mainland!"

He wept as he spoke, and everyone felt sorry for him. But Medon and the singer Phemius had now woken up and came to them from Odysseus's house. Everyone was astonished to see them alive, but they stood in the middle of the assembly, and Medon said, "Listen to me, men of Ithaca! Odysseus didn't do these things against the will of heaven. I myself saw an immortal god take the form of Mentor and stand beside him. This god appeared sometimes in front of him, encouraging him, and sometimes rushing furiously around the courtyard attacking the suitors, and that's when they fell thick upon each other."

When he said this, pale fear gripped them all, and old Halitherses, son of Mastor, stood up to speak. He was the only man among them who could see both the past and the future, so he spoke to them clearly and honestly, saying:

"Men of Ithaca, it's your own fault that things have turned out this way! You wouldn't listen to me or to Mentor when we told you to control your sons' foolishness. They were doing much wrong because of their selfish hearts—wasting the property and dishonoring the wife of a chief whom they thought would never return. Now, however, listen to me and do as I say: Don't go out against Odysseus, or you may find that you're bringing evil upon your own heads!"

This was what he said, and more than half the people raised a loud shout and immediately left the assembly. But the rest stayed where they were, because Halitherses's speech displeased them, and they sided with Eupeithes. They therefore hurried off to get their weapons, and when they had armed themselves, they met together in front of the city. Eupeithes led them in their foolishness, thinking he was going to avenge his son's murder, when in truth he would never return home but would die in the attempt.
Then Athena said to Zeus, "Father, son of Cronus, king of all kings, answer me this question: What do you plan to do? Will you let them keep fighting, or will you make peace between them?"

Zeus answered, "My child, why do you ask me? Wasn't it by your own plan that Odysseus came home and took revenge on the suitors? Do whatever you like, but I'll tell you what I think would be the most reasonable solution. Now that Odysseus has had his revenge, let them swear a solemn peace treaty, so he can continue to rule while we make the others forgive and forget the killing of their sons and brothers. Then let them all become friends as they were before, and let peace and prosperity reign."
This was exactly what Athena was eager to bring about, so she darted down from the highest peaks of Mount Olympus.

When Laertes and the others had finished dinner, Odysseus began by saying, "Some of you go out and see if they're getting close to us." So one of Dolius's sons went as he was told. Standing at the doorway, he could see the angry crowd quite near and said to Odysseus, "Here they come! Let's put on our armor at once!"

They put on their armor as quickly as they could—that is, Odysseus, his three men, and Dolius's six sons. Laertes and Dolius also armed themselves—warriors by necessity despite their gray hair. When they had all put on their armor, they opened the gate and marched out, with Odysseus leading the way.

Then Zeus's daughter Athena came up to them, having taken the appearance and voice of Mentor. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and said to his son Telemachus, "Telemachus, now that you're about to fight in a battle that will test every man's courage, be sure not to disgrace your ancestors, who were famous for their strength and bravery throughout the world."
"You speak truly, dear father," answered Telemachus, "and you will see, if you watch, that I have no intention of disgracing our family."
Laertes was delighted when he heard this. "Good heavens!" he exclaimed, "What a wonderful day I'm having! I truly rejoice in it. My son and grandson are competing with each other in bravery!"
Then Athena came close to him and said, "Son of Arcesius—dearest friend I have in the world—pray to the gray-eyed maiden and to Zeus her father, then aim your spear and throw it!"

As she spoke, she filled him with fresh strength, and when he had prayed to her, he aimed his spear and hurled it. He struck Eupeithes's helmet, and the spear went right through it, for the helmet couldn't stop it. His armor clattered as he fell heavily to the ground. Meanwhile, Odysseus and his son attacked the front line of their enemies and struck them with swords and spears. Indeed, they would have killed every one of them and prevented them from ever returning home, but Athena raised her voice loudly and made everyone stop. "Men of Ithaca," she cried, "stop this dreadful war and settle the matter at once without more bloodshed!"

When she spoke, pale fear seized everyone. They were so frightened that their weapons dropped from their hands and fell to the ground at the sound of the goddess's voice, and they fled back to the city to save their lives. But Odysseus gave a great battle cry and, gathering himself together, swooped down like a soaring eagle. Then Zeus sent a thunderbolt of fire that fell just in front of Athena, so she said to Odysseus, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, stop this fierce fighting, or Zeus will be angry with you."
Athena spoke these words, and Odysseus obeyed her gladly. Then Athena took the form and voice of Mentor and made a peace agreement between the two opposing sides.
